docs.title: XTM One Documentation Space
docs.text:
Welcome to the XTM One Documentation space. Here you will be able to find all documents and resources about the platform.

Release notes

Please, be sure to also take a look at the XTM One release notes, they may contain important information about releases and deployments.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
XTM One is an open source AI-native assistant platform allowing organizations to deploy autonomous agents for email triage, messaging support, knowledge management, and operational automation. It can be used standalone or as the AI layer inside the XTM Suite (OpenCTI, OpenAEV).

Docker deployment of the full XTM suite (OpenCTI – OpenAEV – XTM One)

If you're looking for information about the deployment of the full eXtended Threat Management (XTM) suite using Docker, please refer to this repository and documentation.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: This page covers how to set up a local development environment and contribute to XTM One.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.14+
  • Node.js 24 (22.18 at minimum) with Yarn
  • Docker and Docker Compose (for dependencies)
  • Git

docs.title: Local setup
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one.git && cd xtm-one

# Copy environment file
cp .env.sample .env

# Start dependencies (PostgreSQL + pgvector, Redis, Silo)
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d

# Run the full stack (backend + worker + frontend)
./dev.sh        # Linux/macOS
.\dev.ps1       # Windows

The dev script installs dependencies, runs migrations, and starts all services with hot reload.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
xtm-one/
├── backend/           → Python / FastAPI (see backend/AGENTS.md)
├── frontend/          → React 19 / TypeScript (see frontend/AGENTS.md)
├── docs/              → Product documentation (MkDocs)
├── apps/              → Platform app packages
└── docker-compose.yml → Production stack

docs.title: Running checks
docs.text:
# Backend lint
cd backend && ruff check app/

# Frontend lint and type check
cd frontend && yarn check

# Office add-in type check (an npm package of its own; its unit tests run in `yarn check` above)
cd apps/microsoft-office && npm ci && npm run check

# Backend tests
cd backend && SECRET_KEY=test python -m pytest -m "not integration" -q -n auto

docs.title: Running tests in parallel
docs.text:
CI runs every backend suite under pytest-xdist (-n auto locally, -n logical in CI), and so can you. CI also splits each suite between several jobs: with PYTEST_SHARD=<index>/<total> a run keeps every <total>-th test of the sorted test ids (tests/sharding.py), so a test runs in exactly one job. What that asks of a test:

  • No test depends on another one. The suite already runs in random order (pytest-randomly); xdist spreads it over processes too.
  • Every process collects the same test ids. A parametrize value built from uuid.uuid4(), time.time() or a freshly generated key turns into a different id in each worker, and the run stops with Different tests were collected between gw0 and gw1. Give such a parametrization ids= (or pytest.param(..., id=...)): the value can stay random, its name cannot.
  • A PostgreSQL test works in a database of its own, through tests/scratch_database.py. The schema is built once per process into a template database and every scratch database is a copy of it, so a new suite should use scratch_database(...) rather than a CREATE DATABASE + create_all of its own.
  • A test reading the backend's own source (a tripwire over every module under app/) reads it through tests/app_sources.py, which parses the tree once per process instead of once per suite.
  • A module that owns a fixed resource stays on one process. tests/test_bootstrap.py starts one backend on port 8099; it is marked pytest.mark.xdist_group(...) so that all its tests run in the same worker. The group only applies under --dist loadgroup, which CI and scripts/ci-local.sh pass: add it to a local -n run (python -m pytest -m integration -n auto --dist loadgroup).

The integration suite needs PostgreSQL, Redis and Silo, and a database role allowed to create databases: ./scripts/ci-local.sh --only integration starts them and runs it the way CI does.

The Playwright suite runs in CI as several jobs, each with a stack of its own: E2E_SHARD=<index>/<total> deals the spec files of a project to the jobs by the seconds each took on CI (frontend/tests_e2e/shard-timings.json). Refresh the timings after a large change to the suite from the test-results-* artifacts of a green run: cd frontend && yarn e2e:shard-timings <path>/timings.json....

docs.title: Live LLM smoke suite (opt-in)
docs.text:
The provider unit tests run against mocked SDK clients, so they cannot tell whether a real API accepts the requests the platform builds. backend/tests/live/ sends those requests to the real Anthropic, Gemini and OpenRouter APIs with tiny prompts. It spends real money (cents per run), never runs in CI, and is skipped unless LIVE_LLM_SMOKE=1 is set and the provider's key is exported as LLM_PROVIDER_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, LLM_PROVIDER_GEMINI_API_KEY or LLM_PROVIDER_OPENROUTER_API_KEY:

cd backend && LIVE_LLM_SMOKE=1 SECRET_KEY=test python -m pytest tests/live -v -rfEs

A provider whose key is not set is skipped. backend/tests/live/README.md lists the cases, the model overrides and how the keys are kept out of the test output.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Schema changes must use Alembic migrations. Never use inline SQL.

cd backend
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "description of change"

The platform auto-migrates on startup — no manual alembic upgrade needed in production.

docs.title: One head, always
docs.text:
The migration history must have exactly one head. Two pull requests that each add a migration chained off the same parent fork the history the moment both land — and each one is green on its own, because pull request CI validates the branch against main as it was when that run started. This has happened twice on main, and both times it surfaced days later as an unrelated pull request going red.

Three guards catch it:

Guard Where Catches tests/test_migration_integrity.py Migrations (Alembic) job, every pull request A fork you created yourself Post-merge integrity check Migrations (Alembic) job, pull requests targeting main A fork created by another migration landing on main after your branch was cut CI on push to main Whole CI workflow A fork that landed anyway — flagged on the merge commit that created it

If the post-merge check fails, main has moved under you:

git fetch origin main && git rebase origin/main
# re-point your earliest migration's down_revision to main's new head
cd backend && python -m pytest tests/test_migration_integrity.py

When a migration lands on main, every open pull request that touches backend/alembic/versions/ also gets an automatic comment asking for that rebase.

Pull requests stacked on an integration branch

CI runs in full whatever branch you target. The post-merge check is the exception: it merges your branch into main, which only says something when that merge is what your pull request proposes. A fork you introduced is still caught by the first guard above. Rebase the integration branch itself onto main to clear what the post-merge check would have flagged.

Repository settings

The guards above detect a fork; they cannot prevent two green pull requests from being merged seconds apart. That needs a repository setting: either a merge queue on main, or required status checks with "require branches to be up to date". The merge_group triggers in .github/workflows/ci.yml and .github/workflows/e2e.yml are the prerequisite for the merge queue — enabling the queue itself is done in the repository settings, and every required check must run on merge_group events or the queue never drains.

docs.title: Commit conventions
docs.text:
All commits follow Conventional Commits:

type(scope?): description (#issue)

Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, revert.

docs.title: AI governance
docs.text: This page describes what XTM One shares with AI providers, where that data is processed, and how to control it. Read it alongside Data flow, which covers the request lifecycle and where data is stored.

docs.title: What is shared with an AI provider
docs.text:
When the platform calls an AI provider, the request contains only what the model needs to answer:

  • the agent's persona and system instructions
  • the current conversation or assignment prompt, including recent message history
  • context the agent pulls in to answer — for example, snippets retrieved from a knowledge base, tool results, or an incoming trigger payload
  • the definitions of the tools the agent may call (names and parameters, not their results until a tool runs)

What stays private and is never included in the request to the model:

  • stored integration and channel credentials (encrypted at rest — see Configuration)
  • user passwords and session tokens
  • knowledge bases in full — when an agent answers, only the snippets it retrieves are sent (the full text is sent once to the embedding model when you first add the content, as described below)

XTM One does not train on your data

XTM One never uses your prompts, documents, conversations, memories, or any other data to train, fine-tune, or improve an AI model. Your data is sent to the AI provider you configure only to answer your own requests, in real time. The platform itself trains nothing.

Your AI provider sees your prompts

Whatever an agent puts into a prompt — including retrieved documents and tool results — is sent to the AI provider you configured. The platform does not anonymize, tokenize, or redact prompt content before sending it, and prompts are stored unredacted in your own deployment (see Data flow). Whether the provider retains or trains on the prompts it receives is governed by its terms, not by XTM One — review them, and scope agents' knowledge and tools accordingly. For maximum control, run a local model so no prompt data leaves your network.

docs.title: Adding documents to a knowledge base
docs.text:
To make a knowledge base searchable, XTM One first has to turn its documents into numbers a computer can compare — these numbers are called embeddings. Creating them means sending the document text to an embedding model, which is an AI provider just like the one that answers questions.

Two things are worth knowing:

  • This happens when you add the content, not on every question. The same applies to an agent's saved memories.
  • The embedding model can be a separate provider from the one that answers chats — and it can be a local one (for example Ollama), so the document text never leaves your network. You set it under Settings → AI Models.

docs.title: Where the AI provider runs
docs.text:
You choose the AI provider under Settings → AI Models, or pre-provision it (see the supported providers in Configuration). The provider determines where prompt data is processed:

  • Hosted providers (such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Mistral) process prompts on their own infrastructure, subject to their terms.
  • Self-hosted or local providers (Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint on your network) keep prompt data inside your perimeter. This is the recommended option for air-gapped deployments.

docs.title: Scope what agents can access
docs.text:
Because an agent only shares what it is configured to use, you control exposure by scoping the agent:

  • limit which knowledge bases an agent can read
  • limit which integrations and tools an agent can call
  • use assignment-level scoping to further narrow tools and knowledge bases per automation

See the User Guide for how agents, knowledge bases, and tools are configured.

docs.title: Guardrails and safety
docs.text:
XTM One adds several safety layers around every agent run. They lower the risk of misuse, but they are not a substitute for limiting what each agent can access and choosing your AI provider carefully.

  • Per-agent rules — every agent has a separate "guardrails" box where you write hard rules it must always follow (for example, "never send external email" or "only answer questions about our products"). These rules are kept apart from the agent's persona, so an edit to its personality can't accidentally erase them.
  • Injection detection (alert only) — messages coming into an agent are checked for known tricks that try to make the AI ignore its rules ("prompt injection" and "jailbreak" attempts). When one is spotted, XTM One records it as a security event for administrators to review — but it does not block the message. Treat this as an alert to check, not a wall that stops every attack.
  • Treating outside content as data, not orders — anything an agent pulls in from the outside world (web pages it fetches, incoming webhook or integration messages) is wrapped so the AI treats it as information to read, never as instructions to obey. This helps stop a malicious web page or email from hijacking the agent.
  • Built-in security rules — a fixed set of security instructions is added to every agent so it resists attempts to reveal its hidden instructions, override its rules, or pretend to be someone else.
  • Link checking — when an agent's answer includes links to other XTM Suite products, XTM One checks and corrects them automatically, so the agent never hands out made-up links.

docs.title: Data retention
docs.text:
All platform data lives in your own deployment (see Data flow). XTM One applies these defaults:

Data Where it is stored Default retention How to control it Conversations and messages PostgreSQL Kept until deleted Delete the conversation, or the agent it belongs to Assignment runs and results PostgreSQL Kept until deleted Delete the run, or the assignment Agent memory — recent interactions Redis 24 hours (auto-expires) Automatic Agent memory — rolling summary Redis 30 days (auto-expires) Automatic Agent memory — long-term facts PostgreSQL 90 days, max 200 per agent Admins can clear an agent's memory at any time LLM traces PostgreSQL (or ClickHouse) Purged after the retention period — 90 days by default Adjustable from 1 to 365 days under Settings → Observability, where Store full payloads off keeps no prompt, answer or tool content and Enable local trace storage off keeps no trace (see What a trace keeps); individual traces can be deleted Daily observability aggregates PostgreSQL Kept indefinitely — they outlive the trace purge on purpose Not covered by the trace retention setting; see What survives the trace purge Audit logs PostgreSQL Kept indefinitely (immutable) Admin-only visibility

docs.title: What survives the trace purge
docs.text:
Deleting an expired trace does not delete the KPI it contributed to. Once a day is complete, XTM One rolls its traces up into a small daily aggregate and keeps that aggregate indefinitely, so the Analytics dashboard can still answer "what did last quarter cost?" long after the individual traces are gone. This is why a 30-day or 90-day chart still has data on a platform with 7-day trace retention.

What you keep, and for how long:

Individual traces Daily aggregates Retained for The retention period (1–365 days, default 90) Indefinitely Granularity Every request, with prompts, tool calls and errors (the prompts and tool content only while Store full payloads is on) One row per day, agent, model, source and user Answers "What exactly happened in this conversation?" "How much did this agent, model or person cost, and how fast was it?" Where in the UI Trace explorer, individual trace detail, top errors Cost, volume and latency charts on Analytics

Consequences worth knowing before you choose a retention period:

  • Prompt and response content is not aggregated. Only counts, token totals, cost, latency distributions and feedback averages survive. Nothing a user typed, and no tool result, outlives the retention period.
  • Aggregates are per user. A day's row is keyed by agent, model, source and the user who made the request, so per-person usage and cost stay answerable after the traces are gone. If your retention policy requires per-user usage records to expire as well, treat these aggregates as in scope — the trace retention setting does not clear them.
  • Error details and per-request diagnostics do not survive. The "Top errors" table and trace detail are served from raw traces only, so they are always limited to the retention window.
  • Latency beyond the window is a distribution, not the raw timings. Each day stores a bucketed histogram of its durations, which is what lets percentiles be merged correctly across a long window. Expect percentile values to be accurate to within a bucket rather than exact.
  • A day is never purged before it is aggregated. The maintenance job aggregates first and refuses to delete a day that has no aggregate yet, so lowering the retention period (or a restart longer than it) cannot silently drop a day's KPIs. If a window you select reaches back further than any surviving data, Analytics says so instead of showing zeroes.
  • ClickHouse retention is out-of-band. With tracing_store_provider=clickhouse, the retention setting governs the PostgreSQL copy; expiry of the ClickHouse tables is up to your own TTL or housekeeping. Long-window dashboards read the PostgreSQL aggregates either way.

To remove the aggregates as well, delete the llm_daily_stats rows (or the deployment's PostgreSQL volume, as below).

Two categories are not retained by XTM One and are governed entirely by your own infrastructure:

  • Application logs are written to standard output. Your container runtime or log aggregator decides how long they are kept and how they are rotated — see Monitoring.
  • Metrics are exposed on the /metrics endpoint and scraped by your Prometheus. The platform holds only current values; historical retention lives in your monitoring stack.

To remove all data, delete the deployment's PostgreSQL, Redis, and object-storage volumes. For selective deletion, delete the specific agents, conversations, or knowledge bases from the application.

docs.title: Editions and licensing
docs.text: XTM One ships as one platform with two editions. Which one you are on decides a single thing: whether AI is licensed, and therefore available. Whether it actually runs is a separate, administrator-held switch (see Running Enterprise Edition without AI).

docs.title: The two editions
docs.text:
Edition When What you get Community Edition No XTM One license is installed and no connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platform is in Enterprise Edition The platform runs with AI off. Identity, settings, platform connections, integrations and the exposure dashboards keep working. Agents, chat and automations are listed and reachable, marked unavailable. Enterprise Edition An XTM One license is installed, or at least one connected platform is in Enterprise Edition Everything is on as long as AI is switched on: agentic chat across your platforms, autonomous agents and assignments, flows, knowledge bases, skills, prompts, MCP servers, custom tools, integrations, Agent-to-Agent interoperability, the full integration catalog and AI adoption analytics.

There is nothing in between. A connected Enterprise Edition platform activates every capability of XTM One, exactly as a license does.

Nothing to redeploy

Every deployment already contains the whole platform. Moving to Enterprise Edition never means installing something new: it is a license key, or a platform connection, away.

docs.title: What a license decides
docs.text:
An XTM One license carries two things and nothing else:

  • Agentic capacity - the number of agentic executions allowed per day, per month and per year. One agentic execution is one complete request handled by the platform - a chat turn, an assignment run, or a background task - however many agents and tools it involves. Requests with no account behind them count too: anonymous channel users, visitors of a public chat widget and calls made with the platform MCP key (see Requests with no account).
  • Module editions - which connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platforms are in Enterprise Edition.

A license never switches individual features on or off. Every capability of XTM One is available to every Enterprise Edition deployment.

docs.title: The included allowance
docs.text:
When Enterprise Edition comes from a connected platform and no XTM One license is installed, the platform runs under an included agentic allowance: 30 executions per day, 100 per month and 300 per year, shared across the deployment. It is sized to discover, test and demonstrate value.

Installing an XTM One license replaces the allowance with the capacity the license carries. Settings > Quotas shows which ceilings apply and where they come from, and lets you set per-user defaults and group or user overrides within them.

A license period with no quota has no ceiling, whether the certificate carries no quota for it or a quota of 0, and whatever the license's start date. Licenses issued from 27 September 2026 write an unlimited period as no quota.

docs.title: Activating Enterprise Edition
docs.text:
You have two ways to activate it, and both work without a redeploy:

  • Connect an Enterprise Edition platform. Register an OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platform that holds its own Enterprise license. XTM One inherits Enterprise Edition as soon as the registration validates.
  • Install an XTM One license. Paste the license PEM in Settings > Parameters, or set the ENTERPRISE_LICENSE environment variable and restart. The instance ID shown on the same page is required to generate the certificate. Set the variable on the platform and on the worker; a worker without it still runs the background AI of the licensed deployment, and says so once in its log.

If you have neither, Start free trial and Contact sales are offered wherever an AI capability is locked - on the home page, in the navigation, on the creation buttons and in the AI settings.

docs.title: What Community Edition looks like
docs.text:
On Community Edition the platform tells you once, clearly, and stays out of the way:

  • The home page leads with the upgrade path and the platform connection instructions.
  • AI entries in the navigation carry a lock; hovering one explains why.
  • A creation button opens the same explanation with the three ways forward.
  • The AI Models settings say that a provider configured now is used as soon as Enterprise Edition is activated, instead of warning that the platform is blocked until one is configured.

You can prepare LLM providers, users, groups and platform connections ahead of activation. Nothing you configure is lost when the edition changes.

docs.title: When Enterprise Edition ends
docs.text:
A deployment returns to Community Edition when its last source of Enterprise Edition goes: the connected Enterprise Edition platform loses its license or is disconnected, or the XTM One license is removed. Within a few seconds the automations configured while it was Enterprise stop running AI too, exactly like the interactive surfaces:

  • Scheduled assignments, integration events, webhooks and channel bots start no AI work. A person writing to a bot, where the bot would answer (a direct message, a mention, a channel it listens to), is told that Enterprise Edition is required and how to activate it; a webhook sender receives a 403 carrying the same explanation.
  • A flow containing an AI step is held back and recorded as skipped with the reason. Flows without AI steps keep running.
  • Work that was scheduled but had not started does not start: it is held. An assignment run waiting on its configured delay, a run resumed from a human-review pause (the answer is kept), a background task that had not begun and the pending runs of an evaluation are shown as Held and run by themselves within about five minutes of Enterprise Edition becoming active again; a conversation waiting on a held background task hears back when the task finally runs. Work held longer than AI_UNAVAILABLE_HOLD_MAX_SECONDS (one week by default, 0 to fail it at its start instead) is recorded as failed with the cause AI not licensed. Deliveries waiting in an assignment's queue stay queued and documents waiting to be indexed stay pending; both are picked up once Enterprise Edition is active again.
  • Nothing is charged to the agentic quota, and nothing is disabled, paused or deleted. Schedules, integration events, webhooks, channel bots and flows resume on their own once Enterprise Edition is active again; a scheduled assignment or flow catches up with one run, not one per occurrence it missed.

Work already running when the edition changes finishes under its own time limit. If the platform briefly cannot read its license state when scheduled work comes due, for example during a database failover, that work is not failed: it is retried shortly afterwards. A channel bot written to meanwhile answers a direct message that the AI service is temporarily unavailable, and stays silent in a group channel.

docs.title: Running Enterprise Edition without AI
docs.text: Enterprise Edition and the AI switch are independent. An administrator can switch AI off on a fully licensed platform; see Running without AI.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Review the Settings page for where the license, the quotas and the AI switch live.

docs.title: Evaluations
docs.text:
An evaluation runs one or more agents, on one or more models, against the test cases of a dataset, and scores each answer. Use it to pick a model for an agent, or to check that a new model or persona does not make the answers worse. Evaluations and datasets are administrator tools: they live under Evaluations, and Evaluations > Datasets holds the test cases.

  • A dataset is an ordered list of entries. Each entry has a prompt, the answer you expect, and optionally files attached to the prompt.
  • An evaluation links agents and datasets, says which models to run (the agent's default model, a list of models, or both), and how to score: a judge model compares every answer with the expected one.

docs.title: The built-in OCR benchmark
docs.text:
XTM One ships one ready-made benchmark: the OCR benchmark dataset and the OCR benchmark evaluation. It measures how faithfully a model reads a document it is given.

The dataset holds six short cyber threat intelligence documents: four text PDFs (an advisory, a table of indicators, a notice in French, a two-page incident report) and two scanned pages (a memo and a table, skewed and speckled like a photocopy). Every entry asks for a verbatim transcription, and the expected answer is the document's exact text. The documents are fictional and written by Filigran for this benchmark; their licence and source are recorded in backend/app/evaluations/seed_data/SOURCES.md.

The documents reach each model the way a file attached in a conversation does:

  • A PDF is read natively by the providers that support it (Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock). Other providers receive the text extracted from the PDF, so for them the entry measures how well the model restores the document's structure from that text.
  • A scanned page is an image, so it needs a vision-capable model. A text-only model fails those two entries: that result is expected, not a platform error.

To run it:

  1. Open Evaluations and select OCR benchmark.
  2. Add the models you want to compare. Out of the box it runs the agent's default model only.
  3. Start a run, then compare the scores per model and per entry.

The evaluation runs the built-in Document Transcriber agent, which is hidden from chat and carries no tools, so the scores compare models, not agent configurations. The evaluation is created once: its models, agents and schedule are yours to change, and restarting the platform does not reset them. If you delete it, it is created again, with its default settings, at the next start. The dataset, on the other hand, is re-synced at every startup; to build a variant of it, export it and import the copy. When an upgrade changes the text or the document of one of its entries, the dataset's entries are replaced: earlier runs keep their scores, but their per-entry results are removed, so a score measured on one document is never shown against another. A run in progress keeps the entries and documents it started with; the dataset is then updated at the next start.

The documents are stored in the platform's object storage when it starts. If the object storage cannot be reached at that moment, the dataset appears without its documents and the OCR benchmark evaluation is not created yet: both are completed at the next start that can store the documents, so the benchmark is not offered before the documents it scores are there. When an upgrade changes a document and the object storage cannot be reached, the benchmark keeps the entries and documents it had until a start that can store the new one.

docs.title: Intents
docs.text:
Intents are the mechanism that makes XTM One agents appear inside the other XTM Suite products. A connected platform declares the AI capabilities it wants — summarize this container, translate this question into a search filter, process this bundle in a playbook — and you decide which agent answers each one.

Administrators choose Intents from the left sidebar to open the page.

docs.title: How routing works
docs.text:
An intent is a named capability, written in dotted notation, such as cti.container_summary or global.assistant. It says what has to be done, never who does it. The link between the two is a binding.

The full path from a click in OpenCTI to an answer from one of your agents looks like this:

  1. OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ registers with XTM One and declares the intents it uses, along with its business vertical.
  2. XTM One adds any missing intent to the registry and tags it with the platform that declared it.
  3. You bind one or more agents to each intent, optionally scoped to a vertical and ordered by priority.
  4. A user triggers the feature in the platform. The platform asks XTM One which agents are bound to that intent for its vertical, and uses the one with the highest priority.
  5. The bound agent runs in XTM One with the context sent by the platform, and the result is returned into the product.

Step 3 is the one you control. Everything a user sees — or does not see — in another Suite product follows from it.

No binding, no feature

An intent that no agent is bound to is shown with an Unbound badge. The platform that declared it treats the corresponding feature as unavailable and usually hides or disables it. Binding an agent is what turns the feature on.

docs.title: Verticals
docs.text:
A vertical is the business coloration of a connected platform — cti, aev, grc, and, depending on the deployment, labels such as fimi or fraud. It lets the same intent resolve to a different agent depending on the context the request comes from.

The Verticals panel at the top of the page lists them all with the number of bindings that use them:

  • Verticals declared by a platform at registration are created automatically.
  • Administrators can add their own with Add Vertical.
  • Renaming a vertical updates every binding that uses it.
  • A vertical still used by a binding cannot be deleted.

A binding scoped to All verticals applies to every platform, whatever its business context. A binding scoped to one vertical only applies to platforms declaring that vertical.

docs.title: Bind an agent to an intent
docs.text:
From the Intents page:

  1. Expand the intent you want to serve.
  2. Choose Add Binding.
  3. Search for the agent.
  4. Select one or more verticals, or All verticals. One binding is created per selected vertical.
  5. Confirm.

You can do the same from the agent side: open the agent, go to Configuration, and use the Intent Bindings card. It shows every intent that agent already answers and lets you add or remove bindings without leaving the page.

The agent cannot be private

An agent exposed through an intent is offered to users of the connected platform, so it has to be company-managed or shared with at least one group. XTM One refuses every default binding to a private agent, whatever vertical it is scoped to, and a private agent is never offered to a connected platform even when someone binds it for their own use. Disabled agents are skipped too, even when a binding exists.

Some surfaces in the connected products list several agents for the user to choose from and filter that list by the product tag carried by the agent, such as opencti or openaev. Tagging your agent with the product identifier is what allows it to show up in those lists.

docs.title: Priorities when several agents share an intent
docs.text:
Several agents can be bound to the same intent. In that case the highest priority wins, and priority arrows appear next to each agent in the expanded intent card so you can reorder them.

Priority is evaluated per vertical. An agent can carry a base priority plus a per-vertical override, which is what you adjust when you move it up or down inside a vertical group. Bindings scoped to All verticals are listed inside each vertical group as well, since they compete with the vertical-specific ones.

To take over a capability that a built-in agent currently handles, bind your own agent to the same intent and vertical, then raise its priority above the built-in one.

docs.title: Built-in bindings
docs.text:
XTM One ships with a set of bindings that connect its built-in agents to the intents the Suite products declare. They are marked builtin and cannot be edited or deleted — they are restored at every startup, so a removed one comes back.

These are the shipped bindings:

The Intents page is always the authoritative view for your own platform: it reflects what the connected products actually declared and what is bound today.

How the general assistant resolves

Several agents are bound to global.assistant. The CTEM Assistant carries the highest priority, so it is the one a connected product reaches first; it then hands the conversation over to the product specialist — OpenCTI Assistant, OpenAEV Assistant, or OpenCRQ Assistant. Bind your own agent above it if you want a different front door.

docs.title: Personal overrides
docs.text:
The bindings an administrator creates are the platform-wide defaults. A single intent can also carry a personal binding, which applies to that user's own requests only and leaves everyone else on the default.

A default binding can also be locked, which is how a capability is forced to resolve the same way for the whole organization. A locked default cannot be overridden, and an attempt to override it is rejected with a message stating that an administrator locked the binding.

docs.title: Custom intents
docs.text:
Administrators can add an intent with Create Intent, using dotted notation such as product.feature.action and a short description.

A custom intent is only useful when something asks for it by name — a platform that declares it at registration, or your own integration calling XTM One. Creating an intent no product asks for has no effect on what users see. An intent that has no binding left can be deleted; one that is still bound cannot.

docs.title: When a feature does not appear in a connected product
docs.text:
Work through this list when a user reports a missing AI action:

  • The intent shows an Unbound badge — no agent is bound to it yet.
  • The bound agent is disabled.
  • The bound agent is private, so it is never offered to platform users.
  • The binding is scoped to a vertical the platform does not declare. Check the vertical on the platform's registration and either rebind to that vertical or use All verticals.
  • The intent is not listed at all, which means the platform never declared it. Confirm the platform is registered and running a version that requests that capability.
  • The user's own permissions on the connected platform do not allow the underlying operation.

For the user-facing side of the same question, see XTM One in OpenCTI and XTM One in OpenAEV.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Settings for the rest of the platform configuration, or read XTM One in the XTM Suite to see how these bindings surface for end users.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This chapter is for administrators. It covers the areas used to manage the platform, monitor usage, and configure shared settings.

docs.title: Administration is for
docs.text:
Use the administration sections when you need to:

  • review and route intents
  • manage users and groups
  • inspect platform objects and logs
  • adjust shared platform settings

docs.title: Intents
docs.text:
Intents connect user needs to agents. They are also how an agent becomes available inside OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ.

Use this section when you want to:

  • review which intents exist
  • see which agents are bound to them
  • check which platforms declared them
  • adjust routing priorities
  • make one of your own agents answer a capability in a connected product

For most teams, this is the page that explains why one request reaches one agent instead of another. The Intents page covers bindings, verticals, and priorities in detail.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
The Users section is where administrators manage user accounts.

Use it to:

  • review users
  • create users
  • edit user details
  • manage access and profile-level settings

This is also where administrators usually confirm whether a user should be an admin or a standard user.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Groups help you organize users and share entities with a selected audience.

Use it to:

  • create groups
  • manage membership
  • control group-based sharing

If your organization uses team-based access, this page is often the key to who can see and edit shared agents and resources.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
Objects gives administrators a cross-user view of the platform's library entities, whoever owns them: agents, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, MCP servers, custom tools, integrations, presentations, templates, machines (the computers enrolled with XTM One Desktop or the headless runner), flows, datasets, evaluations, variables and channel bots. A type whose pages your deployment does not offer (Flows, Evaluations, custom variables, XTM One Desktop) is not listed either.

The library pages (Agents, Presentations, Templates, Flows, Evaluations, Variables, the XTM One Desktop page, and so on) list the same three tiers for everyone, administrators included: your own items, the items shared with you, and the items published to the whole company. Objects is where you find an item of one of these types that another person owns and has not shared.

Once you open an item, you see it whole, whoever owns it: an agent shows every integration, knowledge base, tool, skill, prompt, handover and assignment it is bound to, its runs, its chats and its delegations, and each of them opens and can be edited, as can the item itself. Reading the delegations of an agent that other users started (the consultations, transfers and background tasks on its Delegations tab carry their task descriptions and results) is recorded in Logs (action break_glass, entity Agent Delegations), naming the agent and the users whose delegations you read, one entry per administrator, agent and fifteen-minute window; your own delegations are not counted. The same holds the other way round: an integration, a knowledge base or a tool lists every agent that uses it. When you edit a colleague's agent, its pickers keep what the agent is already bound to, next to the items you can see yourself.

Use it to:

  • search any of these entities by name
  • filter by type or by owner
  • open any item directly (a row leads to the item's own page)

This is helpful when you need a cross-platform inventory, or when a user asks you to look at something they built, rather than a page-by-page review.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text:
Filter by Machines to see every computer enrolled with the platform, whoever enrolled it: how many there are, who owns each one, and whether it is still deployed. Each row shows the machine's operating system, whether it is Online, Offline (with the time it was last seen) or Revoked, and the version of the runner it runs. The connection state is the live one the XTM One Desktop page shows, not a stored flag, so a machine that stopped without disconnecting reads as offline here too.

Opening a row shows the machine's own page: its host details, its permission model, its pending approvals and its recent commands, with the same edit, revoke and delete actions an administrator has on the XTM One Desktop page. Reading the command history of a machine you neither own nor hold a configure-level share on (a view-only share is not enough - the full history then comes from your administrator role; a company-managed machine is yours to manage and is not counted) is recorded in Logs (action break_glass, entity Runner Commands): the commands carry shell output and file contents, so the trail says who looked at whose machine, one entry per administrator, machine and fifteen-minute window. Machines are not listed when the runner feature is disabled for the deployment.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Logs show the audit trail of user actions and important platform events.

Use them when you need to:

  • review configuration changes
  • check who changed what
  • investigate activity
  • support troubleshooting

When something changed and no one is sure why, this is usually the first admin page to check.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Settings is where administrators configure the shared behavior of XTM One.

Common areas include:

  • AI models
  • general assistant behavior
  • channels and bots
  • integrations
  • quotas
  • MCP endpoint settings
  • security
  • observability
  • platform parameters

The Settings page covers those tabs in more detail.

docs.title: What may vary by deployment
docs.text:
The standard XTM One administration menu focuses on intents, users, groups, objects, logs, and settings.

Some deployments may include additional administration modules beyond this core set.

docs.title: What regular users should know
docs.text:
Regular users usually do not need the administration sections.

If you cannot see them, that is normal. Access is usually limited to administrators.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Intents to route capabilities to agents, Settings for the detailed platform configuration areas, or My profile for the settings users manage themselves.

docs.title: Running without AI
docs.text:
You can run the platform with AI switched off. No model or embedding provider is contacted, no AI work is scheduled, and nothing leaves the deployment for an AI service. Everything that does not need a model keeps working.

This suits a platform installed before the AI capability is bought, a deployment where policy forbids sending data to a model, and an air-gapped install with no provider to reach.

No licence is required

A platform running without AI needs no licence. You can install it, hand it to your users, and buy the AI capability later.

docs.title: What keeps working
docs.text:
• Deterministic flows, their triggers and their schedules
  • Integration syncs, importing and exporting as usual
  • Sign-in and single sign-on, users, groups, roles and invitations
  • Platform settings, branding, audit logs, health and metrics
  • Every existing agent, knowledge base, flow, run and trace, readable as before

docs.title: What is unavailable
docs.text:
• Chat, and every agent or assistant that answers with a model
  • Creating agents, knowledge bases, prompts, skills and templates
  • Knowledge-base indexing, and searching a workset
  • Evaluations, and the MCP endpoints

AI areas stay listed and reachable in the navigation, marked unavailable rather than removed, so you can still see what is configured. AI actions are visibly disabled and explain why instead of failing when used.

docs.title: Turning AI off or on
docs.text:
An administrator changes this from Settings → Parameters, under Artificial Intelligence. No restart is needed.

The setting has three values:

  • Enabled — AI runs, whatever the deployment default is
  • Disabled — AI does not run, whatever the deployment default is
  • Deployment default — follow the PLATFORM_MODE the platform was started with

Deployment default is a distinct choice, not the same as Disabled: it hands the decision back to the deployment, so a later change to PLATFORM_MODE takes effect.

docs.title: Turning AI on
docs.text:
Saving provisions the built-in content that a normal startup would create, so the first save after enabling takes a moment. Wait for it to finish rather than reloading — an interrupted save leaves the platform enabled with some content still missing, and saving again completes it.

You also need at least one model provider configured before agents can run. Add one from Settings → AI Models.

docs.title: Turning AI off
docs.text:
New AI work stops within one scheduler interval and AI actions begin refusing immediately.

Runs already in progress finish

Work already running is left to complete under its own time limit rather than being cancelled, so you may see AI activity for a few more minutes after saving. Cancelling mid-run would leave half-written runs and traces.

Work that was scheduled but had not started yet does not start: it is held. An assignment run waiting on its delay, a run resumed from a human-review pause (the answer you gave is kept), a background task that had not begun and the pending runs of an evaluation are shown as Held and run by themselves within about five minutes of AI being turned back on. A conversation waiting on a held background task hears back when that task finally runs. Held work is never charged. Deliveries waiting in an assignment's queue stay queued until AI is on again.

A hold is bounded: work held for longer than AI_UNAVAILABLE_HOLD_MAX_SECONDS (one week by default) is recorded as failed with the cause AI disabled on the platform and a message saying how long it waited. Set it to 0 to fail such work at its start instead of holding it. See Configuration.

Nothing is deleted. Agents, knowledge bases, flows, runs and traces are all kept and stay readable, and turning AI back on needs no repair.

docs.title: Setting the deployment default
docs.text:
PLATFORM_MODE=ai_disabled starts the platform with AI off, and is the right setting for an install that should never contact a provider unless someone deliberately changes it. See Configuration.

A platform started this way seeds no AI content at all: no built-in agents, assignments, templates, skills or knowledge bases are created, and the startup log states what was skipped. They are created the first time AI is enabled.

docs.title: Flows
docs.text:
A flow runs as long as none of its steps needs AI. Flows built from schedules, webhooks, HTTP requests, notifications, conditions and scripts are unaffected.

A flow containing at least one AI step does not start. It is recorded as skipped, with the reason on the run, so you can see in Operations that it was held back rather than silently missed. No part of it executes.

Its triggers wait rather than being used up: a schedule that comes due and the integration events that arrive meanwhile are picked up once AI is available again (a schedule catches up with one run, not one per occurrence it missed), a webhook delivery is answered with a 429 its sender retries, and a work item stays on its queue. Nothing has started, so this is not the hold described above: AI_UNAVAILABLE_HOLD_MAX_SECONDS does not end the wait.

In the flow editor, AI steps appear locked rather than absent, and a flow that already contains one tells you it will not run. Removing the AI step lets the flow run again on its next trigger — the decision is made from the flow as it is at that moment, not from a stored verdict.

A flow that hands off to another flow

If a flow calls another flow, the AI steps of the called flow count too. A deterministic flow that hands off to an AI-bearing one is held back.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: To configure model providers once AI is enabled, see Settings. For what the platform shares with an AI provider and how to control it, see AI governance.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Settings is where shared platform behavior is configured. Unlike My Profile, this page affects the whole environment rather than just one user.

Some tabs are visible to all users, while others are admin-only.

docs.title: The main Settings tabs
docs.text:
The current Settings page can include:

  • Parameters
  • AI Models
  • General Assistant
  • Channels & Bots
  • Integrations
  • Quotas
  • MCP Endpoint
  • Security
  • Observability
  • Quality

Non-admin users usually see fewer tabs. That is expected.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameters is an admin area for platform identity and licensing.

It currently includes:

  • platform branding
  • platform logo
  • instance ID
  • license management
  • the default presentation template

The instance ID is especially important during licensing and support work. The page can also show whether the active license comes from the environment or from a value stored in the platform, and which edition the deployment runs. A license carries your agentic capacity and the edition of each connected module; it never switches individual features on or off. See Editions and licensing.

Default Presentation Template is the brand template applied to every deck an agent generates when the request names no template. Only company-managed presentation templates qualify — the default is applied for every user, so a private template would leave everyone else's decks unstyled. When none is chosen, the platform's seeded brand deck is used — the XTM One Brand Deck on an XTM One platform, the Filigran Brand Deck on Filigran Copilot; clearing the field returns to it, and so does a default template that has been removed. See Templates.

docs.title: AI Models
docs.text:
AI Models controls the model providers used by the platform.

This tab can include:

  • chat and reasoning providers
  • default reasoning effort
  • embedding model configuration
  • image model configuration
  • provider-specific model lists

If your environment manages providers outside the UI, XTM One shows that clearly and treats those values as locked.

docs.title: Deleting a provider
docs.text:
Deleting a provider asks for confirmation first, and the confirmation says what happens to everything that used it:

  • The platform default model and the General Assistant chat model move to a replacement provider and stay pinned to it. Each always lands on a model the replacement lists: it keeps its model when the replacement's model list contains it; otherwise it takes the replacement's own default model if that is in the list, else the first model of the list, and the dialog names the exact model and provider. A provider that lists no model is not offered for a default that runs on a model (the dialog says which providers were left out, and why). The oldest remaining provider that qualifies is proposed; you can pick another one in the dialog.
  • Agents and users that picked a model on the deleted provider are counted and named. Their choice is cleared, so they follow the platform default model from then on.
  • Image generation keeps its image model on the replacement when the replacement can serve it, otherwise on the first remaining provider that can. When none serves that model, it moves to the built-in image model of the replacement or, failing that, of the first remaining provider that has one. Only providers that generate images are considered (a gateway listing an image model does not). When none can, the image default is cleared and image generation stops until one is configured. When the image model is set by DEFAULT_IMAGE_MODEL alone, it is only kept, never switched to another model, since the environment restores that model at the next restart.
  • The embedding default is never switched automatically. Knowledge base search only matches content embedded with the same model, so a different embedding model would make every indexed document unsearchable. It is cleared instead. Until you set a new one, embeddings fall back to a remaining embedding-capable provider (OpenAI first, then Gemini, Azure OpenAI, Mistral, Bedrock, Ollama) on its built-in embedding model, which cannot find content indexed with a different model; with no such provider left, knowledge base search and document ingestion stop. The dialog names the fallback and how many knowledge bases hold indexed content. Setting a new embedding default re-embeds every knowledge base.
  • The routing and fallback models are cleared when they used the provider: routing then uses the platform default model, and failover uses the other providers' default models.

When no remaining provider offers a chat model, the dialog says so: the platform default and General Assistant models are cleared instead of moved. If a remaining provider is not embedding-only (for example one listing only image models), chat still goes to it on its provider's built-in chat model, and the dialog names that provider and model. Only when no such provider remains do chat, agents and assignments stop working until a provider is configured. The image default still moves if a remaining provider can serve images. The deletion itself still goes through.

When no default chat model is set (neither the platform default nor the General Assistant model), chat that no agent or user choice decides goes to the oldest provider that lists a chat model. If that is the provider being deleted, the dialog names the provider and model chat goes to next.

When no embedding default is set and embeddings currently fall back to the provider being deleted, the dialog says where they fall back to next, and whether that model can still find the content already indexed.

A provider provisioned from environment variables is deleted when its variable is removed (at the next restart, or when AI is switched back on): the same rules apply, and the audit log records the deletion under a system actor.

The deletion applies what the dialog showed, or nothing. If another change is saved while the dialog is open (another administrator deletes a provider or edits a model list, for example), the provider is not deleted: the dialog reads the impact again and asks you to review it before you confirm. Deletions run one at a time, so two administrators deleting providers at once can never move a default onto a provider the other one is removing.

What was applied is recorded on the audit log entry of the deletion: the replacement provider and model, what each default became, and how many agents and user preferences were reset.

When no default is set at all, requests go to the first remaining provider that offers a chat model, in the order the provider list shows them (oldest first).

docs.title: Emailing users about model changes
docs.text:
When email is configured (SMTP_HOSTNAME), an administrator can tell the users about the models they work with. The email follows the Filigran layout, is in English, and goes to every active user except the bootstrap administrator account.

  • Changing the default agent model asks whether to email the users that it is now their default model: Save without email, or Save and email N users.
  • Adding or retiring models (saving a provider's model list, adding a provider, deleting one) saves the change first, then offers to email the users the models they can now use and the ones that were retired: Don't email, or review and email them. Only models users pick from count; routing, fallback, embedding and image models are never announced.
  • Both dialogs offer Send me a test email first: the same email, marked [Test], sent to you alone.

Every model list save you have not emailed is kept. The changes offered are those saves combined, per provider, over the last MODEL_CATALOG_CHANGES_WINDOW_HOURS (24 by default): a model added then retired again (or the reverse) cancels out, whatever the number of back and forths, and a change the live catalog no longer holds is left out. Before sending you can edit what the email announces. The dialog puts every model in one searchable list: the models users can pick now, the ones they could pick before, the models your providers say they serve (asked when the dialog opens; Ask the providers again refreshes them, at most 10 times in 10 minutes; a provider serving more than 2,000 chat models has its first 2,000 listed, and the dialog says so), and any id you type.

  • New models: any model users can pick right now, even one that was not part of the saved changes. Only these can be announced as new; a new model users can no longer pick has to be removed before emailing.
  • Retired models: any model at all, listed or typed, for instance one retired in an earlier change that was never announced. A typed id is announced under the provider you choose next to it; a model recorded under a provider an email cannot name (the embedding server) is announced under none. A model users can still pick can be announced as retired too: the dialog says it is still offered.
  • Search by model id, name or provider, narrow the list with Users can pick, Not offered, In the email and the provider filter, and pick with the mouse or the keyboard: the Up and Down arrows move through the list, Enter adds or removes the highlighted model (as new when users can pick it, as retired otherwise) and Shift+Enter retires it. A typed id no list holds is offered above the list: Enter adds it when nothing else matches, and when the search also finds longer ids (gpt-4 finds gpt-4o) the Up arrow reaches it first. Esc clears the search before it closes the dialog.
  • Pasting a list of ids, one per line or separated by commas, adds them in one go: Add all announces the ones users can pick as new and the others as retired, Retire all retires them all.
  • Preview shows the email as the users will receive it, updated as you edit.
  • Reset to the saved changes goes back to what the saves add up to.

Saves made while you review are kept for the next email: sending covers the changes you reviewed, and the panel then offers the newer ones.

The User announcements panel under the active default agent model shows the latest announcement and how it went (emailed to how many users, refused addresses, or why it was not sent). The users are emailed MODEL_CATALOG_EMAILS_BATCH_SIZE at a time, one batch a minute, so an announcement to many users takes a while: while it goes out the panel shows how many users it reached out of how many, and about how long the rest takes. When the email server refuses a batch for a while (a hosted mailbox's hourly sending limit, for instance), the next batch waits, 1 minute after the first failure and up to an hour after several: the panel says when it runs next and shows the server's last error. An address the server refuses for now (an unknown domain, a full mailbox, greylisting) does not hold the others: it is set aside, tried once more 10 minutes after everyone else was emailed, and counted as refused if it fails again, a sending limit still in force at that point included. While it waits for that retry, the panel says how many addresses refused the announcement for now, when they are tried again (or that they are being retried), and the last address refused, which is not an email server error. Four addresses refused for now in a row read as the server refusing the platform, and the batch stops and waits as after a server error, longer each time a batch gets no email out - except, once the server accepted an email of the announcement, a refusal that names the address itself (no such domain or mailbox, a full or disabled mailbox): a list holding many dead addresses goes on past them. More than 25 addresses refused for now in a row since the server last accepted an email of the announcement, whatever the batch size, read as the server failing again (a relay that lost its DNS answers "domain not found" to every address), and the batch stops as above. The retries are not held to that bound: they are the refused addresses alone, one after the other. An announcement that waits for an earlier one says so, and when the earlier one is tried next; so does a change a deployment made that waits for the deployed models to stop changing (MODEL_CATALOG_EMAILS_SETTLE_MINUTES, 30 by default): the panel says when it goes out, and a model change deployed before then is added to it. From there you can email the users about the current default model at any time, including one set by DEFAULT_MODEL or a change the platform recorded while its emails were off, review and email the model changes you saved without emailing them (the panel says since when and how many saves they combine), and announce models of your choice with Announce model changes when nothing is waiting.

An email never describes a catalog that no longer holds: a queued change that has not reached anyone yet goes back to the saved changes when you save again, and an announcement whose news was undone before it went out is dropped. Announcements sent from Settings do not depend on MODEL_CATALOG_EMAILS_ENABLED and ignore MODEL_CATALOG_EMAILS_RECIPIENTS, which govern the emails sent when a deployment changes its environment-managed catalog (see Configuration). Every announcement sent is recorded in the audit log.

docs.title: General Assistant
docs.text:
General Assistant is an admin tab for the shared assistant used across the platform.

This is where admins can define:

  • the default prompt
  • the default model
  • the maximum number of reasoning steps
  • how long an agent may pause when it is waiting for work it delegated
  • which tools and resources the assistant can use
  • which agents it can hand work to
  • how it behaves across channels

Two of these deserve a word, because they bound different things:

  • Max Iterations limits how many tool-calling rounds an agent may take. It is about work done, not time spent.
  • Waiting sets two time limits for the wait tool — the longest single pause, and the total an agent may spend waiting in one run. An agent uses it when it has delegated a task and wants to re-check in a few minutes rather than poll for it continuously. A pause deliberately does not count against Max Iterations, which is why it needs its own limits; the run's own time budget still applies, and users can skip or cancel a wait at any time from the chat.

Built-in Tools lists every built-in suite the General Assistant can run. Work items, shared state and trace inspection are keyed to an agent, so they are only offered on agents.

Agent Handover only offers enabled company-managed agents that every user can reach: the General Assistant serves every user, and a private agent, or a company-managed one restricted to the people granted access, would only be reached by the people who can see it. Each target is used as a Delegate, Consult or Transfer handover (Mandatory Transfer is only available on agents). Targets saved without a type are shown as All types: the General Assistant can delegate to, consult or transfer to each of them, and an agent you add next to them joins them as All types. Types are set per target, so picking a type for one of them gives every target a type; before it does, the screen names the targets that will become Delegate and asks you to confirm. A first agent, or an agent added once the targets have types, starts as Delegate. A target saved earlier that is no longer company-managed, is restricted, is disabled or was deleted stays listed with the reason until you remove it.

This tab affects the assistant experience seen by the whole organization unless a user overrides part of it in My Profile.

docs.title: Channels & Bots
docs.text:
Channels & Bots is the shared routing and channel administration area.

It currently covers:

  • always-on web chat
  • external channel bot setup
  • receive and publish whitelists
  • bot-specific tools
  • anonymous access
  • private conversation handling
  • mention-only behavior in group channels

This is also where admins can review or edit the connection details for Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, and other supported messaging platforms when those channels are enabled in the deployment.

For the setup of each platform, step by step, see Channels and bots.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
Integrations is an admin tab with its own sub-navigation.

It currently includes:

  • Catalog
  • OAuth Defaults

Use this tab when you want to manage which integration types are offered in the platform and what default OAuth behavior should apply when users configure them.

The webhook URL shown for an OAuth default belongs to that admin app. By default, a verified event it receives reaches every assignment it reached before: those whose agent is bound to an integration of that provider. With Require verified integration notifications on (or INTEGRATION_NOTIFICATIONS_REQUIRE_VERIFICATION=true) it reaches only the integrations running on that app (created with its OAuth defaults; for an integration created before XTM One recorded that, the one whose client ID is the OAuth default's) whose agent owner may use them, and for a GitHub App event, only integrations that record its installation or, recording none, whose own GitHub token sees it (read in the background: a delivery never waits on GitHub, and one reaching an integration whose installations are not known yet is handed over as before; an integration holding no usable token, or a token GitHub lists no installation for, receives none); the Security Audit reports the default, and each delivery that reaches an assignment the strict rule would leave out is logged. An integration on a user's own app receives its events through its own webhook URL, shown on the integration page. The webhook verifies an event with the webhook secret set on the OAuth default (for LinkedIn, its client secret). For a provider with no OAuth default, or with one that holds no webhook secret, an event is accepted without a check, as before: the delivery is logged, and the Security Audit names the provider and the assignments it can trigger. LinkedIn notifications sent to /api/v1/integrations/notifications/linkedin follow the same rule: that URL belongs to the same admin app, whose client secret verifies each notification. With no LinkedIn client secret configured, a notification is accepted unverified as before (logged and reported by the Security Audit), and dropped in strict mode.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text:
Quotas is the platform-wide usage control area.

In XTM One, it is mainly about:

  • agentic execution quotas
  • license-driven limits
  • per-user or per-group quota overrides

Some other deployments also show extra quota types such as LLM proxy usage.

Use this tab when you need to understand whether the environment is operating under a shared license limit or a manually configured quota policy.

docs.title: How the limits read
docs.text:
• A limit on a user, a group, or the per-user default is what one user may spend in the period. 0 is a hard stop: the user cannot run any agentic action. This holds under an XTM license too - a user blocked by a 0, their own, a group's or the per-user default, stays blocked even while the license pool still has room.
  • A platform-wide cap (the Platform-wide limit field, or a period of your XTM license) caps every user combined. Empty means no cap, and a license period issued without a quota has none either. The field no longer accepts 0; a 0 saved by an earlier version is read as no cap, as it always was. What a platform-wide cap has counted is saved to the database with the rest of the quota usage, every few minutes, so a Redis restart or eviction does not start the period over: at most the last few minutes of usage before it are lost.
  • An empty field on a user or a group inherits: the user falls back to their groups, then to the per-user default. To lift the limit for a user or a group instead, turn on its Unlimited switch.
  • When a user belongs to several groups, the most permissive group limit applies, and an Unlimited group is the most permissive of all. A group whose field is empty sets nothing and does not take part.

The platform configuration API reports a license period without a cap as null, and a deployment with no allowance at all (Community Edition) as 0.

These rules apply to every value saved from this release on. A value saved by an earlier version keeps the effect it had until you save it again: a 0 under the license pool gives way to the pool, a group without a limit yields to a member's other group that has a number, and a user or group quota type holding no limit counts as Unlimited. Where saving such a value would change what it does, its quota card says so.

docs.title: Requests with no account
docs.text:
Some agentic requests have no XTM One account behind them: a message from someone without an account on a channel that allows anonymous users, a visitor of an agent's public chat widget, and a call to the global MCP endpoint (/mcp/global) made with the platform MCP key. They count against the platform-wide limits exactly like everyone else's requests - the periods of your XTM license, or the Platform-wide limit - and against nothing else: no per-user default, user or group limit applies to them, since there is no user.

  • At the limit, the person gets This service is at capacity right now. Please try again later. rather than a message about quotas or licenses they have no way to act on. On a channel, it goes wherever the bot would otherwise have answered, like the message a Community Edition deployment answers with.
  • While the quota store is unreachable, they are refused like every agentic request in xtm_one mode, with This service is temporarily unavailable. Please try again later.; in copilot / dev mode they follow Quotas when their store is unreachable.
  • A request that never reached a model (no provider configured, a provider that could not be reached) gets its action back. Any other failure keeps it: the Agent Failure Pool below is an allowance per user, and there is no user to draw it from.
  • Where they show: the platform-wide usage of this page, and the platform-wide gauge of a user whose limit is the platform-wide pool, include them. They are never attributed to anybody - not in a user's own usage, the top consumers or the Agent Failure Pool card.

An assignment run that no user can be attributed to (a company-managed assignment saved before every assignment kept its owner, with no Run as user) counts the same way.

docs.title: Agent Failure Pool
docs.text:
An agentic action is deducted from the user's action quota before the agent starts, so a run that fails has already spent an action on work nobody received. The Agent Failure Pool card is where that is accounted for: each agent's first few failures are credited back instead of deducted, and the card shows how much of that allowance each agent has spent, how many pools are exhausted (and therefore spending actions on failures again), and the date the allowance renews.

The allowance renews once a year, on your XTM license anniversary. Its size is set by the operator in the environment and is deliberately not editable here — it decides what is billable.

The pool only concerns users who have a limit to give back to. When a user's agentic quota is unlimited at every level — no license ceiling or platform limit, no default per user, no limit on the user or their groups — a failed run costs them nothing, so their agents' pools are left untouched. The card says so: a notice appears when the platform-wide quota is unlimited (the pool then only applies to users or groups carrying a limit of their own), and a row belonging to such a user reads Not applicable instead of Spent. It is never counted under Pools exhausted.

The credited-back totals count every credit granted in the window, including those of a user and an agent that have both been deleted since: those have no row left in the list, and the card says how many of the total they account for (including N for deleted users and agents), so the per-cause breakdown under each total always adds up to it.

Resetting a user's quota usage (Reset usage on the user's page) gives their agents a full allowance again: their credits leave the totals, and their causes leave the breakdown with them. Causes recorded by earlier versions cannot be traced back to a user, so a reset that removes credits from the current window files those older causes under No cause recorded rather than leave a breakdown larger than its total.

A reset or a support-code recharge never runs while quota usage is being saved to the database: the save in progress stands aside, usually within a fraction of a second. On the rare occasion it cannot, the action is refused with Quota usage is being saved right now, so nothing was changed. Try again in a few seconds., and a support code refused that way is not used up. A reset or a recharge that fails part-way leaves every counter as it was; the causes it had already removed from the breakdown then read No cause recorded.

The card separates the two reasons an action comes back, because only one of them is rationed:

  • Agent failure — the run failed on its own merits. This spends one slot of that agent's allowance, and the per-agent table shows how many slots are left.
  • No LLM call — the run never reached a model: the provider was unreachable, down or not configured, or the platform abandoned the work itself (worker lost, deadline blown) — assignment runs and background sub-agent tasks alike. Credited back for free, outside the allowance, however often it happens: no LLM was called, and an incident on the platform's side must not ration what a user gets. The Provider column counts those per agent.

Some agents carry a Platform badge. Those are the seeded platform automations, whose scheduled runs never consume the action quota at all — so they can never appear here for that work. A row exists for one only because someone triggered it manually, which is charged like any other run.

One action is available: Enter a support code. Filigran support can issue a single-use code that gives every agent on the platform a full allowance again without waiting for the renewal date — after an incident on their side, for instance. Paste the code (XTMP-…) and it is verified on the spot, with no outbound call; a refusal explains itself (not issued by Filigran, expired, issued for another platform, already used). Codes already redeemed are listed underneath with the date and the administrator who used them.

docs.title: MCP Endpoint
docs.text:
MCP Endpoint is the admin version of MCP exposure.

It lets administrators:

  • generate or revoke the global MCP key
  • copy the platform MCP endpoint
  • choose which agents are exposed globally
  • review the connection snippet for external clients

This is the shared endpoint, separate from the personal MCP exposure available in My Profile. A call made with the global MCP key has no account behind it: it counts against the platform-wide agentic limits (see Requests with no account). A call made with an OAuth token counts against its user's limits, like any other request of that user.

The page also contains the Platform MCP Servers card, which controls the native OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ MCP servers (/mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, /mcp/opencrq):

  • a global enable/disable toggle (on by default)
  • the endpoint URL and live connection status for each platform

These servers activate automatically when a platform is registered with XTM One and expose business and knowledge tools only. See Platform MCP servers for details.

A separate Platform Tools MCP Server card controls /mcp/xtm, which exposes XTM One's own tools — agent traces, agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, and variables — to external MCP clients:

  • a global enable/disable toggle, off by default
  • the endpoint URL, with a copy button

It is off by default because it exposes this instance's configuration surface rather than a connected platform's content. Each caller only reaches what they can already see and manage in the UI, and every write goes through the same permission gates as the REST API.

Once enabled, the card also offers downloadable installer packages (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Agent Plugins) — the same ones users get in their profile, so you can review exactly what is handed out. With One-click install on, a download creates a new personal API key for the downloading user and writes it into the package; those key creations appear in the audit log like any other, and revoking a key cuts off only the client it was made for. See Platform tools MCP server for details.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Security is where administrators check the platform's security posture, set its security options and configure sign-in. It has four sections, each with its own address:

  • Security audit (/settings/security, the section the tab opens on)
  • Security options (/settings/security/options)
  • Authentication (/settings/security/authentication)
  • Memory purge (/settings/security/memory)

docs.title: Security audit
docs.text:
The security audit reviews the configuration the platform runs with: encryption, sign-in (SSO, self-registration, local sign-in, two-factor coverage, password, session and link lifetimes, the automations of accounts nobody signs in to), the platform registration token and the registered platforms (any the integration catalog does not list), integrations, agents and the public chat widget, channel bots, runners, webhook assignments, custom tools and their sandboxes, the code interpreter, MCP and A2A, LLM providers and traces, and the infrastructure (Redis and the fail modes, debug mode, CORS, the reverse proxy). Each check reports a finding with a severity:

  • Critical - exploitable now: a secret everyone knows, a dependency failure that switches protections off.
  • Warning - a protection is off or misconfigured while what it protects is in use, or a setting silently weakens one.
  • Info - a protection is off with nothing it protects in use, a protection only monitors, or context.
  • Passed - enforced, or nothing to fix. A check that can warn also reports its pass whenever what it protects is in use, so the report shows what is enforced, not only what is not.

"In use" means the audit sees something the protection would refuse or change right now: an embedded widget, a webhook assignment with no secret, a stored OAuth token URL on loopback, runner or MCP credentials issued while the platform is served over plain HTTP, the answers or tool results a connected prompt guard does not evaluate. While it is in use, a protection that is off is a Warning, one that only monitors is Info, one that is enforced is Passed. An opt-in protection off with nothing in use is Info: a deployment that changed nothing is not warned about it.

The page shows:

  • the overall posture: At risk while a critical finding remains, Needs attention while a warning remains, Healthy otherwise, and how many security controls are enforced (and how many only monitor);
