A value typed in Settings > Security is validated like the variable is at startup (a malformed origin or an out-of-range number is refused). The API behind the card is GET / PUT /api/v1/settings/security-options (administrators only); every change is recorded in the audit log.

docs.title: XTM Hub sign-in gate
docs.text:
Restricts sign-in to people XTM Hub has entitled to this XTM One instance, and lets the Hub decide who is an administrator here. OIDC only — XTM Hub does not provide SAML.

Variable Required Default Description XTM_HUB_ADMIN_GROUP No — The role, in this instance's XTM Hub claim, that means administrator. Matched exactly, including case. Setting it enables the gate; empty leaves OIDC behaving exactly as it does without this feature.

The gate reads a claim named after this instance — {PLATFORM_ID}_groups — so PLATFORM_ID must be set when you enable it. It is the switch that is XTM_HUB_ADMIN_GROUP rather than PLATFORM_ID, because forcing a platform identifier is an ordinary thing to do for clone/restore identity continuity and must not enable a sign-in gate as a side effect. Enabling the gate without PLATFORM_ID refuses to start, rather than silently refusing every sign-in.

Enabling it changes three things at once:

  • Every sign-in is checked, not only the first. Someone who already has an account and has since lost their Hub entitlement is turned away too.
  • A refused sign-in creates no account and lands on the login page with a neutral message. The reason is in the server log, not on the page — the person is unauthenticated, and the criteria describe how your IdP is configured.
  • Administrator follows the Hub in both directions: granted when the Hub asserts it, and removed when it stops. The account named by ADMIN_EMAIL is exempt from removal, so a Hub-side group change cannot lock you out of your own instance.

If a misconfigured gate refuses everyone, sign in with a local account — that route stays available and is the way back in.

docs.title: MCP OAuth
docs.text:
MCP OAuth runs in two independent directions, and each has its own switch.

Inbound — an external MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, …) connecting to XTM One. The platform acts as the authorization server and lets clients self-register, which the MCP specification requires because a client has no credentials before any user session exists.

Outbound — XTM One connecting to a remote MCP server. With no client ID configured, the platform discovers the remote authorization server and registers itself, so a server can be added from its URL alone. This is the MCP specification's intended onboarding path: modern remote MCP servers do not issue static credentials to paste into a form.

Variable Required Default Description MCP_DCR_ENABLED No true Inbound. Allow external MCP clients to self-register against this platform (POST /mcp/oauth/register, RFC 7591). The endpoint is unauthenticated by specification, so it is protected by a per-IP rate limit and a bounded client table rather than a login. Set false to turn registration off entirely (the endpoint then returns 403). A confidential client receives its client_secret in the answer, so under CREDENTIAL_TRANSPORT_STRICT a registration the platform cannot confirm arrived over HTTPS is refused first (400 {"error": "invalid_client_metadata", "error_description": "https required"}). Also in Settings > Security; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field. MCP_DCR_MAX_CLIENTS No 500 Inbound. Upper bound on dynamically registered clients. At the cap the oldest registrations are evicted; RFC 7591 clients re-register transparently. Values below 1 are clamped to 1. MCP_OUTBOUND_DCR_ENABLED No true Outbound. Let the platform register itself with a remote MCP server that advertises a registration endpoint, so remote servers can be connected without pre-provisioned credentials. Set false to require every outbound OAuth client to be provisioned by hand — connecting a remote server then needs an explicitly configured client ID. Also in Settings > Security; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field.

docs.title: OpenSandbox
docs.text:
Only used when CUSTOM_TOOL_SANDBOX=opensandbox. Governs the OpenSandbox-managed sandbox used by the code interpreter and by custom tools.

Variable Required Default Description OPENSANDBOX_DOMAIN Yes (if opensandbox mode) localhost:8090 Host (and optional port) of the OpenSandbox service. The default matches local dev (see dev.sh) and isn't enforced at startup — a production deployment that forgets to set this won't fail loudly, it will just try to reach localhost:8090 and fail to connect. OPENSANDBOX_PROTOCOL No http Protocol used to reach OpenSandbox (http or https). OPENSANDBOX_API_KEY No — API key for authenticating to OpenSandbox. OPENSANDBOX_IMAGES No python:sandbox-python:0.1,nodejs:sandbox-nodejs:0.1 Per-key container image, as comma-separated key:image pairs (split on the first : per entry, so a registry:port-qualified image survives intact). Overrides merge on top of the defaults, so overriding one key leaves the other on its default. OPENSANDBOX_K8S_POOL_NAMES No — (cold start, k8s-only) Per-key Kubernetes Pool binding, as comma-separated key:pool-name pairs, e.g. python:my-python-pool,nodejs:my-js-pool. A Pool's warm pods run one fixed image, so one name can't back both sandbox kinds — a key missing from the mapping (or the whole variable unset) cold-starts for that key. OPENSANDBOX_NETWORK_ALLOW No — (all egress denied) Comma-separated list of domains/IPs to allow as egress from every OpenSandbox container. Empty means all egress is denied. SANDBOX_CPU No 1 CPU requested for each OpenSandbox container (code interpreter + custom tools). Passed through as-is to the OpenSandbox SDK's resource argument on the cold-start path. When OPENSANDBOX_K8S_POOL_NAMES binds that sandbox kind to a k8s Pool, this is not read at all — the Pool manifest's own resources.requests governs warm-pod sizing instead, so there's no sync requirement between the two - see dev-docs/opensandbox-pool-management.md. SANDBOX_RAM No 128Mi Memory requested for each OpenSandbox container. Same cold-start-only pass-through as SANDBOX_CPU. OPENSANDBOX_USE_SERVER_PROXY No false Route sandbox traffic through the OpenSandbox server instead of connecting directly to each sandbox's endpoint. Useful for any deployment topology where this process can reach the OpenSandbox server but not the individual sandbox endpoints it hands back — e.g. a native dev.sh backend against a containerized server, where the server advertises endpoints via a hostname like host.docker.internal that only resolves from inside other containers (dev.sh sets this automatically in that case), or a production/k8s deployment where sandbox pods aren't directly routable from this process but the server's service is.

docs.title: Running the OpenSandbox server itself
docs.text:
The variables above configure how the platform connects to an OpenSandbox server. These configure how that server itself runs:

Variable Required Default Description OPENSANDBOX_SERVER_DOCKER No false Local dev only (dev.sh / dev.ps1 / dev-podman.sh). By default the launcher runs opensandbox-server natively; set true to run it as the opensandbox Docker Compose service (docker-compose.dev.yml, plain bridge networking) instead. The native default remains preferred on WSL2, where Docker Desktop's port-publish relay has been observed to fail, or hang unpredictably, for this container. dev.sh also sets OPENSANDBOX_USE_SERVER_PROXY=true automatically when this is enabled, since the backend runs natively but the server does not — see that variable above. KUBECONFIG_PATH Yes (if the opensandbox-k8s Compose profile is enabled) — Production only (docker-compose.yml). Path to a kubeconfig, authorized against the target cluster, mounted into the opensandbox-k8s service so it can manage sandbox pods there instead of local Docker containers. That cluster must already have the BatchSandbox CRD, opensandbox-controller, and the kata-fc RuntimeClass installed.

docker-compose.yml (production) exposes two mutually exclusive, opt-in profiles for the OpenSandbox server, matching where sandbox containers/pods should run: docker compose --profile opensandbox-docker up -d (Docker containers on the same host) or docker compose --profile opensandbox-k8s up -d (pods on an external Kubernetes cluster).

  • Target namespace for the opensandbox-k8s profile: set via the namespace key in [kubernetes] in backend/sandbox/sandbox.k8s.firecracker.toml (mounted into that service) — there's no env var for this specific setting, it's TOML-only. (opensandbox-server itself does read two env vars: OPENSANDBOX_SERVER_API_KEY for its API key, and SANDBOX_CONFIG_PATH as a fallback for --config when no CLI flag is given — dev.ps1 relies on the latter — but neither substitutes for TOML settings like namespace.) Defaults to null (server default) if omitted. See the OpenSandbox server configuration reference for the full [kubernetes] section.

docs.title: Sandbox call log fields
docs.text:
Every OpenSandbox-routed call (code interpreter, custom JS tool, custom Python tool) emits one structured sandbox_call log event to stdout (JSON in production — see Logging above), independent of the quota_usage counters. These fields are stable across releases so a log pipeline (e.g. shipping stdout into Grafana/Loki) can filter and aggregate on them; a field not listed here (e.g. level, timestamp, logger) is generic structlog metadata, not part of this schema.

Field Type Present when Description usage_type string Always One of code_interpreter, custom_tool_js, custom_tool_python. user_id string (UUID) Only when the call had a known user context The caller's user ID. outcome string Always success or failure. failure_reason string Only when outcome=failure One of sandbox_ready_timeout (the sandbox never became ready in time), sandbox_create_failed (other sandbox-creation error), sandbox_create_error (unexpected error creating the sandbox), nonzero_exit (the executed code/tool exited with a non-zero status), execution_error (an unexpected error while running the code/tool). cpu_used_percentage float Successful calls and nonzero_exit failures, when metrics could be retrieved CPU used, as a percentage. cpu_count float Same as cpu_used_percentage Number of CPU cores allocated to the sandbox. memory_used_in_mib float Same as cpu_used_percentage Memory used, in MiB. memory_total_in_mib float Same as cpu_used_percentage Memory allocated to the sandbox, in MiB. tte_ms integer Successful calls and nonzero_exit failures, when the sandbox backend reported a completed execution Time-to-execute: the sandbox's own reported execution duration, in milliseconds (not overall call time, which also includes sandbox creation/setup). Can be absent even on a nonzero_exit failure if the process errored before an execution-complete event was ever emitted (e.g. an immediate crash). egress_default_action string Always Always "deny" today. egress_allow_list array of strings Always (may be empty) The egress allow-list (OPENSANDBOX_NETWORK_ALLOW) applied when the sandbox was created.

CPU/RAM/TTE are omitted (not emitted as null) whenever they aren't available — e.g. no sandbox was ever created (sandbox_ready_timeout, sandbox_create_failed, sandbox_create_error), or the metrics lookup itself failed or timed out. A slow or unreachable metrics lookup is bounded to a few seconds and never delays or fails the underlying sandbox call.

docs.title: Webhook delivery
docs.text:
Governs POST /api/hooks/assignments/{assignment_id} — the endpoint an external system (SIEM/SOAR, ticketing, CI) posts to in order to drive an agent.

A delivery that finds its assignment busy is queued, not discarded: it becomes a run in the queued status, and an accepted delivery produces exactly one run, eventually. Queued runs start the moment they are queued and whenever a run ends, up to ASSIGNMENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS runs of one assignment at once, in turns across agents and assignments so one busy assignment cannot starve the others. Runs that must not overlap - the same ticket, the same thread - are kept one at a time by an assignment's ordering_key (below). Schedules, manual triggers and follow-ups keep their own overlap guard: they never start beside an active run.

Variable Required Default Description ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_ENABLED No true Per-assignment webhook (POST /api/hooks/assignments/{id}) only: queue its deliveries that arrive while the assignment is busy. Integration events follow INTEGRATION_EVENT_QUEUE_ENABLED instead. Set false only to restore the legacy behaviour, where such a delivery was discarded and still answered 200. INTEGRATION_EVENT_QUEUE_ENABLED No false Pushed integration events - a Slack event, a Microsoft Graph or LinkedIn notification, a provider or agent webhook - that arrive while every slot of their assignment is taken. false: the overlap guard skips them, as it always did (a Slack message is still fetched by the poller). true: they are queued, past the queue cap with a warning if need be, and start as slots free. Polled events (email, Teams and Slack messages) are always queued, whatever this says - see below. ASSIGNMENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS No 10 Runs of one assignment started from its queue at once (webhook deliveries, polled and pushed integration events), clamped to 1-50. An assignment's trigger_config.max_concurrent_runs overrides it. To keep up, the cap must exceed deliveries per second times the seconds a run holds its slot: 30 deliveries a minute of 6-22 s runs keep 8 in flight on average. 1 restores one run at a time. ASSIGNMENT_DISPATCH_MAX_PENDING_RUNS No 0 Queued runs promoted and still waiting for a worker, across the platform. The drain stops there, so a promoted run starts within a reconciler cycle and one busy assignment cannot fill the worker pool ahead of the others. 0 = MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS. ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_BACKLOG_SECONDS No 300 Once an assignment's oldest queued delivery has waited this many seconds, the drain alternates its newest and oldest deliveries, so fresh work does not wait behind the whole backlog (nothing is dropped), and logs Assignment dispatch lag at WARNING at most once a minute. 0 disables both. ASSIGNMENT_DISPATCH_RATE_LIMIT_BACKOFF_SECONDS No 60 How long an assignment's concurrency cap stays halved after one of its runs met an HTTP 429, from a model provider or an integration. Only that assignment backs off; a 429 met anywhere else (a chat, an evaluation, an embedding) throttles nothing. The window starts at the first 429 and is not extended by the ones that follow. The providers' own retries are unchanged. 0 disables the back-off. ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_MAX_DEPTH No 20 Maximum deliveries held per assignment. Bounds the backlog a slow or stuck assignment can accumulate. ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_OVERFLOW_POLICY No reject Per-assignment webhook only: what happens to one of its deliveries arriving at a full queue (a queued integration event is never dropped). reject: HTTP 429 + Retry-After, so a sender with retry logic loses nothing. drop_oldest: the oldest waiting delivery is finalized as a skipped run (visible, payload preserved) and the new one takes its slot. drop_newest: the incoming delivery is discarded with a 200 and a warning — no run row is created. ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_RETRY_AFTER_SECONDS No 30 Retry-After value returned with the reject policy's 429. ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_HOLD_ON_AWAITING_HUMAN No true Whether a run paused for human input holds the queue. true starts nothing more for its assignment until the approval is answered, whatever the cap - bounded and visible, unlike the old silent drop. false lets queued runs start beside a paused run; only safe when a HITL pause leaves no half-written shared state. ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_DRAIN_BATCH No 20 Maximum assignments that start queued runs per drain. Only assignments with a free slot are counted: one whose slots are all taken keeps its backlog without taking a turn. The drain runs on every reconciler cycle, on every enqueue and at the end of every run, so the rest follow within a cycle. WEBHOOK_REQUESTS_PER_MINUTE No 60 Per-assignment delivery throttle, applied before the request body is read. Over-limit deliveries get 429 + Retry-After. Raise it for a high-cadence alert feed — the queue still bounds how many accepted deliveries become runs. WEBHOOK_EXACT_EVENT_MATCHING No false Event matching of integration-event and webhook triggers. A trigger created on this version, or whose events are chosen again, matches its event exactly: pull_request runs on pull_request.opened, never on pull_request_review.submitted. A trigger saved on an earlier version keeps its prefix match through every other edit and every copy (duplicate, import, catalog clone); its assignment page says which mode it uses and what it matches, with a one-click switch, and the first delivery it matches only by prefix is logged. true applies exact matching to every trigger without editing them; it does not read the old event_type key of an agent-builder trigger, which only that trigger's own switch does. Also in Settings > Security ("Exact event matching for every trigger"); the variable, when set, wins and locks the field. See Event matching. WEBHOOK_DEDUP_TTL_SECONDS No 300 Idempotency window. A delivery whose key was already seen within the window replays the first delivery's response instead of firing a second run.

ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_ENABLED, ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_OVERFLOW_POLICY and ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_RETRY_AFTER_SECONDS govern the per-assignment webhook (POST /api/hooks/assignments/{id}) only; the concurrency, depth, hold, backlog and back-off settings apply to every queued delivery.

A polled email, Teams or Slack message is always queued. Each poll reads its provider's events oldest first, up to 5 pages - 15 Microsoft emails, 10 Gmail messages, 20 Teams or Slack messages a page - and queues them, so a backlog drains as fast as the assignment's slots allow instead of one event per poll. When the queue is full, the rest is given back to the poller with its position and fetched again on a later tick; nothing is dropped. A backlog larger than one poll is logged once at INFO level. What a poll cannot fetch is logged as a warning: more than 250 new messages in one Teams channel or 1,000 in one Slack channel, more than 100 unread Gmail messages, or more than a page of new events sharing one timestamp. Events that arrived while the platform was down stay with their provider and are read the same way once it is back: the poll resumes from its saved position (kept 30 days) and skips events it already dispatched (kept 7 days).

A pushed event - a Slack event, a Microsoft Graph or LinkedIn notification, a provider or agent webhook - starts in a free slot. With every slot taken, it is skipped unless INTEGRATION_EVENT_QUEUE_ENABLED is true, in which case it is queued past the cap with a warning in the log.

An assignment's trigger configuration can refine the queue:

trigger_config key Effect max_concurrent_runs This assignment's cap, overriding ASSIGNMENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS (1-50). 1 runs its deliveries one at a time. ordering_key A dotted path into the trigger payload, such as issue.number. Runs whose payload has the same value there start one at a time, in arrival order; runs with different values, or none, run side by side. Mail triggers are ordered by thread without it (Microsoft conversation_id, Gmail thread_id); "" turns that off.

A run that is not a delivery - a manual trigger, a follow-up, a scheduled or chained run - has its assignment to itself: deliveries wait until it ends, as they did before parallel runs. A delivery that cannot be queued (a pushed event with INTEGRATION_EVENT_QUEUE_ENABLED=false, the per-assignment webhook with ASSIGNMENT_QUEUE_ENABLED=false) never starts ahead of a queued run of its own ordering_key: it is skipped instead. One without a key may start in a free slot ahead of the queue.

The worker logs one line per drain (Assignment dispatch: promoted ...) and /metrics serves, per assignment (labelled by assignment_id, never by its name), xtmone_assignment_queue_depth, xtmone_assignment_queue_oldest_age_seconds, xtmone_assignment_runs_active, xtmone_assignment_concurrency_cap, xtmone_assignment_queue_held and xtmone_assignment_dispatch_lag_p95_seconds (created-to-started p95 over the last 15 minutes), plus xtmone_assignment_queue_oldest_age_max_seconds across assignments. k8s/prometheus-rules/assignment-dispatch-alerts.yaml alerts when a delivery has waited more than 5 minutes.

docs.title: Response statuses
docs.text: status Meaning ok A run started. triggered[0].run_id is its id. queued Accepted, waiting behind the active run. run_id is the queued run, queue_depth the current backlog. duplicate (with deduplicated: true) The same idempotency key already arrived within the window. The original response is replayed; nothing new was triggered. dropped The queue was full under drop_newest. This delivery will never run. ignored The target does not resolve (unknown, disabled, or not a webhook trigger), or an event filter excluded it. HTTP 429 Not accepted — retry after the Retry-After delay. Either the per-assignment throttle or a full queue under reject.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
Duplicate deliveries — proxy retries, sender at-least-once redelivery, a double-submitted test POST — are deduplicated so a retry returns the original run_id without re-running the assignment. The key is derived in this order:

  1. An explicit header: Idempotency-Key, X-Idempotency-Key, X-GitHub-Delivery, Webhook-Id / Svix-Id, or X-Hook-Signature-Id.
  2. A provider-specific id in the payload (OpenCTI notification_id, Slack event_id, HubSpot eventId, or a JSON-API type + id pair).
  3. A SHA-256 of the URL scope + raw request body.

Send an Idempotency-Key

Step 3 cannot tell a retry apart from a genuine recurrence. Two distinct events carrying byte-identical bodies inside the window — a repeated detection with no timestamp, a state notification with no counter — collapse into a single run, and the second delivery is answered with deduplicated: true. Sending an Idempotency-Key that is unique per logical event removes the ambiguity entirely. Failing that, shorten WEBHOOK_DEDUP_TTL_SECONDS below the sender's event cadence.

docs.title: Assignment auto-pause
docs.text:
A scheduled assignment whose configuration points at a resource its integration can no longer see - a Notion database that was deleted or is no longer shared with the integration - would otherwise fail on every run, forever. Once the integration has reported the same resource missing in two separate runs, the run that uses it again is recorded as failed with the cause Integration resource missing (its summary is kept), and the assignment owner is notified once. After the number of consecutive scheduled runs below, the assignment is paused; the assignment page says which resource and integration are involved and offers Resume. See Work history.

Variable Required Default Description ASSIGNMENT_STALE_REFERENCE_PAUSE_AFTER No 3 Consecutive scheduled runs failed on a stale integration reference after which the assignment is paused. Re-enabling the assignment starts a fresh count; a scheduled run that succeeds or fails for another reason resets it; manual, webhook and event-triggered runs neither advance nor reset it. Built-in and per-user fan-out assignments are reported, never paused. 0 disables the pause (runs still fail and are still reported).

docs.title: Messaging channels
docs.text: Variable Required Default Description CHANNEL_AGENT_MENTIONS_ENABLED No false On Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord and Google Chat, let an identified user's @agent-key (an agent's slug, else its hyphenated name) make that agent answer after the routed one, in the same reply - only an agent whose own channel settings let it answer that message (enabled, set to Receive and Publish on that channel, past the bot's receive whitelist, private-conversation and only-mention rules). Each agent that answers counts as one agentic action. false: a channel message is answered by its routed agent alone, whatever it mentions. The web chat's mentions are not affected by this setting.

docs.title: Runners and XTM One Desktop
docs.text:
A Runner is the pull-based native daemon behind XTM One Desktop (the native client users install on their own machine - chat window plus local execution) and behind the headless runner installed on servers and fleets. A user enrolls it once from the XTM One Desktop page (bottom of the left navigation) and leaves it running. It makes only outbound connections and pulls commands from the platform (the platform never opens a connection to the machine), giving agents genuine full-desktop screenshots, real-browser control, shell + file operations, and synthetic input through the computer_use built-in tool. Enrollment is a single-use, short-lived token exchanged once for a durable credential stored in the machine's OS keychain. Single sign-on from the Desktop app runs in the system browser and hands the session back through the runner-authenticated /api/v1/desktop-login handoff (short-lived Redis records; no extra configuration).

The installers, bare-binary archives, and self-update artifacts are built by the release pipeline and embedded in the platform image — every instance serves its own version-matched downloads directly from the XTM One Desktop page and answers the runners' self-update checks from the same embedded set. There is no external download URL, CDN, or GitHub Releases dependency to configure, and an air-gapped deployment is fully self-sufficient. A source/dev build (no embedded distribution) simply reports downloads as unavailable while everything else — enrollment, transport, computer_use — keeps working with runners you built yourself (apps/runner/build.ps1 / build.sh).

Variable Required Default Description RUNNERS_ENABLED No true Master switch for the whole Runner subsystem: enrollment, the runner transport (WebSocket + long-poll), and the computer_use agent tools. Set false to remove it entirely (every runner endpoint then returns 404 and the Profile tab is hidden). RUNNER_DIST_DIR No runner_dist Directory of the embedded runner distribution inside the image, populated by CI at image build time. Only needs changing if you repackage the image and relocate the artifacts. Empty/absent (source builds) reports downloads as unavailable. RUNNER_MIN_SUPPORTED_VERSION No — Minimum runner binary version accepted at connect (protocol gate). Empty means no floor; a runner below it is told to self-update. Format MAJOR.YYMMDD.SEQ. RUNNER_MAX_PER_USER No 200 Cap on active runners a single user (or the company-managed fleet) may have enrolled at once, enforced at enrollment so an unattended roll-out cannot create unbounded records. 0 = unlimited. RUNNER_MAX_INFLIGHT_COMMANDS No 10 Cap on concurrent in-flight commands per runner; a burst past this is refused with a transient "busy" so parallel tool calls cannot swamp one machine. 0 = unlimited. RUNNER_STRICT_PATH_CONFINEMENT No false What a restricted runner does with a file command whose path lies inside its allowed folders but leads outside them through a link (symbolic link, junction, mount point). false: it runs, as it always has, with a warning in the command result and the runner log; the security audit (Settings → Security) reports the default while a restricted runner has allowed folders. true: it is refused. The same switch covers a file that is not a regular file - a device (/dev/urandom, a serial port, NUL on Windows), a named pipe or a socket, as the operating system reports the object the command opened, never guessed from its name - on every runner, full control included: false reads and writes it as before, with a warning in the result and the runner log; true refuses it. Needs a runner from this release or later; an older runner ignores it. Also in Settings > Security; the variable, when set, wins and locks the field. RUNNER_RESULT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS No — (derived) How long an agent's computer_use call waits for a command's result. Unset: as long as the machine may take to report it, counted from the command's delivery - its execution limit (RUNNER_COMMAND_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS + 30 s, the wait for its turn on the machine included), then the 50 s it retries a result upload through a platform restart, plus 5 s. That is 205 s with the default limit, and it ends before the command's lease, so a command the wait gives up on is never sent to the machine again. A number: a fixed wait of that many seconds from dispatch. Either way a call never waits past the time the agent run allows one tool call (300 s at most): when that limit comes first, the tool stops 5 s before it and tells the agent the command may still finish, its output then landing in the machine's command history. Upgrading: the default used to be a fixed 180 s, which could end before a command near its limit whose upload rode out a restart had reported (see UPGRADING.md); set 180 to keep it.

Tuning knobs

The transport cadence and timeouts (RUNNER_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS, RUNNER_OFFLINE_AFTER_SECONDS, RUNNER_LONG_POLL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, RUNNER_COMMAND_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, RUNNER_MAX_RESULT_BYTES, RUNNER_ENROLLMENT_TTL_SECONDS) have sensible defaults and rarely need changing; .env.sample lists each with its default. RUNNER_COMMAND_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (120 s) is the execution budget every command is handed: the machine stops a command at that budget + 30 s, the wait for its turn included (a run_shell timeout argument can only shorten it), and both the time before the platform sends a silent command again and the default RUNNER_RESULT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS follow it.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.text:
Variable Required Default Description ENABLED_FEATURES No — (none enabled) Comma-separated list of feature flag ids to turn on experimental/in-development features, e.g. MY_FLAG,OTHER_FLAG. Use * to enable all of them. Leaving this unset enables none of them. Changing it requires a restart — there is no toggle in the Settings UI. An unrecognized flag id (e.g. left over from another branch) is logged as a warning and ignored — it never enables anything and never prevents the platform from starting.

The resolved list of enabled flags is also sent to the frontend (as part of the public, boot-time GET /auth/config response), so a flag can control both backend behavior and whether a UI element is shown — with the backend independently enforcing the same flag on any route it gates.

docs.title: Presentation export
docs.text:
Exporting a presentation to PDF or PowerPoint is a server-side render: the platform opens the deck in its own headless Chromium — the same browser that already ships in the image for the browser tool and the PDF path of generate_file — at a fixed 1920x1080 slide size, and hands back the file. This is what makes an exported slide pixel-identical to the slide on screen, independently of the user's browser, zoom level or print dialog. Nothing needs to be installed for it; the unified and worker images both carry the browser.

The browser loads the deck's render page from the platform itself, authenticated with a short-lived token bound to that one deck (three minutes, read access to the deck's own images only, refused everywhere else in the API). Every other request the page could make — external fonts, scripts, images — is blocked; the deck is entirely self-contained.

Variable Required Default Description PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL No Automatic Origin the headless browser loads the render page from. Empty means automatic: the unified image uses its own loopback address (http://127.0.0.1:4000), so no request goes through the ingress and the pod does not need to resolve its own public hostname; a split development setup (Vite dev server + API) falls back to FRONTEND_URL. PRESENTATION_LAYOUT_CHECK_ENABLED No true Render a deck in the same headless browser right after an agent saves it and report what the schema cannot see — a slide body shrunk to fit, text cut by its box, text painted past the slide's edge — back to the agent in the tool result, so it fixes the slide before answering. Set to false to skip the check everywhere (tool result, get_presentation, POST .../layout-check; the viewer then offers no Layout check button), for example on a deployment without the headless browser.

When to set it

Set PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL when the platform runs behind an ingress the pod cannot reach from the inside, or behind an authentication proxy that would intercept the render page before it reaches the platform — the render token is that page's only credential, and a proxy login screen in its place shows up as an export that fails with a rendering error. Point it at an address that reaches the platform container directly, for example the Kubernetes service name.

At most two exports render at the same time per process; further requests wait for a slot, and a user may request at most six exports a minute from the export buttons (decks and reports together; past that the request is answered 429 with a Retry-After). A render that has not settled after 60 seconds (fonts, images and diagrams all loaded) fails with an explicit error rather than hanging, and the Print to PDF (browser) action on a deck's chat card remains available as a fallback that needs no server rendering.

An agent-generated report exports to PDF the same way, through the same browser, slots, timeout and PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL: the platform opens the report's render page (with a three-minute token bound to that one report) and prints it on A4, exactly as the report's viewer prints it, every annex open. The Export menu of a report (its chat card and its viewer) offers that PDF and Print to PDF (browser) as the fallback; an agent with the report tool exports it as a file of the conversation when the user asks for one.

docs.title: Layout check
docs.text: A slide is a fixed surface, and a schema cannot tell whether six cards and a callout fit on it. So the same headless browser also serves as the layout check that runs after every save an agent makes: the deck is rendered, each slide is measured, and what the audience would see go wrong is reported to the agent in the tool result — a body that had to be shrunk to fit (with the ratio, so "dense" and "overloaded" are told apart), text cut off by a box or the footer, a badge whose text runs past its pill, anything painted past the slide's edge, a statement quote that runs past four lines — and, in the other direction, a content slide whose blocks leave the bottom third bare (reported as advisory, with the remedies that slide actually has: spreading a grid block's rows, spreading the blocks over the body, a footer block, or a merge with the neighbouring slide). The agent then trims or fills the slide it is told about and saves again, instead of leaving it for the presenter to discover. On screen, a slide whose content does not fit is scaled down to fit rather than overlapping its footer, and the exported PowerPoint carries the same scaled sizes. The check is bounded (45 seconds, then it is skipped with a note) and never fails a save; the same measurement is available on demand at POST /api/v1/presentations/{id}/layout-check to whoever can edit the deck (a read-only reader gets a 403).

docs.title: Waiting arcade
docs.text:
While an agent works, the chat shows a small self-playing Space Invader. Users can take control of it and play a full-screen game over the interface, with a leaderboard shared by everyone on the platform — see The waiting arcade. Scores are stored in the platform's database; a game that cannot reach the server still plays, it just is not saved.

Variable Required Default Description ARCADE_ENABLED No true Offer the playable arcade and its leaderboard. Set to false to keep only the self-playing waiting animation: every /api/v1/arcade route then answers 404, the chat offers no way to take control, and a ?arcade=play link (the invitation of the chat embedded in OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ) just opens the page. This is the only switch: users cannot hide the game themselves, and it is left out only for a user whose system asks for reduced motion.

docs.title: Skill loading
docs.text:
An agent's prompt carries a catalog of its attached skills (name + description) and the agent pulls a skill's full content in on demand with the load_skill tool, so prompt size scales with the number of attached skills rather than with the size of their content. A skill that must stay in the prompt at all times can be pinned per agent on the agent's Configuration tab.

These caps bound the worst case and rarely need changing:

Variable Required Default Description SKILL_LOAD_MAX_CHARS No 60000 Maximum characters returned by one load_skill call. Longer content is truncated with an explicit marker naming how much was cut. SKILL_LOAD_BUDGET No 8 Maximum number of distinct skills one run may load. Re-loading an already-loaded skill never counts again. 0 = unlimited. SKILL_RESOURCE_MAX_BYTES No 40000 Maximum bytes returned by one read_skill_resource call (files bundled with a packaged skill).

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text: This page explains what happens when you send a request, which components are involved, and where your data is stored. It is written for administrators and security reviewers deciding how to deploy XTM One. For what leaves the platform to reach an AI model, see AI governance.

docs.title: How the pieces connect
docs.text:
At a high level, everything goes through the platform. It is the only component that talks to the AI provider (for example OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, or a local Ollama model), your knowledge bases and integrations, and the trace store — nothing else reaches the AI provider directly.

flowchart LR
    U[You] <--> P[Platform]
    P <--> AI[AI provider]
    P <--> KB[(Knowledge bases)]
    P <--> INT[Integrations]
    P --> TR[(Traces)]
  • Platform — the XTM One application itself (API and UI). It authenticates you, builds prompts, runs tools, and streams answers back.
  • AI provider — the service hosting the language model the agent uses. See Configuration.
  • Knowledge bases — your vectorized document collections. Agents search them to ground answers in your own content.
  • Integrations — connections to external services (email, messaging, ticketing, and more) that agents act on through tools.
  • Traces — the recorded history of each AI interaction (prompts, tool calls, tokens, timing, errors), used for observability. Settings → Observability can keep them without their prompts and tool content, or turn them off. See Monitoring.

docs.title: The request lifecycle
docs.text:
A chat message or an assignment run follows the same broad path across the platform services:

  1. Your request reaches the platform (API + UI), which authenticates you and loads the target agent's configuration.
  2. The platform assembles a prompt: the agent persona and instructions, relevant context, and the list of tools the agent is allowed to use.
  3. The platform sends the prompt — and the tool list — to the configured AI provider.
  4. The model reads the request and either answers directly or asks the platform to run a tool. It cannot run anything itself; it only sends back the name of a tool and the arguments to use.
  5. When the model asks for a tool, the platform executes it — searching a knowledge base, calling an integration, running a sub-agent — and sends the result back to the model. The model can then ask for another tool or write its answer. This repeats until the model is done.
  6. The final answer is streamed back to you and recorded as a trace.
sequenceDiagram
    actor You
    participant Platform
    participant AI as AI provider
    participant Tools as Tools (e.g. search a KB, call an integration, run a sub-agent)

    You->>Platform: Send a request
    Platform->>Platform: Build prompt + tool list
    Platform->>AI: Prompt + available tools
    loop Until the model has an answer
        AI->>Platform: Ask to run a tool
        Platform->>Tools: Run the tool
        Tools-->>Platform: Result
        Platform->>AI: Tool result
    end
    AI->>Platform: Final answer
    Platform->>You: Stream the answer
    Platform->>Platform: Record a trace

What is a tool?

A tool is a function that lives on the platform, such as "search this knowledge base" or "send a Slack message". The AI provider is given a description of each available tool but never touches your systems directly: it can only request a tool call, and the platform decides whether and how to run it. This is why credentials and full data sources never need to be sent to the model — see AI governance.

Assignments follow the same loop without a live user: a trigger (schedule, webhook, or event) starts the run, and the worker carries out any delayed or background work.

docs.title: Where data is stored
docs.text:
All data stays in the backing services you deploy:

Data Where it lives Agents, assignments, users, configuration PostgreSQL Knowledge base documents and embeddings PostgreSQL (pgvector) Uploaded files and attachments Object storage (Silo / S3) Task queue, caching, short-term memory Redis LLM traces PostgreSQL, or ClickHouse if configured (see Monitoring)

All integration and channel credentials are encrypted before being written to the database. See Configuration for the keys that protect them.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with AI governance to understand what is shared with AI providers and how to control it.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This page covers the step-by-step deployment of a self-hosted XTM One instance using Docker Compose. Before starting, read the Overview to understand the deployment models and the architecture.

docs.title: Infrastructure requirements
docs.text: Every deployment runs the same five services. What changes is how much CPU, RAM, and storage you give them. Start from the baseline below, then adjust with What drives sizing.

docs.title: Resource baseline
docs.text:
The official XTM One Helm chart sets the following per-component resource requests and limits. Use them as a starting point and tune to your observed load:

Component CPU request Memory request CPU limit Memory limit Storage Platform 2 4 Gi 4 8 Gi — Worker 1 2 Gi 2 4 Gi — PostgreSQL (per instance, 2 instances) 1 2 Gi 2 4 Gi 64 Gi Redis 0.5 512 Mi — 2 Gi 2 Gi Silo (S3) 0.5 1 Gi — 2 Gi sized to your object volume

The platform and the worker scale differently. See the Scaling model for how to add worker replicas and keep the database connection budget in range.

OS: Any Linux distribution that supports your chosen container runtime. The Docker images are based on python:3.14-slim (Debian).

Disk: 20 GB minimum for the OS, container images, and initial database. Plan for more based on your knowledge base size and file attachment volume — PostgreSQL data and Silo object storage grow over time.

docs.title: What drives sizing
docs.text:
The baseline above suits a typical deployment. Whether you should size up or down depends on how the customer uses the platform. Each resource is driven by a different part of the workload, so profile the use case against these drivers — you rarely need to grow everything at once.

The two dimensions that matter most:

  • Interactive use — how many people chat with agents at the same time, and how heavy each conversation is (long streams, large tool results). This drives the platform and, indirectly, Redis.
  • Automation and data — how many assignments run, how often, and how much content agents ingest and remember. This drives the worker, PostgreSQL, and Silo.

Platform — CPU / RAM. Driven by concurrent interactive users and live chat streaming (WebSocket/SSE, LLM proxy). Size up when many people use chat at once or you see request latency climb — add CPU/RAM and raise WEB_WORKERS. A mostly-automation deployment with few human chat users can stay at the minimum. Chat is stateless per request, so this scales with concurrency, not total user count.

In numbers

WEB_WORKERS is the number of concurrent HTTP/chat processes. The default is 2; the production rule of thumb is 2 × CPU cores + 1, so a 4-core platform runs 9 — roughly ×4 the default's request capacity.

Worker — replicas / CPU. Driven by background-job volume and concurrency — the number of active assignments, how frequently their triggers fire, and how bursty they are (many schedules landing together), plus evaluations and sub-agent fan-out. Size up when jobs start queuing or embedding lags. A deployment with a few daily assignments needs one worker; hundreds of assignments, tight schedules, or heavy sub-agent use need replicas.

In numbers

Each worker runs up to WORKER_CONCURRENCY jobs at once (default 20). One worker = 20 concurrent jobs; ×3 workers = 60. Throughput scales linearly with replica count, so match the replica count to your peak simultaneous-job count.

PostgreSQL — storage / RAM. Driven by total data volume — knowledge-base documents and their vector chunks (RAG), agent memory, and run/audit history retention. Storage grows with knowledge bases and history; RAM helps vector search stay fast as embeddings grow. Size up for large or many knowledge bases, long retention, or slow semantic search.

In numbers

Storage is roughly proportional to content — ×2 the ingested documents and history is about ×2 the disk. Start from the chart's 64 Gi baseline and scale from your own corpus size; add RAM only if semantic search slows as embeddings grow.

Redis — RAM. Driven by peak job-queue depth and active-session count — pub/sub for the live activity feed and notifications, plus transient agent state (short/medium-term memory, in-flight chat markers, quota and rate-limit counters). It holds working state, not your data, so it stays small; size up only if you run very high job throughput or many simultaneous active agents. Storage never needs to grow with your knowledge bases.

In numbers

The chart baseline is a 512 Mi request with a 2 Gi limit — roughly ×4 headroom for bursts. Most deployments never approach the limit because working state is transient; treat a rising limit as a signal of extreme queue depth or session concurrency, not routine growth.

Silo / S3 — storage. Driven purely by stored bytes — uploaded knowledge-base documents, chat attachments, and agent-generated files (images, code-interpreter charts). CPU/RAM stay negligible; only disk grows. Size the volume to the customer's expected document and attachment footprint, and prefer a managed S3 (via S3_*) when that footprint is large or must be highly available.

In numbers

Storage equals the sum of stored file sizes — ×2 the uploaded documents and attachments is ×2 the volume. There is no compute multiplier to plan for; provision disk to the customer's raw file footprint plus headroom.

docs.title: Container runtime
docs.text:
You need Docker Engine 24+ with Docker Compose v2.

The repository includes a ready-to-use docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: Get the deployment files
docs.text:
Check Releases for the latest version tag.

Option A — clone a release (builds images from source):

git clone --branch <version-tag> --depth 1 https://github.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one.git && cd xtm-one

Option B — use pre-built images (no build required):

VERSION="<version-tag>"

mkdir xtm-one && cd xtm-one
curl -fSLO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one/${VERSION}/docker-compose.yml"
curl -fSLO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/XTM-One-Platform/xtm-one/${VERSION}/.env.sample"

Then create an override to pull images instead of building:

# docker-compose.override.yml
services:
  platform:
    image: xtmone/platform:<version-tag>
    build: !reset null
  worker:
    image: xtmone/worker:<version-tag>
    build: !reset null

docs.title: Configure environment
docs.text:
cp .env.sample .env
chmod 600 .env
touch .gitignore
grep -qxF ".env" .gitignore || echo ".env" >> .gitignore

Edit .env and fill in the required values. At minimum you must set:

  • SECRET_KEY — generate with python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))"
  • ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD
  • BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL — the public URL of your instance
  • DB_PASSWORD — password for the bundled PostgreSQL
  • S3_ACCESS_KEY and S3_SECRET_KEY — credentials for the bundled Silo object storage

If you connect OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ platforms, also set:

  • PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN — the secret those platforms register with (use the same value on each); generate with python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))". A standalone deployment that connects none can leave it empty. Left empty, Docker Compose falls back to a published placeholder, which only keeps platforms that are already registered connected - it cannot register a new one - and is reported at startup and in the security audit (Settings → Security) until you replace it. While it is in use, the XTM One license certificate is withheld from registration answers, so platforms sub-licensed by your XTM One license cannot prove their Enterprise Edition.

The complete list of available parameters is documented in the Configuration section.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
docker compose up -d

The platform waits for PostgreSQL, Redis, and Silo health checks to pass, then automatically runs migrations, creates the admin user, and seeds default templates.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
docker compose ps          # all services should show "healthy"
curl localhost:4000/api/health/ready   # 200 = fully ready

docs.title: Configure the platform
docs.text:
1. Open your BASE_URL in a browser.
  2. Sign in with ADMIN_EMAIL / ADMIN_PASSWORD.
  3. Go to Settings → AI Models — add at least one LLM provider.
  4. Configure authentication if needed — see Authentication.

docs.title: Inbound
docs.text: Port Purpose 4000/tcp Platform HTTP + WebSocket

docs.title: Exposing the platform
docs.text:
The platform serves plain HTTP on port 4000. In production you put something in front of it that terminates TLS (so users get HTTPS) and forwards traffic to port 4000. Whatever you choose, it must satisfy the same requirements:

Requirement Why Nginx example Forward client IP Needed for rate limiting and audit logs, with FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS naming the proxy (below) proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; Forward protocol OAuth callbacks need the real scheme proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; Allow large request bodies Knowledge base uploads can reach 50 MB client_max_body_size 50m; WebSocket upgrade Required for chat streaming proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; Generous read/idle timeout LLM calls and streams can run 60s–5min proxy_read_timeout 300s; Trust the proxy The platform honours the forwarded protocol and client IP only from the proxy you name: without it the audit log records the proxy's address for every user, rate limiting sees one client and the A2A endpoints refuse every request (403 https required) On the platform, not the proxy: FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=<proxy address> (Client address and protocol behind the proxy)

Set BASE_URL to the public https:// URL you expose, regardless of which option you pick.

Option A — Reverse proxy (default). Best for a standard host with a public IP or load balancer. Terminate TLS with any reverse proxy — Nginx, Caddy, Traefik, or a cloud load balancer — and forward to port 4000. Caddy and Traefik obtain and renew certificates automatically; with Nginx, pair it with your own certificate or a tool such as Certbot.

Option B — Connection tunnel. Instead of opening an inbound port, you can front the platform with a tunnel. This fits three cases:

  • Evaluation or demo — a tunnel such as Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) or ngrok gives you a public HTTPS URL in seconds, with no proxy or certificate to configure.
  • No public IP — for a host behind CGNAT, a home lab, or an edge site, an outbound-only tunnel exposes the platform without any inbound firewall rule.
  • Private-only access — a mesh VPN such as Tailscale or WireGuard reaches the platform over a private overlay with no public exposure at all.

A tunnel must meet the same requirements as a reverse proxy above. Two points need particular attention:

Watch the tunnel timeout

XTM One makes long LLM calls and holds long-lived WebSocket/SSE streams for chat. A tunnel with a short origin/idle timeout will cut these off — for example, Cloudflare's proxy enforces a ~100-second origin timeout (HTTP 524). Use a tunnel that allows long-lived connections, and confirm chat streaming works end to end before relying on it.

Data residency with public tunnels

A public tunnel (Cloudflare, ngrok) terminates TLS on that provider's edge, so your traffic transits a third party. If you self-host XTM One specifically for data-residency or air-gapped requirements, prefer a reverse proxy you control or a private mesh VPN (Tailscale, WireGuard), which keeps traffic on your own network.

docs.title: Client address and protocol behind the proxy
docs.text:
Behind a proxy the platform's peer is the proxy, not the user: the user's address arrives in X-Forwarded-For and the original scheme in X-Forwarded-Proto. Tell the platform which peer may speak for the client with FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS. Uvicorn, which serves the platform, then rewrites the client address and the scheme from those headers for requests from the listed addresses only, and reads X-Forwarded-For from its end, so a client cannot choose its own address even behind a proxy that appends to the header. Without it (uvicorn trusts only 127.0.0.1 by default) every request looks like plain HTTP from the proxy: per-IP rate limiting on /auth/login and /auth/forgot-password becomes one bucket shared by everyone, the audit trail records the proxy's address, and the A2A endpoints, /runners/enroll, /mcp/oauth/register and /mcp/oauth/token report an unconfirmed transport.

TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS trusts any peer

TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true reads the headers from any peer and takes the client from the leftmost X-Forwarded-For value, which the client itself writes behind a proxy that appends to the header, so it suits only a proxy that overwrites the header and is the only thing that reaches the platform. It also takes precedence over FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS when both are set. It is also the Trust proxy headers field of Settings > Security > Security options (the variable, when set, wins and locks it). While it is on, the platform logs a warning at startup, or when the field is switched on, and the security audit (/api/v1/security-audit) reports it. FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS is the recommended setting: switch to it with the steps below.

  1. Find the proxy's address as the platform sees it. Every request writes an access-log line whose client_ip field is the peer; with the default settings it is the proxy's address. Name that address, or the network it lives in.
  2. Make sure the proxy sends both headers, as in the examples below. X-Forwarded-Proto must be one value (https): uvicorn ignores a comma-separated list there.
  3. Set FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS on the platform container and restart: an IP, a CIDR or a comma-separated list. It is read from the container's environment when the platform starts, so it is not a Settings > Security field. Hostnames are not resolved and a CIDR needs its host bits at zero (10.42.0.0/16); any other entry trusts nobody, and the platform names it in a startup warning. Behind several proxies (a CDN, then a load balancer, then an ingress), list every hop between the user and the platform, since the client is the rightmost address that is not listed. Avoid * unless the platform is reachable only through the proxy: it trusts every peer and reads the start of the chain again.
  4. Check it before relying on it: browse to the platform and read your request's access-log line. Its client_ip field is the address the platform uses without TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS, and must now show your own address rather than the proxy's (while the flag is on, forwarded_for shows what the flag reads). If it still shows the proxy, the list does not name it: correct it and restart.
  5. Turn TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS off where it is set: remove TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS (or set it to false) and restart the platform, or, when the variable is not set, turn off Trust proxy headers in Settings > Security > Security options.
  6. Check the result: the startup log no longer carries the warning about the flag, the security audit no longer reports it, and the access log's forwarded_for field, written only under TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS, disappears.
NginxTraefikKubernetes ingress 
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

Appending with $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for is safe here: the platform reads the chain from its end. For nginx on the Docker host in front of the Compose stack, the platform sees the Docker bridge gateway of the Compose network (for example 172.18.0.1, docker network inspect <project>_default); for nginx in the same Compose network, its container address or the network's subnet:

FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=172.18.0.1

Traefik sends both headers by default and drops the X-Forwarded-* values a client sent unless the entry point lists the sender in forwardedHeaders.trustedIPs (list a load balancer or CDN in front of Traefik there, not in the platform). Name Traefik itself, by its address or its Docker network's subnet:

FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS=172.20.0.0/16

The peer is the ingress controller's pod, so name the cluster's pod network (for example 10.42.0.0/16 on k3s, 10.244.0.0/16 on a kubeadm cluster with Flannel) on the platform container:

env:
  - name: FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS
    value: "10.42.0.0/16"

Neither Helm chart sets it yet: until they gain a first-class value, set it in the platform's env map, xtmOne.platform.env in helm-xtm-one and xtmone.platform.env in helm-xtm-suite:

xtmOne:
  platform:
    env:
      FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS: "10.42.0.0/16"

For an ingress controller on the host network, name the node addresses instead. ingress-nginx writes into X-Forwarded-For the address it received the connection from; behind a cloud load balancer that is the load balancer's unless the service keeps the client address (externalTrafficPolicy: Local, PROXY protocol) or the controller trusts the load balancer's header (use-forwarded-headers with proxy-real-ip-cidr).

docs.title: When the platform reports an undeclared proxy
docs.text:
The platform reads the client address from X-Forwarded-For only, never from X-Real-IP or Forwarded, and only from a peer FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS names. When an audited request - a sign-in, a change an administrator makes - carries X-Forwarded-For from a peer it does not name, whether no proxy is declared or another one is, or names its client only in Forwarded or X-Real-IP, the platform logs one warning naming that peer and what to do, once a day for all its processes and replicas, and again after a restart with another FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS:

A request carried X-Forwarded-For while no reverse proxy is declared - "Trust proxy headers" (TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS) is off and FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS names none beyond this host - so the audit trail recorded the address of the peer that relayed it, 10.42.0.17, instead of the user's. If that peer is your reverse proxy or ingress, set FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to its address or CIDR (behind a Kubernetes ingress, the cluster's pod network) and restart. Said once a day for the whole platform; the security audit (Settings > Security) reports it too.

The security audit (Settings → Security) reports it as the warning "The audit trail records a proxy's address, not users'", naming the latest such peer any replica saw in the last day, with the exact remedy. A proxy declared under another address than the one it connects from - the Docker host's LAN address for a proxy on that host, which reaches the container from the Compose network's gateway - is reported the same way: name the address the warning gives. With no reverse proxy in front of the platform, such a request carried headers a client sent itself: nothing needs to change, the platform ignores them.

Once the platform has restarted with the proxy named, sign out and sign in again, then open the Audit Logs page: your login shows your own address, not the proxy's. The warning is no longer logged, and the security audit stops reporting the proxy - a proxy it reported for sending no X-Forwarded-For drops out 24 hours after its last such request.

docs.title: Serving under a path prefix
docs.text:
By default the platform expects to be reached at the root of its host (https://xtm.example.com/). To serve it under a path prefix instead — one host shared by several products, such as https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one/ — set BASE_PATH to the prefix and include it in BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL:

BASE_PATH=/xtm-one
BASE_URL=https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one
FRONTEND_URL=https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one

The platform then serves its interface, API, WebSockets and MCP endpoints under /xtm-one/..., and every absolute link it hands out (OAuth callbacks, webhook URLs, SSO redirects, the embeddable chat widget, e-mails) carries the prefix. Both reverse-proxy styles work — the platform recognises a request whether the proxy forwarded the prefix or stripped it — so use whichever your proxy makes natural:

Nginx (prefix forwarded)Nginx (prefix stripped)Traefik 
location /xtm-one/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000;   # no trailing slash: the prefix is forwarded as is
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;
    client_max_body_size 50m;
}
location = /xtm-one { return 301 /xtm-one/; }

location /xtm-one/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000/;  # trailing slash: nginx strips /xtm-one before forwarding
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Prefix /xtm-one;  # tells the platform the prefix was stripped
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_read_timeout 300s;
    client_max_body_size 50m;
}
location = /xtm-one { return 301 /xtm-one/; }

http:
  routers:
    xtm-one:
      rule: "Host(`intranet.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/xtm-one`)"
      service: xtm-one
      # Optional - the platform accepts the prefix either way:
      # middlewares: [xtm-one-strip]
  services:
    xtm-one:
      loadBalancer:
        servers:
          - url: "http://xtm-one-platform:4000"
  middlewares:
    xtm-one-strip:
      stripPrefix:
        prefixes: ["/xtm-one"]

Three constraints:

  • BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL must carry the prefix. The platform routes requests by BASE_PATH, but it builds outgoing links from BASE_URL (OAuth callbacks, webhooks, the MCP resource identifiers) and sends the browser back to FRONTEND_URL after an SSO or OAuth round-trip; when either disagrees it logs a warning at startup and every such link lands on the proxy's 404.
  • The prefix must not start with a namespace the platform serves itself — /api, /v1, /mcp, /xtm, /a2a, /office, /metrics, /assets, /.well-known — nor with the name of one of its static files (/favicon.ico, /logos, /robots.txt, /site.webmanifest, ...), because a stripped request under such a prefix could not be told apart from a direct request for that resource. Such a value is refused at startup.
  • The prefix is a plain path: ASCII letters, digits and -, _, ., ~ between slashes, no percent-encoding, no query string. /xtm-one and /apps/xtm-one are fine (xtm-one/ and /xtm-one/ are read as /xtm-one); /xtm%20one or a prefix with an accented letter is refused.
  • A prefix that is also the address of a platform page (/tools, /agents, /chat, /settings, /login, ...) is refused until you declare the proxy with BASE_PATH_MODE. The platform tells the two proxy styles apart per request - an X-Forwarded-Prefix header naming the prefix means the proxy stripped it, otherwise a path under the prefix was forwarded - and for such a prefix the second reading is ambiguous: behind a stripping proxy the public /tools/tools/123 arrives as /tools/123, which is also the forwarded form of another page. BASE_PATH_MODE=forwarded declares that the proxy keeps the prefix (nginx proxy_pass without a trailing slash, Traefik without StripPrefix); BASE_PATH_MODE=stripped declares that it removes it and sends X-Forwarded-Prefix - Traefik's StripPrefix does so by itself, nginx needs the proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Prefix line of the example above. Any other prefix needs no declaration.

BASE_PATH is the one source of the prefix: X-Forwarded-Prefix is read only as the per-request signal that the prefix it names was stripped (a header naming anything else is ignored), and uvicorn's --root-path is not needed (a deployment that already sets it to the same value keeps working). A request for the bare prefix (https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one, no trailing slash) is answered with a redirect to /xtm-one/ when the proxy forwards it, and served directly when the proxy strips it; that redirect is built from the scheme the platform sees, so behind a TLS-terminating proxy declare it with FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS (as for any HTTPS deployment; an nginx reaching a Docker Compose deployment at 127.0.0.1:4000, as in the examples above, connects from the Compose network's gateway - see Client address and protocol behind the proxy) - or keep the location = /xtm-one rule of the examples, which lets the proxy answer it. With Docker Compose, BASE_PATH, BASE_PATH_MODE, BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL set in .env reach both the platform and the worker containers (the worker builds absolute links too). The same values apply to the Helm chart's environment (BASE_PATH / BASE_PATH_MODE on the platform and worker deployments, through the chart's extra env until it gains a first-class value) and to the ingress path; PRESENTATION_RENDER_BASE_URL, when set, is an origin and the platform appends the prefix to it itself (a value that already carries a path is used as is). The container itself still answers /api/health, /api/health/ready and /metrics on its own port without the prefix, so liveness / readiness probes and Prometheus scrapes are unchanged.

docs.title: MCP clients authenticating with OAuth
docs.text:
An MCP client (Claude, Cursor, ...) that signs in to this platform's MCP endpoints with OAuth discovers the authorization server from the issuer https://intranet.example.com/xtm-one. RFC 8414 and RFC 9728 put the well-known segment before the issuer's path, so the client asks the root of the host — https://intranet.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/xtm-one and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/xtm-one/mcp/user — which the /xtm-one/ rule above never sees. The platform serves both forms (the path-inserted one and the /xtm-one/.well-known/... one); forward the well-known paths to it as well, without stripping anything:

NginxTraefik 
location /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000; }
location /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/  { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:4000; }

http:
  routers:
    xtm-one-oauth-discovery:
      rule: "Host(`intranet.example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/.well-known/oauth-`)"
      service: xtm-one   # no StripPrefix on this router

Clients authenticating with an API key (fcp-...) and the platform's own connections to other MCP servers need nothing of this.

Not served under a prefix in this release

The Microsoft Office add-in (/office/) is built for the root of the host: its bundle references /office/assets/... and it recognises the platform by that path. Under BASE_PATH the add-in's page is served at /xtm-one/office/ but the add-in itself does not load there; deploy it from a platform served at the root, or wait for the follow-up.

docs.title: Air-gapped deployments
docs.text:
Air-gapped deployments work if you use a local AI provider (Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint on your network) and the built-in Silo for storage. To get Docker images into an air-gapped network:

# On a machine with internet access — export the images (pre-built images setup from Option B):
docker compose pull
docker save xtmone/platform:<version-tag> xtmone/worker:<version-tag> pgvector/pgvector:pg17 redis:8-alpine pgsty/silo:latest > xtm-one-images.tar

# Transfer xtm-one-images.tar to the air-gapped host, then load:
docker load < xtm-one-images.tar

docs.title: Scaling model
docs.text:
What drives sizing tells you which resource to grow for a given use case. This section covers the mechanics — the structural reason the platform and the worker scale in fundamentally different ways, and the one constraint that couples them.

Two different \"workers\"

The word worker means two separate things here. The worker service (the worker container / Helm worker replicas) is the background-job runner you scale horizontally. WEB_WORKERS is unrelated: it sets the number of uvicorn HTTP worker processes inside the platform container, which serve the API and chat. Adding worker replicas does not change WEB_WORKERS, and vice versa.

  • The platform scales vertically first, and can run more than one replica. Give it more CPU/RAM and raise WEB_WORKERS for more throughput. Extra platform replicas are supported for availability (a rollout or a node drain never leaves zero pods serving) and for load: every background service it runs is coordinated across processes, because a single pod already runs WEB_WORKERS processes (2 by default) that each run all of them. See Running more than one platform replica for what is shared, and the few things that stay per process.
  • The worker service scales horizontally — it holds no singleton state, so you add replicas for more background-job throughput. Scaling is manual (there is no autoscaler) and the reference deployment starts with one replica. See What drives sizing for when to add more.
  • The connection budget couples the two — every platform HTTP worker process and every worker replica opens its own PostgreSQL pool, so max_connections must accommodate (DB_POOL_SIZE + DB_MAX_OVERFLOW) × (WEB_WORKERS × platform replicas + worker replicas) + overhead. Count the rollout too: with a surge rollout (maxSurge: 1) one extra platform pod runs next to the others until the old one is gone. Recalculate it whenever you change a count or the pool sizes (see Configuration).

docs.title: Running more than one platform replica
docs.text:
Each platform process (every uvicorn worker of every replica) runs the same startup and background work. What makes that safe:

What How it is coordinated Database migrations and built-in data seeding PostgreSQL advisory locks: one process migrates / seeds at a time, the others wait and re-run the idempotent steps Vector index builds PostgreSQL advisory lock Assignment scheduler (cron triggers, integration event polling, sweeps, maintenance) Redis window lock: one tick per minute across all processes and replicas Anonymous usage telemetry Redis window lease: one process exports per interval for the whole install, with values read from the database; a process that dies hands over when the lease expires, and a Redis outage skips the export rather than sending one per process A2A stale-task reaper, A2A partner card sweep Rows claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: concurrent sweeps take disjoint work Chat WebSockets Turn state and frames through Redis: a socket on any replica follows a turn running on another Runner connections (XTM One Desktop / headless runners) Redis pub/sub wakes the replica holding a runner's socket; results are awaited through Redis on any replica Activity stream (SSE), presence, rate limits, OAuth / MCP OAuth state, desktop sign-in Redis Discord bot Each process opens its own gateway session; the first to claim a message (Redis) answers it Platform branding (name, logo) Each process, the worker service included, re-reads it every minute: an admin change reaches every process within a minute Channel webhooks (Slack, Teams, Telegram, WhatsApp, Google Chat), REST and MCP endpoints Stateless per request; Slack events are also de-duplicated in Redis

What stays per process, and what it means:

  • Browser tool sessions. The headless browser an agent drives lives in the process that ran the turn. A later turn served by another process opens a fresh browser (the page and its cookies are gone). A chat WebSocket stays on one process for its lifetime, so turns sent over the same socket keep their browser; enable session affinity on the ingress if agents rely on a browser session across reconnects.
  • Outbound rate limiters for integrations (for example the HubSpot search pacer) are per process: with more processes the combined request rate against a provider can exceed what one process allows itself. Integrations retry on 429, so the effect is extra retries, not failures.
  • Prometheus metrics (/metrics) are per process: a scrape is answered by whichever WEB_WORKERS process takes it, so apart from xtmone_quota_usage (recomputed on every scrape) a series is a sample of one process, not a counter to read with rate() or increase(). The logs are the exact record.
  • Caches of licence state, AI settings and LLM provider clients are per process with short expiries (seconds to a few minutes): after a change, other processes follow within that time.

Migrations run on the first new pod to start, while the previous version still serves: a rolling update (with any replica count) relies on every migration staying compatible with the version before it, which the project's migration rules require.

Running multiple workers (Docker Compose). The default docker-compose.yml sets container_name: worker, which limits you to one instance. To run several, remove (or comment out) the container_name: worker line, then scale:

docker compose up -d --scale worker=3

Each worker creates its own connection pools, so recalculate the PostgreSQL connection budget accordingly. On Kubernetes, add replicas through the Helm chart instead.

docs.title: Kubernetes and Helm
docs.text:
XTM One can be deployed two ways: the Docker Compose stack described above, which runs the full stack on a single host, or the official Helm chart, which runs the same container images on Kubernetes. Choose the one that fits your infrastructure.

The chart deploys the platform and worker images and can optionally provision the backing services. Its prerequisites are:

  • Kubernetes 1.28+ and Helm 3.12+
  • the CloudNativePG operator for managed PostgreSQL with pgvector
  • an S3-compatible object store: the chart ships Silo, the community-maintained fork of MinIO (or point the platform at an external S3)
  • Redis (deployed separately, or an external Redis)

Wire the health probes as livenessProbe (/api/health) and readinessProbe (/api/health/ready). The worker scales horizontally by adding replicas; the platform scales vertically first and can run more than one replica (see the Scaling model above).

Under construction

The Helm chart deployment guide is under construction. The chart location, its release status, the full values.yaml reference, and a validated production topology will be documented here soon.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
This page covers how to monitor a self-hosted XTM One instance in production: health probes, metrics, request tracing, and logs. Filigran SaaS instances are monitored by Filigran.

The environment variables referenced here are documented in full in the Configuration section — this page explains what each signal tells you and how to act on it.

docs.title: Health probes
docs.text:
The platform exposes two unauthenticated endpoints for orchestrators and uptime checks:

Endpoint Use for Returns 200 when GET /api/health Liveness probe The HTTP server is running GET /api/health/ready Readiness probe Database, Redis, and object storage are reachable and migrations are complete

Use /api/health as a liveness probe (restart the container if it fails) and /api/health/ready as a readiness probe (stop routing traffic until it passes). The Docker Compose stack already wires /api/health/ready into its health checks so dependent services wait for full startup.

Kubernetes probes

Point livenessProbe at /api/health and readinessProbe at /api/health/ready. Readiness returns non-200 until the database, Redis, and object storage are reachable and migrations have completed, so traffic is held back until the platform is fully started.

Each web worker process (WEB_WORKERS) runs its own startup, and a probe is answered by whichever worker takes it. A worker can therefore be starting while its pod already receives traffic: the replacement uvicorn starts for a worker recycled after MAX_REQUESTS, or a second worker still starting when the first one made the pod ready. Such a worker holds the requests it receives until its startup completes, for up to 8 seconds, and only then answers 503 with Retry-After. It also skips the migrations and the seeding already applied since the container started, so it is serving within about a second. A seeding step the startup logged as retried "on next startup" (the built-in brand assets while the object store was unreachable, for instance) is therefore retried when the container next starts, not by a replacement worker. A worker whose startup failed answers 503 at once, and its /api/health/ready keeps reporting the error.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
XTM One exposes Prometheus metrics on a token-protected /metrics endpoint.

  1. Set PROMETHEUS_ENABLED=true.
  2. Set PROMETHEUS_BEARER_TOKEN to a secret of at least 16 characters.
  3. Scrape /metrics with an Authorization: Bearer <token> header.

The token is mandatory

When PROMETHEUS_ENABLED=true, the platform refuses to expose /metrics unless a valid PROMETHEUS_BEARER_TOKEN is set. This prevents an unauthenticated metrics endpoint from leaking operational data.

The endpoint exposes usage metrics in the Prometheus text format. The main application metric is xtmone_quota_usage, a gauge of quota consumption labelled by user_id, usage_type, model, period (daily, monthly, yearly), and platform_id. The standard per-process metrics from the Prometheus client library (Python runtime and garbage-collection counters) are included as well.

Scrape this endpoint to chart quota usage per user and per period, and combine it with the health probes to build a basic availability dashboard.

docs.title: Request tracing
docs.text:
XTM One records a trace for every LLM interaction so you can inspect what an agent did, which tools it called, how many tokens it used, and where time was spent.

A run's trace counts every token of every model call it made, including a run whose calls different providers answered (a provider failover, or a budget downgrade to another provider's model). When different models answered its calls, or their providers report usage in different formats, the run's cost is the sum of its calls' costs, as each call's own trace entry shows them; a run one model answered is priced at that model's rates.

docs.title: Native trace store
docs.text:
By default, traces are stored inside the platform's own database and are browsable from the application under Traces. The store backend is selected with TRACING_STORE_PROVIDER:
