  • postgres (default) — traces live in the bundled PostgreSQL. No extra service required.
  • clickhouse — traces are read from a dedicated ClickHouse instance for higher-volume analytics. Provide the CLICKHOUSE_* connection settings.

docs.title: What a trace keeps
docs.text:
Two switches under Settings → Observability decide what the native trace store keeps, under both store backends:

Enable local trace storage Store full payloads What is stored On (default) On (default) Every trace with its payloads, as described below On Off Every trace without what was said: the prompts, the conversation, the answers, the model's reasoning, tool arguments and tool results are dropped, and an error message keeps its first 200 characters (a provider error can quote the request it refused). Timings, token counts, cost, model, trace and tool names, status, failure cause and metadata are kept, so the Traces list, the analytics and the cost reports keep working Off On or off Nothing: no trace, no span and no user feedback score is written. An administrator's own score on a trace already stored (POST /api/v1/traces/{id}/scores) is still recorded

A change applies within a few seconds on every server and worker, to the traces written from then on — including a trace that was still queued when the switch changed. Traces already stored keep what they hold until the retention period deletes them; delete individual traces from the Traces page to remove them sooner. The switches govern the native trace store only: the Langfuse export, while it is enabled, still receives each call's payloads (bounded per field). Turn it off as well to keep payloads inside the platform.

While a switch is off, an agent reading traces (inspect_my_traces, inspect_agent_traces, get_trace_payload, and the same tools on the XTM One MCP server) is told so in the result, so it does not read a run missing from the list, or an empty input or output, as something the run did.

docs.title: Trace payload storage
docs.text:
While Store full payloads is on, trace payloads — the prompt, the conversation, the model's reasoning, tool arguments and results — are stored whole. They are audit material, and the trace store holds the only copy, so nothing is clipped on the way in.

Large payloads are moved out of the database rather than truncated. Above TRACE_PAYLOAD_OFFLOAD_THRESHOLD_BYTES (default 1 MiB), the payload is written to object storage and the trace row keeps a pointer with the exact size, a SHA-256 digest and a short excerpt. In the Traces UI those payloads show a Load full payload action that fetches the complete value on demand; the panes show a bounded preview until you ask for it, so opening a trace with megabyte-sized payloads stays fast.

Images and PDFs inside a payload are stored the same way, one object each: the payload keeps a reference with the blob's content type, byte size and SHA-256, and the span inspector lists them as attachments that render the actual image on demand. This is what makes the screenshot an agent received — or the chart it produced — recoverable from its trace; previously media was replaced by an [image] placeholder, and since the trace store holds the only copy, the picture was gone for good.

Variable What it controls TRACE_PAYLOAD_OFFLOAD_THRESHOLD_BYTES Size above which a payload goes to object storage (default 1 MiB). 0 disables offloading and always stores inline. TRACE_PAYLOAD_HARD_MAX_BYTES Inline fallback ceiling used only when object storage is unreachable (default 32 MiB). Below it the payload is stored inline anyway; above it the trace records that the payload could not be stored, so the gap is visible instead of silent. TRACE_MEDIA_OFFLOAD_ENABLED Whether media blobs are stored (default true). Set to false to replace them with an [image] placeholder instead, as earlier versions did.

Offloading requires the same object storage as file attachments (the S3_* settings). Everything one trace owns — offloaded payloads and media alike — lives under a traces/<trace_id>/ prefix. Plan disk for both volumes accordingly. Trace retention bounds how long payloads and their objects are kept — the retention purge deletes the objects along with the rows, under both store backends.

Langfuse export

When Langfuse is configured, the payloads exported to it still have media replaced by placeholders and long strings truncated, regardless of TRACE_MEDIA_OFFLOAD_ENABLED. Langfuse ingestion has its own size limits, and its SDK would otherwise upload every blob to its own separate media storage. Only the export is reduced; the durable trace keeps everything.

docs.title: Trace retention
docs.text:
How long traces are kept is a platform setting, not an environment variable: set it under Settings → Observability → Trace retention (days) (1–365, 90 by default). It applies to both store backends, in the same maintenance cycle, and each cycle deletes the offloaded payload objects belonging to the traces it expires.

  • PostgreSQL — expired traces are deleted in batches roughly hourly. A day's aggregated statistics (llm_daily_stats) are built before its raw traces are deleted and outlive them, so dashboards keep reporting on days whose traces are gone. A day whose statistics are due to be rebuilt (a repricing filled in costs they were built without) keeps its traces until that rebuild has run.
  • ClickHouse — the same cycle sweeps the expired window: it reads the payload pointers off the expiring rows, deletes the rows, then deletes the objects they pointed at. The tables also carry a TTL as a backstop, re-declared whenever the retention setting changes and re-checked on each cycle, so retention still applies to tables that already exist and to a platform whose maintenance loop is not running.

Why ClickHouse keeps a few extra days

The ClickHouse TTL is deliberately set a week beyond the retention window rather than exactly on it. Offloaded payload objects can only be found through the rows that point at them, so the rows have to outlive the object purge — a TTL on the exact boundary would let ClickHouse drop rows before the sweep had read their pointers, orphaning objects in the bucket. In normal operation the sweep enforces the exact window and the TTL never fires. If the maintenance loop stays down for longer than that margin, the TTL still expires the rows (retention is never silently extended) but their objects are left behind; that is a storage cost, and the sweep logs when it cannot reach object storage.

docs.title: Langfuse (optional)
docs.text:
You can additionally forward traces to Langfuse for external observability. Set LANGFUSE_HOST, LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY, and LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY. LANGFUSE_HOST defaults to Langfuse Cloud; point it at your self-hosted Langfuse to keep trace data on your own infrastructure.

Langfuse is complementary to the native store — enabling it does not disable native traces. Payloads sent to Langfuse are bounded per field, because its ingestion rejects oversized events; the native store keeps the unabridged copy. The Enable local trace storage and Store full payloads switches do not apply to the export: Langfuse receives each call's payloads for as long as it is enabled.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
The platform emits structured logs to stdout, which your container runtime or log aggregator collects.

Variable What it controls LOG_LEVEL Verbosity (debug, info, warning, error, critical) LOG_FORMAT json (structured, for aggregators) or console (human-readable)

One structured http_request line is emitted per HTTP request on the app.access logger. Successful requests to /api/health and /metrics are logged at debug so routine probes and scrapes do not flood your logs; client errors are logged at warning and server errors at error.

In production, keep LOG_FORMAT=json and ship logs to a central aggregator (Loki, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch, etc.) so you can search and alert across replicas.

docs.title: Sandbox call logs
docs.text:
Every OpenSandbox-routed call (code interpreter, custom JS tool, custom Python tool) emits one additional structured line, sandbox_call, carrying CPU/RAM usage, execution time, egress policy, and outcome. It ships through the same stdout path as everything else above — no extra infrastructure required. The full field reference (names, types, units, when each is present) lives in Configuration § Sandbox call log fields; this section covers how to query it once it's in Grafana.

Example line (LOG_FORMAT=json):

{"event": "sandbox_call", "usage_type": "code_interpreter", "outcome": "success", "user_id": "3fa85f64-5717-4562-b3fc-2c963f66afa6", "cpu_used_percentage": 12.5, "cpu_count": 1.0, "memory_used_in_mib": 64.2, "memory_total_in_mib": 128.0, "tte_ms": 842, "egress_default_action": "deny", "egress_allow_list": [], "level": "info", "logger": "app.services.sandbox_call_logging", "timestamp": "2026-07-31T12:00:00.000000Z"}

With logs shipped into Loki, these LogQL queries build directly on the fields above — swap {container="platform"} for whatever stream label your Promtail/Grafana Agent config actually attaches (container name, job, Kubernetes pod label, etc.):

  • All sandbox calls (base query for a Logs panel):
{container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call"
  • Failure rate by usage_type (stat/alert panel — ratio of failing to total calls per interval):
sum by (usage_type) (count_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | outcome="failure" [$__interval]))
/
sum by (usage_type) (count_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" [$__interval]))
  • Failure breakdown by reason (table/pie panel — sandbox_ready_timeout, sandbox_create_failed, sandbox_create_error, nonzero_exit, execution_error):
sum by (failure_reason) (count_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | outcome="failure" [$__interval]))
  • Average execution time (TTE) per usage_type (time series panel):
avg_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | outcome="success" | unwrap tte_ms [5m]) by (usage_type)
  • CPU / memory usage trend (swap cpu_used_percentage for memory_used_in_mib or memory_total_in_mib):
avg_over_time({container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | unwrap cpu_used_percentage [5m]) by (usage_type)
  • Egress policy audit (confirm what's actually live, per call):
{container="platform"} | json | event="sandbox_call" | line_format "{{.usage_type}}: {{.egress_default_action}} allow={{.egress_allow_list}}"

CPU/RAM/TTE fields are simply absent (not null) on records where the sandbox never reached completion — sandbox_ready_timeout, sandbox_create_failed, and sandbox_create_error records have none of them. unwrap queries skip lines missing the unwrapped field rather than erroring, so a TTE/CPU/RAM panel naturally reflects only the calls that actually ran, without extra filtering.

docs.title: What to watch
docs.text:
At a minimum, alert on:

  • /api/health/ready failing for more than a few minutes (platform not serving)
  • A rising rate of 5xx responses in the access logs
  • Worker containers repeatedly restarting (background jobs and assignment runs stall)
  • PostgreSQL connection saturation — see the connection-budget formula in Configuration
  • Disk usage on the PostgreSQL and object-storage volumes, which grow with knowledge bases and file attachments
  • A rising sandbox_call failure rate or an unfamiliar failure_reason for OpenSandbox-routed code interpreter/custom tool calls — see Sandbox call logs above

Under construction

Recommended alert thresholds and a reference set of Prometheus alert rules for self-hosted deployments are being prepared and will be added here.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: If a signal points to a problem, continue with Troubleshooting for common issues and how to diagnose them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Before starting the installation, let's discover how XTM One is built, which services it relies on and how it can be hosted.

Docker deployment of the full XTM suite (OpenCTI - OpenAEV - XTM One)

If you're looking for information about the deployment of the full eXtended Threat Management (XTM) suite using Docker, please refer to this repository and documentation.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The diagram groups the deployment by role, following the flow from triggers (inbound) through the platform and workers you run, out to LLM providers and integrations, and down to storage.

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text: What starts work: a chat message, an incoming channel message (Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Google Chat, web), a webhook, a scheduled tick, or an integration event. All arrive at the platform.

docs.title: XTM One platform — xtmone/platform
docs.text: The service you run: API + web UI (port 4000), chat (WebSocket/SSE), the LLM proxy (/v1), the MCP endpoints (/mcp/*), and webhooks. Also runs the cron scheduler and event poller, applies migrations on startup, and runs the agentic loop for chat. Scales vertically first — add CPU/RAM and raise WEB_WORKERS; more platform replicas are supported too, for availability or load (see Running more than one platform replica).

docs.title: Workers — xtmone/worker
docs.text: Run all background jobs — assignment runs, knowledge-base embedding (via SAQ), evaluations, sub-agent tasks — plus the orchestration reconciler that drives the durable run state machine. They run the agentic loop for assignments; no interactive chat. Scale horizontally — add replicas when jobs queue (WORKER_CONCURRENCY, default 20).

docs.title: LLM providers
docs.text: External model endpoints reached at runtime (OpenAI, Anthropic, … or local Ollama). Configured in Settings; LLM calls are outbound only. 10 provider types are supported.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text: The outbound tools the agent acts through: integrations (Internal XTM Suite — OpenCTI, OpenAEV — plus 90+ External third-party), MCP servers, and custom tools. Integrations are two-way — the native Suite platforms call back in via their embedded "Ask AI" (see XTM Suite integration).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL + pgvector — system of record: relational data, run state (orchestration_executions), and vector embeddings (RAG + memory). Back it up.
  • Redis — coordination, not durable: SAQ queue, pub/sub, cache, transient memory. Evicts LRU when full; durable state lives in PostgreSQL.
  • Object storage (Silo / S3) — files: knowledge-base documents, attachments, generated files. Any S3-compatible service.

All three are sized to your data and set via DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, and S3_* — bundled container or managed equivalent (RDS/Aurora, managed Redis, S3).

The Installation page turns this into a deployment: Infrastructure requirements gives the concrete CPU/RAM figures and the database connection-budget math, and the Scaling model covers adding worker and platform replicas.

docs.title: Deployment models
docs.text:
XTM One can be deployed in two ways: Filigran SaaS (Filigran-hosted) and Self-Hosted (you run it).

Filigran SaaS Self-Hosted Hosting Filigran-hosted cloud instance Your infrastructure — on-premises or your own cloud Maintenance Filigran Your team Upgrades Handled by Filigran Manual Network Outbound HTTPS only Your choice — on-premises, private cloud,internet-facing, or fully air-gapped Best for Fastest start, no infrastructure to run Full control, on-premises or data-residencyrequirements, air-gapped environments

docs.title: Filigran SaaS
docs.text:
Filigran hosts and operates XTM One for you as a fully managed cloud private instance. You access the platform through a Filigran-provided URL.

What you need

  • A Filigran subscription
  • A supported web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge)
  • Outbound HTTPS access (port 443) to the platform URL provided during onboarding
  • Outbound HTTPS to your identity provider (if SSO is configured)
  • Outbound HTTPS to any external service your agents connect to (AI providers, messaging platforms, etc.)

Onboarding

  1. Filigran provisions your tenant and sends you a URL and initial admin credentials.
  2. Sign in, then go to Settings to configure AI providers, SSO, and integrations.

Access provisioning

Users can access the platform through:

  • Admin invitation — admins create user accounts from Settings → Users.
  • SSO auto-provisioning — when OIDC or SAML is configured, users are created automatically on first login. SAML supports automatic group mapping from IdP group claims.
  • Self-registration — if enabled by the admin, users can register with a valid email domain.

Your responsibilities

  • User accounts, SSO, and access control
  • AI provider configuration (API keys configured from the Settings UI)
  • Agent, integration, and knowledge base setup

What Filigran manages

  • Infrastructure provisioning and monitoring
  • Platform upgrades and patches
  • Database backups and disaster recovery
  • Availability, performance, and scaling

Infrastructure-level requests — custom domains, network peering or VPN access instead of the public internet, and sizing or capacity changes — go through Filigran. Share your sizing and capacity needs with Filigran so the instance is provisioned accordingly.

Limitations

  • No access to the underlying infrastructure, database, or containers
  • No control over environment variables or performance tuning (worker count, pool sizes)
  • Upgrade timing is controlled by Filigran
  • Custom tool sandbox mode is not configurable

docs.title: Self-Hosted
docs.text:
You deploy and operate XTM One on your own infrastructure. The Architecture above describes the services you run; the Installation page covers the infrastructure requirements and the step-by-step procedure.

What self-hosting means

When you self-host, you take on responsibilities that Filigran handles in the SaaS model:

Area Managed (SaaS) Self-Hosted Upgrades Automatic or coordinated You pull images and restart manually Database backups Managed by Filigran Your responsibility TLS certificates Included You provide certificates and a reverse proxy Monitoring and alerting Included You set up your own (Langfuse, Prometheus, log aggregation) Scaling Managed by Filigran You scale workers and tune connection pools Infrastructure security Managed by Filigran You harden the host, network, and containers

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with the Installation procedure to deploy the platform.

docs.title: Security headers
docs.text:
XTM One sends a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) on every HTML page it serves: the web application itself, the API reference, the MCP OAuth consent page, the Microsoft Teams tab and the Office add-in task pane. API responses, file downloads and streams carry none.

A CSP tells the browser which scripts, styles, images and connections a page may use. It is defence in depth: if some injected content ever slipped past the platform's own output checks, the browser would still refuse to run a script or load a resource the page never needed.

docs.title: Report-only first
docs.text:
The policy is sent in report-only mode by default (CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_MODE=report-only), as a Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header. In this mode the browser blocks nothing. It only reports what the policy would have blocked, so turning the policy on cannot break any deployment. The reports tell you whether enforcing it would.

CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_MODE Header Effect report-only (default) Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only Nothing is blocked; violations are reported. enforce Content-Security-Policy The browser blocks whatever the policy does not allow, and still reports it. off none No policy at all.

Any other value stops the platform at startup rather than silently meaning another mode. With the policy enforced, the pages also carry Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, the browser's own default stated explicitly. In report-only and off modes the platform sends no Referrer-Policy, so one your proxy or CDN adds keeps applying.

The platform never sends X-Frame-Options: it cannot name the Teams and Office hosts or the embedders a deployment declares. The frame-ancestors directive of the policy does that job once the policy is enforced (see Who may frame the platform).

docs.title: Reading the reports
docs.text:
Browsers send their reports to /api/v1/csp-report, the policy's report-uri (under BASE_PATH when one is set). The policy names no report-to: a browser that supports it would then ignore report-uri and deliver only to an absolute HTTPS endpoint, which the platform cannot name correctly for every deployment. The endpoint needs no authentication, accepts both the report-uri format (application/csp-report) and the Reporting API format (application/reports+json), and is bounded: 64 KiB per request, 32 violations per request, 120 requests per minute per client address. Behind a reverse proxy, the client address is known only once the platform trusts that proxy (FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS, or TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS); otherwise every browser shares one budget of 120 requests a minute, and the reports past it are refused and not counted.

Reports are never stored, and never logged one per report:

  • the first time a violation is seen, the platform logs one warning line:

    CSP violation first seen: directive=img-src blocked=https://cdn.example.com document=/chat disposition=report source=https://xtm.example.com/assets/index-abc123.js

  • every five minutes, one line summarises the counts of the violations seen in that window:

    CSP violation summary: 42 violations (3 distinct) in the last 300s, 5 from browser extensions, 0 not tracked; top: img-src blocked https://cdn.example.com on /chat (report) x40; ...

Every URL is cut down before anything reads it: the query string, the fragment and any credentials are dropped (a signed download link carries its token in the query), a blocked resource is reduced to its origin (or to inline, eval, data:, blob:), a page to its path with identifiers replaced by :id.

The Prometheus counter csp_violation_reports_total{directive, disposition, origin} counts violations per directive, per disposition (report or enforce) and per origin (page, or extension when a browser extension caused it). Like the platform's other counters it is per process.

Browser extensions inject scripts and styles into the pages they run on, and those violate the policy too. They are not the platform's: they are counted under origin="extension" and in the summary, but never logged one by one.

You can also watch the browser itself: with the developer tools open, a report-only violation appears in the console as [Report Only] Refused to ....

docs.title: Deciding when to enforce
docs.text:
The security audit (Settings > Security, or GET /api/v1/security-audit) reports the policy's mode and the violations browsers reported over the last 7 days, summed across every replica:

  • off is a warning: no policy is sent at all, so framing is not restricted either.
  • report-only lists the violations of the last 7 days by directive, largest first, browser extensions counted apart. When there is none, enforcing would have blocked nothing the platform's pages loaded in that period. When Redis cannot be read, the audit says the counts are unknown, never zero.
  • enforce is a pass; a violation reported since is a load the browser blocked, which users may have hit.

Switch to enforce once the violations it lists are understood.

The audit also says who may frame the platform (see Who may frame the platform). Only an enforced policy restricts framing: a report-only one blocks no frame, and the platform never sends X-Frame-Options.

Mode CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_FRAME_ANCESTORS Finding off anything none - the off warning says framing is not restricted report-only admits every site (*, a bare scheme such as https:, https://*) web.csp_frame_ancestors_any, warning: once enforced, it would still admit every site report-only anything else, empty included web.csp_frame_ancestors_not_enforced, info: any site can frame the platform until the policy is enforced; it names who may frame it then enforce admits every site web.csp_frame_ancestors_any, warning enforce anything else, empty included web.csp_frame_ancestors_restricted, pass: it names who may frame the platform

While the policy is report-only, a page another site frames is reported as a frame-ancestors violation and counted under frame-ancestors with the other violations.

Only these counts are kept: one Redis hash per UTC day (csp:violations:<YYYYMMDD>), a number per directive, for 8 days. A Redis that does not answer within 2 seconds is read as unknown; the report is still accepted and logged.

The audit's Controls view lists both settings as security controls: web.content_security_policy (CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_MODE) and web.csp_frame_ancestors (CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_FRAME_ANCESTORS). Both read Monitoring in report-only mode, since browsers then report what the policy would block without blocking it, and Enforced once the policy is enforced; the framing control reads Off whenever an entry admits every site.

docs.title: Switching to enforce
docs.text:
1. Run in report-only for a while under normal use: the chat, presentations, reports, settings, the Desktop app if you use it, and any embedding (the Teams tab, the Office add-in, an intranet portal).
  2. Read the security audit (see Deciding when to enforce), then the CSP violation first seen log lines (browser extension violations never appear there). Each one names a resource that enforce would block on that page; if it is something the platform legitimately uses, report it rather than working around it: the policy is part of the platform and is fixed there.
  3. Set CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_MODE=enforce and restart. The pages now carry Content-Security-Policy instead of the report-only header.
  4. To roll back, set report-only again and restart. Nothing is stored; the change is immediate.

Three pages stay report-only even in enforce mode, because the platform cannot guarantee what they load: the API reference (/api/reference, which runs a pinned, integrity-checked Scalar release from its CDN whose run-time loads no test exercises), the Microsoft Teams tab and the Office add-in task pane (both run inside Microsoft hosts). They keep reporting.

One MCP client setup cannot be expressed in a policy at all: a client whose registered redirect URI is an IPv6 loopback address (http://[::1]:<port>/...), because a Content-Security-Policy has no syntax for an IPv6 address. With the policy enforced, signing in through the consent page's email and password form ends on a blocked redirect for such a client. Sign in to the web application first - the consent page then offers Authorize for the existing session - or use single sign-on: both leave the consent page by a navigation the policy does not check. Clients that use 127.0.0.1, localhost or an HTTPS redirect URI are not affected.

docs.title: The policy
docs.text:
The web application's policy:

Directive Sources Why default-src 'self' Everything else comes from the platform itself. script-src 'self' The application's own bundle. Inline scripts are allowed by their SHA-256 hash, never by 'unsafe-inline'; no eval. style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' Diagrams, the diff viewer and the branding colours use inline style elements. img-src 'self' data: blob: https: http: The chat shows images an agent links to, integration pickers show provider avatars, previews and generated images use data: and blob:. font-src 'self' data: The typefaces are bundled with the application. connect-src 'self' ipc: http://ipc.localhost wss://<host> ws://<host> The API, the chat WebSocket (named explicitly for older Safari) and the XTM One Desktop bridge. media-src 'self' blob: Text-to-speech playback. worker-src 'self' blob: The diff viewer's worker. frame-src 'self' The application frames no other site. object-src 'none' No plugins. base-uri 'self' form-action 'self' Every form is submitted by the application; single sign-on starts with a redirect, not a form. frame-ancestors see below

The other pages add what they need to it: the MCP OAuth consent page loads its typeface from Google Fonts, cannot be framed by another site, and allows its sign-in form to reach the platform's own BASE_URL and the MCP client it redirects to (browsers check that redirect against form-action too), the API reference loads Scalar from cdn.jsdelivr.net (whose bundle needs 'unsafe-eval', allowed on that page alone), the Teams tab loads the Teams SDK from res.cdn.office.net, and the Office add-in loads Office.js from appsforoffice.microsoft.com / ajax.aspnetcdn.com (which reports telemetry to Microsoft) and its typefaces from Google Fonts.

docs.title: Who may frame the platform
docs.text:
With the policy enforced, frame-ancestors decides which sites may show a page in an iframe. In report-only mode it decides nothing: the browser reports a page framed by a site the policy does not allow, but shows it, and since the platform never sends X-Frame-Options, any site can frame the platform until the policy is enforced.

Page May be framed by, once the policy is enforced The web application The platform itself, the origins listed in CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_FRAME_ANCESTORS, and - only when PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN is a value of your own, not unset and not the published default, which lets anyone register - the platforms registered with it (their registered URLs, picked up at registration, dropped as soon as a platform unregisters, is purged or moves to another origin, and re-read every five minutes). MCP OAuth consent page Only the platform itself - it is opened in a browser window, never framed. API reference Any site: the page stays report-only in every mode, so its frame-ancestors is only reported. Microsoft Teams tab, Office add-in Any site (their Microsoft hosts).

If another site embeds XTM One in an iframe, an intranet portal for example, list its origin before enforcing:

CONTENT_SECURITY_POLICY_FRAME_ANCESTORS=https://portal.example.com,https://*.intranet.example.com

The same goes for an OpenCTI or OpenAEV instance that frames XTM One while PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN is unset or the published default: a registration then proves nothing, so its origin is not trusted until you list it here. Registered platforms past the first 20 (in sorted order) are not named either, since each lengthens the header of every page; the platform logs a warning with their number, and you list the others here.

A malformed entry stops the platform at startup. An entry that admits every site - *, a bare scheme such as https:, or https://* - is accepted, but the platform logs a warning at every startup: once the policy is enforced, any such site may show the platform in an iframe, which is what frame-ancestors is there to prevent. Name the sites that embed the platform instead.

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text:
• The platform sends the headers itself; the proxy does not need to add any. If it adds its own Content-Security-Policy, the browser enforces both policies, and a request must satisfy both.
  • Do not add X-Frame-Options at the proxy: it would break the Teams and Office embeddings and any portal you declared.
  • A script the proxy or a CDN injects into the pages (an analytics snippet, Cloudflare Rocket Loader or email obfuscation) is not in the policy: it is reported in report-only mode and blocked once the policy is enforced.
  • Under BASE_PATH, the report endpoint carries the prefix automatically.

docs.title: The embeddable chat widget
docs.text: The public chat widget (/api/v1/public/widget.js) runs inside the page of the site that embeds it, not in a page of the platform, so the platform's policy does not apply to it. If that site sends its own Content-Security-Policy, it must allow what the widget loads - the XTM One origin, Google Fonts and inline styles among others: see Embedding the chat widget on a site with its own Content-Security-Policy.

docs.title: Development mode
docs.text: In development (./dev.sh, .\dev.ps1), the Vite development server serves the web application itself, so no policy is sent. The policy applies to the platform image, where the backend serves the built application.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
This page helps you diagnose common issues on a self-hosted XTM One instance. Filigran SaaS issues are handled by Filigran support.

Start every investigation with the health probes and logs described in Monitoring.

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
Before digging into a specific symptom, gather the basics:

docker compose ps                       # are all services healthy?
curl -s localhost:4000/api/health/ready # 200 = fully ready
docker compose logs platform --tail 100
docker compose logs worker --tail 100

Most startup and runtime problems surface in the platform or worker logs. Set LOG_LEVEL=debug temporarily for more detail, then revert.

docs.title: Readiness never turns green
docs.text:
If /api/health/ready keeps returning a non-200 status, the platform cannot reach one of its dependencies or migrations are still running.

  • Confirm PostgreSQL, Redis, and Silo/S3 are healthy in docker compose ps.
  • Check the connection settings (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, S3_ENDPOINT) match the running services.
  • Watch the logs for migration progress — a large existing database can take time on the first upgrade.

docs.title: Migration errors on startup
docs.text:
Migrations run automatically on startup. If startup fails inside a migration, the logs name the failing revision.

  • On a multi-replica deployment, startup migrations are serialized — a replica may wait for another to finish. This is expected.
  • Never run migrations manually against production. If a migration fails repeatedly, capture the log and see the Upgrade rollback procedure.

docs.title: Decryption or login failures after a restart
docs.text:
If integrations stop working or the admin cannot log in after a restart, SECRET_KEY most likely changed.

SECRET_KEY is permanent

SECRET_KEY encrypts every stored credential and signs sessions. If it changes, all encrypted data becomes unrecoverable and existing sessions are invalidated. Restore the original value — there is no recovery path once it is lost.

Webhook deliveries are refused while the configuration that holds their secret cannot be decrypted: an unreadable configuration may hold a secret, so a delivery is never accepted unverified. The sender gets a 503 and the backend logs an error naming the integration (Webhook delivery refused (...)) or, for LinkedIn notifications, the LinkedIn OAuth default. Restore the original SECRET_KEY or re-enter the secret; senders that retry a 5xx deliver again once it is readable. The security audit (GET /api/v1/security-audit) names the integrations and OAuth defaults concerned. It also names those whose stored webhook secret is not text (a JSON boolean, float, list or object): no sender can sign with it, so every delivery to them is refused with a 401 until the secret is re-entered as text.

Slack events are the exception: a Slack integration whose signing-secret configuration cannot be read is treated like one with no secret, so its deliveries keep being accepted without a verified signature and the logs name the configuration that cannot be read. With Require verified integration notifications on (Settings > Security, or INTEGRATION_NOTIFICATIONS_REQUIRE_VERIFICATION=true) they are answered 401 instead; do not wait for Slack to redeliver then: it retries a refused event only a few times within minutes, and until the secret is readable again the messages are polled every 5 minutes.

With that option on, the webhook URL of an OAuth default (and, for LinkedIn, the notification URL) answers 503 with Retry-After while the OAuth default's client ID cannot be decrypted (by default the delivery is handed out as before and the error is logged): no integration can then be matched to the admin app, so a delivery is refused rather than dropped. The backend logs one error naming the provider. An integration whose own client ID cannot be decrypted receives none of the admin app's deliveries until it is re-entered, and a warning names it.

docs.title: Admin cannot sign in
docs.text:
The admin account is reset to the .env values on every startup.

  • Confirm ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env, then restart to re-apply them.
  • If you changed the password in the UI, the next restart resets it back to the .env value — keep them in sync.

docs.title: Chat or streaming does not work behind a proxy
docs.text:
If chat hangs, never streams, or disconnects, the reverse proxy is usually the cause.

  • Ensure the proxy forwards the WebSocket Upgrade header.
  • Raise the proxy read timeout — LLM calls can take 60 seconds or more.
  • Forward X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For so OAuth callbacks and audit logs work, and set FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to the proxy's address so the platform honours them (Client address and protocol behind the proxy). While TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS is on, a startup warning names the same fix.

See the ingress requirements in Installation.

docs.title: The audit log shows the proxy's address for every user
docs.text:
If every entry of the Audit Logs page carries the same address - your ingress controller's, your nginx or Traefik host's, or the Compose network's gateway - the platform runs behind a reverse proxy it does not trust, so it ignores the client address the proxy sends (a client could have set it itself). The platform says so: each process logs one warning naming that address (A request carried X-Forwarded-For ..., or A request named its client in X-Real-IP ...), and the security audit (Settings → Security) reports it as "The audit trail records a proxy's address, not users'", with the value to set. That includes a proxy declared under another address than the one it connects from.

  • Set FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS in the platform container's environment to that address, or to a network covering it (the pod network on Kubernetes), and restart the platform: it is read at startup and is not a Settings > Security field.
  • Make sure the proxy sends X-Forwarded-For: the platform reads neither X-Real-IP nor Forwarded.
  • Entries recorded before the change keep the proxy's address; new ones carry each user's own.

See When the platform reports an undeclared proxy and Client address and protocol behind the proxy.

docs.title: Blank page or 404s when the platform is served under a path
docs.text:
If you expose the platform at https://host/xtm-one/ and get an empty page, the browser is loading /assets/... and /api/... from the root of the host instead of from under /xtm-one/.

  • Set BASE_PATH=/xtm-one and include the prefix in BASE_URL and FRONTEND_URL, then restart. The platform accepts the prefix whether the proxy forwards it or strips it.
  • A startup warning BASE_PATH is /xtm-one but BASE_URL (...) does not end with it (or the same for FRONTEND_URL) means OAuth callbacks, webhook URLs and post-SSO redirects will point at the wrong place until both URLs carry the prefix too.
  • The platform refuses to start with BASE_PATH ... starts with '/api' (or another platform namespace, or a static file name) or BASE_PATH may only contain ASCII letters, digits ...: pick another prefix - the refused values could not be routed unambiguously.
  • The platform refuses to start with BASE_PATH '/tools' is also the address of a platform page: behind a stripping proxy such a prefix is ambiguous. Set BASE_PATH_MODE=forwarded if your proxy keeps the prefix, or BASE_PATH_MODE=stripped if it removes it (and make it send X-Forwarded-Prefix, as Traefik's StripPrefix does and as the nginx example shows) - or pick another prefix.
  • An MCP client that cannot complete OAuth sign-in against a prefixed platform (404 on /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/xtm-one) is asking the root of the host, as RFC 8414 requires: forward /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/ and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/ to the platform as well - see MCP clients authenticating with OAuth.

See Serving under a path prefix.

docs.title: A platform is connected but every call to it fails
docs.text:
OpenCTI, OpenAEV or OpenCRQ registers, yet the assistant cannot read its data, or the platform's own calls to XTM One are refused with 401. The platform and XTM One usually reach each other on internal URLs that differ from the ones your users browse (in Docker, http://opencti:8080 and http://xtm-one:4000 instead of http://localhost:...).

  • Set OPENCTI_API_URL / OPENAEV_API_URL / OPENCRQ_API_URL on XTM One to the URL it reaches the platform on, and leave the platform registering with its public URL: XTM One fetches the platform's keys and calls its API on the internal URL, and keeps addressing its tokens, and every link it gives your users, to the public one. The change applies at the platform's next registration, a few minutes later.
  • Set BASE_URL on the XTM One worker to the same value as on the platform container: the worker signs the tokens of background work.
  • The XTM One log names the refusal: Untrusted JWT issuer means the platform signs with a URL other than the one it registered with; Failed to resolve signing key for <platform> from <url> means XTM One cannot reach that URL; audience mismatch (this platform accepts ...) means the platform addresses its tokens to another URL than BASE_URL.
  • For an audience mismatch, upgrade the platform to a version that reads GET /xtm/auth/metadata, or accept the URL it addresses with XTM_AUTH_ACCEPTED_AUDIENCES (see Public and internal URLs).

docs.title: Agents give no answer or fail immediately
docs.text:
• Confirm at least one AI provider is configured under Settings → AI Models with a valid API key.
  • Check outbound HTTPS access from the platform (and worker) containers to your AI provider. Air-gapped deployments must use a local provider such as Ollama.
  • Check your quota. If the agentic execution quota is exhausted, chat is refused with "You have reached your agentic execution quota for the current period" and assignment runs fail with a Quota exceeded error. Users see their usage in My Profile → Quotas; admins manage limits and per-user overrides in Settings → Quotas. Wait for the period to reset or raise the limit.
  • Inspect the run in Traces or the agent's Activity tab to see which tool or model call failed.

docs.title: Assignments do not run
docs.text:
Assignments and their delays are driven by the worker's orchestration reconciler and the platform's scheduler.

  • Confirm the worker container is running and not crash-looping.
  • Confirm Redis is reachable — the task queue and scheduling rely on it.
  • Check the run's quota. A run whose owner is over the agentic quota is marked failed with a Quota exceeded error rather than executing — verify usage in Settings → Quotas.
  • A run stuck for a long time is swept and marked failed automatically; re-trigger it after fixing the underlying cause.

docs.title: Real-time Slack, Microsoft Graph or LinkedIn events do not arrive
docs.text:
By default nothing is refused that was accepted before: a delivery the platform cannot verify is still accepted, with a warning in the log and a Security Audit finding. Refusals come from a stored secret that does not prove a delivery, or from the Require verified integration notifications option (Settings > Security, or INTEGRATION_NOTIFICATIONS_REQUIRE_VERIFICATION). To go back to the previous behaviour at once, turn the option off (or unset the variable and restart, when it is set); every process applies the change within seconds.

  • Slack answers 401 Invalid Slack signature (Slack shows the delivery as failed, and the Request URL check fails): the option is on and no Signing Secret is stored for the app that sent it, or the stored secret is not that app's current Signing Secret (rotated in Slack, or another app). Copy the Signing Secret from the Slack app's Basic Information into the integration's Signing secret field, or into the Slack OAuth default's for integrations on the administrator's app. Then re-enable the app's Event Subscriptions if Slack turned them off.
  • The log says Slack delivery ... accepted without a verified signature: expected by default while no Signing Secret is stored for the app. Store it to verify that app's events.
  • Slack answers 200 but an assignment does not run in real time once a Signing Secret is stored: a verified event reaches only the integrations of the workspace it was sent for, and a message outside a public channel only the integration of its author or of the user Slack authorized the event for. An assignment connected only to integrations whose Signing Secret is stored does not receive a delivery that secret does not prove (another Slack app, for example). The poller still delivers, within 5 minutes, what the integration's own token can read.
  • The log says Graph change notification discarded: the notification does not echo the clientState of its subscription, or that clientState cannot be decrypted. With the option on, a subscription record holding only the assignment id is discarded too: recreate the subscription so it is stored with a clientState.
  • LinkedIn answers 401 Invalid LinkedIn signature: the notification is not signed with the LinkedIn OAuth default's client secret, as before this release. 503 means that secret cannot be decrypted: restore the SECRET_KEY or re-enter it. With the option on and no LinkedIn client secret configured, notifications are answered 200 but trigger nothing: configure the LinkedIn app in Settings > OAuth defaults.
  • An admin OAuth app webhook (/api/hooks/providers/<provider>) no longer reaches an assignment with the option on: its agent has no integration created on that app that its owner may use (or, for a GitHub App, none recording the delivery's installation). While the option is off, the log reports (at most every 15 minutes) the deliveries that reached an assignment it would leave out, so they can be checked before turning it on.

docs.title: Knowledge base uploads fail
docs.text:
• Large uploads need a permissive proxy body-size limit (client_max_body_size 50m; in Nginx).
  • Confirm the S3 / Silo credentials and bucket are correct and the endpoint is reachable from both the platform and worker.

docs.title: PostgreSQL connection errors under load
docs.text: Errors about too many connections mean the pool budget exceeds PG_MAX_CONNECTIONS. Recalculate using the formula in Configuration, accounting for every web worker and every scaled worker container.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
When opening an issue or asking the community, include:

  • the platform version (shown in the UI and container image tag)
  • relevant platform and worker log excerpts (with secrets redacted)
  • the output of docker compose ps and /api/health/ready

Community support

For questions the documentation does not answer, join the Filigran Community on Slack or open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Review the Upgrade procedure before your next version bump, and keep Monitoring alerts in place to catch issues early.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text: This page covers the upgrade and rollback procedures for a self-hosted XTM One instance. Filigran SaaS instances are upgraded by Filigran.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Read the release notes.
  2. Apply the update based on your deployment option:

Pre-built images (Option B):

docker compose pull
docker compose up -d

Source-based (Option A):

git fetch --tags
git checkout <new-version-tag>
docker compose build --pull
docker compose up -d

Migrations run automatically on startup. Wait for /api/health/ready to return 200 before verifying.

Image tags follow the format <major>.<YYMMDD>.<patch> and are listed on Docker Hub.

docs.title: Deprecated environment variables
docs.text:
Environment variables renamed by a release keep working under their old name for a while, so an upgrade does not silently change what your deployment does. While an old name is in use, XTM One logs a warning naming the replacement. Rename them in your compose files, Helm values and CI secrets before the removal date.

Old name New name Read until Notes OPENGRC_API_URL OPENCRQ_API_URL 2026-12-31 Renamed with the OpenGRC -> OpenCRQ product rename. When both are set, OPENCRQ_API_URL wins. See Network reachability.

docs.title: Platform registration token (Docker Compose)
docs.text:
This note applies when PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN is not set in your .env, or is set to xtm-default-registration-token: Docker Compose then runs XTM One with that published default, which authenticates nobody. After upgrading such a deployment:

  • The OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ platforms already registered keep their heartbeat, but the published default can no longer register a new platform, change the URL of a registered one, rename one or unregister one: a registered platform's URL is trusted to sign XTM One users in, and its name is what the agents bound to it read. Nor does its heartbeat change the intents and business vertical a platform declares (those of an upgraded platform are recorded once you set your own token), or replace a platform's license with anything but its renewal.
  • The XTM One license certificate is no longer sent to the connected platforms, so a platform whose Enterprise Edition comes from your XTM One license (a sub-license) cannot prove it. The registration answer says why: xtm_license_withheld_reason: registration_token_published_default.

To leave the published default:

  1. Generate a token: python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))".
  2. Set it as PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN in the .env of XTM One, and set the same value as the registration token of every connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ platform. A platform still presenting the old value is refused.
  3. Restart XTM One (docker compose up -d) and the platforms.
  4. Check the security audit (Settings → Security, or GET /api/v1/security-audit): the platform registration token finding now reads pass. Then review the registered platforms and purge any you do not recognise: earlier releases let anyone holding the published default register one, and changing the token does not end the trust a registration carries. The integration catalog in Settings lists the OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ registrations; the security audit names any registration under another identifier with its id, which DELETE /api/v1/platform/registrations/{id}/purge removes.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
Warning

Migrations run automatically on startup and may alter the database schema. Once a migration has run, the previous application version may not work against the new schema. Rollback requires restoring the database and object storage from the same pre-upgrade recovery point.

  1. docker compose down
  2. Restore the database from the pre-upgrade backup.
  3. Restore Silo/S3 to the same recovery point.
  4. Revert image tags to the previous version.
  5. docker compose up -d

docs.title: XTM Suite integration
docs.text:
XTM One is the AI layer of the Filigran XTM Suite. This page covers the technical wiring that connects XTM One to the other Suite products — OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ — from a deployment and operations point of view.

For the end-user experience of these features, see XTM One in the XTM Suite. For connecting external MCP clients, see Platform MCP servers.

docs.title: How the products connect
docs.text:
Each Suite platform registers itself with XTM One. Once registered, the platform can surface the embedded "Ask AI" experience, and XTM One can call back into the platform on behalf of the requesting user.

flowchart LR
    subgraph suite["Other XTM Suite products"]
        direction TB
        octi["OpenCTI"]
        oaev["OpenAEV"]
        ogrc["OpenCRQ"]
    end

    xtmone["XTM One"]
    client["External MCP client<br/>Cursor, Claude, ..."]

    suite -->|"1 · Registers"| xtmone
    suite -->|"2 · Embeds assistant"| xtmone
    xtmone -->|"3 · Reads & updates data"| suite
    client -->|"4 · Uses tools via MCP"| xtmone

The diagram shows four ways XTM One and the Suite products work together:

  1. Registration — each platform registers with XTM One at POST /api/v1/platform/register, authorized by the shared PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN (see below). This one-time handshake enables everything else.
  2. Embedded AI assistant — once registered, OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ surface an in-product AI assistant. The platform streams each request to XTM One over HTTP with Server-Sent Events (/api/v1/platform/chat). The assistant panel also reads the signed-in user's usage quota (GET /api/v1/platform/chat/quota, null on Community Edition), lists their chat prompts (GET /api/v1/platform/chat/prompts) and records their rating of an answer (POST / DELETE /api/v1/platform/chat/conversations/{conversation_id}/messages/{message_id}/feedback), all as that user, like the chat itself.
  3. Reads & updates platform data — to answer, XTM One calls the platform's own GraphQL / REST API. Every call runs as the signed-in user: XTM One signs a short-lived per-user token that the platform verifies against XTM One's public keys at GET /xtm/auth/jwks, so each user's permissions and audit trail apply exactly as if they acted directly (see Acting as the user).
  4. Platform tools over MCP — connecting a platform also exposes its native tools to external MCP clients (Cursor, Claude, custom agents) through XTM One at /mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, and /mcp/opencrq. This is a separate capability from the in-product assistant — see Platform MCP servers.

Registration is authorized by a shared token:

Variable Where it is set Purpose PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN XTM One and each Suite platform Shared secret authorizing a platform to register. Must be identical across all services.

Use the same token everywhere

Every product that registers with XTM One must use the exact same PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN. Set a strong shared secret before connecting production instances, for example the output of python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))".

  • Unset: registration is disabled. Every registration request is refused with a message naming the variable to set.
  • The published default xtm-default-registration-token (the docker-compose.yml fallback): accepted only so the platforms already registered with it stay connected. It cannot register a new platform, change a registered platform's URL, rename one or unregister one: a registered platform's URL is trusted to sign XTM One users in, and its name is what the agents bound to it read, so a token everyone knows must never choose either. Nor can it change the intents and business vertical a platform declares, or clear, downgrade or swap a connected platform's license: only a renewal that XTM One validates - a newer license issued to the same customer and instance - replaces the one registered. XTM One logs a warning at startup and the security audit (Settings → Security) reports a critical finding until you replace it on XTM One and on every platform. Meanwhile the license certificate described below is withheld, so a platform sub-licensed by your XTM One license cannot prove its Enterprise Edition; the registration answer says why (xtm_license_withheld_reason: registration_token_published_default), so the platform can point you to this setting.
  • Failed attempts: after 10 failed attempts in a minute, a client is refused with HTTP 429 until the minute ends, whatever token it presents. A call the published default may not make counts as a failed attempt.

The registration answer can carry your XTM One license

When your XTM One license is what puts a platform in Enterprise Edition (it sub-licenses that platform, or every platform of its type), the registration answer carries the license certificate itself, so the platform can verify its entitlement against Filigran's certificate authority instead of taking XTM One's word for it. That certificate is a license: whoever obtains it can use it until it expires. XTM One sends it only to a caller that presents the registration token, and only in that case, and it refuses every registration while PLATFORM_REGISTRATION_TOKEN is unset - so treat the token like the license itself: a strong secret, shared only with the platforms you connect, never the placeholder.

Once a platform is registered, its native capabilities become available automatically — including the platform MCP servers (/mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, /mcp/opencrq), which activate as soon as the corresponding platform is connected.

Under construction

The exact registration procedure on the OpenCTI / OpenAEV / OpenCRQ side (which settings to fill, in which UI or configuration file, and how to verify a successful registration from XTM One) is being documented and will be added here.

docs.title: Network reachability
docs.text:
XTM One calls the registered platform's API when an agent works with its data. By default it uses the public platform_url supplied during registration.

For deployments where XTM One and the platforms share an internal network, you can override the API URL XTM One calls:

Variable Effect OPENCTI_API_URL Call the OpenCTI API, fetch its signing keys and send its callbacks on this internal URL instead of the registered public URL OPENAEV_API_URL Same, for OpenAEV OPENCRQ_API_URL Same, for OpenCRQ. The pre-rename name OPENGRC_API_URL is still read, with a deprecation warning in the logs, until 2026-12-31 - see Upgrade

Links stay on the public URL

The override is only where XTM One calls the platform. Every link a person is given - the "Open in ..." links of the platform tools, the platform URL the agents build their links from, the links in their answers, trigger.platform_url in an assignment prompt - is on the registered public URL, the one a browser reaches. A link the agent writes on the internal URL (from a conversation older than the upgrade, for example) is shown on the public URL too, except inside code blocks, which are left as written. With URL_GUARD_ENABLED=false the answers are left as written.

docs.title: Public and internal URLs
docs.text:
In Docker Compose or Kubernetes, each product usually has two URLs: the public one your users open in their browser (http://localhost:8080), and the internal one the other containers reach it on (http://opencti:8080). The signed calls between the products use them for different things:

  • The public URL is the product's identity. It is BASE_URL for XTM One and the base URL a platform registers with (for OpenCTI, APP__BASE_URL). Every token a product signs names it as the issuer, and every token sent to a product must be addressed to it.
  • The internal URL is only where the other side connects: the platform's API, its signing keys and, for OpenAEV, the autonomous run callbacks. No link a person is given is ever on it.

On the XTM One side, the internal URL of a platform is the *_API_URL override above, recorded at the platform's next registration (its heartbeat, every few minutes). On the platform side, it is the XTM One URL the platform is configured with (XTM__XTM_ONE_URL for OpenCTI, OPENAEV_XTM_ONE_URL for OpenAEV): the platform reads XTM One's public identity from GET /xtm/auth/metadata on that URL.

Two settings keep the signed calls working when the URLs differ:

Variable Where Purpose BASE_URL XTM One and its worker The worker signs the tokens of background work (assignments, delegated tasks, autonomous runs). Without it, those tokens carry a default issuer the platforms refuse. Set it to the same value on both containers. XTM_AUTH_ACCEPTED_AUDIENCES XTM One Comma-separated URLs the platforms reach XTM One on when they differ from BASE_URL, for example http://xtm-one:4000. Platform versions that do not read /xtm/auth/metadata address their tokens to that URL, and XTM One refuses them unless it is listed here.

If the embedded assistant answers but every action on the platform's data fails with 401, check the XTM One logs for XTM JWT rejected: the message names the issuer, the audience or the key URL that did not match.

docs.title: Acting as the user
docs.text:
When a Suite platform calls XTM One (or when a request from XTM One calls back into a platform), the action runs as the requesting user, not as a shared service account.

XTM One signs a short-lived, per-user token that the platform verifies, and verifies the platform's tokens the same way. Each product signs its tokens for 10 minutes; XTM One refuses a platform token that carries no expiry or is signed to live longer than 15 minutes, and tolerates up to 60 seconds of clock difference between the products. Keep their clocks synchronised (NTP): a token from a clock more than 60 seconds ahead is refused. Users are matched by email between the two products, so each user's platform permissions, data markings, and audit trail apply exactly as if they acted directly. Platform API tokens are never stored in or proxied through XTM One.

The public keys used to verify these tokens are served from XTM One:

Endpoint Purpose GET /xtm/auth/jwks Public JWKS keys for verifying XTM One's cross-platform tokens (unauthenticated, public) GET /xtm/auth/metadata The issuer XTM One's tokens carry, the audience it expects (both its public BASE_URL, whichever URL you reach it on), its jwks_uri and signing algorithm (unauthenticated, public)

Under construction

The cross-platform token verification setup on the platform side — including how each platform is configured to trust XTM One's JWKS endpoint and how key rotation is handled — is being documented and will be added here.

docs.title: Verifying the integration
docs.text:
After registering a platform, confirm the connection from XTM One:

  • The platform MCP server for that product reports Connected in My Profile → MCP Endpoint (and in Settings → MCP Endpoint for admins).
  • The embedded "Ask AI" experience appears inside the registered product.

If a platform shows as not connected, see the platform MCP troubleshooting table and the general Troubleshooting page.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Review Data flow to understand how cross-product requests are processed, and AI governance for what is shared with AI providers.

docs.title: Run budgets
docs.text:
A run budget caps what one run costs. A run is a single piece of agent work: one chat turn, or one assignment execution. The budget bounds it along four dimensions at once — money, tokens, tool calls and wall-clock time — and stops the run when any of them is reached.

Budgets exist because the natural limits are the wrong shape. Max iterations counts tool-calling rounds, and a single round can fan out into a dozen parallel tool calls. A model change can multiply the cost of the same work without changing anything you configured. A budget measures what you actually care about instead.

docs.title: Where a budget is configured
docs.text:
There are two places, from broadest to narrowest.

The platform, set by an administrator in the deployment's environment. This is the default every run inherits and, just as importantly, the ceiling nobody else can raise. See Agent run budget for the settings themselves.

One agent, on its Budget tab. This is where you say "this research agent may spend more than the platform default" or "this triage bot must never spend more than a few cents". It applies wherever that agent runs.

docs.title: The agent's Budget tab
docs.text:
Open an agent and choose Budget. Each of the four limits is a single field, and an empty field means "inherit", not "zero". The placeholder tells you what it would inherit, so you can see the effective budget without saving anything.

That distinction is the whole point of leaving fields empty. A budget that only pins the cost keeps tracking the platform's token, tool-call and time limits — including any later change an administrator makes to them. Typing the inherited numbers in to "be explicit" freezes a copy that silently stops following the platform.

Use the Inherit link next to a field to hand a dimension back.

docs.title: Who may raise a limit
docs.text:
Anyone who can edit an agent may lower any limit. Spending less is never a privilege.

Raising a limit above the platform budget requires an administrator. That is what the platform setting is for: it is the budget a user cannot exceed on their own. If you are not an admin, the tab says so up front, and a field you push above the ceiling is flagged with the platform's value before you attempt to save — you will not discover it as a rejected save.

If your agent genuinely needs a larger budget than the platform allows, ask an administrator to set it. Once they have, the value stays: you can keep editing everything else about the agent without the budget being questioned again, and without being able to raise it further yourself.

Three settings that need no admin

The final-answer reserve, the cheaper-model failsafe and the choice of fallback model are not gated, because none of them can increase what a run spends. The reserve only moves the in-run limit down, and the failsafe keeps the same cost ceiling — it just buys more work under it.

docs.title: The final-answer reserve
docs.text:
A run that spends its entire budget on work has nothing left to pay for the call that turns that work into an answer, so it would return a raw digest of tool output instead of a written result.

The reserve prevents that: a slice of the cost and token ceilings is held back for the closing answer. Work is gated at the remainder; the final answer may spend the full budget. The platform default is 10%, which comfortably covers one closing call.

docs.title: Finishing on a cheaper model instead of stopping
docs.text:
A cost ceiling of, say, $0.50 on an expensive model usually means "don't spend more than $0.50 at this quality" — not "abandon the task". The same $0.50 buys several times more work on a cheaper model.

Turn on Finish on a cheaper model and a run that reaches its cost ceiling switches to a cheaper model and carries on instead of stopping. The rest of the run, including its closing answer, is charged at that model's rates, so the ceiling still holds. The agent is told the switch happened, and the run's trace records it, so cost attribution stays readable per call.

Deliberately bounded:

  • Once per run. Never a ladder that limps along on progressively worse models.
  • Cost only. Tokens, tool calls and time are model-independent — a cheaper model buys no extra wall clock.

Fallback model chooses which model that is. Left on Platform fallback model, it uses the one configured in Settings > AI Models > Fallback Model — the same model the platform already falls back to when a provider fails, so there is one cheaper model to reason about rather than two.

The switch is refused — and the run stops at its ceiling instead — when it could not be made safely: when no pricing is known for the fallback (with no price there is no way to know the next call is actually cheaper), when the fallback's context window cannot hold the agent's system prompt, or when switching would silently drop a structured-output guarantee the run depends on. In each case stopping is the honest outcome; failing mid-run is not.

docs.title: How the layers resolve
docs.text:
Nearest wins, dimension by dimension. For any agent step, each limit is taken from the first layer that pins it:

  1. the agent's own Budget tab,
  2. the platform.

Per-dimension is what makes partial budgets safe. A tab that pins only the cost does not unbound the token limit — the platform's still applies. Worked through:

Cost Tokens Agent's Budget tab $2.00 (not set) Platform $5.00 1,000,000 Effective $2.00 1,000,000

docs.title: A budget you did not type yourself
docs.text:
Who may raise a limit governs every way a budget can reach your account, not just a value you type into the tab. Which of two things happens depends on whether you chose the number:

  • you typed it — editing an agent: the save is refused, naming the dimension and the platform's value, so you know exactly what to change;
  • you copied it — duplicating an agent, importing one, restoring an older version: the action goes through and any limit above the platform ceiling arrives lowered to that ceiling. Blocking a duplicate over a number somebody else typed would get in the way of the ordinary "copy the company agent and adapt it" workflow, and lowering it prevents the same escalation.

Either way you cannot end up holding a budget an administrator did not grant. An admin's copy keeps its values, since they could have typed them.

docs.title: What happens when a budget runs out
docs.text:
The run stops making model calls and writes its final answer from the work it completed, using the reserve. The answer says which limit was reached, so the outcome is a shorter result rather than a failure with nothing to show.

Time is the exception in one respect: the duration limit is folded into the run's existing deadline, and whichever bound is tighter applies.

docs.title: When a budget does not apply
docs.text:
Cost needs pricing. The cost ceiling is enforced from the platform's model price table, which is seeded for known models. If no price is known for the model a run uses, cost is not enforced for that run — a warning is logged and the token, tool-call and time limits still apply. Missing pricing data must never be able to stop every run on the platform.

Platform limits bound autonomous work. The platform's own settings apply to assignment runs. A budget you configure on an agent applies wherever that agent runs, chat included — configuring a budget is an explicit act, so it takes effect everywhere.

A budget smaller than one call

A model call the remaining budget cannot cover at the model's full maximum output is made with a lower maximum output, sized to what is left. A limit below the cost or tokens of a single call even with its maximum output lowered to 1,024 tokens makes every run stop immediately and return a summary of tool output. The platform logs an explicit warning at the start of such a run. Raise the budget.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Read Agentic flow for how agents hand work to each other, or Agents for the other tabs on an agent's detail page.

docs.title: Agentic flow
docs.text: Agentic Flow is the global handover graph opened from the main sidebar. It helps you understand how agents cooperate.

docs.title: What Agentic Flow is for
docs.text:
Use this view when you want to:

  • understand how one agent hands work to another
  • see the structure behind a shared workflow
  • inspect the path a task can follow
  • review or adjust that structure, if you are allowed to edit it

docs.title: Understand the handover types
docs.text:
The graph uses named connection types between agents.

  • Delegate sends work to another agent in the background.
  • Consult asks another agent for help and returns to the original agent.
  • Transfer moves the conversation to another agent.
  • Mandatory transfer forces the conversation to continue with another agent.

These labels matter because they change how the user experience behaves in chat and in automation.

An agent whose handover agents have no type yet (configured before handover types existed, or through the API without types) shows each of them as All types: it can delegate to, consult or transfer to each one. Types are set per agent, so giving one of them a type, on the agent's configuration page or on this graph, gives every one of them a type: the others become Delegate, and you are shown which ones and asked to confirm first. Saving the agent's handovers without picking a type keeps them All types, and so does adding a handover agent next to them. Once the handover agents have types, removing the only typed one, or deleting that agent, leaves the others Delegate: they never switch back to All types on their own.

docs.title: The global Agentic Flow page
docs.text:
Choose Agentic Flow from the left sidebar to open the platform-wide graph.

This page shows:

  • all visible agents in one graph
  • the handover links between them
  • a warning that changes affect global behavior
  • a focus field so you can isolate one or more agents
  • a graph you can pan and zoom

docs.title: Use the focus field
docs.text:
Large graphs are easier to read when you focus on a few agents.

Use the focus field to:

  • highlight one agent
  • compare a few related agents
  • reduce visual noise in a large environment

You can add and remove focused agents directly from the filter area.

docs.title: Open an agent from the graph
docs.text:
You can open an agent directly from the global graph.

This is useful when you want to move from a visual connection view to the full agent detail page.

docs.title: Editing the global graph
docs.text:
If your role allows it, the global graph is not only a viewer. It can also be an editing surface.

Authorized users may be able to:

  • create a new handover between two agents
  • change the type of an existing handover
  • remove a handover

Because these are global relationships, a change here affects all users who rely on that agent behavior.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter explains Work History, where you review runs, waiting items, notifications, and execution details.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text: Agents are the main assistants in XTM One. Each one is configured for a particular role, team, or workflow.

docs.title: What an agent is for
docs.text: Use an agent when you want a more focused assistant than the General Assistant. An agent can answer questions in a specific domain, use selected tools and integrations, search one or more knowledge bases, hand work to other agents, and run background tasks automatically.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text:
Choose Agents from the left sidebar to open the list. You can browse all visible agents, search, filter by visibility or tag, import an agent from a file, and — if your role allows it — create a new one. Each card is a quick summary: the agent's status, what is attached to it, and whether it is company-managed or shared. Some cards also offer quick actions such as opening a chat or enabling and disabling the agent.

Click the star on an agent's card or row to make it a favorite. Favorites are pinned to the top of the list in both views, above everything else and whichever column you sort by, so the two or three agents you actually work with stay one glance away in a long fleet. The choice is yours alone — it is stored on your account, follows you to any browser, and changes nothing for anyone else. Click the star again to remove it. Filters still come first: a favorite that does not match your search or tag filter is not shown.

The toggle at the right of the filter row switches between the card grid and a sortable list. The list view is the better choice once you manage more than a handful of agents: it puts status, model, assignment count, and attached resources in sortable columns so you can answer questions like "which agents run which model?" by scanning one column. See grid and list views for how sorting and persistence work.

Not every visible agent is editable. Company-managed agents are shared broadly and often read-only for standard users, shared agents come from a group or another owner, and built-in agents are typically read-only. If you open an agent and cannot change it, the page is behaving as designed for your access level.

Connecting a resource to an agent or to one of its assignments (an MCP server, an integration or a channel bot) is limited to the ones you can see yourself, and a save that adds another one is refused; what the agent or the assignment already names stays in place when you save, whoever connected it. An agent shared with you runs with what its owner connected to it - their MCP servers, custom tools, knowledge bases, channel bots and integrations - in its assignment runs, and in your chats too with one exception, integrations: in a chat, an integration you cannot see, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with you, is not used for you (see Sharing an OAuth integration). Your own or a company-wide integration of the same service takes its place when the agent resolves one for you; otherwise a note under the answer names the integration (by its service only when it is not shared with you) and says why, and the agent is told too, so it can say what it cannot do.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text:
Click an agent card to open its detail page. The header gives you direct actions — Chat with Agent, Duplicate, Export, enable or disable, and delete when you can manage the agent. If the agent is designed mainly for assignments, the chat button still works but XTM One warns that it is not optimized for conversation.

The page is organized into tabs (some appear only when your role can see them):

  • Overview is the best first stop: a quick understanding of what the agent does and what is attached to it, without reading the full configuration.
  • Configuration is how the agent is set up — persona and instructions, tools and integrations, knowledge and memory, handovers, channels, and intent bindings. For most users this is a reading page; editing is usually reserved for admins. The Intent Bindings card is what makes the agent available inside OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ; see Intents. A built-in tool the agent carries but this deployment has switched off (the code interpreter, Runners, a feature not enabled here) is shown greyed as Unavailable: it does nothing until an administrator enables it, and while editing you can remove it from the agent, not add it. On a company-managed agent that carries Work Items or Shared State, the same card holds its Coordination access: which agents can read and change the company-managed work items it creates and the shared state it owns (see Work history).
  • Budget caps what one run of the agent may spend — money, tokens, tool calls or time — and can let a run that reaches its cost ceiling finish on a cheaper model instead of stopping. Lowering a limit is open to anyone who can edit the agent; raising one above the platform's own budget is an administrator's decision. See Run budgets.
  • Versioning lists every version of the persona and of the tracked settings, to compare them and roll back. It also holds the agent's persona rewrites (see below).
  • Memory shows the agent's longer-term memory, where authorized users can search it, review its health, and run maintenance.
  • Chats shows conversations associated with the agent, to review or reopen context.
  • Delegations shows work the agent sent to or received from other agents, useful for understanding how handovers behaved.
  • Feedback gathers every thumbs up and thumbs down given to the agent's work — its chat answers, its assignment runs, its background tasks and the answers it gave when another agent consulted it — with the comments people left, filterable by kind of work and by rating. When feedback criteria are defined (Settings > Quality), it also shows the agent's weighted score and, per criterion, the average, the distribution and the last 30 days. It is shown to the people who can manage the agent.
  • Activity is the agent's run history — review recent executions and spot failures.

docs.title: What an assignment or a roster may name
docs.text:
