An assignment whose trigger listens to an integration reads that integration's events with its credentials, so when you save it, the integration it names must be one you can see: yours, one shared with you or one of your groups, or a company-wide one. Admins may name any. Otherwise the save is refused with the same answer whether the integration exists or not. Editing anything else, or saving the trigger again with the integration it already names, is never refused, even if that integration is no longer visible to you. The agent builder tools apply the same rule; when strict admin access for agent tools is on, an administrator's agent may name only the integrations the administrator sees as their own, shared with them or company-wide.

An agent you create from a template gets the template's assignments. A template trigger that names an integration you cannot see is created without it, and then listens to the new agent's own integration of that provider.

The agents you let an agent hand work items to (the Work Items tool's roster) follow the same rule: you can add only agents you can see (admins may add any), and the ones already in the roster stay when you save.

docs.title: Improve the persona
docs.text:
An administrator can ask for a rewrite of an agent's persona from its Versioning tab (Ask for a rewrite), measured against one of the evaluations the agent is part of (evaluations, and so this button, are not offered in XTM One mode). The agent's latest completed run of that evaluation is the baseline, so it must have measured the persona the agent has now; if it has not been run yet, run it first. The rewrite is written from that run's lowest-scoring cases and from the feedback people gave on the agent's work. Only the persona is rewritten, never a skill, and with targeted changes: a rewrite that would grow the persona by more than half (or by more than 2,000 characters, for a short one) is refused, and a persona of more than 20,000 characters is not rewritten. The rewrites are shown to the people who can manage the agent.

Nothing changes until someone who may manage the agent approves it: an administrator for a company-managed agent, and for a private agent its owner or someone it is shared with for configuration (an administrator's access alone is not enough). Approving shows the changes line by line; Apply makes the rewrite the active persona as a new version and runs the evaluation again for this agent, on the same model.

When that run ends, the two quality scores are compared (the evaluation's judge score, or its F1 score, never the overall score with speed). A drop of more than 2 points rolls the persona back to what it was, again as a new version; anything within 2 points keeps the rewrite. If someone edited the persona after the rewrite was applied, their edit is kept and the verdict is only reported. Every step is in the version history and the audit log, so any of them can be undone by hand.

docs.title: Duplicate and export
docs.text:
Two header actions are easy to overlook. Duplicate creates a private copy you can adapt without changing the original, and Export downloads the agent so it can be stored, shared, or imported elsewhere. This is especially helpful when your organization uses standard company-managed agents but you need a private variation.

The copy is yours, so it keeps only what you could connect to an agent of your own. When you copy an agent someone else owns, the integrations, MCP servers, knowledge bases, custom tools, skills, prompts, handover agents, work-item owner agents and channel bots you cannot use are left out, in the copied assignments too, and the confirmation says how many of each kind were left out and why (the warnings of the duplicate response). Everything you can use is copied as it is, a personal OAuth integration shared with you included. Whoever copies, an assignment trigger that listens to an integration you cannot see loses it: the copied trigger then listens to the copy's own integration of that provider. The original agent is not changed: it keeps running with everything its owner connected. Copied assignments start disabled.

Export asks which format you want. The XTM One native bundle (default, JSON) carries everything — assignments, handover routing, memory settings, prompts, skills and variables — so use it for backups and for moving an agent between XTM One instances. Microsoft AgentSchema (YAML) is an open, cross-vendor agent definition that other agent platforms can read, and only what that specification can express goes into its standard fields.

Choosing AgentSchema shows you exactly which of your agent's settings will not be included as standard fields — handover, memory tiers, assignments, integration bindings, prompts and skills among them — before the file is created. Nothing on that list is thrown away: it is preserved in an XTM One section of the document's metadata, so re-importing the same file into XTM One restores everything, while other platforms ignore that section.

Exporting everything is for the people who can manage the agent: its owner, someone it is shared with for configuration, and administrators. If you can see an agent but not manage it, such as a company-managed agent or one shared with you as read-only, Export gives you what its AI Catalog download carries instead, in either format. A credential passed to an MCP server as an argument or in its URL is masked. Custom tools that are not company-managed are left out, unless the agent is published with its personal tools included. A company-managed tool, MCP server, skill or prompt restricted to a group you are not in is left out too, and variables come without their values. The file still imports: re-enter the masked values and fill in the variables afterwards.

docs.title: Importing an agent
docs.text:
You do not have to say what kind of file you are uploading. The platform reads the file, works out whether it is an XTM One bundle or an AgentSchema document, checks it against that format's rules, and only then creates the agent. Both JSON and YAML are accepted.

After a successful import you are told which format was detected, along with anything the platform had to assume about your file or could not resolve here. A tool declared in an AgentSchema document arrives without its code, because the specification describes what a tool takes rather than how it works, so you need to fill in the implementation before enabling it. An MCP server arrives as a placeholder, since no server address or credentials travel in the document. A knowledge base or file-search source may be referenced but not included, in which case you bind the agent to a knowledge base on this instance to restore retrieval.

If the file is neither format, fails its format's rules, or is an AgentSchema document describing a hosted or workflow agent — kinds XTM One has no equivalent for — the import is refused and the reason names the specific fields or rules that failed. Nothing is created in that case.

Whichever format you import from, integration bindings, knowledge bases and links to other agents are not imported: they belong to the instance the agent came from. Imported assignments always start disabled so nothing runs before you have reviewed it.

An assignment limited to some of the agent's MCP servers keeps that limit. A server included in the file is mapped onto the copy the import creates, and a server outside the file is kept only if you can already use it on this instance; any other server is removed from the assignment's scope and the import says so. An assignment left with none of its servers runs without MCP tools rather than with every server of the agent.

An assignment's integration setting is never widened on the way in. An assignment set to use no integrations imports the same way, and one limited to specific integrations imports with no integrations at all, because those integrations do not exist here: the import report names it so you can re-select them. An assignment that uses all of the agent's integrations keeps doing so, as does any assignment from a file exported before this setting was carried.

An assignment whose trigger listens to an integration keeps it only if you can already see that integration on this instance (an admin keeps any that exists here). Otherwise the integration is removed from the trigger and the import names the assignment, so you can pick one of your integrations before enabling it.

docs.title: Exposing an agent on a messaging platform
docs.text:
An agent answers in web chat by default and nowhere else. To let it work in Slack, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, or Google Chat, enable the channel in Configuration > Channels & Bots, where you choose whether the agent receives messages, publishes messages, or both, and on which channels.

The bot itself is connected once by an administrator. See Channels and bots for the platform setup and the rules that govern mentions, direct messages, and anonymous users.

docs.title: When an agent is disabled
docs.text: A disabled agent stays visible but does not behave like an active one: it looks dimmed in the list, chat is limited, and assignments do not run normally. If an agent you expected to use is disabled, contact the person who manages that workflow.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter explains Agentic Flow, which shows how agents connect to one another.

docs.title: AI catalog
docs.text:
The AI Catalog is where you browse published AI resources and add them to your account.

It helps you start faster by reusing ready-made content instead of building everything from scratch.

docs.title: What you can find here
docs.text:
The catalog is organized into these sections:

  • Agents
  • Skills
  • Prompts
  • MCP Servers
  • Tools, including custom tools

You can browse all resources together or open one category at a time.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Use search to find a resource by name or description.

This is useful when the catalog grows and you want to quickly narrow down what you need.

docs.title: Resource cards
docs.text:
Each card shows a short summary of the resource.

You can usually see:

  • the resource name
  • a short description
  • tags
  • who shared it
  • basic counts or status information

docs.title: Add to my account
docs.text:
Open a resource to see its details, then add it to your account.

The detail page lets you:

  • review the content before adding it
  • copy the resource URL when available
  • download the JSON definition
  • add the resource to your account

For agents, you may also see an install step that asks for a name and any setup choices that are needed before the resource is added.

docs.title: What happens when you add something
docs.text:
What gets copied depends on the resource type.

  • Agents are added to your account as usable agents
  • If an agent includes assignments, they are installed disabled by default
  • Skills are copied into your account automatically
  • Prompts are copied into your account automatically
  • MCP Servers are copied, but you still need to configure any secrets or environment values they require, including a credential passed as a command argument or in the server URL: the catalog shows, downloads and copies it masked
  • Custom Tools are copied into your account and may need follow-up setup

Company-managed resources you have access to are bound as they are, without extra binding. When one is restricted to a group you are not in, a knowledge base is recreated empty and an integration asks you to pick your own, while an MCP server, custom tool, skill or prompt is left out: it is not listed on the catalog page, installed or included in the download for you. Others need you to connect an existing integration or complete a setup step after installation.

When you publish an agent, you decide whether its downloadable JSON includes the code of your personal custom tools, the ones that are not company-managed: the Include the code of my personal custom tools in the catalog download switch sits under Include in AI Catalog on the agent's configuration. It is off for a new publish, and agents published before the switch existed keep including them until you change it. When it is off, the download leaves those tools out and says which, both in the file and on the catalog page. Company-managed custom tools are always included, except for a reader outside a restricted tool's group, and adding the agent to an account never copies a personal custom tool either way. An assistant with the agent builder can set it for you too, with the same rules.

For an agent, an integration you pick during installation must be one you can use. The publisher's own integrations, channel bots, sharing and run-as settings never come with the agent, and its run budget is lowered to the limits that apply to you. The variables named in its persona, guardrails, assignments and copied prompts and skills are copied into your account as well, a secret one without its value. The end of the installation lists the variables that still need a value, and the agent's page shows a notice until you set them in Variables.

Nothing is left out silently. The end of the installation also lists, per kind and with the reason, what your copy does not carry or carries only in part: an integration, MCP server, custom tool, skill or prompt that is not shared with you, an MCP server copied as yours without any credential, a knowledge base copied empty, the handovers and channel settings a catalog copy never carries, and an assignment limited to an MCP server the agent does not have, which runs without it. The same list is the warnings field of the install response (POST /api/v1/public/catalog/{type}/{id}/add).

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Agent detail pages show what the agent does and what it needs.

You can review:

  • the agent persona
  • assigned integrations
  • knowledge bases
  • MCP servers
  • custom tools
  • skills
  • prompts
  • built-in tools
  • variables

If the agent includes assignments, you can also see how much work it is designed to automate.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Skill detail pages show the skill URL and its content.

Use this when you want to inspect the instructions before importing them into your account.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
Prompt detail pages show the full prompt content.

This helps you review reusable text before adding it to your own workspace.

docs.title: MCP Servers
docs.text:
MCP Server detail pages show:

  • the transport type
  • the command or URL
  • arguments, when present
  • the tools exposed by the server

These entries help you understand which external tool server the resource connects to.

docs.title: Custom Tools
docs.text:
Custom Tool detail pages show:

  • the code size
  • the input parameters
  • the JavaScript function
  • the timeout

This helps you understand what the tool does before you add it.

docs.title: What to remember
docs.text:
The AI Catalog is a starting point, not the final setup.

After adding a resource, you may still need to:

  • connect an integration
  • add documents to a knowledge base
  • configure secrets or environment values
  • review the imported setup before using it with users

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with the Common experience across the XTM Suite page, then move to the product-specific pages that match your environment.

docs.title: Chat API
docs.text:
The web app, the Office add-in and your own scripts talk to a conversation over the same WebSocket. This page describes that protocol: how to connect, what you receive while an agent works, how to tell your own requests from the ones sent elsewhere, and what you can count on when a request ends.

To create a conversation and read its messages, use the REST routes under /api/v1/chat/conversations.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Open a WebSocket on the conversation, with a session token (the access_token that POST /api/v1/auth/login returns):

wss://<your-xtm-one>/api/v1/chat/conversations/<conversation_id>/ws?token=<access_token>

Only the conversation's owner receives the requests described under Requests you did not send. Send {"type": "ping"} every 25 seconds or so; the platform answers {"type": "pong"}, and while a request runs it sends one itself after about 20 seconds without other frames.

docs.title: Send a message
docs.text:
Send the message as JSON:

{"content": "Summarize the last incident report"}

The platform answers with a sequence of frames, all JSON objects with a type:

Frame Meaning thinking Your message was received. It is sent before the request starts running. turn_started Your message started a request of its own; turn_id identifies it. A message folded into a running request gets folded_into_active_turn instead (below). status Progress: status says which step (preparing, tool_start, thinking_text, streaming...). stream A piece of the answer as it is written (content). done The answer: content and message_id, the stored assistant message. error The request ended without an answer (content says why). cancelled The request was stopped.

A done with "intermediate": true is part of the answer that was already delivered while the agent keeps working: the request is not over. Send {"type": "cancel"} to stop a request that is running.

docs.title: Messages that mention several agents
docs.text:
To have several agents answer one message (@mentions), add their ids to the message, in the order they should answer:

{"content": "@mail-desk @deal-desk what do you think?", "mentioned_agent_ids": ["<agent id>", "<agent id>"]}

The conversation's agent answers first, then each mentioned agent, all in the same request: every frame carries the same turn_id. Each reply but the last arrives as a done with "intermediate": true, and a status frame with "status": "mention_answering" (agent_name, position, total) announces the next agent. The last reply is the request's final done. On such a request every reply carries answered_by (agent_id, agent_name, and agent_icon when the agent has one) naming the agent that wrote it - the conversation's agent included, except the General Assistant, whose replies carry none - and a note written in place of an agent that did not answer carries "mention_failed": true. Over REST, the replies after the first are in mention_messages.

A request you sent can become such a request without you mentioning anyone: a message another place folds into it (below) may mention agents, and they answer inside your request, after its agent. To tell your agent's reply from theirs, compare answered_by.agent_id with the conversation's agent: voice mode speaks only its agent's reply and shows the others as text with their name, and the Office add-in, like the web app, labels every reply with the agent that wrote it.

docs.title: Requests you did not send
docs.text:
A conversation can be open in several places: another browser tab, another device, voice mode, a script calling the REST API, or a background task reporting back. Every open WebSocket of the conversation's owner receives what the others do, so each one can show the same answer as it is written. Two fields tell those frames apart:

Field Where Meaning relayed Every frame of a request this WebSocket did not send, and user_message frames true: the request was sent somewhere else. Frames of your own requests never carry it. turn_id turn_started, and every thinking, status, stream, done, cancelled and error frame of a request, once it runs Identifies the request. Your own frames and the copies other WebSockets receive carry the same value. The thinking that acknowledges your message arrives before the request runs and carries none.

A WebSocket that connects while a request is running first receives a thinking frame flagged "resumed": true, then the steps, the reasoning and the answer written so far, then the rest as it happens. A user_message frame (message) is a user message stored from another place.

If your script only cares about its own messages, ignore every frame flagged relayed, except for the request your message was folded into (below).

docs.title: Messages folded into a running request
docs.text:
A conversation runs one request at a time. A message you send while another request is running is folded into it: that request takes your message into account, and you receive:

{"type": "folded_into_active_turn", "conversation_id": "<id>", "folded": true, "turn_id": "<turn id>"}

turn_id names the request that answers your message: its frames reach you flagged relayed, with that turn_id, after this frame. The agents your message mentions answer it in that request, after the agents of that request, or in the next request when it ends before it can ask them. The REST route that sends a message answers 202 with "status": "folded_into_active_turn" and the same turn_id in that case. Rarely, the message is kept for the next request instead ("folded": false on the WebSocket, "status": "queued_for_next_turn" over REST). turn_id is then present only when a request is running, and that request picks the message up.

docs.title: How a request ends
docs.text:
Every request you are shown ends with a done, cancelled or error frame, including one sent somewhere else, even when the connection to the platform's message broker was briefly lost or the process running the request stopped. When the platform itself had to end it, the error frame carries a reason:

reason Meaning interrupted The request was stopped before it produced its answer (a server restart, for instance). lost The request is over, but how it ended could not be delivered. Read the conversation to see what it stored.

A request stopped from the WebSocket that runs it can end with two cancelled frames: the acknowledgement of the stop, then, once the stop is stored, a second one carrying message_id. In the same way, a request whose agent failed can end with an error (without reason), then, once that reply is stored, a done carrying message_id. Both frames mean the request is over; the second one says what to read back.

Keep a safety check

If your script waits for an answer, also read GET /api/v1/chat/conversations/<conversation_id> when the request stays silent for a long time: is_processing is false once no request is running, and the stored messages show the answer. The platform guarantees the end frame; the check covers a network that drops frames on your side.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Go back to Chat to see how the web app shows the same conversation.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: Chat is where you work directly with XTM One in natural language. It supports both the platform-wide General Assistant and individual agents.

docs.title: What Chat is for
docs.text:
Use Chat when you want to:

  • ask a question in plain language
  • work with a specific assistant
  • upload supporting files
  • reuse a saved prompt
  • continue an earlier conversation
  • speak instead of typing, if your browser supports it

docs.title: The chat layout
docs.text:
Chat has two main areas:

  • the left sidebar for assistant selection and conversation history
  • the main panel for the active conversation

If you are on a smaller screen, the sidebar can collapse so the conversation has more space.

docs.title: Choose who you want to talk to
docs.text:
At the top of the sidebar, you choose the assistant for the conversation.

You may see:

  • General Assistant
  • chat-enabled agents
  • assignment-oriented agents shown in a Not recommended for chat section

Choose the General Assistant when you want a broad helper. Choose a specific agent when you want an assistant with a focused role or built-in context.

docs.title: Start a new conversation
docs.text:
To start a new conversation:

  1. Open Chat from the sidebar.
  2. Choose the assistant you want.
  3. Click the New conversation button.
  4. Type your message and send it.

If you open Chat from an agent card or an agent detail page, XTM One can preselect that agent for you.

docs.title: Manage conversations from the sidebar
docs.text:
The sidebar is not only a list of past chats. It is also your main control area.

From here you can:

  • search conversations by title, preview text, or agent name
  • open an earlier conversation
  • archive a single conversation
  • archive all conversations from the Clear all conversations action
  • switch assistants without leaving the page

Archiving removes a conversation from the active list. It is not the same as simply closing the page.

docs.title: Write your message
docs.text:
The composer at the bottom of the screen supports several input methods.

You can:

  • type a normal message
  • attach files with the paperclip button
  • paste files into the composer
  • drag and drop files onto the page
  • insert a saved prompt template
  • use voice dictation
  • start a full voice conversation

If a response is still being generated, the send button becomes a stop button so you can interrupt the response.

The lightning icon among the composer buttons counts the agentic actions consumed in the current quota period (the day, month or year your administrator configured), out of your limit when there is one. Hover it for the details. While an assistant works on your message, the action this reply consumes is shown in brackets: 4(+1)/10 means 4 actions before this reply, 1 for it, out of 10. It joins the total when the reply ends, along with any sandbox code runs counted toward the same limit; a reply that fails may have its action credited back instead (see Configuration). The counter is refreshed as well when a reply is stopped or fails, and when a reply you left running by opening another conversation ends. A message you send while a reply is running can count as one more action.

docs.title: Ask several agents at once with @mentions
docs.text:
Type @ in the composer and pick an agent from the list to mention it. You can mention several agents in the same message.

  • In a new conversation, the first agent you mention becomes the conversation's agent.
  • The conversation's agent answers first. Then every other agent you mentioned answers in turn, in the order you mentioned them. Each reply is its own message, labelled with the agent's name.
  • Every mentioned agent receives your full message, including attachments, and can read the replies given before its own in the same turn.
  • An agent you mention twice answers once.
  • Only agents you can chat with answer: a mention of an agent that is not available to you (not shared with you, disabled, or not open to chat) is ignored, and the others still answer. If an agent fails while answering, a short note replaces its reply and the agents after it still answer.
  • Clicking stop ends the turn: the agents that have not answered yet are not asked.
  • The mentioned agents of one message share a time limit. An agent still answering when it runs out is stopped, and a note names the agents that were not asked.
  • Each agent that answers counts as one agentic action, charged before it starts, exactly as if you had asked it alone; an agent it consults while answering adds nothing. If your agentic quota runs out, the agent that could not be charged says so and the agents after it are not asked. An agent that fails is credited back like any failed answer.
  • Each reply keeps what its own agent produced: its trace (for feedback) and the files it generated.
  • A message you send while an answer is still being written is held and sent as its own message when the answer ends if it mentions another agent, or while several mentioned agents are answering. A message that reaches a running answer anyway (from another device, or through the API) goes to the agent already answering, and the other agents it mentions then answer it, after the agents of the running turn and under the same rules. One that arrives as the answer is ending is answered by them after the next answer in the conversation.

Once an administrator turns them on (CHANNEL_AGENT_MENTIONS_ENABLED=true, see Configuration), mentions also work in messaging channels (Slack, Teams, WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord and Google Chat), for people with an XTM One account. Until then, a channel message is answered by its routed agent alone, whatever it mentions. There is no picker there: type the agent's key after @, the same key the web composer inserts, such as @mail-desk. A mentioned agent answers only when its own channel settings let it answer that message: it is enabled, open to chat, set to Receive on that channel (and on that channel conversation, if it is restricted to some), past the bot's receive whitelist, the private-conversation and only-mention rules, and set to Publish there. With mentions turned on, an administrator decides which agents can answer on a channel in each agent's Channels settings. Any other @ word - a person, a handle, an agent not set up on that channel - is plain text: the routed agent answers alone, as it would without the mention, and no note is added. Anonymous senders cannot mention agents. Each agent that answers counts as one agentic action, as in the web chat. The replies arrive together in one bot message, one section per agent, with a link to every file an agent produced, and are stored as separate messages in the conversation, each with its own agent's files.

docs.title: Ask for changes to a file the agent produced
docs.text:
When an agent hands you a file — an HTML briefing, a CSV export, a Markdown report, a JSON bundle — you can ask for a change in plain words: "remove the paragraph about X", "rename the column to Y", "fix the date in the footer". The agent reads the file it produced, applies exactly the change you asked for and returns a new revision of the file. The version you already downloaded is never altered under you.

  • Text-based files (HTML, Markdown, CSV, JSON, YAML, source code, ...) are edited in place, so a one-line change stays a one-line change — the rest of the document is untouched.
  • Rendered documents (PDF, Word) have no editable source: the agent regenerates them from the corrected content.
  • Files you uploaded yourself can be corrected the same way; the result is a new file next to your original.

Tip

Name what you want changed as it appears in the document. The agent matches your words against the file's exact text, so "remove the sentence about JP" works when the document says "JP"; a paraphrase may need one round of clarification.

docs.title: How a reply shows its files
docs.text:
• The files an answer names are shown as cards in the answer. The other files the agent wrote while working on it (a first draft, a scratch file) are listed under a collapsed Working files row below it, still downloadable.
  • An answer that names none of its files shows them all as cards, as before.
  • When the agent wrote a file twice under the same name in one answer, the older one is marked Superseded and Go to the newer version takes you to the newer one.
  • Files that share a name and type in a conversation are numbered v1, v2, ... in the order they were written, and their cards show the exact size in bytes. Every card shows the time its file was written; hover a card to see its file id and the start of its SHA-256 digest.

docs.title: Use prompt templates
docs.text:
If prompts are available in your environment, the prompt button opens a list of reusable prompt templates.

Use this when you want to:

  • start from a standard request
  • keep your wording consistent
  • save time on recurring questions

Selecting a prompt inserts its content into your message box.

docs.title: Use session tools
docs.text:
The wrench button opens the session tools panel.

Depending on the conversation, you may be able to enable or disable:

  • built-in tools
  • custom tools
  • integrations
  • MCP servers
  • knowledge bases

When you use the General Assistant, this panel lets you build a temporary toolset for the conversation. When you use a specific agent, the panel starts from that agent's own toolset and lets you switch built-in tools on or off for the conversation. Work items, shared state and trace inspection act as the agent itself, so they are only offered when the agent already has them or when you can configure the agent.

A message can only add to the conversation what you could connect to an agent of your own: one that adds a custom tool, MCP server, knowledge base or integration you cannot see is refused with an error that says which kind it is, and nothing is sent. Saving your profile's default tools follows the same rule. What the conversation already has - the tools you selected earlier, your profile defaults, the agent's own toolset and the General Assistant's configuration - is used as it was set up, including what the owner of an agent shared with you connected to it.

Integrations are the one exception, as they always were: an integration you cannot see, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with you, is never used for you in a chat (see Sharing an OAuth integration). Nothing is hidden: when an answer could not use one, a note under it names the integration - by its service only when it is not shared with you - and says why, and the agent is told as well, so it can say what it cannot do. Connect your own integration of that service, or ask the owner to share theirs.

The panel also lets you:

  • reset back to the default configuration
  • enable all visible tools (the ones already on stay on)
  • disable all visible tools
  • temporarily hide integrations from the picker and restore them later

docs.title: Voice options
docs.text:
If your browser supports speech features, Chat can offer two voice modes.

  • Voice input converts your speech into text in the message box.
  • Voice conversation opens a more continuous spoken interaction.

If these controls do not appear, your browser or device does not currently support them.

docs.title: What you may see above the messages
docs.text:
The conversation header can show extra context.

You may see:

  • the active agent name
  • the current channel, such as web chat
  • a transfer banner if another agent handed the conversation over
  • a Return action if you want to go back to the source agent

This is especially useful when the conversation moved from one agent to another.

docs.title: A conversation open in several places
docs.text:
When the same conversation is open in several tabs, on another device, or in voice mode, each one shows the answer as it is written, wherever the message was sent from. Voice mode reads out only the answer to what you said.

When XTM One is updated while a tab stays open, that tab shows A new version is available: select Reload to use the new version. Until you do, the tab keeps working, but it may show an answer started elsewhere as if you had asked it.

To connect your own scripts to a conversation, see the Chat API.

docs.title: Background task banners
docs.text:
Some requests continue in the background.

When that happens, Chat can show:

  • a banner while background tasks are still running
  • a completion banner when those background tasks finish
  • a failed count if some delegated tasks did not complete successfully

This means the request involved delegation or longer-running work. It is normal behavior, not an error by itself.

Files a delegated task produces (a CSV export, a spreadsheet, a report) belong to the conversation: they appear as download chips on the message the agent posts once the task finishes, and the agent itself can open, check and merge them with its own file tools when it summarizes the result.

docs.title: The waiting arcade
docs.text:
While an agent works through a longer request, a small Space Invader appears under the conversation and shoots the waiting message away, letter by letter. It is more than an animation: click it, or its Take control button, and a full Space Invaders game opens over the whole interface. When the agent is showing its reasoning instead, the gamepad button in the corner of the reasoning window opens the same game. You can also start a game at any time, no wait needed: Play Space Invaders in your user menu (top right), or the command of the same name in the command palette.

The chat embedded in OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ invites you here too: while its agent works, its Play Space Invaders in XTM One link opens <your XTM One address>/chat?arcade=play in a new tab, and the game starts as soon as you are signed in - even if you have to sign in first, or wait for an administrator to accept the platform's Terms of Use, as long as that happens within ten minutes of the click.

  • Controls: arrow keys or A/D (Q/D on an AZERTY keyboard) to move, Space to fire (hold it for autofire), right-click or X to send a missile where you aim, P to pause, M to mute, Esc to leave (the first press pauses, the second ends the game and saves it). On a touch screen, drag to move and fire, and tap the rocket for a missile.
  • Waves and bosses: every wave marches faster than the last, and every fifth wave brings a boss. Falling capsules hold power-ups: rapid fire, spread shot, laser, shield, extra missiles, and a few rarer ones.
  • The interface is fair game: your shots and the invaders' leave holes in whatever they hit - buttons, messages, the sidebar. Nothing is really broken: the damage is cosmetic, and everything is rebuilt the moment you leave. Your conversation keeps running underneath.
  • Your answer comes first: when the agent has finished answering, a banner says so - a message it posts along the way before carrying on with its work does not count. Esc (or Read it) takes you straight back to it, and if you had stopped playing, the arcade takes you back by itself after a few seconds. Keep playing lets you finish your game. The game waits for the conversation you started it from: if you switch to another conversation or leave the chat while you play, the game goes on but no longer announces that answer.

docs.title: Leaderboard
docs.text:
Every game you play is scored and saved. The leaderboard - Arcade leaderboard in your user menu, the trophy button next to the waiting game, the Open the leaderboard command, or the pause menu - ranks the best game of each player over the last 24 hours, the last 7 days and all time, shows who is playing right now, and names the holders of three titles: top vandal, sharpshooter and marathon. During a game, the score bar shows whose score you are about to beat.

  • Your callsign is three letters or digits, like on a real arcade cabinet. It defaults to your initials; change it in the leaderboard's My arcade tab. Other players only ever see your callsign - never your name or your email.
  • Turn off Show me on the public leaderboard to keep your scores, titles and live games to yourself, from that moment on - even in a game already running. You still see your own rank.
  • Scores are checked by the server: a score, a number of shots or a count of destroyed interface elements that is not plausible for the time played is refused, and so is a score higher than the waves you reached can yield. The arcade tells you why a score was not recorded. A game in which a cheat code was used is saved but not ranked.

docs.title: Achievements and secrets
docs.text: The leaderboard's Achievements tab lists what you have unlocked. Many achievements are secret until you find them: old cheat codes, a very rare saucer, certain dates on the calendar, and a few things you probably should not shoot. Explore.

docs.title: When the game is not offered
docs.text:
The gamepad always means play: on the waiting panel and in the reasoning window it opens the game, and nothing in the chat hides it. When your system asks for reduced motion, the waiting panel shows a plain rotating message instead of the invader and the chat offers no game; Play Space Invaders (in your user menu or the command palette) and a ?arcade=play link still start one, since you asked for it. The arcade is not offered while an administrator impersonates a user: nothing is ever recorded under someone else's name. Nor is it offered while the platform's Terms of Use are waiting to be accepted. Administrators can turn the arcade off for the whole platform with ARCADE_ENABLED (see Configuration).

The game and the leaderboard load in the background shortly after you sign in, so a page left open while XTM One is updated can still play. If they could not load before the update (on a Data Saver or 2G connection, for instance), opening them shows Reload to play or Reload to open the leaderboard: Reload reloads the page and opens the game or the leaderboard right away.

docs.title: When an agent is shown as not recommended for chat
docs.text:
Some agents are built mainly for background execution rather than direct conversation.

These agents still appear in the picker, but XTM One marks them so you know they are not optimized for normal chat use.

You can still try them, but the best experience usually comes from:

  • the General Assistant
  • a chat-enabled agent

docs.title: Practical tips
docs.text:
• Start with the General Assistant if you are unsure which agent to use.
  • Use a dedicated agent when the topic belongs to a specific workflow.
  • Attach documents when the answer depends on exact wording or evidence.
  • Open the same conversation again if you want XTM One to keep the discussion context.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter explains Agents, including what the list page shows and how to read an agent detail page.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Files is the one place that lists every file you and your agents exchanged — the documents you uploaded in a conversation and the outputs your agents produced (reports, exports, generated images, spreadsheets), wherever they were made.

Until now each file lived only behind the context that produced it: the files panel of one conversation, the attachments of one run. Files collects them all so you can find a deliverable again without remembering which chat or which assignment produced it.

docs.title: Open Files
docs.text:
Choose Work > Files from the left sidebar. The Work group holds what your agents produce — Operations (their runs), Presentations (their decks) and Files (everything else they output, plus what you gave them).

The Work hub page itself shows the three at a glance, with counts and the most recently changed items of each.

docs.title: What is listed
docs.text:
You see exactly the files you are allowed to download:

  • files you uploaded, and files generated for you, in your own conversations
  • files of conversations that were shared with you
  • outputs of assignment runs you can open — your own agents' runs, and runs of company-managed agents

Nothing is listed that you could not open: a file that appears in the list can always be downloaded.

Generated files include what an agent brought in from the web: every page or document it reads with Web Fetch is kept as a file of the conversation (a PDF, a spreadsheet or a data file as the document itself, a web page as its HTML source), so it can be downloaded, handed to another tool or added to a knowledge base. Reading the same page twice with identical content keeps one file. A report an agent exported to PDF is a file too.

What is not here

The design assets of presentation templates (logos, diagrams, fonts) are managed from their template under Agent Studio > Templates and are not repeated here — a fresh install ships a few hundred of them, and they would bury your real files. Presentations themselves have their own page, Presentations; a deck exported to PDF or PowerPoint does show up in Files, because the export is a file.

Administrators do not get a wider view here. An administrator reaches another user's conversation files only through the audited break-glass access on the conversation itself, never through this list.

docs.title: Find a file
docs.text:
Three filters sit next to the search box. Each is a segmented control; pick one segment of each.

Filter Segments Question it answers Where the file lives Everywhere · Conversations · Runs · Other in a chat, from an assignment run, or unbound (dataset uploads, tool tests, flow uploads) How it got there Any origin · Uploaded · Generated did a person upload it, or did an agent produce it Whose files Everyone · Mine · Shared with me your own files and contexts, or files you can see because they were shared with you

Search matches the file name. The counter on the right of the filter row is the total for the current filters, and the list is paginated when it is long.

Group (on by default) folds the list by conversation or run, so the files of one piece of work sit together under its title and owner. Switch it off for a flat, most-recent-first list where each row also shows its context.

Filters, search, grouping and page are kept in the URL, so a filtered view can be bookmarked or sent to a colleague — they will see the same view, limited to what they may read.

docs.title: Act on a file
docs.text:
Each row shows the file name, type and size, when it was added and by whom, and a badge telling whether it was Uploaded or Generated. From the row's menu:

  • Download fetches the file.
  • Open conversation / Open run takes you to the place the file came from, so you can read it in context or ask the assistant for a new version.
  • Delete removes the file and its storage object. It is available to the file's owner, the owner of the conversation it lives in, or whoever can manage the run that produced it — someone a conversation was merely shared with can read the file but not delete it.

Deleting a file does not break the message or the deck that referenced it: they show the file as no longer available.

docs.title: Jump from a chat or a run
docs.text: Anywhere the platform shows a file — a chat message, a run's attachments — a link to it in Files opens the page already scoped to that conversation or run, with the file highlighted. The Showing files of chip at the top of the list names the scope; close it to return to the full list with the same filters.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Agents also produce slide decks. See Presentations for how decks are created, shared, and exported.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This chapter introduces what XTM One does, who it is for, and how to find your way around.

docs.title: What XTM One is for
docs.text: Use XTM One to work with AI assistants built for cyber, intelligence, operations, and business workflows. You can ask for summaries, explanations, extractions, and recommendations; launch or monitor automated work handled by agents and assignments; reuse shared resources such as knowledge bases, prompts, skills, tools, and integrations; and review execution history before acting. Across the wider XTM Suite it acts as a common AI layer with shared authentication and platform services.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: XTM One is designed for business users, analysts, and operators — you do not need to be an AI specialist. It is useful for teams working with OpenCTI, OpenAEV, threat intelligence, investigations, reporting and summarization, operational triage, security operations, and email or messaging workflows.

docs.title: Key words in this guide
docs.text:
A few recurring terms appear throughout this documentation:

  • Agent: an AI assistant configured for a specific use case, role, or workflow
  • Assignment: an automation rule that tells an agent when to run and what to do
  • Knowledge Base: searchable internal knowledge used to ground answers and actions
  • Prompt and Skill: reusable instructions that shape how agents behave
  • Tool or MCP Server: capabilities that let agents query, fetch, or act outside the chat itself
  • Integration: a connection to another system such as messaging, email, or external platforms

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text: Open the XTM One sign-in page and choose the login method available in your organization — a company account, email and password, or a local account if that is allowed. If your organization uses single sign-on, you are redirected to your identity provider and brought back automatically.

docs.title: Find your way around
docs.text:
After signing in you land in the main application. A left sidebar moves you between sections, a top bar holds your profile, notifications, and quick actions (including the AI Catalog of shared, published items), and the center shows the current page.

The most common places to start are the Dashboard for an overview, Chat to work with an assistant, Agents to open a specific assistant, and History to review completed work. Administrators also see the administration sections (such as Users, Groups, Logs, and Settings).

What you can access depends on your role and your organization's license: some users only use the shared platform experience, some can use ready-made assistants, and some can create and manage their own agents and resources. If a section is missing, it may not be enabled for your account. This guide explains those differences only when they matter for a task.

docs.title: XTM One in other XTM Suite products
docs.text: Depending on your deployment, you may also use XTM One from inside another Filigran product such as OpenCTI or OpenAEV. In those cases it appears as an embedded AI capability — an assistant panel or AI action inside the product where you already work — rather than as a separate destination, while the resources and automations are still managed centrally in XTM One.

docs.title: Start with the dashboard
docs.text: If you are not sure where to begin, open the Dashboard first. It is the best place to see recent activity, check what is already in progress, and find the next action you need to take.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Once you are signed in and comfortable with the layout, move to the Foundations section. Start with Foundations Overview, then continue to Data model before moving into the Dashboard and the rest of the UI chapters.

docs.title: Home dashboard
docs.text: The Dashboard is the landing page for XTM One. It changes based on how far your organization is in setup, so the first thing to understand is which dashboard state you are looking at.

docs.title: What the Dashboard is for
docs.text:
Use the Dashboard to:

  • confirm that OpenCTI and OpenAEV are connected
  • see whether XTM One is active and healthy
  • open the main work areas quickly
  • check recent agent activity without going into detailed history

docs.title: The three dashboard states
docs.text: XTM One currently shows one of three dashboard experiences.

docs.title: 1. Welcome and connection setup
docs.text:
If no platform is connected yet, the Dashboard becomes a setup landing page.

You will see:

  • a high-level introduction to XTM One in the XTM Suite
  • connection cards for OpenCTI and OpenAEV
  • setup instructions for administrators
  • a registration token area for administrators

This screen is mainly for the initial rollout. If you are a regular user, you usually do not need to act here. Your administrator completes this step.

docs.title: 2. Connected platforms overview
docs.text:
If at least one platform is connected but the full CTEM operations experience is not yet enabled, the Dashboard focuses on connection status.

You will usually see:

  • a greeting and status summary
  • one card per connected platform
  • connection health indicators
  • last heartbeat information
  • a reminder to connect the missing platform if setup is incomplete

This view is useful when you want to confirm that the XTM Suite is online before you start using agents and chat more heavily.

docs.title: 3. Full operations dashboard
docs.text:
When the full experience is available, the Dashboard becomes an operational workspace.

You will usually see:

  • a greeting and current activity summary
  • a prominent Start chatting action
  • KPI cards for Agents, Conversations, Agentic Executions, Connected Platforms, and Integrations
  • connected platform cards
  • an Agents panel
  • a Live Activity panel with recent runs

This is the main dashboard most end users will work from day to day.

docs.title: What the platform cards mean
docs.text:
Platform cards represent connected XTM Suite products such as OpenCTI and OpenAEV.

They help you check:

  • which product is connected
  • whether the connection is healthy or stale
  • the platform version
  • when the last heartbeat was received

You can also open the connected platform directly from these cards.

docs.title: What the KPI cards mean
docs.text:
On the full dashboard, the KPI cards are meant to answer simple questions at a glance.

  • Agents shows how many assistants are active and how many assignments are configured.
  • Conversations shows how much direct chat activity has happened.
  • Agentic Executions shows how much automated work has run recently.
  • Connected Platforms shows how many XTM Suite products are linked to XTM One.
  • Integrations shows how many connected services are available to agents.

Most of these cards are also shortcuts. Clicking them opens the related page.

docs.title: Use the Agents panel
docs.text:
The Agents panel on the full dashboard gives you a short list of available agents.

From here you can:

  • open an agent directly
  • create a new agent
  • jump to the full Agents page

This panel is helpful when you already know which assistant you want to use.

docs.title: Use the Live Activity panel
docs.text:
The Live Activity panel shows recent runs as they happen.

Use it to:

  • see which assignments ran most recently
  • spot failures quickly
  • jump to the full History page

If nothing has run yet, the panel stays empty until the first execution is triggered.

docs.title: How to use the Dashboard day to day
docs.text:
A practical pattern is simple:

  1. Check that the connected platforms look healthy.
  2. Use Start chatting if you want help right away.
  3. Open an agent if you need a more specific assistant.
  4. Open History if you want to understand what has already run.

docs.title: If the dashboard looks different from another user's
docs.text:
That is usually normal. The dashboard varies based on:

  • whether OpenCTI or OpenAEV has been connected
  • whether the full licensed experience is enabled
  • whether your account has access to the related areas

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter explains Chat, which is the fastest way to start working with XTM One.

docs.title: My profile
docs.text: My Profile is where you manage your personal experience in XTM One. Unlike Settings, which is shared platform configuration, this page is about your own account.

docs.title: What you can do here
docs.text:
Use My Profile to:

  • update your account details
  • set your time zone and theme
  • change your password, if you use a local account
  • protect your account with two-factor authentication
  • choose your default chat agent
  • tailor the General Assistant to your needs
  • control your private channel routing
  • review and clear memory
  • check your quotas
  • create API keys
  • manage your personal MCP exposure

docs.title: The main profile tabs
docs.text:
The current profile page is organized into:

  • Profile
  • Channels & Bots
  • Memory
  • Quotas
  • API Keys
  • MCP Endpoint

Looking for the runners tab?

Downloading the native app and managing your machines moved to the XTM One Desktop page - the entry at the bottom of the left navigation, also in your user menu. The old Profile > Runners address redirects there. See XTM One Desktop and runners.

docs.title: Profile tab
docs.text:
The Profile tab contains your personal account information.

You can usually review or update:

  • full name
  • title
  • email address
  • time zone
  • theme
  • authentication method

If you use SSO, the page shows that clearly so you know sign-in is handled by your identity provider.

docs.title: Password changes
docs.text:
If you use a local account, the Profile tab also includes a password change area.

If you sign in with SSO, password changes are usually managed outside XTM One by your identity provider.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.text:
Right below the password area, the Profile tab lets you protect your account with a second factor: a six-digit code from an authenticator app, asked for every time you sign in — after your password, or after your identity provider if you use SSO.

To turn it on:

  1. Select Set up. A QR code appears.
  2. Scan it with your authenticator app — Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, KeePassXC, 1Password, Bitwarden, or any other. If you cannot scan (for example KeePassXC on a desktop), choose Enter the key manually and type the key it shows.
  3. Type the six-digit code your app displays and select Enable two-factor.

XTM One then shows 10 recovery codes.

Save your recovery codes now

This is the only time they can be displayed. Each one signs you in once, in place of your app, if you lose your phone. Nobody can retrieve them for you afterwards — not even an administrator.

Once enabled, signing in becomes two steps: your password, then the code. If your phone is not to hand, choose Use a recovery code on the code screen.

From the same area you can:

  • Generate new recovery codes — replaces your current set. Requires a code from your app.
  • Disable two-factor — requires both your password and a current code, so neither an unlocked browser nor your phone alone is enough to remove it.

If you lose both your device and your recovery codes, ask an administrator to reset your two-factor enrollment. Your account then signs in with your password alone until you set it up again on a new device.

Works with SSO too

If you sign in through an identity provider, you can still enable two-factor here. XTM One asks for the code after your provider signs you in, so the extra factor applies even when your organisation's identity provider does not enforce one. If your account has no XTM One password, disabling only asks for a code.

docs.title: General Assistant Tools
docs.text:
The Profile tab also contains your personal General Assistant tool overrides.

This is where you can review or override access to:

  • built-in tools
  • integrations
  • MCP servers
  • custom tools
  • knowledge bases

This matters when you want your own General Assistant experience to differ from the platform default.

You can also reset your personal choices back to the platform default.

docs.title: Channels & Bots tab
docs.text:
Channels & Bots controls how your own chat routing works.

This tab currently lets you:

  • choose your default web chat agent
  • assign a different agent for your private conversations on supported channels
  • fall back to default routing when you do not want a personal override

If connected channel bots are available, you can set a different direct-message agent for each channel. Group-channel behavior remains governed by the shared admin routing, described in Channels and bots.

docs.title: Memory tab
docs.text:
Memory shows what XTM One remembers about you.

It is split into two main parts:

  • a Cross-Agent Profile shared across agents
  • per-agent memory for agents you have interacted with

From this tab you can:

  • review consolidated memory
  • inspect recent interactions
  • clear the cross-agent profile
  • clear memory for one specific agent
  • purge all your memory if you want a full reset

This is the best place to check when an agent seems to be remembering something you no longer want it to keep.

docs.title: Quotas tab
docs.text:
Quotas shows your personal usage against the limits that apply to your account.

In XTM One, this usually focuses on agentic executions. Some other deployments can also show additional quota types.

When your limit is the platform-wide pool of the license, the gauge shows the whole platform's usage against it, including requests with no account behind them (anonymous channel users, public chat widget visitors, calls made with the platform MCP key).

Use this tab to understand:

  • your current consumption
  • your limit period
  • whether the limit comes from a user rule, group rule, or platform default

docs.title: API Keys tab
docs.text:
API Keys lets you create personal keys for controlled programmatic access.

From this tab you can:

  • create a named key
  • copy it when it is first shown
  • review existing keys
  • delete a key you no longer need

The page also shows the Platform API endpoint and basic usage guidance. In some non-XTM deployments, an additional LLM proxy section can appear.

docs.title: MCP Endpoint tab
docs.text:
MCP Endpoint is for users who want to connect external MCP clients (Cursor, Claude Desktop, and others) to XTM One.

From this tab you can:

  • copy your personal MCP endpoint URL
  • review the connection snippet
  • choose which agents are exposed
  • remove agents from that exposed list

If you do not choose a restricted list, the endpoint can default to all eligible visible agents.

The same tab also shows the Platform MCP Servers card (unless an administrator has disabled the feature). Each connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ platform gets its own native MCP server (/mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, /mcp/opencrq) exposing its business tools, with the endpoint URL, live connection status, and a ready-to-copy client configuration; platforms that are not yet connected appear dimmed as Not connected until they are registered. See Platform MCP servers for the full guide.

When an administrator has enabled it, a Platform Tools MCP Server card appears too. It exposes XTM One's own tools on /mcp/xtm — agent traces, agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, and variables — scoped to what you can already see and manage. It is how you read an agent's traces from Claude Desktop or Cursor and fix its configuration there. The card also offers a downloadable installer package for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and any Agent Plugins client — with One-click install on, the package already contains the endpoint URL and a freshly created API key, so there is nothing to configure (and the file is then a secret: delete it once installed). See Platform tools MCP server.

docs.title: What to change first
docs.text:
For most customer users, the most useful first changes are:

  • name and title
  • time zone
  • default chat agent
  • General Assistant tool preferences

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The Settings page explains where administrators manage shared platform behavior.

docs.title: Presentations
docs.text:
A presentation is a slide deck your assistant builds for you, in a conversation, from a plain-language request. It renders right inside the chat, plays like a real deck (keyboard, touch, fullscreen, speaker notes), stays editable by asking for changes, and exports to PDF and PowerPoint that look exactly like the slides on screen.

Every deck you can see is listed under Work > Presentations in the sidebar — your own, the ones colleagues shared with you, and the ones published to the whole company. The Work group is where what your agents produce lives: their runs under Operations, their decks here, and every other file they output or you gave them under Files.

docs.title: Create a deck
docs.text:
Ask any assistant that can generate presentations — the General Assistant, or an agent with the presentation tool enabled — for slides, in your own words:

Create a 10-slide all-hands deck for Q3: highlights, the three numbers that matter, the roadmap for Q4, and a closing slide with my contact details.

The assistant composes the slides, and the deck appears in the conversation as an interactive card. When several templates are available to you and your request does not name one, the assistant first asks which template to use (see Template and theme). You can also start from the Presentations page: New presentation lets you pick the template and the theme, then opens the chat with the beginning of a request already typed for you.

Brief it like a designer

A good brief names the audience, the one message to remember, and the numbers you want on screen. The assistant chooses the slide compositions — a two-column comparison, a wall of key figures, a before/after, a diagram with an explanation, a roadmap, a takeaways slide — and keeps each slide readable from the back of the room. Ask for a short outline first when the deck is long, then let it build the whole thing in one pass.

Slides can carry text, bullet and check lists, callouts, key figures, tables, feature grids, timelines, process flows, numbered cards, quotes, images, logo grids, native charts, and diagrams drawn from a text description (flowcharts, sequences, mind maps). The assistant can highlight a word or a phrase with bold, emphasis, code style, or a colored tone — for example an accent to point at the one thing that matters, or success / warning / error for a verdict.

Architecture and ecosystem diagrams

Ask for "an architecture diagram of the platform", "how the modules feed each other" or "the ecosystem around the product" and the assistant draws a native diagram in the deck's own palette and fonts: product logos from the template inside the boxes, labeled arrows between them ("Threat data", "Findings"), a highlighted core the rest runs on, a band across the top for a portal or a marketplace, a titled panel around the modules of a platform, and a legend. A box or a panel can also wear a colour of the template's palette — on the brand decks, the product colours: XTM One purple, OpenCTI blue, OpenAEV orange, OpenCRQ blue — as its border, a tint of its body, its icon and the chips inside it (ask for "each product in its own colour"); the colour follows the slide's theme, dark or light, and the PowerPoint exports carry it as shown. The arrows are routed so they never run through a box, an exchange in both directions runs as two parallel lines that do not cross, and every arrow lands on the middle of a side. In the live deck the diagram is interactive: hover or focus a box to light up what it connects to, click it to read the detail the assistant wrote for it, Escape to release. Everything is vector — the PDF export stays sharp at any size.

Charts and dashboard slides

Give the assistant the numbers — "ARR by quarter for the last eight quarters", "the share of Community versus Enterprise", "trials against a target of 150" — and it draws a native chart in the deck's own palette and fonts: bar, stacked bar, line, area, pie, donut, a gauge against a target, or a bar and line combined. Values read the way a board expects (€29.5M, 86%, thousands separators in your language), a target shows as a dashed reference line named in the legend, and the chart follows the theme when you switch it between dark and light. In the live deck a chart is interactive: hover a bar or a point for its exact value, click a legend entry to hide or show a series. For a slide that reproduces a dashboard, ask for a dashboard slide: a row of key figures across the top — each can carry a small trend line beside its value — and up to six panels of charts, tables or figures on a grid below, sized to fit the slide without shrinking.

Agenda slides

A short agenda is a numbered list — one column up to four items, two columns up to six. From seven items the assistant lays it out as a board-deck grid: three columns of N. | TITLE cells, each with a one-line description under the title, so a long agenda still reads from the back of the room. The grid holds six to nine items — two to three full rows — and past nine the agenda returns to a two-column list rather than shrinking. Ask for "the agenda as a grid" or "as a list" to choose the look yourself, or "in three columns" to get the grid from six items; a description on any one item reserves that line on every cell, so the board stays even.

Logo walls

Ask for "our customers by sector" or "a logo wall of our partners" and the assistant groups the logos into equal cards — one per sector or category, its title and icon on one line — that fill the slide, each card's logos spread across its full width. Every logo is sized by its visible mark, not by its file: the transparent margin a logo was exported with is cropped away, so "small", "medium", "large" and "extra large" (28 / 40 / 56 / 72 px on the slide) are the height you actually see, and a round seal is drawn a little taller than a long wordmark so both carry the same weight. A logo row that is too narrow shrinks all its logos together, never one alone. Ask for the logos in one colour (the slide's text colour, or a muted grey) for a quiet "trusted by" band — it is also how white brand logos stay visible on a light slide; hovering a logo in the live deck shows its original colours. Labels under the logos are off unless you ask for them. Boxes of text follow the same idea: ask for "a card" instead of a tinted panel, with the icon on the title line and the content using the full width.

Customer quotes

Ask for "a customer quote slide" or "the customer's quote as a statement" and the assistant makes the quote the slide itself: large and bold, centred on the slide, with an oversized quote mark in the deck's accent colour, the speaker's name, role and company underneath and, when you give them, two to four facts about the customer ("Employees 80K", "Revenue $30B") as figures in the accent colour. A quote can also sit beside other content as a pull quote with a large accent rule, or be a testimonial card with the speaker's portrait or the company logo. In the editor, a selected quote offers its four looks as thumbnails, the size (up to the size of a title-slide headline), the alignment, the quote marks, the portrait and the logo picked from the deck's template, and the figures. Key figures anywhere on a slide can drop their card the same way (the plain variant of a metric), so a row of numbers sits under a paragraph without turning into boxes.

Funding rounds and partner logos

Ask for "our funding rounds with the lead investors' logos" and the assistant draws a timeline whose steps each carry their investor's logo, under the step's description and centred on its step, all the logos on one row. In the editor, each step of a timeline has a logo picker over the template's logos. A logo grid with a set number of columns shares its width in equal cells, each logo centred in its own, so a grid placed under a timeline of as many steps lines up with it; Stretch spreads the logos edge to edge instead.

Sales and marketing collateral has its own building blocks: a feature matrix (a comparison table with an accented "us" column and check / cross marks), editions and plans as tier cards with one recommended tier and a call-to-action button each, a fact sheet made of badges (certifications, hosting regions, community numbers) and label / value rows, personas — two to four audience cards naming the role, what hurts today and what changes for them — and a banner for a hero header or a closing call to action with buttons that link to a page or an e-mail address. Ask for "a battlecard against a legacy TIP", "the editions slide", "who it is for" or "a closing slide with a demo button" and the assistant reaches for them.

Pages, not only slides

Not everything is presented from a stage. Ask for a product brief, a one-pager, a datasheet or a case study and the assistant lays it out on a portrait page — A4 or US Letter — instead of a 16:9 slide: a hero banner, a fact sheet, a feature matrix, the editions, and a call to action, denser than a slide because it is read, not projected. A page exports to a PDF on real A4 / Letter paper and to a portrait PowerPoint of the same size. On screen it is not a slide show — see Read a page.

Images come from the predefined assets of the deck's template rather than from the assistant's imagination: add your architecture diagram, product screenshots or partner logos to a template, ask for "the architecture diagram" or "a logo wall of our partners", and the assistant places the actual figure — every one is described so it can be picked by what it shows, and the assistant asks the template for one role or keyword at a time rather than reading the whole inventory. See Templates.

docs.title: Play a deck
docs.text:
The card in the chat is a live deck. Everything you operate it with sits in the toolbar along its top edge — nothing is drawn over the slide itself: no corner arrows, no progress bar, no counter on the slide.

  • The middle of the bar is navigation: previous / next, and the slide counter (3 / 12), which opens a go-to-slide menu listing every slide by title, with a number field for long decks.
  • Present — the one highlighted button on the bar — takes the deck, toolbar included, to the whole screen. The slide fills the screen edge to edge: a 16:9 deck on a 16:9 monitor has no border at all, and on a screen of another shape (a 16:10 laptop, an ultrawide) the bands around it are black, like any player, whatever theme the deck or the app is in. The bar floats over the top edge for a moment, then slides away with the pointer after a moment of stillness and comes back as soon as you move the pointer — never when you press a key, so stepping through the slides with the arrows or a clicker never makes it flash; press Esc (or the bar's exit button) to leave. The keyboard is always active while presenting. Where the browser will not hand over the screen — a locked-down kiosk, an embedded desktop window — the deck fills the application window instead, with the same bar and the same keys; and from a chat embedded in another product, Present opens the standalone viewer, which can go fullscreen.
  • Open in studio, on the card in the chat, lands on the standalone viewer at /presentations/<id> — the same page a deck opens on from the Presentations list, with the editor, the comments, the history and the sharing controls — and opens the studio beside it, carrying this very conversation along so the assistant keeps everything it already knows about the deck. It is also the page you put on a projector or share as a link: no product menus, only the deck's own toolbar. Open in a new tab, in the More menu, opens that page beside the chat.
  • Comments opens the review notes on the deck and History its revisions (see Work on a deck together); the count on Comments is the number of notes still open. The initials beside Present are whoever else has the deck open right now.
  • The More menu holds the rarer presenter actions: the slide overview, the black screen, the speaker view with your notes and the next slide, the printable notes handout, and the list of keyboard shortcuts.

In the chat, the keyboard belongs to the page until you click the deck or its toolbar; from then on the deck has the keys, until you click somewhere else. In the viewer and while presenting the deck always has them.

Keys What they do Right Space N Page Down / Left P Page Up Next / previous slide Home / End First / last slide G Go to a slide O Slide overview F / Esc Present / stop presenting (Esc also closes the overview) B or . Black screen S Speaker view ? or F1 Keyboard shortcuts

Shortcuts pause while you type in a field or use a menu, so a key never turns the page by accident.

The deck is authored at a fixed 16:9 slide size (or 4:3 if you asked for it) and scales to whatever space it is given — a chat card, a laptop screen, a projector — so what you rehearse is what the room sees.

docs.title: Present with your notes
docs.text:
Every slide can carry speaker notes — what you say over it, not what the room reads. The assistant writes them with the deck (ask for "speaker notes on every slide, conversational, two or three sentences each" and it does; the note under each slide in the editor panel shows the words and the speaking time it adds up to), and reports back which content slides still have none. They live in the deck, travel with it in the PowerPoint export, and are read from the speaker view.

S, or Speaker view in the More menu, opens the speaker view in a window of its own — from the standalone viewer or from the card in the chat alike. Put the deck on the room's screen and keep this window on your laptop:

  • The current slide on top, so you know what the room sees without turning round — with a "screen is black" notice while the deck is paused.
  • Your notes in large type under it, the reason the window exists: bullets as bullets, emphasis as emphasis. + / - set the type size once and it is remembered.
  • The next slide in the side column, so the transition is spoken before it appears.
  • A stopwatch that starts on your first slide change (pause, resume, reset at will), the wall clock, and your pacing: the notes give every slide an estimated speaking time, so the window knows how far ahead of or behind the plan you are, and how much spoken time is left. Type a target length in minutes and the plan is re-scaled to the slot you actually have.
  • The transport: previous / next, a go-to-slide menu, the black screen — every one with the same key as the deck.

The window follows the deck: whichever screen is playing it — the viewer, a chat card, the fullscreen stage — announces where it is, and the keys pressed in the speaker window move the room's screen. Your clicker moves both. With no deck window open it runs in rehearsal mode, and says so: same notes, same timer, its own position — the way to practise the talk before the room is there. Edits made from the studio while you rehearse land in the notes and the previews without a reload.

Notes handout, in the same menu (and in the speaker window's header), opens every slide with its notes as one printable document at /presentations/<id>/notes — the sheets for the lectern, or for the colleague who presents the deck in your place. Only slides with notes leaves the section dividers out; print it to paper or to PDF from the browser.

If the speaker window does not open

Browsers block windows a page opens without a click behind them. Allow pop-ups for this site and press S again — the speaker view is a new window, never a popup drawn over the deck.

docs.title: Read a page
docs.text:
A portrait presentation — a brief, a one-pager, a datasheet on A4 or Letter — is a document, and the platform treats it as one. Instead of a stage it opens as a reader: every page stacked on a scrolling surface as a sheet of paper, the same toolbar along the top edge, and nothing that only makes sense for a slide show — no fullscreen, no transitions, no speaker view.

  • The middle of the bar is navigation: previous / next page, and the page counter (1 / 2), which opens a go-to-page menu listing every page by its heading. Scrolling moves the counter too — the current page is the one under the top of the reader.
  • The zoom controls sit beside it: zoom in / out in steps, and Fit width, which sizes each sheet to the reader. Ctrl + mouse wheel zooms as well.
  • Open in studio, on the card in the chat, lands on the standalone reader at /presentations/<id> with the studio open beside it and the document's actions (edit, comments, history, share, export) alongside; Open in a new tab in the More menu opens it beside the chat.
Keys What they do Right N Page Down / Left P Page Up Next / previous page Home / End First / last page G Go to a page + / - / 0 Zoom in / zoom out / fit width ? or F1 Keyboard shortcuts

What you see is what prints: each sheet on screen is the page the PDF export produces, scaled as a whole, so a line that fits on screen fits on paper.
