In the library, pages carry a paper badge (A4, LETTER) and open with Open rather than Present; the Decks / Pages pills above the list show one kind at a time.

docs.title: Change a deck
docs.text:
You never rebuild a deck from scratch. Ask the assistant for the change in the same conversation, and it changes the deck in place: the card in the chat and the link you already shared show the new version, and the viewer keeps your current slide instead of jumping back to the first one.

Move the roadmap before the numbers, add a slide comparing the two options, and make the closing slide warmer.

A small change stays small. "Change revenue to ARR on slide 12", "shorten this title", "swap the two columns", "delete the second bullet" edits exactly that slide, block or word: the assistant applies the change to the deck as it is stored rather than writing the whole deck again, so the other slides are not redrawn, reworded or reshuffled along the way — on a forty-slide deck as much as on a five-slide one. The reply says which slides changed and confirms that the rest are untouched, and the deck's History records the same thing (Edited slide 12). The layout check that follows every save looks at the slide that was edited — if the new wording no longer fits, the assistant trims that slide, not the others — while anything that was already tight elsewhere is left for you to raise, or for the viewer's Layout check; a change to the whole deck (a new theme, another aspect ratio) is checked on every slide, since every slide was redrawn. When two people edit the same deck, the second edit is applied to the deck as the first one left it — and if slides were added or reordered in between, the assistant re-reads the deck before touching a slide by its number, rather than editing whatever slide now sits there. Only a request that is genuinely a rewrite — a new outline, a different story — regenerates the deck.

Point at the slide

Naming the slide ("on slide 12", "the closing slide", or, in the studio, "this slide") is what keeps an edit surgical. A word that appears on several slides is changed only where you pointed; without a pointer, the assistant is shown every slide the word appears on before anything changes, so it changes them all on purpose or asks you which one you meant.

Small fixes need no assistant round-trip. In the standalone viewer, Edit slides turns the deck itself into an editor, the way a slide editor is expected to work, with a side panel beside it.

docs.title: Edit slides by hand
docs.text:
On the slide. Click a text and type: the caret lands where you clicked, the slide keeps its look while you type, and the panel's fields follow. Click a block — a list, a callout, a card, a table — to select it: an outline shows what you have, a small bar above it carries its actions (move up or down, duplicate, insert a block after it, delete), and the Selection tab of the panel shows every setting the block has. Clicking a selected list row, tile or card opens the one text it holds; a double-click does both at once; clicking the empty part of a slide selects the slide.

While a text is open, the bar above it formats the selection or the word at the caret: bold, emphasis, code, a tone (accent, info, success, warning, error, muted, gradient), clear formatting, a line break. What you see is what the deck stores — a formatting the deck's grammar cannot carry (an emphasis glued to the middle of a word, say) is written as plain text rather than as broken markup.

From the keyboard, with a block selected: Enter edits its main text, Tab / Shift+Tab move the selection to the next / previous block of the slide, Del deletes it, Ctrl+D duplicates it, Alt+Up / Alt+Down move it, Ctrl+S saves, Esc leaves the text, then the selection, then hands the keys back to the deck. While typing in a text: Enter inserts a line break, Ctrl+Enter (or a click elsewhere) keeps the change, Esc drops it, Ctrl+B / Ctrl+I / Ctrl+E toggle bold / emphasis / code.

Undo and redo — Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z; Cmd on a Mac) — work from anywhere while the panel is open: on the slide, on a floating bar, in the panel and in its fields, so a word typed in the inspector is taken back with the same keys as a block moved on the stage (the Undo / Redo buttons in the panel footer do the same, and the shortcuts sheet — ? or F1 — lists every editor key while the panel is open). A save does not end the history: undoing past it makes the deck dirty again, and the next save writes what you went back to as a new revision, the saved one staying in History. Discard is one more step, so it can be undone too. Inside a text you are editing in place, the same keys walk that text's own history — a burst of typing, a line break, each formatting — until you leave the field, and undoing puts the caret back where the change was made. The history starts over only when you leave the deck or take on someone else's version of it: a change a collaborator or the assistant saved while you had nothing unsaved is adopted as is, and Reload the latest version after the "changed since you started editing" notice drops your unsaved edits for good (as the button says) — the steps behind them were made on the deck as it no longer is.

In the panel:

  • Slides — a filmstrip of the deck: click a slide to go to it, reorder, duplicate or delete slides, change the composition of a slide with its layout picker (the layouts the deck's template offers, every layout for a deck without one; the slide's words move into the new shape and a toast says what was kept, derived or could not find a home), and Add slide with any layout after the current one — the stage lands on the new slide. Everything else about a slide — its look included — is one click away in Selection.
  • Selection — the slide or the block you selected, with every one of its settings: the title and subtitle, the alignment and the spread of a slide, its theme, its hero and overlay, its speaker notes; for a block, its content (the items of a list, the rows of a table, the tiles of a metrics grid — add, reorder, remove) and its style (size, tone, density, columns, alignment, icons, variants...). A setting left on Default follows the deck's design, exactly as when the assistant writes the slide. A setting that only acts on another shape of the slide — a column ratio on a slide with a single flow of blocks, a spread with one block — says so under its control rather than changing nothing silently; the value is kept and takes effect when the slide takes that shape. Insert a block from the palette here too — text, heading, quote, list, callout, metrics, table, badges, cards, timeline, columns, comparison... Blocks that need a file, numbers or a graph (an image, a logo grid, a chart, a diagram) are the assistant's: ask it in the studio.
  • Deck — the title, the template and the theme (Dark / Light, among the ones the template supports — see Template and theme), the header and footer pattern (the event, the classification, the footer text, the logo, the footer and the slide numbers — see Header and footer) and the slide transition.

To add a block, click the + under the last block of the slide (or of a column, or of the callout, comparison or columns block you selected) and pick one: it lands at the end of that run, selected. A slide's Selection tab offers the same under Add a block. On a slide with columns, or in a columns block, Equal row heights lines the blocks up as rows: the cards at the same place in each column share one height.

Nothing is written until you Save: every change is one undo step, Discard drops them all (and is itself undoable), and closing the panel (or the tab) with unsaved changes asks first. One save is one revision in the deck's History, named after what it touched (Edited slides 3, 7, Inserted slide 4, Moved slide 5 to 1). The slides keep the platform's layouts — you arrange blocks, you do not drag boxes around — which is what keeps a hand-edited deck one the assistant can still read, fit and export.

Decks from earlier versions

A deck built with an earlier version of the platform may use slide compositions that no longer exist. It keeps working: such a slide is shown as the closest current composition, with its words, notes and images intact, and is stored that way the next time the deck is saved. Nothing to do on your side — and if you ask the assistant to change one of these slides, its reply mentions the conversion.

Anything that needs judgement or material — a new argument, a chart from your numbers, an image, a whole section — is the assistant's job, and the place for it is the studio; the two work on the same deck, so a hand edit and a prompted edit follow each other in the same History.

docs.title: Edit in the studio
docs.text:
Studio, in the viewer toolbar, opens a chat beside the deck: the conversation on the left, the presentation on the right as a live preview. Edit with my assistant, on a card in the library, lands on the same screen.

  • The assistant you talk to already knows which presentation is open — its title, its slides, the revision you are looking at, and what you are allowed to do with it. There is nothing to load and no identifier to paste: "make the title shorter", "add a slide comparing the two options after this one", "warm up the closing" is enough. It also knows which slide is on your screen, so "this slide", "here" and "it" mean the one you are looking at.
  • Pick any of your chat agents from the menu at the top of the rail, or stay with the General Assistant. Whichever you pick has the presentation tools while it is in the studio, even if it does not carry them elsewhere — you never have to find "the agent that can edit slides" first.
  • Every change is applied to this presentation, in place: the deck on the right refreshes the moment the assistant saves, the link you shared stays the same, and the change lands in the deck's History like any other edit. The assistant only creates a new presentation if you ask for a copy.
  • The assistant shows you what it changed. When it edits a slide, the deck on the right moves to that slide as the save lands (unless you are presenting), its reply links the slides it touched — "done, see [slide 4]" — and clicking such a link moves the deck rather than opening a new tab (hold Ctrl or Cmd to open the viewer instead). The saved-receipt line in the rail reads Saved - slide 4 changed. with a Go to slide 4 shortcut. The same links work in the main chat: the inline preview opens on that slide, and a link pasted or shared elsewhere (/presentations/<id>#/<slide>) opens the viewer on it.
  • The rail is a full conversation: attach a file (a brief, numbers, a logo) with the paperclip, send a follow-up while the assistant is still working to steer it, and scroll up for earlier turns. If the deck came out of a conversation, the empty rail offers to continue that conversation, so nothing the assistant learned while building it is lost.
  • Make the rail as wide as you read. Drag the divider between the chat and the deck to widen the rail — up to half the screen, for the outline of a whole deck or a slide-by-slide review that would otherwise wrap every few words — and back again; the deck rescales as you drag. Double-click the divider to return to the default width. The divider works from the keyboard too (focus it, then Left / Right, Shift for bigger steps, Home / End for the narrowest and the widest). The width you pick is remembered in your browser for every presentation; it is not part of the link you share.
  • Collapse the rail with the chevron to give the deck the whole width; a thin Studio strip stays at the left edge to bring it back, with the conversation exactly where you left it. Present leaves the studio first — a chat beside a fullscreen deck would be invisible. While the rail is open, colleagues who have the deck open see you as editing.
  • The studio is for the people who can edit the deck. Someone who can only view it does not see Studio (nor the strip at the left edge, nor Open in studio on the card in a chat); Copy and edit with my assistant, on the library card, makes them a copy of their own and opens the studio on it.
  • The studio remembers the conversation in the page address (?studio=1&c=…), so reloading, bookmarking or pasting the link to yourself reopens the same chat beside the same deck.

The keyboard follows the focus: arrows typed in the composer never turn the page, and the deck's shortcuts work again as soon as you click back on it.

Two people, one deck

If a colleague or their assistant changes the deck while your edit panel is open, saving does not overwrite their work. The panel tells you the presentation changed and offers to reload the latest version before you apply your change again. The studio is subject to the same rule from the other side: the assistant reads the current revision before it edits, so a collaborator's change made a minute ago is not silently rewritten.

docs.title: Share a deck
docs.text:
A deck starts private to you. Share (on the card in the chat, in the viewer toolbar, or on the library card) opens the sharing dialog. Access is granted in the dialog, never by the link on its own:

  • share with specific people or groups, choosing Can view or Can edit for each
  • administrators can publish the deck to the whole company (optionally restricting it to the people and groups listed)
  • then copy the link to paste into a message

Under the link, Who can open this link says in words who it will open for — only you, the people and groups listed, or everyone in the company — and, while you have unsaved changes, that the new audience applies when you save. Anyone else who follows the link is told the presentation is not available.

Someone who can edit can open the deck, use Edit slides, and ask their own assistant to change it in place from the studio — the link stays the same for everyone. Someone who can view can open, present, export, duplicate and comment on it, and browse its History; the editing tools (Edit slides, the studio, the Layout check) are not offered to them, and their Copy and edit with my assistant action works on a copy of their own, leaving the original untouched.

Sharing never changes the slides: opening the dialog while someone's assistant is mid-edit cannot disturb their work.

docs.title: Work on a deck together
docs.text:
A shared deck is reviewed where it is presented. Three things in the viewer's toolbar are there for the people working on it with you:

Who is here. The initials beside Present are the people looking at the deck right now — hover one for the name, and for whether they are editing and which slide they are on. They appear as someone opens the deck and disappear within a minute of them leaving.

Comments. Comments opens a side panel of review notes. A note is attached to the slide you are on (or to the whole deck, if you say so), so a reviewer can write "this number is last quarter's" on the slide it concerns; clicking a note takes the deck to that slide. Anyone the deck is shared with can read and add notes and reply to them — reviewing is exactly what read-only access is for; you can edit and delete your own, and whoever manages the deck can tidy up any of them. When a note has been dealt with, Resolve moves it out of the way (the author or a manager decides) — Open and Resolved at the top of the panel switch between the two, and This slide narrows the list to the current slide. The count on the Comments button (and on the card in the library) is the number still open.

Your assistant works the comments with you. In the deck's conversation, ask it to "address the review comments" and it reads each open note with the slide it is about and changes the deck in place; ask it to "implement Ada's comment on slide 5 and close it" and it makes the change, then resolves that note — with a reply saying what was done, if you like. It can also leave notes for you ("comment on every slide where a number has no source"), read the resolved ones back, or reopen a thread that was closed too early. Everything it posts appears under your name, in the panel, the moment it is saved, and it can only close what you could close yourself: on a deck you merely view, it will reply to a note rather than resolve it. Nothing is resolved unless you ask — a reviewer asked a question, and you decide when it is answered. A note on a slide that was later deleted stays in the panel, marked Slide removed, so nothing a reviewer wrote is lost.

Writing a note yourself, Generate with AI under the text box drafts it for you: say what the note should convey ("ask for the source of the revenue figure") and the assistant writes it against the slide you are on — it sees the slide's content, not just your words — or against the thread you are replying to. If you have already typed a draft, the same button becomes Improve with AI and tightens what you wrote. The draft lands in the text box for you to edit and post, or discard; nothing is sent until you press Comment.

The panel is as wide as you read: drag its left edge to widen it — up to a third of the screen — and back again, or double-click the edge to return to the default width; the divider works from the keyboard too (focus it, then Left / Right, Home / End). The width you pick is remembered in your browser for the editor, history and comments panels alike.

History. Every save — an assistant generation, an edit in the panel, a restore — is kept as a numbered revision, with who made it, when, and what changed (Edited slides, title), the last thirty per deck. History opens the list; clicking a revision previews it in place, with a banner naming what you are looking at and Back to current beside it. Restore brings a revision back as the current version, and is itself a new revision, so a restore can be undone the same way. Restoring, like editing, needs edit access.

Working alone, none of this gets in your way: the buttons are quiet until someone leaves a note or a second person opens the deck.

docs.title: Export a deck
docs.text:
Export is available on the chat card and in the viewer toolbar. Every export is rendered by the platform itself from the same slides you see, so the result does not depend on your browser or zoom level:

Format What you get PDF (vector) One page per slide, with selectable text and the deck's own fonts. Page size matches PowerPoint's slide size, so a PDF page and a PowerPoint slide of the same deck have identical dimensions. PowerPoint (pixel-perfect) One full-slide image per slide, with the speaker notes attached. Opens anywhere and looks exactly like the screen. PowerPoint (editable shapes) Text boxes, cards, tables, badges, buttons and dividers as real PowerPoint shapes placed where the platform placed them — tinted columns, check marks and outlined display numbers included — so a colleague can keep editing in PowerPoint. Charts are real PowerPoint charts: a bar, stacked bar, line, area, pie or donut chart opens with its series, categories, colours and number formats, ready to be edited or re-pointed at new figures (see below). Icons, diagrams (architecture diagrams included), logos and gradient surfaces are embedded as images.

Print to PDF (browser), in the More menu of the card and of the viewer, is the fallback that needs nothing from the server: it opens the deck in your browser's print layout and starts the print dialog. In that dialog pick Save as PDF as the destination: the browser then uses the deck's own page size and every slide lands on a landscape page. Sending it to a printer instead - including a virtual one such as Microsoft Print to PDF - uses that printer's paper (usually portrait Letter or A4), so the slides come out rotated and boxed in the middle of each page.

The print dialog opens once every chart, diagram, icon and logo on the deck is drawn. A figure that cannot be drawn - its code could not be loaded, or it never finished loading - does not hold it forever: after a short wait the deck prints as it stands, and a notice (Part of the deck was not finished) says so when the dialog closes. Use the PDF (vector) export for the complete deck: it never exports a figure that could not be drawn, and fails with the reason instead, so it can be tried again.

Which PowerPoint export?

Use pixel-perfect when the deck is finished and only has to be presented from PowerPoint. Use editable shapes when someone will keep working on it there.

Charts in the exports. A chart on a slide is data the platform draws, not a picture, and each export treats it that way. The PDF keeps every chart as vector graphics in the deck's own colours and fonts — as sharp as the text next to it. The editable PowerPoint rebuilds bar, stacked bar, line, area, pie and donut charts as native PowerPoint charts: same series and categories, the palette of the deck's template, the same axis range and the same number formats (€29.5M, 86%, 12,400 users), the legend and the target line where the slide had them. Two kinds have no PowerPoint equivalent — a gauge and a combo chart (bars and a line on one plot) — and are placed as a high-resolution picture of the rendered figure instead. When that happens the export says so: a short note appears when the download starts (Exported with notes, naming the slide and the chart), and an assistant that exported the file for you lists the same notes in its reply, so nobody opens the file expecting to edit a chart that is a picture.

docs.title: Move a deck to another platform
docs.text:
The last entry of the Export menu, JSON package (import elsewhere), is not a rendering: it is the deck itself — its slides, the name of its template and every logo, diagram or image it uses, embedded in one <title>.presentation.json file. Import on the Presentations page reads that file back and creates the deck under your name, so a deck built on a staging or local platform continues on production, and a deck can be kept as a backup outside the platform.

On import, the platform first looks for what it already has: a template with the same name (a built-in brand deck the destination also ships, or a company template you recreated) and, inside it, the assets by filename — so a deck that uses the brand logos points at the destination's own logos and nothing is duplicated. When the template holds several files of that name (a dark and a light logo.svg), the one with the same content is used; if none has it, the one the template lists first is used and the confirmation says so. Only what is missing is copied out of the file, as files that belong to you. The confirmation says what happened: how many assets were matched, how many were copied, and which template the deck ended up on. If the template does not exist on the destination, the install's default template is used and the message says so; if a file can be neither matched nor copied, the import is refused naming it, rather than silently producing a deck with a hole in it. A picture that was already missing from the deck when it was exported is the exception: the deck imports without it, and the confirmation says how many.

The imported deck is a new deck — revision 1 in its history, with none of the original's shares or comments — and validates like any other: a package written by a newer platform whose slides use a layout the destination does not know yet is refused with the exact slide and field. A package embeds only the files you could download when exporting; a shared deck exports the files its owner shared with the deck, never anything else of theirs.

docs.title: Template and theme
docs.text:
Two words describe how a deck looks, and each means exactly one thing:

  • The template is the deck's design: a palette per theme, the heading and body fonts, the logos drawn on every slide, the predefined assets the assistant may place, and a few sentences of composition guidance. A deck wears one template, or none.
  • The theme is the colour scheme the deck is drawn in: Dark or Light, nothing else. A template supports the themes it has a palette for — a template designed only on a dark background supports Dark alone — so the theme picker of a deck only ever offers what its template supports. A deck with no template offers both.

Out of the box every platform ships with the read-only XTM One Brand Deck (the product's purple palette, Dark theme only). Creating your own — by hand, or from a brief and a logo with Generate with AI — is covered in Templates.

docs.title: Choose a template when you create a deck
docs.text:
• New presentation, on the Presentations page (and New presentation with this template on a template's page), asks which template the deck starts in — one of the templates you can see, No template - plain look, or Let my assistant ask me in the chat — the theme among the ones that template supports, and which assistant writes it (Written by: only the assistants that carry the Presentation Generation tool are offered, so the chat you land in can always produce the deck). It then opens the chat with the request written for you; add what the deck is about and send.
  • In a chat, when you ask for a presentation and you can see several templates, the template is your choice, never the assistant's: unless your request names one ("in the Sales template") or asks for "no template" (the plain built-in look), the assistant lists your templates and asks which one to use before creating anything — the platform refuses to create a new deck in a template you did not pick, even one the assistant would have chosen for you. It may recommend one, but the deck is created once you answer. With a single template in view, it is used and the reply says so.
  • Automations, and chats where the assistant cannot ask, use the default template an administrator sets in Settings > Parameters — the platform's built-in brand deck unless another company template was chosen.
  • On XTM One, the CTEM Assistant is the General Assistant of the platform and carries the presentation tools out of the box; on the Copilot edition the General Assistant does, and any agent an administrator gives the Presentation Generation tool to is offered as a writer.

docs.title: Change the template or the theme of a deck
docs.text:
A template is not copied into the deck: the deck stays linked to it. Its colours, fonts and logos are read from the template every time the deck is drawn, so editing the template restyles every deck wearing it, at once. Everything else — the slides, their words, the images you uploaded, the theme you picked — belongs to the deck.

Edit slides, in the viewer, opens the Design section: pick another template from the Template menu (or No template - plain look) and the deck restyles on screen before you save; the Theme toggle beside it offers Dark and Light and greys out what the chosen template does not support — switching to a template with a single palette snaps the deck to that theme. In a chat, "apply the Sales template" or "switch this deck to the light theme" does the same; the assistant tells you when a template cannot draw the theme you asked for. Deleting a template does not touch the decks that wore it: they keep their content and fall back to the plain look.

docs.title: A slide with its own theme
docs.text: A slide can be drawn in the other scheme than the deck: a dark cover and a dark closing slide over a light body is the classic shape of a brand deck. In the Selection tab of Edit slides, Theme offers Inherit, Dark and Light for the slide. Inherit — the default — follows the deck theme; Dark or Light fixes the slide's own scheme, and everything on it follows: its paper, its text, its tones and charts, and the logo variant drawn in its corner. A slide with a theme of its own keeps it whatever happens to the deck theme: switching the deck between Dark and Light changes only the slides that inherit (the Design section says how many slides keep their own theme), and the slide comes back to the deck only when you choose Inherit again. The template's rule applies to slides too — a slide can only take a theme the template supports, and a template that cannot draw a slide's theme snaps that slide the way it snaps the deck. In a chat, "make the cover dark" or "let slide 5 follow the deck again" does the same; the assistant's outline marks the slides that keep their own theme.

docs.title: Covers: hero backdrops
docs.text: A title or a closing slide has a hero — the backdrop behind its headline, drawn in the slide's own colours: Plain (the flat paper), Gradient (the brand gradient washed over the paper, with the template's mark as a faint watermark in the corner — the look of a brand cover), Split (the text on the left, a gradient panel on the right that carries the slide's background image when it has one) and Spotlight (a soft glow behind the headline and two thin arcs in the corner). Pick it in the Selection tab; a dark gradient cover on a light deck is the slide's theme set to Dark plus the Gradient hero. Under the hero, Hero colour says which colour of the template's palette the backdrop is drawn in — each chip is painted in the exact colour the slide will use: Brand gradient (the default — the template's gradient, from its first colour to its second), or one colour alone: Accent, Gradient start, Gradient end, one of the Info / Success / Warning / Error tones, or Muted. On the XTM One Brand Deck the gradient runs from the product purple into cyan, so a cover that should stay purple picks Accent (or Gradient start); an incident review can open on an Error red spotlight. On a title slide, Accent the last line of the title colours the last line of the headline (after a line break — or its last word) in the accent tone, so "Uncover Threats. / Take Action." reads the way the brand deck does without any formatting in the text. Any slide with a background image can also take an overlay — None, Soft or Strong — a scrim between the picture and the text so the headline stays readable. Templates can set the cover defaults for new decks — the hero, its colour and the slide's theme (the XTM One Brand Deck opens and closes on a gradient cover) — and everything exports as it shows: the PDF draws each slide in its own colours, and the PowerPoint carries the backdrop as a picture under editable text.

docs.title: Header and footer
docs.text:
The line at the bottom of every slide is not written on the slides. It is drawn from a handful of deck settings, so it is set once and never edited slide by slide — and it cannot drift: a footer that reads the deck's title changes on every slide the moment the deck is renamed.

A template can define the footer (and, optionally, a header) for every deck wearing it, as a pattern such as {{event}} - {{title}} - {{classification}}. {{title}} is the deck's title, {{subtitle}} the subtitle of its opening slide (as plain text — the footer never shows inline emphasis), {{event}} the event you set; anything else — a classification, a client, a version — is a field the template declares with a label and, optionally, a default. Both built-in brand decks define {{event}} - {{title}} - {{classification}}; like the event, the classification is empty until you set one. An empty part disappears together with its separator, so a deck with no event reads Quarterly review - Confidential, not - Quarterly review - Confidential, and a deck with neither reads Quarterly review.

Edit slides, in the viewer, has a Header & footer section:

  • Show logo, Show footer (and the header, when the template defines one) and Show slide numbers switch each part of the furniture on or off for the whole deck. Opening, section and closing slides never carry the footer; a body slide can leave it out on its own (hide_footer).
  • Event names the occasion — a conference, a customer meeting, a board date.
  • One field per variable the template declares (Classification for the brand deck), labelled by the template, with its default shown greyed until you type. A deck wearing a template with no pattern, or no template at all, gets a free Footer text instead, drawn after the event.
  • The Footer preview line shows exactly what every slide will read as you type; the panel tells you when the footer switch hides it.

In a chat, "mark this deck Confidential", "set the event to FIC 2026" or "hide the slide numbers" changes those settings — one field, not thirty slides — and the assistant's reply says what the footer now reads. Exports (PDF and PowerPoint) draw the same line. How a template declares its pattern is covered in Templates.

docs.title: The Presentations page
docs.text:
Work > Presentations in the sidebar lists every deck you can see, most recently changed first. Search by title, and narrow the list to Mine, Shared or Company. Each card shows the slide count, the template it wears and its theme (Dark or Light), the owner, when it last changed, and - as icons on the right of the attribute row - whether it is shared with you, company-managed, or view only. Click anywhere on a card to open the deck. The card's footer carries Present (or Open for a page), Edit with my assistant (which opens the deck with the studio beside it), and a menu with Share, Duplicate, and Delete for a deck you manage. Import, next to New presentation, reads a JSON package exported from another platform (see Move a deck to another platform).

Deleting a deck removes it for everyone it was shared with; a chat message that embedded it then shows the deck as no longer available.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Set up the brand your decks are generated in with Templates.

docs.title: Webhook triggers
docs.text:
A webhook trigger lets another system start an assignment. Your SIEM raises an alert, your SOAR runs a playbook, your ticketing tool opens a case — each of them can post to a URL, and the agent starts working on what it received.

This page covers where to find that URL, how to authenticate a call to it, and how to wire it up from a SOAR playbook.

docs.title: Find the URL and the secret
docs.text:
Open the agent, find the assignment in the Assignments card, and open it. On the Trigger card of an assignment whose Trigger type is Webhook you will see:

  • Webhook URL — the address the sending system posts to. It already contains the assignment identifier, so there is nothing else to configure.
  • Webhook secret — the credential the sending system must present. Every webhook assignment gets one automatically.
  • How to trigger — a ready-to-paste request you can copy, adapt, and test with before you touch the other system.

Who can see the secret

The secret is only shown to people who can manage the assignment. If the Trigger card shows the URL but no secret, ask whoever owns the assignment for it.

docs.title: Authenticate the request
docs.text:
Send the secret in one of these headers — verbatim, except in the Authorization form, which takes the Bearer prefix:

Header Value X-Webhook-Token the secret, verbatim X-Webhook-Secret the same thing, under the name the Webhook secret label suggests Authorization Bearer <secret>, for senders that only offer standard authentication fields X-OpenCTI-Token the original spelling, still accepted so existing senders keep working — use one of the names above for anything new

This is what almost every SIEM and SOAR webhook action can produce, and it is the scheme to reach for first. A secret with non-ASCII characters is matched whether the sender writes the header in UTF-8 or in latin-1.

If your sender can compute an HMAC over the request body, you can sign it instead and keep the secret off the wire: put the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body in X-Signature. Provider-specific signatures — GitHub, Slack — are recognized as well.

A correct URL is not enough

A request that carries none of these headers is refused with 401, even when the URL and the secret are both right. The most common cause is a header sent under a name that is not on the list above. Every webhook assignment is created with a secret, and administrators can additionally require one platform-wide — see Configuration.

docs.title: Trigger from a Google SecOps SOAR playbook
docs.text:
The native webhook action in a SecOps SOAR playbook only offers a URL and a token, with nowhere to put a header. Use the generic Execute HTTP request action instead, configured like this:

Field Value Method POST URL Path the Webhook URL from the Trigger card Headers {"Content-Type": "application/json", "X-Webhook-Token": "<the webhook secret>"} Body Payload the JSON you want the agent to receive, for example {"case_id": "[Case.case_id]", "alert_name": "[Alert.alert_name]"} Fail on 4xx/5xx true Request Timeout 120

Do not paste the secret in clear

Store it in the SecOps SOAR credential store (or an environment parameter) and reference it as a placeholder instead of the literal value. Playbooks are exported, cloned between environments and often committed, and this credential is long-lived and travels on the wire with every delivery. Anyone who obtains a copy can authenticate any body against your assignment until someone rotates the secret. An X-Signature HMAC is bound to the exact body it signed and never puts the secret on the wire at all, so senders that can compute one should prefer it.

Three things to get right:

  • Write plain JSON in Headers and Body Payload. The field expects JSON as-is. Escaping the quotes — {\"Content-Type\": \"application/json\"} — makes the playbook reject the value before the request is ever sent, with a message about an invalid JSON structure.
  • Keep the placeholders inside the quotes. "[Alert.alert_name]" is valid JSON; an unbalanced quote around a placeholder is not, and the request fails for a reason that has nothing to do with XTM One.
  • Leave Fail on 4xx/5xx on. It is what makes a refused or throttled delivery visible in the playbook instead of passing for a success.

docs.title: Event matching
docs.text:
A trigger that selects events - an integration event such as GitHub pull_request, or the events list of a webhook trigger - runs on exactly the events it selects:

  • pull_request runs on pull_request and its actions (pull_request.opened, pull_request.closed, ...), never on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, whose names only start with it.
  • An events entry works the same way: issues.opened matches issues.opened, never issues.opened_by_bot.

A trigger saved on a version before exact matching keeps the prefix match it always had, so nothing that ran before stops running: pull_request also runs on pull_request_review, an events entry also matches any event whose name starts with it, and a GitHub trigger on its dedicated URL runs on every delivery it receives, ping included. It keeps that through every edit that leaves its events alone - a new name, prompt, delay, filter or integration - and through every copy: duplicate, import, catalog clone.

The Trigger card says which mode an assignment uses: Exact event matching with what it runs on, or Legacy event matching with the events it also runs on because of the prefix match. A legacy trigger switches to exact matching when you:

  • choose Use exact matching on its Trigger card, or
  • choose its events again in the trigger editor - another event, provider or trigger type. The editor says so before you save.

Administrators can apply exact matching to every trigger at once: Settings > Security > Exact event matching for every trigger, or WEBHOOK_EXACT_EVENT_MATCHING=true, which wins. See Configuration.

Triggers the agent builder created before this version

The agent builder used to store an integration event under event_type, a key the platform does not read: such a trigger runs on every event its provider delivers by webhook, and a polled one (a new email, a new message) never runs. It keeps behaving that way until you choose Use exact matching on its Trigger card: it then runs only on the event it names, and a polled one starts with its next new event. The Trigger card and the security audit point these triggers out.

docs.title: When something does not arrive
docs.text:
Read the response the sending system got:

What you see What it means 401 Missing webhook signature… No recognized credential header. Check the header name first — the secret is usually fine. The rest of the message lists the headers you can send. 401 Invalid webhook token A token header is right, its value is not. Copy the secret again from the Trigger card. 401 Invalid webhook bearer token Same, for the Authorization: Bearer form. 401 Invalid webhook signature The body was signed with a different secret, or the signature was computed over a modified body. 429 Too many deliveries, or too many already waiting. Retry after the delay given in the response. "status": "ignored" The delivery was accepted but matched nothing — the assignment is disabled, deleted, or not a webhook assignment. "reason": "event not selected" A GitHub delivery to the dedicated URL of an integration-event assignment that matches exactly, for an event its trigger does not select. Check the event on the Trigger card, or the events the GitHub webhook sends (see Event matching).

Everything that did start is in Work history, including runs still waiting behind an active one. An assignment runs up to ASSIGNMENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS deliveries at once (10 by default, or its trigger's max_concurrent_runs), so a delivery arriving while they are all going is queued rather than lost, and starts as soon as one ends. A pushed integration event arriving then - a GitHub delivery to an integration-event assignment, for example - is skipped instead, unless an administrator turned on INTEGRATION_EVENT_QUEUE_ENABLED; a polled one (an email, a Teams or Slack message) always waits in the queue. See Webhook delivery.

Administrators can tune the delivery limits, the queue depth, and the de-duplication window — see Configuration.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Work history to follow what your triggered runs actually did, or with Agents if you still have to create the agent behind the assignment.

docs.title: Work history
docs.text: History is where you review what agents have already done. It is the operational record for runs, waiting items, notifications, and failures.

docs.title: What Work History is for
docs.text:
Use History when you want to:

  • check whether a task is still running
  • review a completed result
  • respond to a request for human input
  • isolate notifications or digests
  • follow work that moved between agents

docs.title: Open History
docs.text:
Choose Work > Operations from the left sidebar. The Work group gathers what your agents produce — Operations (their runs), Presentations (their decks) and Files (their outputs and your uploads) — and the Work hub page shows the three at a glance.

Operations opens on its Executions tab, which is the run history described in this chapter. The other tabs — Background Tasks, Work Items, Shared State, Worksets — cover the delegations, durable work items, cross-run state and corpora your agents coordinate through.

Work items and shared state written by a company-managed agent are company-managed: everyone who can use that agent sees them, and they are read-only for everyone else. Only company-managed agents (whoever they are working for) and administrators can change them, claim them or delete them; a company-managed flow can also claim and settle the company-managed work items its work-item trigger picks up. Your own agents and flows can read them but not change them, and on these tabs only an administrator can resolve, complete or delete a company-managed entry, including one created while you were chatting with a company-managed agent.

A company-managed agent can narrow this for what it produces: its Coordination access, in the Built-in Tools card of its configuration, says which agents can read and which can change the work items it creates and the shared state it owns - everyone and every company-managed agent (the default), selected company-managed agents, or only itself. An agent that can change them can always read them, and the agent a work item is assigned to, and the agent that claimed it, can always work on it. An agent left out of an entry never sees it, so two groups of agents narrowed to themselves can each use the same key for their own entry. The setting applies at once to what the agent already created. It only concerns agents: these tabs show the same rows as before, and administrators keep full access.

The Executions tab shows runs across your visible agents. It is designed for filtering first and investigation second.

docs.title: Use the main filter tabs
docs.text:
At the top of the page, XTM One provides quick filter tabs.

You can switch between:

  • All
  • Notifications
  • Digests
  • Running
  • Awaiting Input
  • Completed
  • Failed

These tabs are the fastest way to narrow the page to the type of work you care about.

docs.title: Use the other filters
docs.text:
In addition to the main tabs, you can refine the list with:

  • search
  • ownership
  • agent selection

Ownership usually includes:

  • All
  • My Runs
  • Shared Runs

This is useful when you work in a shared environment and only want to focus on your own workload or on cross-team runs.

docs.title: Understand the run cards
docs.text:
Each run card gives you a quick status summary.

You may see:

  • the agent name
  • the assignment or run title
  • a short summary
  • the current state
  • the creation time
  • delegation indicators

Typical states include:

  • running
  • awaiting human input
  • completed
  • failed

docs.title: Notifications and digests
docs.text:
The Notifications and Digests filters are there for communication-oriented runs.

Use them when you want to:

  • review automated updates sent by the platform
  • separate digest-style outputs from normal task runs
  • find communication outputs without scanning every run

docs.title: When a run is waiting for you
docs.text:
Some runs pause and ask for human input.

When that happens:

  • the run appears under Awaiting Input
  • the run detail page shows the question or pending action
  • you can respond directly from the run
  • you can dismiss the waiting item if it is no longer needed

This is the main place where human approval or clarification appears in the UI.

docs.title: When an integration resource goes missing
docs.text:
An assignment can keep pointing at something its integration can no longer see - a Notion database that was deleted, moved, or is no longer shared with the integration. A single miss can be a typo in one run, so it changes nothing. When the integration reports the same resource missing in two separate runs, the platform treats it as the assignment's configuration:

  • the run that used it again is marked failed with the cause Integration resource missing, and its error names the resource and the integration; whatever the agent produced stays in the result
  • the assignment owner gets one notification when this starts, not one per run
  • after a few consecutive scheduled runs like this (three by default), the assignment is paused; the assignment page shows why, and Resume switches it back on

To fix it, share the resource with the integration again, or update the assignment so it no longer uses it, then resume the assignment. Resuming starts a fresh count, and a scheduled run that succeeds ends the episode. Only a resource the agent used counts: an id it only read along the way - the target of a relation, a child block, a search result - never fails a run.

docs.title: When an assignment's owner is deactivated
docs.text:
While an administrator has disabled the account that owns an assignment, nothing starts that assignment unless it is company-managed - an assignment whose agent is shared with a group or a person pauses too: not its schedule, webhooks, integration events or work items, not a chained assignment or a retry, not a flow step, and not a manual run, whoever asks - an administrator included. The assignment page and the agent's assignment list show it as paused because its owner's account is deactivated.

  • nothing about the assignment itself changes: its own on / off switch and any pause its owner set are kept, so re-enabling the account resumes it exactly as it was, and a schedule that came due meanwhile runs once, as after a resume
  • a run that was already waiting to start (a delayed run, a queued webhook delivery, a retry) is marked skipped with the reason when it would have started; a run in progress finishes, but one that stopped to wait (for a partner's answer, for example) is marked skipped - stopped before resuming - when it would go on
  • a webhook delivery to it is answered ignored with the reason; a question it asked stays pending until the account is back (dismissing it still works)
  • company-managed assignments are not affected: they keep running even when the administrator who created them is deactivated
  • to keep one running while the account stays disabled - a shared agent other people rely on, for example - an administrator transfers its agent to an active owner or makes the agent company-managed

docs.title: Open a run detail page
docs.text:
Click any run to open the detailed view.

The run detail page usually includes:

  • the run title
  • the status
  • the agent
  • the trigger that started the run
  • timestamps for created, started, and completed states
  • shortcuts to the related agent, assignment, or parent run

docs.title: Review the result
docs.text:
For completed runs, the detail page helps you understand what happened.

Depending on the run, you may see:

  • a final summary
  • tool actions
  • intermediate reasoning or step history
  • output sent to another system
  • child runs created through delegation

This makes the page useful both for everyday checking and for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Rate the result
docs.text:
Once a run has completed or failed, the Result card asks Was this result useful? with a thumbs up and a thumbs down, like the buttons under an answer in the chat. A thumbs down lets you say what went wrong. Your rating is yours: rating again replaces it, and clicking the thumb you chose removes it.

The same rating is offered wherever an agent's work can be read: on a finished background task that was started from a chat (in Operations > Background Tasks; a task started by an assignment is rated on its run page), and on the answer an agent gave when another agent consulted it for you, in the agent's Delegations tab (a background task is rated as the task or its run, and a transferred conversation in the chat, so the same work is never rated twice). The people who manage the agent see every rating in its Feedback tab, with a link to the rated run or conversation when they may open it.

When your administrators have defined feedback criteria (Settings > Quality), the dialog also asks you to score each of them, such as the accuracy of the answer on a scale of 1 to 5 or its tone. Score what matters to you and skip the rest: a thumb alone is still a complete rating.

docs.title: Follow delegated work
docs.text:
One run can create more runs if work is handed to another agent.

Use the history list and the detail page together to understand:

  • where the work started
  • whether another agent took over
  • which parts succeeded or failed

This is especially important in environments that use multi-agent flows.

docs.title: Bulk actions
docs.text:
The history page also supports selection and cleanup actions.

Depending on your permissions, you may be able to:

  • select multiple visible runs
  • delete selected runs
  • select all runs matching the current filters

Bulk actions are useful when you need to clean up large sets of test runs or old operational records.

docs.title: Administrator-only cleanup
docs.text:
Administrators can also see Cleanup Stale Runs.

This action is meant for recovery situations, such as:

  • a restart left some runs stuck
  • a run exceeded its timeout
  • the page still shows work as running when it should have failed

The cleanup action marks those stale runs as failed so the history becomes accurate again.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: The next chapter covers Resources, which includes knowledge bases, prompts, skills, MCP servers, tools, variables, and integrations.

docs.title: Foundations
docs.text:
This section introduces the concepts behind the product before the rest of the guide walks through individual screens. It is most useful when you are new to XTM One, when the object names still feel abstract, or when you are moving between XTM One and other Filigran products.

The pages cover:

  • Data model — the main platform objects.
  • Relationships and nesting — how one object references another.
  • Containers and scopes — how work is grouped and where visibility applies.
  • Reuse and deduplication — when to reuse a shared object and when to create a copy.
  • Trust, review, and confidence — how to judge AI outputs operationally.
  • Meaning of dates and status — the timestamps and status labels you see across the product.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Start with Data model, then continue through the rest of the Foundations pages before the screen-by-screen guides.

docs.title: Containers and scopes
docs.text: Some pages in XTM One are about one specific object. Others are about a container that groups many objects, or a scope that sets a visibility boundary.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
A container is any object or view whose main role is to hold and organize related work. It usually shows the items it contains and lets you add or remove them. The main ones:

  • Conversations keep the messages, context, and history of one chat thread together.
  • Knowledge bases group documents and import sources into one searchable corpus.
  • AI Catalog entries group shareable resources into published packages that other users can review and clone.

Being inside a container does not always mean ownership: a prompt attached to an agent is still reusable elsewhere, and a catalog item added to your account usually becomes a new local copy rather than a live link to the source.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
A scope is the boundary that decides where an object is visible and who can edit it:

  • Personal — belongs to one user; the safest place to experiment, since edits stay local.
  • Shared — visible to the groups or people it is shared with. Each share has a permission: Can configure lets them edit it too, Full access (incl. chats) (agents only) also lets them read the agent's conversations, and Read only lets them look but not change it; a read-only share shows a Read-only badge and says so instead of offering an Edit button.
  • Company-managed — visible to everyone but usually edited only by admins; the broadest scope in day-to-day use.

docs.title: Before you change something
docs.text: Ask whether you are editing the container itself or an item inside it, and whether the change affects only you, your group, or the whole company. Those two questions prevent most accidental changes.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Reuse and deduplication, which explains when XTM One keeps a shared object, when it creates a copy, and how to avoid duplicate setup.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
XTM One is easier to understand when you treat it as a set of connected objects rather than a set of disconnected screens. The same object can appear in Chat, the Agentic Flow graph, History, and the AI Catalog without becoming four different things.

At a high level there are three kinds of things: assistants that do work, resources those assistants rely on, and records that show what happened.

docs.title: Assistants and records
docs.text:
• Agents are the main assistants. An agent bundles its instructions and persona, tools, knowledge bases, prompts and skills, assignments, handovers, and memory. If you remember one object type, remember this one.
  • Assignments are automation rules inside an agent — they define what triggers the work and what the agent does when it runs. They are not separate assistants.
  • Runs are the execution records created when assignments or other background work happen. They tell you whether the work ran, is still running, failed, is waiting for a person, or what it produced — the operational layer of the product.
  • Conversations are the chat sessions between a user and the General Assistant or a specific agent. The conversation holds the discussion; the agent stays the reusable assistant behind it.

docs.title: Reusable resources
docs.text: The Resources area holds the building blocks agents and chats depend on: knowledge bases (searchable documents), prompts (reusable instructions), skills (reusable instruction packages), MCP servers (external tools over the Model Context Protocol), tools (built-in or custom actions), and integrations (connections to outside systems).

docs.title: Access and sharing
docs.text: Users have personal settings and access; groups are used for controlled sharing. Most objects have one visibility state — personal, shared with a group, or company-managed — which decides who can edit them and whether you should reuse an object or copy it.

docs.title: How it appears in the UI
docs.text: Most areas follow the same pattern: a list page, a detail page, and tabs for overview, configuration, activity, and related records. The UI is not inventing a new concept on every screen — it shows different views of the same underlying objects. In practice they chain together: a user opens an agent, the agent contains assignments and references resources, running it creates a run in History, and chatting with it is stored in a conversation.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Relationships and nesting, which explains how these objects point to one another and where configuration actually lives.

docs.title: Meaning of dates and status
docs.text: XTM One shows many timestamps and status labels, and they do not all mean the same thing. The common confusion is between when a record was created or changed in XTM One, when outside data was last refreshed, when a run started or finished, and whether an assistant or connection is healthy right now.

docs.title: Two families of dates
docs.text:
Technical dates describe what happened inside XTM One — created, updated, refreshed, synced, last heartbeat. They tell you about platform freshness and maintenance state.

Operational dates describe the lifecycle of work — scheduled for, started, completed, awaiting input since, last run. They tell you what happened in the workflow.

A few worth pinning down: created/updated are when a record was made or last changed in XTM One; started/completed are when a run began and finished; last heartbeat is when a connected platform last reported health; synced/refreshed is when imported content was last updated from its source.

docs.title: Status labels
docs.text: Dates read best alongside status. Enabled/disabled describe whether an object is active for use. Connected, stale, or disconnected describe the health of an external connection. Running, awaiting input, completed, and failed describe the state of a run.

docs.title: How to read a page
docs.text: On configuration pages, dates usually describe the object record. On history pages, they describe execution lifecycle. On connection cards, they describe freshness or health. For example, an agent with a recent updated date changed its configuration recently — it does not mean it ran recently; and a run with an old started time and no completion may be stuck or waiting.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Return to the main guide and continue with the Home Dashboard chapter.

docs.title: Reuse and deduplication
docs.text: XTM One works best when teams reuse shared building blocks instead of recreating the same setup many times. Without a clear reuse model, you quickly end up with duplicate agents, copied prompts that drift apart, repeated tool configuration, and confusion about which version is the real one.

docs.title: Reuse first
docs.text:
Before creating something new, check whether the platform already has a shared agent, a reusable prompt or skill, an existing knowledge base, a configured MCP server or integration, or a catalog item you can add instead of rebuilding. In many environments, reuse is the right default.

The platform keeps one shared object when several agents point to the same prompt, skill, MCP server, or knowledge base, or when a company-managed or group-shared object is intentionally reused. It is not silently duplicated.

docs.title: When to make a copy
docs.text:
XTM One creates or expects a copy when you duplicate an agent, add a catalog item to your account, or export and re-import an object. Do this on purpose when you need different behavior, are testing a private variation, do not have edit rights on the shared original, or want the shared object to stay stable for everyone else.

The practical rule: edit the shared object when the whole team should benefit; duplicate it when only your version should change. This matters most for prompts, skills, and agents. Do not create a copy just because you found the shared version first.

docs.title: Avoiding duplicate setups
docs.text:
• Search before creating.
  • Check whether a company-managed or shared version already exists.
  • Use Duplicate only when behavior must diverge.
  • Reuse prompts, skills, MCP servers, and knowledge bases whenever possible.
  • Use the AI Catalog when you want a structured starting point rather than a manual rebuild.

XTM One also deduplicates operationally — for example, agent memory maintenance avoids storing the same fact repeatedly. From a user perspective the key idea is simple: prefer a stable shared source when one already exists.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Trust, review, and confidence, which explains how to judge AI output and understand operational trust signals in XTM One.

docs.title: Relationships and nesting
docs.text: Objects in XTM One are rarely isolated. Most of the platform works because one object references, includes, or configures another. When you look at a page, it helps to know whether you are editing the object itself, editing a child that belongs to it, or linking a reusable object that lives elsewhere.

docs.title: Linked resources vs. nested configuration
docs.text:
Two patterns cover most of the product:

  • Linked resources are references between standalone objects — an agent references knowledge bases, prompts, skills, integrations, MCP servers, and tools; a group gives users access to shared objects. The referenced object keeps its own identity and life elsewhere, so one prompt, skill, MCP server, or knowledge base can serve many agents. Changing a shared resource can therefore affect more than one page.
  • Nested configuration is stored inside a parent object rather than as a separate shared item — an assignment belongs to one agent, a persona belongs to its agent, channel behavior belongs to the agent or the shared bot, personal tool overrides belong to the user profile. Here you are editing the current object, not a library item.

Agents are where most of this comes together — they contain assignments, reference reusable resources, point to handover targets, and expose themselves through chat, channels, or MCP. That is why the agent detail page is often the best place to understand the rest of the model.

docs.title: Overrides and inheritance
docs.text: Some settings inherit rather than link one-to-one: channel behavior can inherit from the channel bot, profile preferences can override platform defaults, and user-level MCP exposure can be narrower than the global setting. When a value is empty, it usually means inherit, not disabled.

docs.title: How to read a page
docs.text: If the page shows a reusable entity card or picker, you are usually linking objects, and a change can affect shared behavior. If it shows inline form fields with no separate entity page, you are usually editing nested configuration that stays local.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Containers and scopes, which explains how work is grouped and where organizational boundaries apply.

docs.title: Trust, review, and confidence
docs.text: XTM One does not reduce trust to a single score. You judge it through ownership, run status, review steps, and source visibility — deciding whether an answer is ready to use, still needs review, where it came from, and who owns the underlying configuration.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: Who manages an object is the first trust signal. Personal objects are yours — good for testing, but not a shared standard. Group-shared objects are collaborative team assets that can change as the group edits them. Company-managed objects usually represent the most stable, broadly approved standard, and are often the best starting point.

docs.title: Run status
docs.text:
Execution state is the second signal. Running means work is still in progress. Awaiting input means the system is waiting for a human decision, so the output is not final. Completed means the run finished normally, though you may still want to review the result before acting on it externally. Failed means the work did not complete and should not be treated as final.

Some workflows pause for a person on purpose — a draft to review before sending, a question that needs a human answer, an approval gate mid-workflow. When you see this, the platform is intentionally asking for human judgment.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: To judge an output, look at which agent produced it, which tools or integrations were used, which knowledge base or source material was involved, and whether the configuration was shared or private. The run detail page and the surrounding object pages are the best places to inspect that context.

docs.title: Good working habits
docs.text:
• Treat AI output as proposed work, not automatic truth.
  • Prefer company-managed or well-reviewed shared resources for important tasks.
  • Review Awaiting Input and draft states carefully.
  • Open the related run or object page when you need more context.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with Meaning of dates and status, which explains how to interpret timestamps and lifecycle signals across XTM One.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Resources is the working area for the reusable building blocks behind agents and conversations. If agents are the assistants, resources are the things those assistants rely on.

This page is the summary view. For a tour of one resource type — its screens, actions, and good habits — continue with the detailed guides:

  • Integrations
  • Knowledge bases
  • MCP servers
  • Platform MCP servers
  • Platform tools MCP server
  • Prompts
  • Sharing and access: who can use what you lend, and through what
  • Skills
  • Templates
  • Tools
  • Variables

You usually come here when you are preparing an agent, improving an existing setup, or checking how a workflow gets its data and actions.

docs.title: The resource types
docs.text:
• Knowledge bases store documents and indexed content that agents can search, so answers are grounded in trusted material. Content can be uploaded directly or kept in sync from external sources such as websites, Notion, cloud storage, and GitHub.
  • Prompts are reusable text instructions that keep wording consistent across chat requests, agent behavior, and recurring workflows.
  • Skills are reusable instruction sets — a packaged behavior or method — that can be attached to agents. A skill can be authored directly or fetched from a source URL.
  • Templates hold the brand behind generated presentations, reports and dashboards — palette, typefaces, layouts, logos and composition guidance — so the same request produces on-brand output for everyone. A read-only brand template, the XTM One Brand Deck, ships with every platform.
  • MCP servers expose external tools to XTM One in a controlled way. Use them when agents need capabilities such as search, data lookups, or system actions provided through MCP.
  • Tools are the actions agents can use directly. In standard XTM One this is mainly built-in tools (image generation, code interpreter, web fetch, browser, and the platform tool); some deployments also allow custom tools.
  • Variables store reusable values that resolve at runtime in prompts, personas, skills, and tools, so key values are not repeated by hand. Values can be marked Secret.
  • Integrations connect XTM One to external services such as email, ticketing, messaging, and cloud document systems, giving agents live access to those systems.

docs.title: Grid and list views
docs.text:
Every resource list page — and the Agents page — can be displayed two ways. The toggle sits at the right of the filter row, next to the item count.

  • Grid is the default: one card per item, optimized for browsing and recognizing things at a glance.
  • List shows the same items as table rows. It fits far more per screen and exposes extra attributes side by side, so you can compare a whole fleet at once — which model each agent runs, which tools are enabled, how many documents each knowledge base holds.

On the Agents page, favorites (the star on a card or row) sit above every other item in both views — sorting a column reorders the favorites among themselves rather than sending them back into the pile.

In list view, click a column header to sort by it; click again to reverse the order. Items with no value for that column (no model pinned, never fetched) always stay at the bottom, in both directions. Every action available on a card — opening the item, enabling or disabling it, starting a chat, copying a variable reference — is available on the matching row.

Your choice is remembered per page and across sessions, so a page you prefer as a table stays a table the next time you sign in.

docs.title: Platform MCP servers
docs.text:
XTM One is not only an MCP client — it is also an MCP server for the connected Filigran platforms. As soon as an OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ instance is registered with XTM One, external MCP clients (Cursor, Claude Desktop, and others) can connect to /mcp/opencti, /mcp/openaev, and /mcp/opencrq with a personal API key and work with threat intelligence, exposure validation, and governance-risk-compliance content directly.

See Platform MCP servers for endpoints, authentication, the tool surface, and client configuration.

docs.title: Platform tools MCP server
docs.text:
XTM One also exposes itself over MCP, on /mcp/xtm: agent traces, agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, and variables — scoped to what the calling user can already see and manage. It is how you read an agent's traces from Claude Desktop or Cursor and fix its configuration without leaving the client. Off by default; an administrator enables it in Settings > MCP Endpoint.

See Platform tools MCP server.

docs.title: How the resource types work together
docs.text:
In a typical workflow:

  • an integration connects to the outside system
  • a knowledge base provides trusted context
  • a prompt or skill shapes the behavior
  • a tool performs an action
  • a variable avoids repeating key values

This is why Resources matters so much. It is the place where assistants become usable and consistent.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with the detailed guide of the resource type you need, starting with Integrations.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
This page complements Integrations in XTM One.

That guide explains when integrations matter. This page gives you a quick tour of the integration screens.

Each first-party provider card in the integration catalog carries a diagonal corner ribbon. Certified marks the integrations Filigran qualifies and supports: OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ (the product marketed as OpenCRQ). Preview marks every other catalog entry. Custom providers you import yourself carry no ribbon — the qualification is ours to make about our own catalog, not about your bundles — and are identified by their Custom badge instead.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text:
In the left navigation, this area is Integrations. The list page answers one practical question fast: which external connections are usable right now.

Each card is status-heavy by design, so the list already works as a health dashboard. The status badge is the signal to read first — it distinguishes a connection that is ready, one that is configured but not yet authorized, and one that needs re-authorization because permissions changed or the provider refused its refresh token or client credentials. You can search by name or provider and filter by visibility, tags, or category to narrow a long list.

If you have permission, New Integration starts a new connection. Credentials are always encrypted in the database.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text:
Opening an integration shows a header with the connection status and the actions that make sense for it — a setup guide for provider prerequisites, Test Connection to validate the live connection, Authorize or Re-authorize to resolve OAuth state, and delete. The detail page itself is organized into Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

When Test Connection reports a failure the platform recorded earlier - such as the last rule sync of the Nova integration - the stored error is shown only to the people who can manage the integration (administrators, for a company-managed integration). Everyone else sees that the check failed and a sentence saying who can see the details; the server log always keeps the full error.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview tells you not only whether the integration works, but why it does or does not. It combines usage figures, the connection state (authentication method, credential readiness, authorized and missing scopes), and cards showing which agents — and, for sync sources, which knowledge bases — depend on it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is a richer screen than most other resources because it mixes three concerns: the integration's identity, its authentication and provider setup, and its visibility and reuse in the workspace. The description field matters more than it looks — the UI passes it to agents as tool context.

This tab is also where you see what the integration actually does:

  • The available tools are split into read tools (retrieve or inspect information) and write tools (change something in the connected system). That split helps you judge risk. When the integration is connected, you can test a tool with real credentials before binding it to an agent.
  • If the provider supports events, an event triggers card explains, in business language, which external changes an agent can react to and how they are delivered (webhook, polling, or hybrid).
  • A webhooks card shows how external events enter XTM One. Depending on the provider it can display a URL to copy or, for GitHub, let you create and remove repository webhooks directly from the UI. What it shows follows the provider and the OAuth app the integration uses:
    • Microsoft 365: new emails and Teams messages are picked up by polling every 5 minutes, so there is no webhook to configure.
    • Slack: new messages are picked up by polling every 5 minutes. For real-time events, the card shows the shared Slack notifications endpoint to set as the Request URL in the Event Subscriptions of the Slack app the integration uses; the integration's Signing secret field (or, on your administrator's Slack app, the Slack OAuth default's) is what verifies them. See Slack message events below.
    • Other providers with events: an integration created on your administrator's OAuth app (you left its client ID empty and the administrator configured OAuth defaults for the provider) gets its events through the webhook the administrator set up, so the card says so instead of showing a URL. An integration on your own OAuth app shows its own webhook URL to configure in that app.
    • Replacing the client ID moves an integration to your own OAuth app. The tokens issued to the previous app are removed, so authorize the integration again before it is used.
    • For integrations created before XTM One recorded which OAuth app they use, the card compares the integration's client ID with the administrator's current OAuth default: the same ID means the administrator's app, any other means your own. Only when that comparison cannot be made does the card follow whether the provider has OAuth defaults, as it did before.

docs.title: Slack message events
docs.text:
New Slack message assignments receive messages in two ways. The event poller reads the monitored channels every 5 minutes with the integration's own token. It needs no setup and serves every assignment whose trigger names the integration (the assignment editor always sets one) or whose agent is bound to it. For real-time delivery, the Slack app the integration runs on sends its Events API deliveries to /api/v1/integrations/notifications/slack.

That endpoint checks every delivery against the app's Signing Secret (Slack app > Basic Information). Nothing has to be set up for events to keep arriving: with no Signing Secret stored, a delivery is accepted without a verified signature, exactly as before signatures were checked, and XTM One says so with a warning in the log and a Security Audit finding. Storing the secret turns verification on for the integrations of that app:

  • An integration running on its own Slack app: put the secret in the integration's Signing secret field.
  • An integration created with the Slack app your administrator provides (Settings > OAuth defaults): the administrator stores the secret in the Signing secret field of the Slack OAuth default, once for everyone.

Once a Signing Secret is stored, a delivery it does not prove never reaches the integrations of that app, and a verified event reaches only what it concerns:

  • It reaches only the integrations running on the app that signed it, and only those of the Slack workspace it was sent for.
  • It then reaches the assignments whose agent is connected to one of those integrations, under the rules the poller applies: for an OAuth integration bound to the agent, the token is the agent owner's own, or shared with its owner's explicit acknowledgement. An assignment whose acting user can no longer see the integration still receives the event, as polled events are delivered, and the log says so.
  • A message outside a public channel (private channel, direct or group message) reaches only the integration of its author or of the user Slack authorized the event for. Everyone else still receives it through the poller if their own token can read it.
  • The trigger's channel selection applies, as the poller applies it.
  • An assignment whose agent is connected to no Slack integration at all has no app or workspace to be matched against: it receives the event as before.

An event the platform cannot verify with what it holds (no usable Signing Secret for the app that sent it) is handed out as before signatures were checked: to every New Slack message assignment whose channel selection admits it, except those connected only to integrations whose app Signing Secret is stored.
