Each message runs an assignment once. The real-time path and the poller claim it under the same key, and a Slack retry of the same event is skipped. A message an assignment's own run posted does not run that assignment again; any other assignment watching the channel still runs on it.

To refuse every event that cannot be verified, an administrator turns on Require verified integration notifications in Settings > Security (or sets INTEGRATION_NOTIFICATIONS_REQUIRE_VERIFICATION=true, which wins and locks the field). The messages of integrations without a stored Signing Secret then arrive through the poller only, and the Security Audit says how many integrations are concerned. If Slack disabled the app's Event Subscriptions after refused deliveries, re-enable them once the secret is stored.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Activity is the change history — when the integration was edited, whether it was tested recently, and whether an issue started after a configuration change.

docs.title: Read-only and managed nuances
docs.text: Integrations can have more nuanced edit behavior than other resources. Company-managed integrations are read-only for non-admins, and some suite-level registrations behave like centrally managed records rather than personal connections. Status, tools, and related usage stay visible even when editing is restricted.

docs.title: Sharing an OAuth integration
docs.text:
An OAuth integration is connected with one person's account: whoever authorized it. You can share it like any other integration - with groups, with individual users, or company-wide by making it company-managed - and once it is shared, everyone it is shared with acts using that connected account. Their agents, assignments and flows use the owner's token, so actions in the external service appear as the owner.

That is the default. When sharing is turned on in Configuration, a notice says so, with one switch below it:

  • Don't share my connected account (off by default; an admin editing someone else's integration sees Don't share the owner's connected account) keeps the integration shared without the owner's account. The stored credentials are removed when you save, and nobody can use the integration until it is authorized again. Only the owner or an admin can turn it on.
  • Reconnecting a shared integration shares the account used to reconnect it; the Authorize button says so. A group-shared or user-shared integration is reconnected by its owner. A company-managed integration can be reconnected by any admin, who then becomes its owner.
  • Saving asks once: a confirmation names whose account it is, who will act with it and how to avoid it. Confirming shares it; cancelling changes nothing.
  • A member who edits a shared integration without being its owner or an admin cannot share the owner's account: if the owner never shared it, saving a new share removes it, and the confirmation says so before anything is saved.
  • Stopping sharing - removing every group and user and turning company-managed off - makes the integration personal again: only its owner uses the account until it is shared again.

In a chat, people who cannot see the integration, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with them, use their own account of the same provider instead when they have one; when they do not, a note under the answer says the integration was not used for them and why, and the agent is told too. What carries it - an agent's runs, public link and channels, a flow, a knowledge base import source, a skill's source - acts with its account for that thing's audience, as the next section explains.

The dashboard reminds owners which of their integrations share their connected account, with a shortcut to stop sharing.

Through the API, the choice is the keep_oauth_credentials_on_share field of POST /api/v1/integrations and PUT /api/v1/integrations/{id}: true shares the connected account, false shares the integration without it. A request that shares the integration without the field keeps the account private, as it always did: an account whose sharing was never consented to is removed. An edit that does not change sharing and sends no choice changes nothing.

docs.title: Sharing a personal credential, everywhere
docs.text:
Any stored credential - an OAuth account, a personal access token, an API key, a bot token, a service-account secret - is used by more than the people an integration is shared with. Everything that carries the integration lends it to its own audience:

  • An agent bound to it: its assignments, its flows, its public web widget, the people who message it on a channel without an account and the platform MCP key all act with the agent's integrations. In a chat, someone the integration is not shared with uses their own account instead, or is told under the answer that it was not used.
  • An assignment that overrides the agent's integrations or listens to an integration's events, for everyone who can use the agent.
  • A flow node, for the flow's audience.
  • A knowledge base import source: its readers see what is synced with it.
  • A skill's private source: it is refreshed with it.
  • The General Assistant's platform bindings, for every user, and a user's own assistant, for that user.

Sharing is never refused. Before a change that lets new people act with someone's credential - sharing an integration, an agent, a knowledge base or a skill, making one company-managed, binding an integration to an agent, an assignment, a flow node, an import source or the General Assistant, enabling an agent's web widget, transferring an owner - one confirmation says whose credential it is ("your GitHub token", "Alice's Jira connected account"), who will be able to use it (with counts, and the public link, anonymous channel users or the MCP key when they apply), through what, what they can do with it (the provider, and the scopes when known) and how to avoid it: Don't share my connected account, switching the agent to per-user integrations, or a company integration. Nothing is asked when nobody new is reached.

The integration's Overview has a Sharing and access section for the people who manage it: every way the credential reaches people, with the reason (shared directly, bound to an agent, an assignment override or trigger, a per-user binding an assignment resolves to the person it runs as, a flow node, an import source, a skill source, the assistants), the audience and a link. An entity you cannot open is named by its owner only. The integration cards show the same thing compactly (Shared - 3 ways), with the breakdown on hover.

The same answers are available to API clients, read-only: GET /api/v1/integrations/{id}/exposure, GET /api/v1/integrations/exposure/summary and POST /api/v1/integrations/exposure/preview (see Sharing and access for every moment you are asked, and the routes every lent resource has).

docs.title: Scope(s): boundary or guidance
docs.text:
An agent, and each of its assignments, can narrow an integration to specific elements in its Scope(s) card (repositories, channels, CRM object types). The card says which kind of selection it is.

By default every selection is Guidance only: it is given to the agent as instructions ("focus your work on these specific resources"), and its tools can still reach other elements. This is also what every selection made before the choice existed stays.

A selection of one of the four element types below can instead be a hard boundary: turn on Enforce as a boundary next to it, in the agent's or the assignment's Scope(s) card, and save. The card then reads Enforced. The choice is made on each selection, so an agent can enforce its repositories while its Slack channels stay guidance. The Security Audit lists, for information, the selections of these types that are kept as guidance; it does not change the audit's score.

  • Enforced - GitHub repositories. The agent's GitHub tools cannot work on any other repository, in assignments and in chat. A request for another repository is refused with the list of allowed ones, whichever way it names that repository. Repository listings and searches, a team's repositories, sub-issues and project boards show only the selected repositories, and a project card of another repository cannot be changed (draft cards belong to no repository and stay available). The tools that reach repositories without naming one - the raw GraphQL query, repository search, the notification inbox - are not offered, and creating or transferring a repository, changing a team's members and comparing with a branch of another repository are refused. Organization, team, project and user details stay readable.
  • Enforced - Slack channels. The agent's Slack tools cannot read, post to, react in or manage any other conversation, in assignments and in chat; a channel may be named by its ID or its #name. Channel listings and message and file searches show only the selected channels, listing files needs a selected channel, and a file named by its ID is read or deleted only when it is shared in one of them. Direct messages and creating a channel are not offered. Workspace members stay readable. A Slack channel bot the agent posts through is bound by the bot's own publish channels, not by this selection.
  • Enforced - Microsoft Teams channels. The agent's Teams tools cannot read, post to, reply in or list the members of any other channel, in assignments and in chat; a channel meeting's recordings and transcripts are read only in a selected channel (by name or ID), and so is an image pasted in a channel message. The teams-and-channels listing shows the selected channels. Teams chats (1:1 and group) and creating a channel are not offered. The selection applies to Teams only: Outlook mail, calendar, OneDrive, SharePoint, To Do and your own online meetings keep their tools.
  • Enforced - HubSpot CRM object types. The HubSpot tools of an object type that is not selected (contacts, companies, deals, tickets) are not offered, in assignments and in chat, and associations, record deletion, record attachments and the associations a record read includes are refused for any other object type. Marketing email campaigns and the file manager (file search and upload) are not a CRM object type and are not offered; a file is downloaded through the record of a selected type it is attached to. Owners and pipeline definitions stay readable. A custom object is selected and named by its object type ID (2-...).
  • Guidance only - every other element type (GitHub organizations, Jira projects, ...): these have no switch and cannot be enforced. The selection is given to the agent as instructions, but its tools can still reach other elements. Do not rely on it as an access boundary; restrict the integration's own credentials instead.

An assignment refines the agent's selection, and the stricter of the two wins: a type is a boundary for an assignment's runs when the agent or the assignment enforces it. A type the agent enforces is a boundary for every assignment of that agent (the assignment's switch shows it on and locked), and an assignment can enforce a type its agent keeps as guidance. The boundary is then the assignment's refinement of the agent's selection, and one that leaves no valid element (an entry that is not a valid owner/name, or an assignment enforcing repositories its agent does not offer) allows nothing.

The work an agent hands over - to a consulted or transferred agent, or as a background task - stays within the boundaries of the run that handed it over, narrowed further by the other agent's own selection of those types. A selection the delegating run only has as guidance does not follow the work: the other agent keeps working from its own selection, as the prompt it receives says.

What the boundary does not cover

The boundary applies to the GitHub integration's own tools. It does not restrict another route to GitHub the agent may have - an MCP server that exposes GitHub, a custom tool, the code interpreter or the web tools - nor a flow's integration nodes, nor the General Assistant, which has no Scope(s). It does not govern the selected repository's own automation either: a workflow the agent starts runs with that repository's own token and secrets, and GitHub serves the commits of a repository's forks through the repository itself. After a transfer, the conversation continues under the new agent's own selection.

docs.title: Who receives an integration's events
docs.text:
An assignment with an integration-event trigger listens to the integration its trigger names, or, when it names none, to its agent's first integration of that provider. A flow's integration-event trigger names one too. XTM One reads those events with the integration's credentials and hands them to a run, and checks whether the run's user can see the integration:

  • for an assignment, the user its runs act as: its Run as user, else its owner (the agent's owner);
  • for a flow, the flow's owner.

Seeing the integration means the usual rule: it is theirs, it is shared with them or one of their groups, or it is company-managed and not restricted to an audience. Admins see every integration. A company-managed assignment with neither an owner nor a Run as user keeps the connected-account rule above, as before.

When that user cannot see it, the events are still delivered, as they always were, and never silently: the worker log names the assignment (or the flow and its trigger node) once an hour, and the security audit (GET /api/v1/security-audit, Settings > Security) lists it as a warning. Share the integration with that user, or pick one they can see.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Read the status badge before editing anything.
  • Use Test Connection before assuming the agent is broken.
  • Use the available tools card to understand what the integration really provides.
  • Check scopes and re-authorization warnings when OAuth behavior changes. The platform also marks an OAuth integration as needing re-authorization, and stops refreshing its token, when the provider says the refresh token is revoked or invalid, or rejects the integration's client ID / secret (invalid_client). GitHub and Slack report both inside an otherwise successful answer, and the platform reads them there too: bad_refresh_token (GitHub) and invalid_refresh_token (Slack) for the refresh token, incorrect_client_credentials (GitHub), invalid_client_id and bad_client_secret (Slack) for the client ID / secret. In that last case, update the client ID / secret in Configuration first, then re-authorize: a new consent with the rejected credentials fails the same way. The mark stays until a new authorization succeeds: the platform never retries such an integration on its own, and saving a new client secret, token URL or scopes alone neither reconnects it nor retries the refresh. Saving a new client ID removes the tokens issued to the previous app, so the integration then shows as configured but not yet authorized until you authorize it. A temporary provider failure (a network error, an outage, rate limiting, such as Slack's ratelimited or service_unavailable) never produces this mark; the platform just retries later.
  • Look at Agents Using before editing a shared integration.

docs.title: Knowledge bases
docs.text:
This page complements Knowledge Bases in XTM One.

That guide explains what a knowledge base is for. This page gives you a quick tour of the knowledge base screens.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, this area is Knowledge. The list page is where you start: search by name or description, filter by visibility or tags, and compare existing collections before creating a new one so you avoid duplicate silos. Each card shows enough to judge a collection at a glance — what it is about, its visibility, and how much indexed content it holds. If you have permission, New Knowledge Base creates one from files, GitHub, Notion, or cloud storage.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text:
Opening a knowledge base shows a header with the name, its badges (System managed, Company-managed, Shared, Read-only), and a few actions that serve different purposes:

  • Test Search lets you judge answer quality before changing anything. It is disabled until the knowledge base has indexed content.
  • Re-embed is a maintenance action that refreshes the searchable index.
  • delete removes the whole knowledge base, not a single document.

The detail page is organized into tabs. Overview, Configuration, and Activity are always present; Documents and Import Sources appear for knowledge bases you populate yourself (Import Sources is hidden for system-managed ones).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview is the fastest way to understand the current state: how much content is indexed, how often it is queried, the embedding model, and which agents are bound to it.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
Documents is the main content view — upload files, paste text, download, delete, and reprocess documents that are stuck or failed. Open it when your real question is whether the source content is actually present, whether ingestion failed, or whether an old file version is still indexed.

Each document keeps its original source text, not just the searchable chunks it was split into. That is what makes download return the file you put in, and it is also what agents read when they need a whole document rather than the fragments semantic search returns.

docs.title: Import Sources
docs.text:
Import Sources manages automatic sync (website, Notion, OneDrive/SharePoint, Google Drive, GitHub, and more). It shows each source's schedule and last-sync status, so it is useful both for setup and for answering "why isn't the knowledge base up to date?". Some source types require a connected integration first; when that is missing, the option stays visible but disabled and the UI explains what is needed.

When you choose a specific integration for a source, you can only choose one you can see. The source then syncs with that integration every time, on its schedule or with Sync now, whoever starts it. If the person the source syncs for (whoever set it up, else the knowledge base's owner) later loses access to that integration - it is no longer shared with them, or Restrict access leaves them out - the source keeps syncing with it, and the security audit lists the source so that an administrator can share the integration with them or have the source use another one.

When a sync fails, the full error is shown only to the people who can manage the knowledge base: its owner, the people it is shared with who may configure it, and administrators (only administrators for a company-managed knowledge base). That text is what fixing the source takes, and it can name internal hosts, addresses or paths. Everyone else who can open the knowledge base sees a short, fixed description instead - for example The sync timed out. or The source was disabled after repeated failed syncs. - followed by a note that people who can manage the knowledge base can see the details. The full error is always kept, and the server log records it with the knowledge base and source ids.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration covers the knowledge base's identity (name, description, tags), its visibility and sharing, and the Read-only content and Index HTML as rendered text switches. System-managed knowledge bases stay read-only here.

Turn Read-only content on when a collection is ground truth — the authoritative version of something other work is checked against. A read-only knowledge base stays fully searchable, so agents keep using it for answers; what changes is that nothing can rewrite it. Agents lose write access to it even if an agent's configuration grants writing, its documents cannot be added, edited or deleted, and the knowledge base itself cannot be deleted until you turn the switch back off.

Two things deliberately keep working on a read-only knowledge base: configured Import Sources still refresh it, and Re-embed still works. That is so a collection whose authority lives in another system — a policy wiki, a specification repository — stays both locked against edits and up to date. To freeze such a knowledge base completely, disable its import sources as well.

Index HTML as rendered text (off by default) decides how HTML documents are searched. Off, an HTML document is indexed as its source markup, exactly as before the switch existed. On, it is indexed as the text a reader sees: the page text in reading order, with a summary of the data its scripts embed first, and styles, scripts and SVG drawing instructions left out. Turn it on for exported pages and reports, whose markup often outweighs their text so much that searches match tags instead of sentences. The stored document does not change either way (opening or downloading it still returns the original HTML), and only what is indexed differs. Changing the switch re-indexes nothing by itself: it applies to documents added or changed afterwards (by hand, by an agent or by an import source), and Re-embed applies it to the documents already there. It only affects documents that are HTML; data, text and code files (JSON, CSV, Markdown, plain text, scripts), and text an import source has already converted, such as Markdown from a crawl, are indexed as they are. A page with no visible text or data, a page too large to render whole, or one that cannot be rendered is indexed as its source; with the switch on, the Embedding completed entry Activity shows for an HTML document says which of the two it was indexed as.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text:
Activity is the audit view — when content changed, whether a sync ran recently, and who edited the configuration. Check it when answer quality shifts. Document updated entries also cover agent write-backs: an agent with write access to a knowledge base can revise a stored document, which re-indexes it. The document shows pending until re-indexing finishes, so a document an agent just changed is briefly not searchable — that is expected, not a failure.

Sync entries follow the same rule as Import Sources: a failed sync, a sync alert, a quarantined source and a configuration error show the full error to people who can manage the knowledge base, and a fixed sentence to everyone else. The activity search only looks through what you are shown, so it never finds text you cannot see.

docs.title: Badges that set expectations
docs.text:
• System managed means the platform maintains the content automatically; Documents may be read-only and point you to Import Sources instead.
  • Content locked (Locked on the list page) means the knowledge base is marked read-only: searchable as usual, but nothing writes to it. This is about the content.
  • Company-managed plus Read-only means you can view it but not change it. This one is about permissions — who may administer the knowledge base — which is why a collection can carry both badges for different reasons.
  • Shared means the knowledge base belongs to a shared group rather than to one person.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Start on Overview before editing anything.
  • Use Test Search before deciding a knowledge base is weak.
  • Check Documents when results look incomplete, and Import Sources when freshness is the issue.
  • Read the badges first — they explain why some actions are missing.
  • Mark authoritative collections Read-only rather than relying on each agent's configuration being right — the lock lives on the knowledge base, so it holds no matter what an agent is granted later.
  • Keep very large documents out of knowledge bases you expect agents to read whole. A document above roughly 200 000 characters is not loaded into an agent's context at all: the platform records it as a work item instead, and the agent is steered to search it for the relevant passages. Splitting it into meaningful documents usually works better than leaving one enormous file.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
This page complements MCP Servers in XTM One.

That guide explains what MCP servers are for. This page gives you a quick tour of the MCP server screens.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, this area is Tools & Integrations > MCP Servers — the first entry of the group, ahead of Tools, Integrations and Variables, because an MCP server is the richest capability an agent acts through (a whole tool server rather than one function). The page also carries the MCP endpoints this platform itself exposes; see Platform MCP servers and Platform tools MCP server. The list page is built for quick scanning: search by name, command, or URL, and filter by visibility or tags. Each card answers two questions at a glance — is the server likely usable right now (enabled or disabled, transport type), and what kind of setup sits behind it (subprocess vs. HTTP, whether OAuth or environment variables are involved) if something goes wrong later. If you have permission, Add Server exposes a new external toolset.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text: Opening a server shows a header with its name, transport, enabled state, and OAuth status when relevant. Test Connection is the main action — try it first after any setup or credential change, because it tells you whether the problem is the server connection itself or something later in the agent workflow. The page is organized into Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview shows whether the server is meaningfully ready: how many tools it discovered, how often they are called, its connection details, and which agents depend on it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is the most operationally important screen. It covers the server's identity and connection (transport, command or URL, environment variables or headers) and its visibility and sharing. You can switch transport directly here between subprocess (stdio), Streamable HTTP, and SSE.

The same screen holds the discovered tools card, where you discover or refresh the server's tools, read each tool's description, and test an individual tool. This matters because most MCP questions are not about the server object itself — they are about whether the expected tool is actually visible and callable. When the server uses OAuth, an OAuth connection card shows whether it is configured but not yet authenticated, with an authorize or re-authorize action. On a company-managed server that action is admin-only, because the resulting connection is a single shared one — every user of the platform calls the server through the token the admin authorized, just as they all share its API key when it authenticates with headers.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Activity is the traceable history — whether the server changed recently, whether calls were made, and whether an issue started after an edit.

docs.title: Files an MCP tool returns
docs.text: A file an MCP tool sends back (an image, a document, an embedded resource) is kept as a file of the conversation or run: the agent reads it, you get a download card, and the agent can hand it to any other tool that takes a file. A tool may instead return a link to a resource without its content, often because it is large. The agent sees the link, and when it needs the file it asks the same MCP server for it (read_mcp_resource), over the server's own connection: the file is then kept like any other. Only a link the server's own tools returned in the run can be read this way, up to the platform's 40 MB file limit.

docs.title: Shared, company, and read-only states
docs.text: Ownership rules shape these pages: private servers are editable by their owner, shared servers are reused across group members, and company-managed servers are visible more widely but read-only for non-admins. Testing may be available even when editing is not.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Use Test Connection before troubleshooting the agent itself.
  • Refresh discovered tools after changing transport or credentials.
  • Read the discovered tool list, not just the server name.
  • Notice the difference between a configured server and an OAuth-connected one.

docs.title: Platform MCP servers
docs.text:
XTM One embeds a native Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for every connected Filigran platform. This means any MCP-compatible client — Cursor, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or your own agents — can connect to OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ through XTM One and work with your threat intelligence, exposure validation, and governance-risk-compliance content directly.

This page explains what the platform MCP servers are, where to find them, and how to connect a client.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
One dedicated MCP endpoint per platform:

Endpoint Platform What it exposes https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencti OpenCTI Threat intelligence knowledge: search, entities (SDOs), observables (SCOs), relationships, indicators, containers (reports, cases, groupings), notes, labels, markings, statistics https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/openaev OpenAEV Adversarial exposure validation: scenarios, simulations, payloads, injects, atomic tests, expectations, findings, vulnerabilities, assets, media content, lessons learned, reports https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencrq OpenCRQ Governance, risk & compliance: frameworks, requirements, controls (maturity), assessments, evidence, risk scenarios, attack outcomes, CRQ financial summaries, assets, CVE search

All endpoints use the MCP Streamable HTTP transport, the modern standard supported by all major MCP clients.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
The platform MCP servers are a Community Edition feature. There is nothing to install and nothing extra to license:

  • A server becomes available as soon as the corresponding platform is registered with XTM One — the same registration that powers the embedded "Ask AI" experience in OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ.
  • While no platform of that type is connected, the endpoint simply answers that the platform is not registered.
  • Administrators can turn all platform servers off globally with the Platform MCP Servers toggle in Settings > MCP Endpoint.

docs.title: Where to find your endpoints
docs.text:
Open My Profile > MCP Endpoint.

The Platform MCP Servers card is always visible there (as long as an administrator has not disabled the feature) and lists every platform server with its live status. For each connected platform it shows:

  • the endpoint URL, with a copy button
  • the live connection status (Connected or Registered)
  • a Config button that copies a ready-to-paste MCP client configuration

A platform that is not yet connected appears dimmed as Not connected, with a reminder that its MCP server activates automatically once the platform is registered with XTM One.

Administrators see the same information, along with the global enable/disable toggle, in Settings > MCP Endpoint.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The servers accept a standard bearer token:

  • a personal API key (fcp-...), created in My Profile > API Keys, or
  • an OAuth 2.1 access token — MCP clients that support OAuth discover the authorization flow automatically.

Every tool call runs as you on the platform. XTM One signs a short-lived token for your user (matched by email on the platform side), so your platform permissions, data markings, and audit trail all apply exactly as if you performed the action yourself. The platform's own API token is never stored in or proxied through XTM One.

docs.title: Connect a client
docs.text:
Copy the configuration from the Config button in your profile, or use this template (keep only the servers you need):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "opencti": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencti",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    },
    "openaev": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/openaev",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    },
    "opencrq": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencrq",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Where to paste it:

  • Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json in your project (or the global MCP settings)
  • Claude Desktop: claude_desktop_config.json
  • Other clients: any client supporting MCP Streamable HTTP with custom headers

You can verify the connection from a terminal:

curl -s -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencti \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}'

docs.title: What the tools cover
docs.text:
The tools are the same battle-tested tools used by XTM One agents through the native platform integrations.

For OpenCTI, you can:

  • search and read any STIX entity, observable, relationship, or container
  • create and update entities, observables, indicators, relationships, containers, and notes
  • manage labels, markings, and container membership
  • promote observables to indicators
  • retrieve statistics, top related entities, and modification history

For OpenAEV, you can:

  • search and read scenarios, simulations, payloads, injects, findings, assets, and ATT&CK content
  • create and manage scenarios, simulations, injects, expectations, and atomic tests
  • create and manage payloads, findings, and vulnerabilities
  • work with documents, media channels, articles, challenges, lessons learned, and reports

For OpenCRQ, you can:

  • browse tenants, organizations, compliance frameworks, and their requirements
  • read and update controls (including maturity levels) and requirement assessments, and attach evidence
  • create and manage risk scenarios, and read attack outcomes and CRQ financial summaries
  • list primary and supporting assets and search CVEs

OpenCRQ is multi-tenant: every tool accepts an optional tenant identifier and resolves your sole tenant automatically when omitted.

docs.title: What the tools deliberately do not cover
docs.text:
The platform MCP servers expose business and knowledge tools only. Platform administration is out of scope by design:

  • no user, group, role, tenant, or organization management
  • no playbooks, dashboards, or workspace administration
  • no notification, customization, ingestion, or data-sharing configuration
  • no connector or platform settings management

This is enforced server-side with a strict allow-list: a tool that is not explicitly allowed can never be listed or executed through these endpoints.

OpenCTI writes are direct

Knowledge changes made through the OpenCTI MCP server are applied directly to the live knowledge graph, with your user's permissions. The draft-review workflow used by XTM One agents does not apply to MCP clients — review changes on the client side before running write tools.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Meaning What to do 401 Unauthorized Missing or invalid token Check the Authorization header and that your API key is active 403 Forbidden Platform MCP servers are disabled Ask an administrator to enable them in Settings > MCP Endpoint 404 Not Found The platform is not registered with XTM One Connect the OpenCTI / OpenAEV / OpenCRQ instance to XTM One first Tool result contains an error message The platform rejected the call (permissions, invalid input, connectivity) Read the message — it reflects your own permissions on the platform

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Create a dedicated API key per MCP client so you can revoke access independently.
  • Remember that every action is performed as you — write tools modify real platform data.
  • If a tool you expect is missing, it is most likely excluded on purpose (platform administration) rather than misconfigured.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text:
If you also want to expose XTM One agents (not platform tools) to your MCP clients, continue with the MCP Endpoint tab described in My Profile.

To read agent traces and manage XTM One's own objects from an MCP client, see Platform tools MCP server.

docs.title: Platform tools MCP server
docs.text:
Alongside the platform MCP servers — which bridge the connected OpenCTI, OpenAEV, and OpenCRQ instances — XTM One exposes itself over MCP.

One endpoint, /mcp/xtm, lets any MCP-compatible client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, your own agents) read your agent traces and manage the objects you work with every day: agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases, prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, MCP servers, and variables.

The typical use: an agent misbehaved, so you read its traces from your client, spot the step that failed, and fix the agent's configuration — without leaving the client.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Endpoint What it exposes https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/xtm XTM One's own tools: agent traces, agents, assignments, runs, knowledge bases (including semantic search), prompts, skills, custom tools, integrations, MCP servers, variables

The transport is MCP Streamable HTTP, the same as every other XTM One MCP endpoint.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• inspect_agent_traces — recent traces, filterable by period, status, source, and model. Naming a target_agent_id scopes to one agent; omitting it lists traces across agents, which is how you find which agent failed before drilling into it.
  • get_trace_payload — the full stored value of any trace or span field. Listings return bounded previews; this reads the rest, one page at a time.

Trace access follows the same rule as the Trace Explorer in the UI: the cross-agent listing is an administrator surface, and a non-admin reads the agents they can manage.

Every inspect_agent_traces listing, and every get_trace_payload read of a trace that is not the calling agent's own, is recorded in the audit log (inspect_traces). The same read by the same person - a listing of the same agents, or the same field of the same trace - is recorded once every 15 minutes: paging through one payload or changing a listing's filters writes one entry, and the entry says so in window_seconds. A listing of other agents, another trace or another field is recorded at once.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Everything the REST API and the UI offer for the objects you own or share:

  • Agents — list, read, create, update, delete, plus templates and the available-resources catalog
  • Assignments and runs — list, read, create, update, trigger, and read execution history
  • Knowledge bases — list, read, create, update, delete, add and read documents, revise a document (with automatic re-embedding), and search_knowledge for semantic search across everything you can read
  • Prompts, skills, variables — full CRUD, plus load_skill / read_skill_resource to open a skill's bundled files
  • Custom tools, integrations, MCP servers — full CRUD

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Off by default. Unlike the platform MCP servers, this one exposes this instance's own configuration surface, so an administrator has to enable it explicitly:

Settings > MCP Endpoint > Platform Tools MCP Server

While it is disabled, the endpoint answers 403 with a message saying so.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The tool surface is resolved per request, from the calling user. There is no separate permission model to configure: every tool enforces the same three-tier gates as the REST API and the UI.

  • Built-in objects are read-only for everyone.
  • Company-managed objects are read-only for non-administrators.
  • Group-shared objects need a config-tier grant to modify.
  • Knowledge bases you can read are searchable; only the ones you can manage are writable.

A caller sees and changes exactly what they could see and change in the interface — never more.

docs.title: Where to find your endpoint
docs.text: Open My Profile > MCP Endpoint. Once an administrator has enabled the server, a Platform Tools MCP Server card shows the endpoint URL, a copy button, and — under Install in your client — a downloadable package for each supported client.

docs.title: Install with a package
docs.text:
Three formats, all carrying the same skill so the model knows how to use the tools rather than guessing:

Package For How you install it Claude Code plugin (.zip) Claude Code claude --plugin-dir ./xtm-one-platform, or add it as a local marketplace to keep it across sessions Claude Desktop extension (.mcpb) Claude Desktop Double-click the file, or drag it into the Claude Desktop window Agent Plugins package (.zip) Any Agent Plugins v1.0.0 client Unzip it and point your client at the directory

Each package already contains the endpoint URL, and the skill inside carries a tool reference generated from the surface that server offered you — so it lists the tools your permissions actually reach, not a maintained-by-hand list.

docs.title: One package, one server
docs.text:
The same three formats also package the platform MCP servers — OpenCTI, OpenAEV, OpenCRQ — for the platforms actually registered with XTM One. When more than one server is live, clicking a format asks which one you want; with only one there is nothing to ask and the download starts.

There is deliberately no "all of them" package. A client loads every tool definition of every server it connects to, and the four servers together currently come to more than two hundred tools — well past the point where tool selection degrades and every request carries the weight. Installing a second package stays available; it is your explicit choice rather than a default.

A bridge package ships the generated catalogue of that platform's tools and no hand-written guidance: those tools belong to OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ, whose own documentation is the authority on what they mean, and invented prose here would rot unnoticed as those products move.

docs.title: Other clients
docs.text:
The Other button covers the clients that install by editing a file rather than by opening a package:

Client File Notes Codex CLI, Codex IDE extension, ChatGPT desktop app ~/.codex/config.toml One file for all three — they share this configuration Cursor ~/.cursor/mcp.json Also accepts .cursor/mcp.json per project VS Code — Needs no snippet: it reads the Agent Plugins package directly, so download that one

Those two files already hold your other MCP servers, so what you get is a fragment to merge, not a file to replace — shown with a copy button and the path to paste it into. The one-click choice applies here too: with a key, it is written into the fragment; without, the fragment points at a XTM_ONE_API_KEY environment variable instead, which is what both clients document for keeping a token out of a file that often ends up in a dotfiles repository.

ChatGPT desktop, outside Codex

ChatGPT's own Developer mode (Settings → Apps) takes a public HTTPS URL and authenticates with OAuth or not at all — it accepts no custom header, so an API key has no place there and http://localhost will not connect. /mcp/xtm publishes OAuth 2.1 Protected Resource Metadata, so that route works on an HTTPS deployment. The ~/.codex/config.toml entry above is what covers the ChatGPT desktop app locally.

docs.title: One-click install
docs.text:
The One-click install switch (on by default) makes the download self-contained: the platform creates a new API key dedicated to that package, names it after the client, and writes it into the configuration files. Install it and you are done — nothing to paste.

The trade-off is stated plainly because it is real: the downloaded file is then a live credential. Do not commit or share it, delete it once installed, and revoke the key from My Profile > API Keys if it goes anywhere it should not. It is a key of its own, so revoking it affects nothing else.

A new key is created rather than reused because there is nothing to reuse: keys are stored as bcrypt hashes and the plaintext exists only at creation, so no existing key can be read back into a package.

Turn the switch off and the packages carry no credential — your client asks for the key at install time and keeps it in its own secure storage. If you have no API key at all, the card says so and points you at the API Keys tab.

docs.title: The Agent Plugins package never carries a key
docs.text: Agent Plugins 1.0.0 states that configured headers are literal, visible package data that must not contain credentials, and defines no portable credential-reference field. Embedding a key would make the package non-conformant — which is the one property that format exists for. It therefore always downloads credential-free, whatever the switch says, and its README explains where to add the bearer token in your own client.

docs.title: Why the Claude Desktop bundle contains a script
docs.text:
The .mcpb format runs a local MCP server over stdio, but this server is remote and speaks Streamable HTTP. The bundle therefore carries a small bridge (server/index.js) that forwards each JSON-RPC message over HTTPS. It has no dependencies, fetches nothing at runtime, and is about a hundred readable lines — check it before installing if you would rather verify than trust.

If you want no local process at all, add the endpoint as a Claude Desktop custom connector instead, using the URL from the same card.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
A standard bearer token:

  • a personal API key (fcp-...), created in My Profile > API Keys, or
  • an OAuth 2.1 access token — clients that support OAuth discover the flow automatically (RFC 9728), and the token is audience-bound to /mcp/xtm, so a token minted for another endpoint is refused here.

docs.title: Configure a client by hand
docs.text:
For a client with no package of its own — Cursor, an internal tool, your own agent — configure it directly:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "xtm-one-platform": {
      "url": "https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/xtm",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer fcp-..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Where to paste it:

  • Cursor: .cursor/mcp.json in your project (or the global MCP settings)
  • Claude Desktop: claude_desktop_config.json
  • Other clients: any client supporting MCP Streamable HTTP with custom headers

Verify from a terminal:

curl -s -X POST https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/xtm \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer fcp-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list"}'

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Meaning What to do 401 Unauthorized Missing or invalid token Check the Authorization header and that your API key is active. A one-click package whose key you later revoked will fail this way — download it again 403 Forbidden The server is disabled, or AI is turned off on this deployment Ask an administrator to enable it in Settings > MCP Endpoint A tool is missing from tools/list You have nothing in scope for it search_knowledge only appears when you can read at least one knowledge base; load_skill only when at least one skill is visible to you A trace listing is refused The cross-agent listing needs administrator rights Name a target_agent_id for an agent you manage

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Create a dedicated API key per MCP client so you can revoke access independently — revoking a user's keys cuts that client off immediately. The one-click packages already do this: each download gets its own key, named after the client.
  • Delete a one-click package file once it is installed. The client has stored what it needs, and the file is a live credential until you do.
  • Remember that write tools change real platform objects. Review what your client proposes before letting it run them.
  • Leave the server disabled on deployments where no one needs it; it is a configuration surface, not a read-only report.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: To expose XTM One agents as tools (rather than platform management), see the MCP Endpoint tab described in My Profile. For the connected OpenCTI / OpenAEV / OpenCRQ platforms, see Platform MCP servers.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
This page complements Prompts in XTM One.

That guide explains when prompts are useful. This page gives you a quick tour of the prompt screens.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, this area is Prompts. The list page is a reusable library: search by name or a remembered wording fragment, filter by visibility or tags, and check whether a prompt already exists before creating another version. Each card shows a content preview so you can judge relevance and style before opening it. If you have permission, Add Prompt creates a repeatable instruction others can reuse.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text: Opening a prompt shows a header with its name, badges (Company-managed, Shared, Read-only), and a delete action when you can manage it. The page is organized into Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview combines usage metrics with a readable content preview. It helps you tell whether the prompt is a draft or already reused in real workflows, and — through the Agents Using card — how many downstream uses an edit would affect.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is where you read and edit the prompt. The distinctions that matter are durable:

  • editing the content changes what the prompt says
  • Hide from chat changes where it is surfaced (it drops the prompt from the chat picker while keeping it available for agent configuration)
  • sharing settings change who can reuse it

The content editor includes a variable insert control, so you can add platform variables without memorizing the syntax.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Activity answers who changed the prompt, when, and whether a recent run problem started after an edit — especially useful for shared prompts.

docs.title: Read-only and shared states
docs.text: Private prompts are editable by their owner, shared prompts are visible in a group context, and company-managed prompts are visible to everyone but read-only for non-admins. When a prompt is read-only, you can still inspect its content and usage.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Read the content preview before creating a duplicate prompt.
  • Check Agents Using before editing a shared prompt.
  • Use Hide from chat when the prompt is operational and not meant for casual use.
  • Keep names and descriptions clear enough that other teams can reuse the prompt without guessing.

docs.title: XTM One Desktop and runners
docs.text:
XTM One Desktop is the native XTM One app for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It gives you two things in one install:

  • A real window for your agents. Your chat, your conversation history and your agent selection - everything the web app does - in a native window that stays in your system tray and comes back with one shortcut (Ctrl+Alt+Space).
  • An assistant that can act on the machine you are sitting at. From that chat, agents can run commands, read and edit files, capture a genuine full-desktop screenshot, and drive a browser you are already logged into - on this machine, within its permission model, with your approval inline in the chat, and with every command audited.

The second half is a runner: the small pull-based daemon the Desktop app embeds, which connects outbound to XTM One and pulls the work agents send to this machine. A runner also exists on its own, without the window: the headless runner you install on servers, VMs, and MDM-managed fleets where nobody sits at a desktop (see Install headless). Both appear as machines on the XTM One Desktop page, both obey the same permission model, and both are what the computer_use agent tools target.

Runners exist for the cases a headless browser cannot cover. When an auditor wants a screenshot with the real desktop, the OS clock, and the signed-in identity - not an AI-generated or headless render - a runner captures the true screen of a real session. The same channel lets an agent operate an authenticated browser or run a check directly on a workstation or server.

Runners are pull-based: the app connects outbound to XTM One and pulls work. The platform never opens a port on your machine, and there is nothing inbound to firewall.

docs.title: Install XTM One Desktop
docs.text:
Everything starts from the XTM One Desktop page: the entry at the bottom of the left navigation (also in your user menu, and in the command palette as Get XTM One Desktop). On a personal machine the graphical installer needs no command line; for servers and fleets there is a fully headless command-line path (see the next section).

  1. Open the XTM One Desktop page and download the installer for your operating system - the page detects it and offers it first; the other platforms are listed below. The main button is the x86_64 (Intel/AMD) build; ARM machines take the arm64 link next to it. Macs need no choice at all - one universal bundle covers both Intel and Apple Silicon.
  2. Run the installer (next, next, finish on Windows; drag to Applications on macOS; an AppImage or a .deb / .rpm on Linux).
  3. Launch XTM One Desktop. On the Connect this machine screen, paste this instance's URL and an enrollment key, then connect. The chat window opens on your instance: sign in as you would in a browser. (Single sign-on opens your system browser - see Signing in below.)

If the OS blocks the first launch

A build that is not code-signed for your operating system trips the first-open gate: Windows SmartScreen shows "unrecognized app" (click More info > Run anyway), and macOS reports it "could not verify ... is free of malware" - click Done (not Move to Trash), then open System Settings > Privacy & Security, click Open Anyway, and launch again. This only ever concerns the first manual install: self-updates are signature-verified and never re-prompt, and the headless install path is not affected.

Create an enrollment key from the same page, under Connect a machine. The key carries the permissions the enrolled machine starts with, as one of three presets:

  • Desktop (recommended) - every capability enabled. This is the preset for the machine you sit at: usable from the very first message. Shell commands run as the agent sends them; turn on Shell commands need approval on the key if you want each one held for your approval in the chat (off unless you turn it on).
  • Locked down - screenshots and browser control only, no approval gate; enable more later from the machine's card. The historical default.
  • Custom - choose the mode, the capabilities and the approval gate yourself (this is where fleet keys for servers are configured).

A key is single-use for the first machine but can be configured for reuse across a fleet, and it can carry labels so an unattended roll-out lands already configured. After enrollment the app stores a durable credential in the machine's OS keychain and stays connected across reboots - you never paste the key again.

One record per machine

Each enrolled machine is one runner. Installing on ten machines gives you ten runners you can name, label, and target individually - not ten integrations. Re-enrolling a machine that is already in the list (a reinstall, a re-run of the install script) updates its existing record - new credential, refreshed host facts, your name/permissions/labels kept - instead of creating a duplicate. Revoked runners stay revoked: enrolling that machine again deliberately creates a fresh record.

docs.title: Install headless (command line)
docs.text:
Servers, VMs, and MDM-managed fleets rarely have someone sitting at a desktop, and have no use for a chat window. For those machines, the XTM One Desktop page also shows a one-line install command per operating system under Servers and headless machines (command line): copy it, replace the key placeholder with an enrollment key, and run it on the target machine - no graphical session is ever needed. What it installs is the headless runner: the same binary as the Desktop app without the window and the tray, serving shell, file and browser commands to your agents exactly as before.

The command downloads the runner build matched to your instance's version, verifies its integrity, installs the binary, enrolls the machine, and registers it to start automatically (a LaunchAgent on macOS, a systemd user service on Linux, a logon task on Windows). The same binary is also a CLI afterwards: xtm-one-runner status, xtm-one-runner run, and xtm-one-runner reset manage it without any UI.

If the integrity check cannot run - the host has no sha256sum / shasum, or no .sha256 is available next to the archive - the installer still installs but warns INTEGRITY NOT VERIFIED and says why. For fleet and MDM rollouts, add --require-checksum (-RequireChecksum on Windows) or set XTM_RUNNER_REQUIRE_CHECKSUM=1 so an unverified binary is refused instead. A checksum that does not match, or a .sha256 that holds no checksum, always stops the install. The checksum is served by your instance next to the archive, so it proves the download arrived intact rather than who built it: use an https:// address for your instance, since over plain HTTP both could be swapped in transit and the installer warns about it. If the installer cannot get the archive from your instance, it reports the HTTP status it received, so a proxy or firewall problem - or a sign-in page from an authentication proxy answering in its place - is not mistaken for a build without embedded downloads.

The installer also checks the release signature: every release signs its runner archives, and the installer verifies the archive's .minisig against the release public keys it carries (the signature names which key made it, so a new release key can be trusted before releases are signed with it), so when that signature is there to check, a binary that was not built by the release - swapped on a mirror or behind a proxy, together with its checksum - is refused. The signature must also have been made for the archive this machine needs, so a signed build of another platform or flavor served in its place is refused too. Release signatures also name the runner version they were made for: when the archive comes from your instance, a signature for another version - an older signed build served in place of the current one - is refused, and the installer prints the version it verified. Archives signed before versions were signed install as before, and say so. The same checks guard the runner's own self-updates, which never install a build older than the running one. On macOS and Linux it uses minisign when installed, otherwise OpenSSL 3, otherwise (when upgrading) the runner already installed; on Windows it needs nothing extra. A signature that does not verify always stops the install. When the signature cannot be checked - no .minisig next to the archive (a build made without the release signing key), one that is not a signature at all (an error page from a mirror or a proxy, for example), a signature whose trusted comment names no file, or no verifier on the host (for example a first install on a macOS machine with neither minisign nor OpenSSL 3) - the installer warns SIGNATURE NOT VERIFIED; add --require-signature (-RequireSignature on Windows) or set XTM_RUNNER_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=1 to refuse instead. Without it, whoever can swap the archive can also withhold its .minisig and leave only that warning, so always add it for a mirror (--download-base) and for MDM or other unattended rollouts, where nobody reads the warning. If you build and sign the runner with your own key, an instance built from your fork serves installers that already trust the key of its tauri.conf.json; an installer taken from anywhere else needs XTM_RUNNER_MINISIGN_PUBKEY set to your public key: the key line of your .pub file, or the base64 value tauri.conf.json carries. The installer then says which key ID it checks against - the ID your .pub file prints - so you can confirm it is yours.

docs.title: The headless build (Linux servers)
docs.text:
On Linux the installer picks between two builds of the same runner:

Build Ships Capabilities Desktop (default) Everywhere else, and any Linux with a graphical session Screenshots, mouse/keyboard, shell, files, browser Headless Linux hosts with no graphical session Shell, files, browser

This is not a matter of taste. The desktop build links the desktop libraries (GTK, X11) at load time, so on a server without them it fails before it runs - no flag or setting can work around that. The headless build links none of them.

The installer decides from the environment: no DISPLAY and no WAYLAND_DISPLAY, and no graphical session on the machine, means headless — so SSH-ing into your own Linux desktop to run the installer still gets you the desktop build. Force either one with --headless or --desktop (or XTM_RUNNER_FLAVOR=headless for cloud-init and MDM). The choice sticks: a headless runner is only ever offered headless updates.

Two things a server does differently:

  • Credential storage. Servers usually run no keyring daemon. When there is no OS keychain, the runner stores its credential in a file readable only by its own user, next to its config, and says so in the log.
  • Staying up after logout. The service runs under your user account, so enable lingering or it stops when your SSH session ends. The installer does it for you when it can: sudo loginctl enable-linger <user>.

Desktop capabilities need a desktop

Screenshots and mouse/keyboard control require a logged-in graphical session. Shell commands, file operations, and browser control work on fully headless servers. A headless runner asked for a screenshot answers with a clear error rather than a black frame - assign that work to a runner on a real desktop.

libxdo.so.3: cannot open shared object file

A runner installed before this error was fixed needs one library that a stock Ubuntu desktop does not ship (it lives in universe). Install it once with sudo apt install libxdo3; the runner then starts and updates itself to a build that no longer needs it. Newer builds synthesize input over the X11 protocol directly and require nothing extra to install. That is a packaging fix, not new Wayland support: synthetic input reaches X11 and XWayland windows, so a Wayland-native application still does not receive computer_action keystrokes or clicks.

docs.title: The XTM One Desktop app
docs.text:
Once enrolled, the app opens your instance in its own window and lives in the system tray (or menu bar) behind the XTM One icon. From there you can:

  • open the chat window - or press Ctrl+Alt+Space from anywhere
  • see live status - Online, Connecting, Reconnecting, or Update required when your instance no longer accepts this version of the app (update it from the connection panel)
  • open the connection panel: the machine's name, the enrolled instance URL, the app version, and the host facts reported to the platform (OS build, available shells, installed browsers, monitors, timezone and locale)
  • change a few settings - automatic updates, launch-at-login, and the browser CDP URL
  • unenroll the machine locally

The same actions are in the app's own menu, so you never have to find the tray icon: the File and Help menus of the chat window on Windows and Linux, the menu bar on macOS (where Cmd+, opens the settings). Check for updates..., in the Help menu (the app menu on macOS), asks your instance for a newer build and, when there is one, installs it and restarts the app.

Closing a window hides the app to the tray; the runner keeps serving. To stop the app, use Quit in the tray or in the app's menu; while an update is being installed, Quit waits up to a minute for you to answer or cancel its password prompt, and the connection panel says so. The window stays on your instance: links that would open a new tab, and any link to another site, open in your default browser, and downloads land in your Downloads folder. The app updates itself from signed bundles matched to your instance, so a fleet stays current without anyone touching each machine. When an update restarts the app, the windows you had open come back, with the chat on the page you were on.

On Linux, only the AppImage updates unattended. A .deb / .rpm install updates through your package manager, which asks for an administrator password, so the app does not install those updates on its own: it opens the connection panel to announce the new version, and Install version ... installs it when you choose to. For a Linux desktop that should stay current with nobody at the keyboard, install the AppImage (or the headless build on a server). A .deb / .rpm install from an earlier version gets this behaviour through one last update applied the old way: until you accept it, that version asks for the password on its own each time it checks for updates.

docs.title: Upgrading from XTM One Runner
docs.text:
An installed runner updates itself into XTM One Desktop; the enrollment, the credential and the launch-at-login choice are kept. A few things change name along the way:

  • Windows: XTM One Desktop installs into a new XTM One Desktop folder and removes the former install. The Start menu and desktop shortcuts and a taskbar pin keep their XTM One Runner name but start XTM One Desktop; XTM One Runner leaves Installed apps. A machine updated before this was fixed may still list XTM One Runner in Installed apps: do not uninstall it, as that removes the machine's enrollment and sign-in. The next update removes it for you.
  • macOS: the app bundle is swapped in place. A Mac upgraded from the runner keeps its old folder name until you reinstall from a fresh download.
  • Linux: the AppImage updates in place. The .deb / .rpm package is now named xtm-one-desktop; it declares that it replaces xtm-one-runner, so a package-manager upgrade removes the old package for you.

Headless runners on servers are not affected: they keep their own update channel and the same command line.

docs.title: Signing in
docs.text:
Email and password work inside the window like anywhere else. Single sign-on runs in your system browser: identity providers refuse or degrade embedded browsers (conditional access, passkeys, Windows Hello, "use the browser you are already signed in to"), and the app's window shares no session with the browser you use all day. So a Continue with ... button in the app opens your browser on your instance's sign-in; you finish there as usual, the browser then shows which machine is asking (the name of your XTM One Desktop machine and who enrolled it) and asks you to confirm, and the app signs itself in a moment later. The browser tab keeps no session - you asked to sign in on the desktop.

The confirmation matters: a sign-in request can only be started by an enrolled XTM One Desktop, and can only land on a machine that is yours (you enrolled it) or company-managed (a shared machine your administrator provisioned). A machine someone else enrolled is refused, even one shared with your group: that share lets the machine run your commands, it does not let whoever holds the machine act as you. If the machine named is not yours, choose Not my machine: the request is dropped so nobody else can complete it, the refusal is recorded in the audit log, and you should tell your administrator.

docs.title: Acting on this machine
docs.text:
Every message you send from the app carries the machine it was typed on, so the agent's computer_use tools default to it: "run the tests", "what is in ~/Downloads", "take a screenshot" act here, without naming a runner. Fleet targeting still works - name another machine and the agent reaches it, within the usual rules. Above the composer, a small bar shows the machine, its connection state and a switch to turn local execution off for a conversation.

When the machine's permission model holds a shell command for approval (the Shell commands need approval switch, on the enrollment key or on the machine's card), the request appears in the chat, above the composer: what the agent wants to run and on which machine, with Approve, Always allow, Reject and Always block. The agent waits for your decision and the command's output lands in the same reply. A decision you do not take in time leaves the command queued on the XTM One Desktop page, where you can still approve it.

docs.title: Seeing what the agent does on a machine
docs.text:
Every command an agent sends to a machine shows up in the conversation as a card, above the reply it leads to - in the Desktop app and in the browser alike:

  • a shell command is a small terminal window: the prompt and the command, a live timer while it runs, then its exit code, how long it took and its output (errors in their own colour), with buttons to copy the command or the output and a larger view;
  • a file read or written shows its path and a preview of the content;
  • a folder listing shows the folder's entries, folders first;
  • a screenshot shows a thumbnail you can enlarge;
  • a mouse, keyboard or browser action says what was done (text typed through the agent is shown as a character count, never as text).

A command held for your approval, blocked by the machine's policy, refused because the machine was busy or offline, or cut short when the reply ended says so on its card. The cards are saved with the conversation, so they are still there after a reload and for the people you share it with; a very long output is shortened on the card, and the reply's reasoning details (the i icon) keep more of it.

Inside XTM One Desktop, the paths on a card whose command ran on this machine get Open (with its default application), Show in folder and Copy path, and so do absolute paths the agent quotes in its reply, such as C:\Users\me\Desktop\disks.txt or a file:/// link: a click opens the item, Alt (Option on macOS) + click shows it in its folder. Only documents, images, media and plain-text files are opened that way - an executable, a script, a shortcut, an installer, a web page or a document able to carry macros is only ever shown in its folder - and a network address (a \\server\share path, a link that leads onto one) is never opened from the chat; a drive letter you mapped to a share yourself works like any other drive.

When a long reply finishes while the app is behind another window, the taskbar entry flashes (the Dock icon bounces on macOS) so you know it is ready.

docs.title: Uninstall and re-enroll
docs.text:
Uninstalling the app removes the local enrollment with it - the stored credential, the configuration, and the launch-at-login entry - so the next install always starts fresh at the Connect form. The runner's record on the platform is deliberately left alone (an uninstall can happen offline): revoke it on the XTM One Desktop page when you retire a machine for good.

If a running runner's record is revoked on the platform, the app shows a fatal error with a Re-enroll this machine button: one click drops the dead local credential and reopens the Connect form, prefilled with your instance URL and ready for a fresh enrollment key.

Revoking takes effect on every server at once: from that moment no new command is queued for the machine or handed to it and nothing more is accepted from it, its queued and running commands end, and its live connection closes right away, or at its next heartbeat (every 30 seconds by default) at the latest. A command handed to it a moment before the revocation may still reach it; it is recorded as cancelled and its result is refused.

docs.title: Permissions the first time
docs.text:
• macOS asks for Screen Recording and Accessibility permission the first time an agent captures the screen or controls input. Grant them in System Settings > Privacy & Security; the app links you straight there and shows whether each one is granted.
  • Linux capture and input need a graphical session. On Wayland, capture goes through the desktop portal; the app warns when the current session cannot be captured.

docs.title: What an agent can do on a runner
docs.text:
When an agent has the computer_use built-in tool and at least one of your runners is online, it can:

  • take a full-desktop screenshot (the audit-evidence case)
  • perform mouse and keyboard actions
  • run a shell command
  • read, write, and list files
  • control a browser you already authenticated

Typing and scrolling are bounded by the command's time budget, never by a length: text of any size is typed in small chunks, and when the budget runs out the action stops between two chunks and says how far it got, so nothing is typed after the command is reported as timed out. A shell command's output and its errors are each kept up to 1 MiB; past that the output is cut and the result says so. The data a command returns - that output, a folder listing, a page's content - may take up to 16 MiB once written as JSON, where escaping counts (a control character takes six bytes), and a file it returns up to RUNNER_MAX_RESULT_BYTES. A larger result is not kept: the command fails at once and its error says why, so the agent can ask for less.

Flows can drive runners too: the Runner command node dispatches the same command kinds through the same transport — the runner's permission mode, allow-lists, and approval gating apply unchanged — and can wait for the result. A flow reads at most 1 MiB of that result, written as JSON: a larger one reaches the node's outputs cut to fit, each cut text ending with a [TRUNCATED ...] marker and flow_truncated giving its full size, while the machine's command history keeps it whole. Flows can also react to runner lifecycle through the built-in Runner online, Runner offline, and Runner command completed event types with the On event and Wait for event nodes. Runner offline fires when a machine is revoked while online, or when it has been silent for RUNNER_OFFLINE_AFTER_SECONDS (75 seconds by default): the scheduler's presence sweep, which runs about once a minute and handles up to 500 machines per pass, then declares it offline. Runner online fires once the machine is heard from again, so the two always alternate. A platform restart or upgrade drops every runner connection for a few seconds; a machine back within that window fires neither. The machine rides the restart out: it retries its polls, heartbeats and result uploads with back-off, so a command that finishes while the platform restarts still reports its result once the platform is back within about 50 seconds.

The agent waits for a command's result as long as the machine may take to report it: from the moment the machine takes the command, its execution limit and then those 50 seconds of upload retries (205 seconds in all by default, RUNNER_RESULT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS sets a fixed wait instead), never longer than the agent run allows one tool call. When that limit ends the wait first, the agent is told the command may still finish.

A command is never sent later to nobody: when the agent stops waiting for it (its wait ran out or you stopped the turn) or the flow run waiting for it ends, a command the machine had not picked up yet is cancelled, including one still waiting for your approval in a flow, and one the machine already took is not sent again. If that one still finishes, its output is in the machine's command history.

Screenshots and file reads come back into the conversation as inline images or downloadable files, exactly like other tool results, so they can flow straight into an evidence workflow. The PNG is also forwarded to the model as a native vision block (high-detail, PNG preserved) so the agent can read the URL bar, labels, errors, and OS clock itself - it should never ask you to describe or verify the capture.

docs.title: Control what a runner allows
docs.text:
Each runner carries its own permission model, set on the XTM One Desktop page (the machine's card):

  • Restricted (default) - least privilege. Only the capabilities you enable are allowed (screenshot, mouse/keyboard, shell, file operations, browser control). Enabling a capability is the consent: once it is on, it runs without further prompts. Shell commands are the exception and get finer control:
    • Allow-list (standing approvals) - a matching command runs immediately and never asks for approval. With approval off, only allow-listed commands can run at all.
    • Block-list (standing refusals) - a command containing a blocked word or phrase is always refused. It never runs and never reaches the approval queue, and the block-list wins over the allow-list.
    • Require approval - any shell command not covered by the lists waits for a human decision: inline in the chat when the command was asked for from XTM One Desktop, otherwise on the XTM One Desktop page. When approving or rejecting, Approve & always allow / Reject & always block saves the exact command, whatever its length, into the corresponding list, so the same command never asks again. Approval applies to shell commands only - screenshots, input, file operations and browser control never queue.
    • File operations can additionally be narrowed with a path allow-list. The platform checks the path as written against it, and the runner resolves links to see where the path really leads. A path inside the allowed folders that leads outside them through a link (a symbolic link, a junction, a mount point) still runs by default, as it always has, with a warning in its result and in the runner log; with RUNNER_STRICT_PATH_CONFINEMENT=true (see Configuration) it is refused (to reach what such a link leads to, add that folder to the allowed paths). A link that stays inside the allowed folders keeps working either way, an allowed folder that does not exist yet can be written into (the runner creates it), and a path written as a network share or automount path (\\server\share, /net/host) is only looked up inside an allowed folder that is itself on it. After opening a file or folder the runner re-checks the handle it actually got: its type in every mode, and in strict mode its real path too, so a link swapped in between the check and the open is caught and nothing is truncated or written until that check passes (only a folder the write has to create is made before it, so a link swapped in at that moment can leave an empty folder where it leads; on a volume the OS cannot resolve paths on, some RAM disks and VirtualBox shared folders, the handle cannot be named and the pre-open check stands). What no mode prevents: a link in an allowed folder that leads onto a share is followed to see where it leads, which can reach that host, and a hard link is the file itself under a second name, so one inside an allowed folder is served like any file there.
  • Full control - a deliberate opt-in that allows every capability and every command with no lists and no approval. It is clearly flagged in the UI, and every command is still audited.

Whatever the mode, every command is recorded server-side with its result, and revoking a runner invalidates its credential immediately - the next command fails and the app stops. A command still queued when a runner's permissions are tightened is checked again when it is delivered, and cancelled if they no longer allow it.

File operations read and write regular files as they always have. A path goes to the operating system as written and is never judged by its name: what the OS opens for it decides, and when the OS refuses it, its error is the result.
