A file that is not a regular file - a character or block device (a serial port, /dev/urandom, /dev/zero, NUL on Windows, a volume or disk opened raw such as \\.\C:), a named pipe (FIFO) or a socket, as the OS reports the object opened - is also read and written as before, on every runner, with a warning in the result and in the runner log saying what it is. With RUNNER_STRICT_PATH_CONFINEMENT=true (see Configuration) it is refused, on every runner, full control included; on Windows a device is refused once it is opened, before anything is read or written, since its handle is what tells. A name Windows opens as a file is a file, whatever it looks like - con.log, aux.c or nul.txt on Windows 11, a folder named aux, a drive, share or volume location behind a \\.\, \??\ or \\?\ prefix, a file in a volume shadow copy (\\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\...) - and is served as one, with no warning, strict or not. Reading a Windows device such as NUL, or a raw volume, fails as it always did: Windows cannot describe it for the size check before the read. Such a file is opened without waiting and then used as a plain open would, so a named pipe with no program at its other end returns at once (empty for a read, an error for a write) instead of holding a runner worker for good; a socket cannot be opened as a file at all. A restricted runner with allowed folders only reaches one inside those folders; a device path never lies under a drive-letter folder.

A read never asks for more than a positive result size limit (RUNNER_MAX_RESULT_BYTES, the largest file a runner may upload) or 256 KiB, whichever is larger. What comes back as a file - binary content, or text past 256 KiB - is cut to the limit and flagged as incomplete; the 256 KiB of text that comes back inline has never met that limit, so under a smaller limit a runner from this release still returns such text whole (an older runner cuts it to the limit, as before). A limit of 0 or less keeps its meaning - every non-empty file result is refused at upload and reads are not bounded - and is reported at startup and by the security audit (Settings → Security).

A read that stops at its size before the end of the file says so in its result: how many bytes were read, and how to read the rest - a larger max_bytes, or, at the result size limit, another way such as a shell command that splits or compresses the file. A runner from before this release cannot tell, so a read it returns at exactly the size it was asked for is flagged as possibly incomplete.

docs.title: Choose which machines an agent can reach
docs.text:
Runners are targeted, not global:

  • Give runners labels (for example audit, eu-west, workstation).
  • On an agent, set a runner selector - specific runners or a set of labels - so the agent can only reach the machines you intend.
  • An assignment can refine that selection further, never widen it, so an agent-driven automation can never reach a machine its agent could not. A flow's Runner command node targets one explicit runner instead — gated by the runner's own permission mode, allow-lists, and visibility (a flow can only use runners visible to the person who runs it: their own, group-shared, or company-managed).

When more than one eligible machine is online, mutating actions require the agent to name the target runner explicitly, so a command can never land on the wrong machine by accident. The list_runners tool lets an agent see which machines are online before acting.

docs.title: Availability and limits
docs.text: The whole subsystem is governed by platform configuration: an administrator enables it, sets where installers are downloaded from, and can cap how many runners a user may enroll and how many commands may run on one machine at once. If downloads are not configured on your deployment, the page explains it and you can still enroll a runner you obtained separately. See the runner variables in Configuration for the full list.

docs.title: Fleet oversight for administrators
docs.text: The XTM One Desktop page lists your machines: the ones you enrolled, the ones shared with you, and the company-managed fleet - for administrators too. To see every machine enrolled with the platform, whoever enrolled it, an administrator opens Administration > Objects and filters by Machines: each row shows the machine's owner, operating system, live connection state (Online, Offline with the time it was last seen, or Revoked) and runner version, and opens the machine's own page with the same permission editor and revoke / delete actions as here. Reading the command history of a machine you neither own nor hold a configure-level share on (a company-managed machine is yours to manage and is not counted) is recorded in the audit log. See Objects.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Name each machine so you can tell an agent exactly where to work.
  • Start in Restricted mode and enable only the capabilities you need; reserve Full control for machines you fully trust.
  • Use labels for fleets and set agent selectors so each agent reaches only its own machines.
  • Turn on shell-command approval when a person should stay in the loop, and build up the allow/block lists from real decisions with "Approve & always allow" / "Reject & always block".
  • Revoke a runner as soon as a machine is decommissioned.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• The XTM One Desktop page (bottom of the left navigation) - where you download the app, create enrollment keys and manage your machines.
  • Agents - bind the computer_use tool and set the runner selector.
  • Configuration - the RUNNERS_ENABLED and RUNNER_* deployment variables.

docs.title: Sharing and access
docs.text: When you share something, you may also be lending what it carries. An agent bound to your GitHub token lets everyone who can use that agent act with your token; an MCP server with your API key in its headers answers for everyone whose agent uses it. XTM One always says so, and never blocks you.

docs.title: What can be lent
docs.text: Resource What the people it reaches act with Integration its stored credential: an OAuth connected account, a personal access token, an API key, a bot token MCP server its headers, its environment variables, or its own OAuth token Custom tool its code, run on their behalf Channel bot its bot token (bots are platform-wide and managed by administrators) Variable its value, secret or not

docs.title: Through what
docs.text:
A resource reaches people in two ways:

  • Directly: it is shared with people, with groups, or with everyone (company-managed, optionally restricted to named people and groups).
  • Through something that carries it: an agent bound to it, an assignment override or trigger, a flow node, a knowledge base sync source, a skill's private source, a prompt or custom tool that references a variable, or the General Assistant's platform bindings. What an agent or the General Assistant attaches carries its resources into their runs too: an attached prompt's or skill's variables, a skill's private source, a knowledge base's sync source (attached prompt, attached skill, attached knowledge base on the card).
  • Through a per-user binding: an agent bound "per user" to a provider has each person use their own integration in a chat, but its assignments run as one person - the agent's owner, or the run-as user of a company-managed assignment - and use that person's own integration of the provider for everyone who sees their work, or, while that person has none connected, the company-wide integration of the provider they may use. The integration's card lists those assignments (per-user binding); a per-user fan-out assignment (Run for all users) uses each user's own.

An agent's audience includes more than the people it is shared with: anyone with its public chat link, anyone who messages it on a channel that accepts people without an account, its A2A partners, anyone holding the platform MCP key when the agent is exposed there, and anyone holding the URL of one of its webhook assignments. A flow's audience includes anyone holding the URL of its webhook trigger once it is active. What the people without an account run counts against the platform-wide agentic limits (see Requests with no account).

Two honest caveats:

  • In a chat, people who cannot see an integration bound to an agent, or whose owner's connected account is not shared with them, use their own connected integration of the same provider instead; when they have none, a note under the answer says the integration was not used and why. The agent's runs, public link, channels and A2A partners act with the bound one.
  • A variable resolves only for someone who can see it, or in a run acting as someone who can (the agent's owner by default).

An OAuth connected account shared without its owner's consent is shared without the account: the people it reaches connect their own.

docs.title: Where you see it
docs.text:
• On the resource's page: a Sharing and access card lists every path - shared with a group, with people, company-managed, through an agent, an assignment, a flow, a knowledge base, a skill, a prompt, a custom tool or the General Assistant - with who it reaches and a link to each one you can open. Something you cannot open is named by its owner, without its name. Integrations, MCP servers and custom tools show it on their overview, variables in their edit dialog, channel bots in their tools dialog (Settings > Channels & Bots).
  • On the resource's card: a Shared - N ways badge, with the breakdown in its tooltip.

Both are shown to the people who can manage the resource, and both follow every change as soon as it is saved.

docs.title: When you are asked
docs.text:
Before a change that lends something to new people, or takes it from people who use it, one dialog lists each resource concerned: whose it is ("your MCP server Tickets and its headers", "Alice's GitHub connected account"), who newly gets it or loses it, through what, what they can do with it and how to avoid it (a company-managed resource instead of a personal one, per-user integrations, Don't share my connected account). One click proceeds; nothing is refused and there is no setting. The dialog only opens when someone other than you and the resource's owner is concerned.

You are asked when you:

  • share a resource or something that carries one: people, groups, company-managed (a flow's too), lifting an access restriction, an owner transfer (an agent, a flow, a skill, a knowledge base, a prompt, an integration, an MCP server, a custom tool), an agent's public web widget, an agent's channels, sharing an agent's personal integrations with its groups from its Sharing card;
  • bind a resource to something shared: an agent's integrations (fixed or per user), pipeline steps, MCP servers, custom tools, channel bots, knowledge bases, skills and prompts, persona, guardrails and human-in-the-loop prompt (variables), an assignment's overrides, trigger, channels, prompt and run-as identity, a flow node, a knowledge base import source, a skill's private source, a prompt's or skill's content, the General Assistant's bindings, knowledge bases and channels;
  • open a public entry point: activating a flow with a webhook trigger, resuming a webhook assignment, letting a channel bot answer people without an account, exposing an agent on the platform MCP endpoint or generating its key;
  • change a group's members: an administrator adding someone to a group (or removing them) is told what its shares lend them, by name;
  • create something already shared: a company-managed integration, agent, prompt, skill, MCP server or custom tool, a channel bot, an assignment on a shared agent;
  • unshare or unbind: the dialog says who stops having access, with Unshare and Keep sharing - switching an agent to per-user integrations, unrouting an agent from a channel bot, removing an agent from the platform MCP endpoint or revoking its key included;
  • delete an agent, an assignment, a flow, an integration, an MCP server, a custom tool, a prompt, a skill, a knowledge base, a channel bot or a variable that others use: the dialog says who loses what, and replaces the usual confirmation.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Every route is read-only and additive:

  • GET /api/v1/exposure/{resources}/{id}: every path of one resource, with its reason and audience. For the people who can manage the resource (an administrator who opens it from a direct link or Administration > Objects included).
  • GET /api/v1/exposure/{resources}/summary: the number of ways each resource you can see and manage is shared, for the list cards.
  • POST /api/v1/exposure/preview: before a change, which resources it lends to new people (gained) and takes from people who could use them (lost). Body: entity_type (a resource type, or agent, assignment, flow, knowledge_base, skill, prompt, general_assistant, and for administrators group and platform_mcp), entity_id (omitted when creating), parent_id (the agent, when creating an assignment) and change (only the fields the change sets, plus new_owner_id for an owner transfer and delete: true for a deletion; remove_channel for an agent unrouted from a channel; add_user_ids / remove_user_ids for a group; mcp_exposed_agent_ids / has_mcp_key for the platform MCP endpoint; status: "active" for a flow's activation).

{resources} is integrations, mcp-servers, custom-tools, channel-bots or variables. GET /api/v1/integrations/{id}/exposure, GET /api/v1/integrations/exposure/summary and POST /api/v1/integrations/exposure/preview give the same answer for integrations, computed by the same engine, with integration-specific names (credential, credential_usable, credentials, reached). The routes never return a secret value, and a carrier you cannot open is listed without its name.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
This page complements Skills in XTM One.

That guide explains what a skill is. This page gives you a quick tour of the skill screens.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text: In the left navigation, this area is Skills. The list page is a reusable behavior library: search by name, description, or purpose, and filter by visibility or tags. Each card answers three questions without opening the detail page — is the skill currently active, is it centrally maintained or locally owned, and (for URL-based skills) whether it should be edited here or refreshed from its source. If you have permission, Add Skill creates one by URL, paste, or file upload.

docs.title: The detail page
docs.text: Opening a skill shows a header with its name, source type (URL-based or direct content), enabled state, and badges. For URL-based skills the header also has Refresh, which re-fetches the content from the source URL — the quickest way to answer "did the source change outside XTM One, and do I need the latest version here?". The page is organized into Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview helps you judge whether the skill is active, up to date, and widely used: how many agents depend on it, its content size, the last refresh for URL-based skills, and a content preview.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration is where you inspect or edit how the skill is defined. The parts that matter serve different purposes:

  • the markdown content is where the actual operating method lives
  • the source URL matters when the skill is maintained outside XTM One and refreshed from a source of truth
  • Enabled controls whether the skill is currently available to agents — a skill can stay saved but stop affecting agents immediately, including mid-conversation
  • Hide from chat controls discoverability in chat, not whether the skill exists
  • sharing settings control who can reuse it

The content editor includes a variable insert control for reusable values.

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Activity is the audit view. During troubleshooting it helps you tell a skill change apart from an agent configuration change or a normal difference in model behavior.

docs.title: How a skill reaches the agent
docs.text:
An agent does not carry the full text of every skill attached to it. Its prompt carries a catalog: one entry per skill with the name, the description, the compatibility note, and the names of any bundled files. When a task matches an entry, the agent calls load_skill and the full instructions arrive at that point in the conversation. If the skill is a package, the agent can then read individual bundled files with read_skill_resource.

This is why the description matters more than it looks: it is the only thing the agent sees until it decides to load. A description that does not say when to use the skill leaves the agent guessing.

Three consequences worth knowing:

  • attaching ten skills costs about the same prompt space as attaching one — the cost scales with the number of skills, not the size of their content
  • every load shows up in the run trace as a tool call, so a trace finally answers "which skill actually influenced this answer?"
  • a skill that is disabled, unshared, or made private stops being loadable immediately, even in a conversation that is already running (detaching a skill from the agent takes effect on the next message or run, like every other change to an agent's configuration)

docs.title: Keeping one skill always loaded
docs.text:
On an agent's Configuration tab, each attached skill has a pin. Pinning it puts the full instructions in the system prompt on every turn, exactly as before this behaviour existed — the right choice for the one skill that defines how the agent works, rather than one it should reach for occasionally. A pinned skill does not appear in the catalog, because there is nothing left to load.

Pin sparingly. Pinning every skill re-creates the oversized prompt the catalog exists to avoid.

docs.title: Skills from a private GitHub repository
docs.text:
A URL-based skill normally fetches its SKILL.md anonymously, which only works for a public file. When the file lives in a private repository, select a connected GitHub integration under Private repository access, and every fetch is authenticated with that integration's stored credential instead.

Both GitHub integration types work, because both authenticate the same API:

  • a personal access token — a fine-grained token must list the repository and grant Contents: Read
  • an OAuth App or GitHub App connection — the current token is read on every refresh, so a rotated token is picked up with no change to the skill

Nothing is copied onto the skill. It stores only a reference to the integration, so rotating the credential in Integrations is the single place a token is ever managed. You can attach any integration you can already see: your own, one shared with your groups, or a company-managed one.

Tracked branch decides which version is served:

  • leave it empty to follow the repository's default branch, which means each refresh returns the latest commit merged there — the usual choice when skills are reviewed by pull request and merged
  • set a branch name to follow that branch instead
  • set a commit SHA to deliberately pin a fixed version that will not move

The URL you paste may point at the GitHub file page (github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<branch>/…), at raw.githubusercontent.com, or at the contents API. All three are recognised. A branch name containing a / is ambiguous in those URLs, so set Tracked branch explicitly in that case.

The content is validated when you save: XTM One reads the file once with the credential you selected, and refuses to save with a specific message when the token is rejected, when the token cannot see the repository, or when the path does not exist on the tracked branch. You therefore find out immediately rather than discovering a stale skill later.

After that, refresh is on the normal schedule: URL-based skills are re-fetched when their cached content is more than a day old, and the check runs hourly. A newly merged change appears within one refresh cycle rather than instantly — use Refresh in the header when you need it right away.

docs.title: When the credential stops working
docs.text:
If the attached credential expires, is revoked, or loses access to the repository, the skill shows a Credential rejected badge on both the list page and the detail header.

That state is deliberately different from a broken URL:

  • the skill stays enabled and agents keep using the last content that was successfully fetched
  • refresh keeps retrying daily instead of quarantining the skill, because the fix is rotating a token, not repairing a URL
  • as soon as the credential works again, the next refresh clears the badge on its own

To recover, re-authorize the integration in Integrations, or attach a different one to the skill. Operators also get distinct log entries for an authentication failure, a missing path, and a provider outage, so a token problem is never reported as a dead URL.

Setting Private repository access back to Public repository (no credential) detaches the credential. That is a configuration change only: it does not re-read the source, so it works even when the repository is private and unreadable without a token. The content already cached is kept, and the next scheduled refresh then behaves like any other unreachable URL.

docs.title: Importing skills from an archive
docs.text:
Import Package on the list page accepts a single SKILL.md / .txt file, or a .zip archive.

A ZIP may hold several skills at once — a folder exported from a repository, or a collection shared by another team. Nothing is written straight away: XTM One reads the archive first and opens a review screen listing the skills it found (with their description, resource and version counts), the files it ignored grouped by reason (a README with no frontmatter, an image, archive metadata such as __MACOSX), and a checkbox per skill. A single-skill package goes through the same review, showing one row.

docs.title: What counts as a skill in the archive
docs.text:
A skill is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter declaring name and description, and the directory holding it is that skill's root. Those roots are found wherever they are in the archive, so all of these work — mixed together in the same ZIP if need be:

  • <skill-name>/SKILL.md with its scripts/, references/, assets/, examples/ and versionning/ folders — the Agent Skills layout, repeated as many times as needed
  • <skill-name>/<anything>.md — folders that name the file after the skill rather than using SKILL.md
  • <skill-name>.md at the root of the archive — a flat folder of skill files
  • any of the above under one or more wrapper folders, which is what zipping a skills/ directory produces (skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md), README included

The frontmatter name is always what the skill is called, even when the folder is named differently — a mismatch is a warning on the review screen, not an error. When a folder contains both SKILL.md and other markdown files, SKILL.md is the skill and the rest is ignored.

Files inside a skill's scripts/, references/, assets/, examples/ and versionning/ folders belong to that skill at any depth, and are never mistaken for skills of their own even when they carry frontmatter — a reference document stays a reference document, and a versionning/ snapshot stays a version. Anything else inside a skill folder (an unmapped templates/ directory, for instance) is listed as ignored rather than imported. When a single folder holds several skill files, resources cannot be attributed to one of them: they are listed as ignored and the skills are imported without them.

docs.title: Collisions and partial failures
docs.text:
A skill whose name you already have is flagged on the review screen, with a choice per skill: Skip leaves the existing skill untouched (the default), Replace overwrites it with the archive's version, Import as new creates a copy under a suffixed name.

Each skill is then imported on its own. A skill that fails — malformed frontmatter, a duplicate name inside the archive, a package requiring a tool this platform does not have — never rolls back the skills that already landed. The result screen lists every skill as created, replaced, skipped or failed, with the reason.

docs.title: What a package's files become
docs.text: A skill package is more than its SKILL.md. The mapped folders are turned into real platform objects at import time.

docs.title: scripts/ become Custom Tools
docs.text:
Every executable script in scripts/ is imported as an enabled Custom Tool, so the agents using the skill can actually run it. The tool is named <skill-name>-<file-name> (pdf-extract-convert for scripts/convert.py), described as Imported from scripts/convert.py, and tagged skill-import plus the skill name so you can find every tool a skill created. Language comes from the extension: .py is Python, .js / .mjs / .cjs are JavaScript. A file with any other extension is not turned into a tool — it is still stored with the skill and downloadable from it, and the import reports Skipped non-executable script resources so the omission is visible rather than silent.

There are two shapes:

  • One tool per file — the default. Each script stands on its own.
  • One tool for the whole folder — used when scripts/ looks like a Python project, which XTM One detects as an __init__.py alongside more than one .py file. Modules that import each other only work if they are unpacked together, so the entire scripts/ tree is embedded in a single tool: at run time it is extracted into a temporary directory, that directory is put on sys.path and becomes the working directory, and the entrypoint runs as __main__. Anything passed as the tool's argv input becomes sys.argv for the script.

The entrypoint of a Python project is chosen among the top-level scripts that contain __main__, preferring main.py, then run.py, then the first in alphabetical order; when several qualify, the import says which one it picked. The embedded workspace is capped at 10 MB compressed — a larger scripts/ folder is refused with a message asking you to reduce or split the package. Imported tools execute in the same hardened sandbox as any other Custom Tool: importing a package does not create a privileged execution path.

docs.title: Who can run them, and what happens on delete
docs.text:
Materialized tools inherit the skill's visibility — a company-managed or group-shared skill produces company-managed or group-shared tools, because agents belonging to other users must be able to execute them. A private skill produces private tools. A tool name that is already taken is suffixed rather than overwriting anything.

Agents that already reference the skill are wired up automatically: the new tools (and reference knowledge bases) are added to their configuration, so an existing agent does not silently miss the scripts of a skill it already uses. Deleting the skill deletes the tools and knowledge bases its import created and removes them from every agent that had been linked; re-importing with Replace does the same cleanup first, so repeated imports never accumulate orphaned tools. The tools a skill created are listed on its Resources tab, next to the resource path each one came from.

docs.title: references/ become Knowledge Base documents
docs.text:
Text files in references/ (or reference/) are imported as documents in a knowledge base named <skill-name>-references, tagged the same way, and bound to the agents using the skill. Files whose type cannot be read as text are skipped and reported as Skipped non-text reference resources.

The knowledge base and its documents exist as soon as the import returns, but the documents are queued for vectorization like any uploaded document — they stay pending until the platform worker processes them, and only then are they searchable by agents. A knowledge base whose documents are all still pending means the worker has not picked them up yet, not that the import missed them. assets/ and examples/ are stored with the skill as-is, and are never turned into tools or documents.

docs.title: Controlling the mapping: assets/xtm-resource-map.json
docs.text:
Everything above is inference — convenient defaults for a package that ships nothing but files. A package can decide for itself instead by including assets/xtm-resource-map.json:

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "builtins": ["web_search"],
  "scripts": [
    {
      "path": "scripts/convert.py",
      "tool": {
        "name": "pdf-to-markdown",
        "description": "Convert a PDF to markdown",
        "language": "python",
        "workspace_mode": "project",
        "input_schema": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": { "argv": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } } }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "references": [{ "path": "references/format.md" }]
}

Points that matter when writing one:

  • listing scripts replaces inference — only the entries you list become tools, which is how a Python project exposes more than one entrypoint
  • workspace_mode is single_file or project, and overrides the detection described above
  • input_schema is the tool's input contract; without it the tool takes no declared input
  • builtins requests platform built-in tools by ID. The platform refuses to import a package asking for a built-in it does not have, and the bulk review screen flags it before you approve rather than at write time
  • a malformed manifest fails the import with the exact field at fault, instead of falling back to inference

Exporting a skill writes this manifest back into the package with the mapping that was actually resolved, so a skill exported from one platform and imported into another creates the same tools.

docs.title: Packaged skills carry their own resources
docs.text:
The skill card and picker show what a skill carries, for example 1 KB · 2 tools. Those resources belong to the skill, not to the agent:

  • attaching such a skill to an agent also attaches the knowledge bases and custom tools it carries, so instructions that say "consult references/playbook.md" actually reach the content
  • detaching the skill removes them again
  • in the agent's Knowledge Bases and Custom Tools sections they are marked Via skill and cannot be detached by hand — detach the skill instead

Two consequences are worth knowing. A company-managed agent only accepts company-managed knowledge bases, so a packaged knowledge base that is not company-managed is skipped rather than attached — publish the skill company-managed if its references must follow it there. And resources you attached yourself are never touched by this: only the ones a package created are added and removed automatically.

Deleting the skill, or re-importing its package with replace, deletes the resources that import created and unbinds them everywhere.

docs.title: Read-only states
docs.text: Company-managed skills can be read-only for non-admins, shared skills stay editable in a group context, and some built-in skills are non-editable. When a page is read-only, inspection still works.

docs.title: Empty states on the list page
docs.text:
If no skills exist yet, the page suggests creating the first skill by URL, paste, or file upload.

If filters remove all visible skills, the page shows No skills match your filter.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Check whether a skill is enabled before blaming the agent for missing behavior.
  • When an agent ignored a skill, read the run trace: no load_skill call means the description did not match the task, which is a description problem, not a content problem.
  • Write descriptions that say when to use the skill, not just what it contains.
  • Use Refresh on URL-based skills when the source was updated.
  • Treat a Credential rejected badge as an integration task, not a skill task — fix the token in Integrations.
  • Review Agents Using before changing a shared skill.
  • Keep compatibility and description fields meaningful so reuse stays easy.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A template is a design your presentations wear: a palette per theme, the heading and body typefaces, the logos drawn on every slide, the predefined assets a deck may place (figures, screenshots, badges, partner / integration / customer logos), the layouts it may use, and a few sentences of guidance on how to compose in that brand. Agents find templates by name, kind, aspect ratio, tag and by the themes they support, so the same request produces on-brand output for everyone. The page lists, for each template, the themes it supports — Dark, Light or both.

A template has one of two kinds, chosen when it is created: Presentation dresses slide decks and pages, Report dresses executive reports. Whatever its kind, its assets are readable by any deck — there is no separate "asset pack" kind, the assets belong to the template whose brand they serve.

Templates live under Agent Studio > Templates in the sidebar. The page opens with the three steps of using one; they are spelled out below.

docs.title: Use a template
docs.text:
1. Design it. A template declares the themes it supports — Dark, Light or both — with two switches, when it is created and at any time on the Configuration tab (Themes this template supports); at least one stays on. Each supported theme gets its own palette: the base palette carries the full set of colours and the typefaces and is read as Dark or Light from its background colour, and the other supported theme gets a variant palette in which only the colours you set differ — the accent, fonts and logos carry over. A template that supports a single theme limits every deck wearing it to that theme; switching a theme off removes the choice from those decks (a deck already in that theme is snapped to a supported one at its next save, and the note says so). The template's Preview renders a sample deck in each supported theme so the palettes can be judged before any deck exists.

2. Choose it when you create a presentation. New presentation, on the Presentations page or on a template's own page (New presentation with this template), asks which template the deck starts in and which of its supported themes to use, then opens the chat with the request written for you. In a chat, when you can see several templates, the template is your choice, never the assistant's: an assistant asked for a presentation without a template named lists your templates and asks which one to use before creating anything (it may recommend one, but a new deck is never created in a template you did not pick); name it ("in the Sales template") and it does not ask, ask for "no template" and the deck is drawn in the plain built-in look. Automations, and chats where the assistant cannot ask, use the platform's default presentation template — the built-in brand deck (the XTM One Brand Deck on an XTM One platform, the Filigran Brand Deck on Filigran Copilot) unless an administrator chose another company template in Settings > Parameters.

3. Change it anytime. A deck stays linked to its template rather than copying it: the palette, fonts and logos are read from the template every time the deck is drawn, so editing the template restyles every deck wearing it, at once. The deck's own Design section (Edit slides in the viewer) applies another template, or none, with a live preview, and offers the Dark / Light theme among the ones the chosen template supports. The slides, their words, the images uploaded to the deck and the theme it picked belong to the deck; deleting a template leaves its decks intact, in the plain look.

A template can also fix the deck defaults of new decks made from it, so nobody has to ask for the brand look each time — the theme (a default theme the template does not support is snapped to one it does), the 16:9 or 4:3 aspect ratio, the slide transition, and the covers: the hero backdrop, its colour and the theme of the title and closing slides, so a brand deck opens and closes on a dark gradient cover whatever the body's theme (the XTM One Brand Deck does: its decks open and close on its purple-to-cyan gradient cover). Deck defaults live in the template's Extra metadata and in the Design editor, and they dress new decks only — an existing deck is never restyled by them. A template can define the header and footer every deck wearing it fills once, and it carries the agent guidance every assistant reads before composing a deck in that brand: which slide opens, where the numbers go, how sparingly to use the accent color. The logo_mark asset — the symbol without the wordmark — is what the gradient cover draws as a faint watermark in its corner.

Only the template's palette, fonts, logos and footer pattern reach a deck. A template can restyle a presentation, but it can never inject arbitrary styling or scripts into the pages that render it.

docs.title: Header and footer
docs.text:
The line at the bottom of every slide of a deck is not written on the slides — it is drawn from a few deck settings. A template decides what that line says for every deck wearing it, as a pattern with placeholders:

{{event}} - {{title}} - {{classification}}
  • {{title}}, {{subtitle}} and {{event}} are always available: the deck's title, the subtitle of its opening slide (as plain text — inline emphasis such as [[accent:...]] is not drawn in a footer) and the event the deck names. They need no declaration.
  • Every other placeholder is a variable the template declares — a key (classification), the label the deck's settings show (Classification), an optional hint and an optional default. A deck fills its variables once, in its Header & footer settings; until it does, a variable reads the template's default, or nothing when the template declares none.
  • An empty placeholder disappears with its separator: a deck with no event reads Quarterly review - Confidential, not - Quarterly review - Confidential. Everything that is not a placeholder is drawn as written.
  • A header pattern is optional and follows the same rules; it is drawn along the top of the same slides as the footer, and hides with it.

The XTM One Brand Deck defines {{event}} - {{title}} - {{classification}}. The event and the classification are both optional and have no default, so a new deck reads its own title on every slide, and "mark it Confidential" is one field, not a slide-by-slide edit.

On the Configuration tab, the Design editor's Header & footer card holds the footer pattern, the optional header pattern and the variables (up to eight), and previews the line with sample values as you type. The declaration is checked before it is saved — a placeholder no variable declares, a variable no pattern uses, a key that is not a lowercase word, a missing label — and a declaration with a problem is refused rather than drawn literally on every slide. Overview shows the pattern and the variables of a template that has them. A template with no pattern leaves the footer to each deck, which writes an event and a free footer text in the same settings. Changing the pattern restyles every deck wearing the template, like the palette; a field a deck set for a former pattern is kept, and the deck's settings say when no footer reads it.

The pattern is part of the design an assistant authoring a template can set (chrome in the template's metadata, with footer, header and variables), and get_template shows it to any assistant composing a deck, which is how "set the event to FIC 2026" reaches the right field.

docs.title: The built-in brand deck
docs.text:
Every platform ships the XTM One Brand Deck, a company-managed template: the product's own purple palette on dark surfaces (it supports the Dark theme only), Geologica and IBM Plex typefaces, six ordered colours for the series of a chart, four brand colours (the XTM One, OpenCTI, OpenAEV and OpenCRQ product colours, which the boxes of an architecture diagram can wear), and the XTM One logo and mark. It is the working example of a template every platform has, and the default presentation template of an XTM One platform; Filigran Copilot, Filigran's internal edition, also ships the Filigran Brand Deck and defaults to it.

The logo is drawn automatically on every slide of a deck made from it. To give an assistant real figures to place — your architecture diagram, product screenshots, your partners' logos — duplicate it or create a template of your own and add them on its Assets tab.

docs.title: Predefined assets
docs.text:
The assets of a template are what an assistant places when you ask for a figure, so it uses the actual one instead of drawing an approximation.

Every asset has a description that says what the figure shows and which surface (dark or light) it is drawn for; assistants read these descriptions to pick the right file, and you see them in the Assets tab. A template can hold hundreds of assets, so an assistant never reads the whole list: it asks the template for one role ("the partner logos") or one keyword and gets only what matches — ask for "a logo wall of our partners" and it lays the right logos out in a logo grid.

Upgrading an XTM One platform

Earlier versions also shipped the Filigran Brand Deck, Filigran's own house style, on XTM One platforms. It is reserved to Filigran's internal edition: on the first start after the upgrade — whether AI is switched on or off — it is removed together with every one of its assets and their stored files, and whatever the object store could not delete at that start is deleted within the hour once it answers again. The decks made from it keep their slides and are drawn in the plain look until you choose another template in their Design section, such as the XTM One Brand Deck. A picture a slide had placed from it is removed with it and nothing is drawn in its place; editing that slide, asking an assistant to rewrite the deck or restoring an earlier revision still works — the picture stays gone and the history says how many pictures were left empty — and you can put another picture in its place at any time. If an administrator had chosen it as the Default Presentation Template, the setting returns to the built-in default. A copy you made with Duplicate is your own template and stays: delete it from the Templates page if it should go too.

Upgrading from the asset libraries

Earlier versions shipped the partner, integration and customer logos as three separate asset-library templates next to the brand deck. On an XTM One platform the first start after the upgrade removes them, logos included. On Filigran Copilot, which ships the Filigran Brand Deck, it moves their logos into that deck instead — the same files under the same identifiers, so every slide that already placed one keeps it — and removes the three emptied libraries. A template of that former kind you created yourself keeps working with its assets, but no new one can be created: give the logos to a Presentation template instead. Import refuses a package of that kind and names it, so edit the kind in the export first; Duplicate copies such a template as a Presentation one, keeping the palette keys and layouts a presentation honours; whatever it had to leave out is listed in the audit log entry of the copy.

Built-in templates carry a Built-in badge and are read-only: they are kept in sync with the platform on every startup, so an edit would be undone by the next upgrade. To derive your own palette from one, use Duplicate — the copy is yours to change.

docs.title: Create a template
docs.text:
From Templates, Add Template opens the creation form: a name, a description, the kind (Presentation for slide decks and pages, Report for executive reports), the aspect ratio, tags, and — for administrators — whether the template is company-managed. A Presentation template also declares the themes it supports with two switches, Dark and Light — both on by default, at least one stays on. Generate with AI drafts the palette from a brief (see below) and proposes the themes its palettes read as, which you can still change; Preview renders a sample deck in it before you save.

Once the template exists, its detail page has three tabs:

  • Overview — the description, the Design (the palette per theme, marked Supported or Not supported), the attributes agents search by (kind, aspect ratio, tags), the layout catalog, and how many times agents retrieved the template
  • Configuration — the editable fields, the Design editor (Themes this template supports, one palette per supported theme with its colours — the base palette comes first and also carries the fonts — and the deck defaults), the layouts and the sharing settings; the raw JSON stays available under Advanced (JSON). Every palette shows its chart series (chart_1 to chart_6, drawn as a small bar preview that follows each keystroke; each theme tunes its own, and an empty series keeps the built-in colour, chart_1 the accent) and its optional brand hues (brand_1 to brand_4, the product colours an architecture node or zone can wear; an empty one falls back to the chart series of the same rank, and a variant palette inherits the base palette's). An empty field shows, dashed, the colour a deck draws instead: the colour it falls back to, or what a variant palette inherits from the base palette - its accent, gradient and brand hues, and every colour when the base palette's background is not set. When Advanced (JSON) also holds a variant for the base palette's own theme, which decks in that theme lay over the base, the form names the keys it sets, and editing one of them in the base palette removes it from that variant - except background, which decides the base palette's theme: remove a variant's background in Advanced (JSON). Preview the unsaved design opens the template preview on everything being edited - the name, the aspect ratio, the layouts, the palettes and the deck defaults - so it shows what saving would produce; a name, an aspect ratio or layouts the save would refuse (a blank or over-long name, an over-long aspect ratio, layouts JSON that does not parse) are previewed as saved, and a palette value the save would refuse is left out of the preview.
  • Assets — the files bound to the template

The old theme label

Templates created before this version could carry a free-text theme label (dark, corporate, …). It never changed a deck's colours — only the palettes do — and is no longer part of the design. Where one is still set, Configuration shows it as Search label (legacy) with a Clear action; older agent instructions that looked templates up by that word keep working until it is cleared.

Templates are shared like every other resource: private to you, shared with groups, or company-managed for everyone. The Export action downloads the whole template as a package (metadata plus assets) that Import on the Templates page recreates on another platform.

docs.title: Generate a template with AI
docs.text:
Rather than typing color values by hand, let the assistant draft the template. Generate with AI is available on the Templates page, on the creation form, and on the Configuration tab of an existing template.

  1. Write a design brief in plain language: the audience, the mood, two or three colors — "a light corporate deck for quarterly reviews, navy and gold, understated".
  2. Add palette hints if you have them: a hex value or a color word, one chip each.
  3. If the template already holds an image asset, pick it under Sample colours from a logo: the dominant colors of the image are handed to the assistant so the palette sits naturally around your logo.
  4. Click Generate. A live preview of a sample deck in the proposed palette appears next to the result, together with the name, labels, layout catalog and agent guidance the assistant drafted, and the colors it read from the logo.
  5. Refine in follow-up rounds — Refine this result with "warmer accent" or "swap the heading font for a geometric sans" — or Regenerate from the brief to start over.
  6. Apply to form fills the fields. Nothing is saved until you save the template, and every field stays editable.

When you generate from the Configuration tab, Start from the current configuration keeps whatever the brief does not mention; turn it off for a fresh design. The proposal is checked against what the renderer supports: a value it would ignore is listed as an adjustment rather than silently dropped.

A logo first

To build a template around a logo, create the template, upload the logo on the Assets tab with the role logo (and the dark-on-light variant as logo_light), then run Generate with AI from Configuration with the logo selected. The logo is then drawn on every slide of the decks made from the template, and the palette is sampled from it.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
The Assets tab holds the files a template brings to a deck. Each asset has a role that tells the renderer and the agents what it is: logo, logo_light, logo_mark, product_logo, partner_logo, integration_logo, customer_logo, people_photo, background, illustration, diagram, screenshot, badge, icon, image, font, or other — and a free-text description that says what the file shows. A template holds up to 400 assets; the tab filters them by role (each role with its count) and by a keyword in the name or the description — the same two handles an assistant uses.

  • The logo asset (and logo_light on the light theme) is drawn by the deck chrome on every slide.
  • Other images are placed by the assistant when you ask for them — a product logo on the title slide, a background on a section divider, a diagram in an image block, several logos at once in a logo grid.
  • The description is what an assistant picks an asset by ("the architecture diagram", "the dark-surface variant"), so write it for a reader who cannot see the file: what it shows, and whether it is drawn for a dark or a light surface.

You can add, relabel, replace and remove assets independently of the rest of the template. Replacing a file keeps its identity, so decks that already reference it pick up the new version. SVG files are cleaned on upload: scripts and remote references are removed before the file is stored.

docs.title: Ask an agent to author a template
docs.text: The built-in Template Designer agent creates and refines templates from a conversation: describe the brand, answer its questions, and it creates the template, attaches the logos you uploaded to the chat, writes the deck defaults and the guidance, and generates a preview deck for you to judge. It cannot read colors out of an image — for that, use Generate with AI in the UI and bring the result back to the agent to refine.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Generate a deck in your new brand: see Presentations.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
This page complements Tools in XTM One.

That guide explains what tools are for. This page gives you a quick tour of the Tools screens.

docs.title: The list page
docs.text:
In the left navigation, this area is Tools & Integrations > Tools. In standard XTM One the main visible section is Built-in Tools — platform-provided capabilities such as Image Generation, Code Interpreter, Web Fetch, Browser, and XTM One. So this page is often less about configuration and more about understanding what the platform already makes available to agents. Each card tells you whether the tool is a standard platform capability, whether it is active, and what category of action it adds.

Some platform variants also expose Custom Tools. When they do, the area behaves like the other resource libraries, gaining search, visibility and tag filters, and an Add Tool action.

docs.title: Built-in tool detail pages
docs.text:
Opening a built-in tool leads to a detail page with Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs.

  • Overview shows what the tool does and whether it is used in real workflows — how many agents use it, how many runs it has, and (for Image Generation) the current image model.
  • Configuration is usually informational. For Image Generation it exposes the platform-wide image model: admins can change it, non-admins can only see it — so the experience differs by role even though the page is visible to everyone.
  • Activity shows runs linked to agents using the tool.

docs.title: Custom tool detail pages
docs.text:
When custom tools are available, their detail page has Overview, Configuration, and Activity tabs, with Test Tool and delete actions in the header.

  • Overview summarizes the tool: what it does, its language and timeout, its input parameters, and which agents use it.
  • Configuration is where you define and edit the tool. The parts that matter are durable:
    • parameters define what the tool expects
    • code (JavaScript or Python) defines what the tool does
    • a timeout defines how long the platform will wait
    • visibility and sharing settings define who can discover and reuse it

Test Tool opens a dedicated test dialog — the fastest way to validate a custom tool before binding it to an agent.

docs.title: Waiting is a tool too
docs.text:
Some capabilities are not on the Tools page because every agent has them. wait is one: it lets an agent pause on purpose — typically after handing a long task to another agent — and re-check when the work is likely done, instead of asking for a status update over and over.

You will see it in the chat as a countdown with the agent's own explanation of what it is waiting for, next to a Continue now link:

  • Continue now ends the pause and lets the agent carry on with whatever it has.
  • The usual stop button cancels the whole response, pause included.

The agent also wakes up on its own as soon as the tasks it named have finished, so a five-minute wait often costs far less. Admins set the ceilings in Settings > General Assistant.

docs.title: Read-only expectations in XTM One
docs.text: In standard XTM One, built-in tools are part of the platform: visible and understandable, but not treated like personal resources. The main experience is usually inspection and understanding rather than ownership and creation.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Use the tool description to understand capability before attaching it to an agent.
  • Check Agents Using before changing shared tool settings.
  • Treat Image Generation configuration as platform-wide, not per-agent.
  • In standard XTM One mode, expect built-in tools to be the main visible UX.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
This page explains what the Variables page shows and how it works in XTM One.

Unlike most other resources, variables do not use a list page plus detail page pattern. They use one management page with create and edit dialogs.

docs.title: The management page
docs.text:
In the left navigation, this area is Variables. The page is a board of reusable values that resolve at runtime in personas, prompts, skills, and tools. You can search by name, description, or value pattern and filter by tags, then create, edit, copy, or delete a variable. If you have permission, New Variable adds one.

Each variable is a card, not a table row. The card shows enough to decide quickly whether it is the right variable, whether it is sensitive, and whether it still looks current. Non-secret variables show their value preview directly; secret variables mask it behind a lock icon and a Secret badge, with a reveal toggle on the card itself. Each card also has a copy action for the variable reference.

docs.title: Editing behavior
docs.text:
Clicking a card opens an edit dialog — there is no separate detail page or tabs. The create and edit dialogs share the same fields; the key decision is whether to mark the variable Secret, which changes how it is displayed and handled later.

For a secret variable, the value field does not reveal the stored value on edit. The placeholder tells you to enter a new value only when you want to update it, which reinforces that secret handling differs from plain text.

docs.title: Copying a reference
docs.text: The UI lets you copy the reference format directly instead of typing it. The copied format uses the variable ID (for example {{var_id.<id>}}) and can be reused in personas, prompts, skills, and tools.

docs.title: Who a reference resolves for
docs.text:
A reference is replaced by its value only for the person the work runs as, and only if that person can see the variable: their own variables, the ones shared with them or one of their groups, and company-managed ones (unless restricted to an audience they are not in). In a chat that is the person chatting. An assignment runs as the person who triggered it, else its run-as user, else its owner. A flow runs as its owner, or as the person who ran it. Administrators get no exception.

When an agent's automations run as someone else, share the variable with that person or their group, or make it company-managed. Otherwise the reference is sent to the model as written. The agent's page lists the variables it references that have no value yet, and the references to variables that no longer exist.

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
• Use Secret for credentials or sensitive values.
  • Copy the reference instead of typing it from memory.
  • Add clear descriptions so other users know where the variable should be used.
  • Use tags when the same workspace contains many operational variables.

docs.title: XTM One in the XTM Suite
docs.text:
This section explains how XTM One can appear inside other products in the XTM Suite, such as OpenCTI and OpenAEV.

You do not always have to open the XTM One application directly to use XTM One capabilities. In some deployments, those capabilities are surfaced inside the product where you are already working.

docs.title: What this section is for
docs.text:
Use these pages when you want to understand:

  • where XTM One features can appear outside the main XTM One application
  • what the user experience usually looks like in another product
  • why some AI actions are available, hidden, or disabled
  • how OpenCTI and OpenAEV can expose XTM One to end users
  • which access point to use for a given task

docs.title: What stays the same across products
docs.text:
Even when you use XTM One from another XTM Suite product, a few principles stay the same:

  • the product you are in remains the main working context
  • XTM One provides the AI layer behind the feature
  • your current user permissions still matter
  • feature availability depends on how your administrators configured the platform

docs.title: How a product knows which agent to use
docs.text:
Each connected product declares the AI capabilities it needs — summarize this container, generate this message, process this bundle. In XTM One, those capabilities are called intents, and an administrator binds an agent to each one. That binding decides which of your agents answers when a user clicks an AI action in OpenCTI, OpenAEV, or OpenCRQ, and whether the action appears at all.

You do not need to configure anything to use the features: XTM One ships with bindings for its built-in agents. If your organization wants its own agent behind one of these actions, see Intents.

docs.title: What can vary by deployment
docs.text:
Not every organization exposes the same XTM One features in the same way.

What can vary includes:

  • which actions are available
  • which objects can trigger those actions
  • which assistant or agent is used behind the scenes
  • whether the result is immediate, streamed, or handled in the background

docs.title: Pages in this section
docs.text:
• Common experience across the XTM Suite
  • XTM One in OpenCTI
  • XTM One in OpenAEV

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Start with Common experience across the XTM Suite, then move to the product-specific pages that match your environment.

docs.title: Common experience across the XTM Suite
docs.text: When XTM One is exposed inside another XTM Suite product, the experience is usually contextual rather than standalone.

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
You usually start from the product you are already using, not from the XTM One home page.

That means:

  • you stay inside the current product
  • the current object or workflow provides the context
  • XTM One is used to interpret, summarize, plan, or automate based on that context

docs.title: How a request usually works
docs.text:
The common pattern looks like this:

  1. You open an object or workflow in the current product.
  2. You trigger an XTM One action from that context.
  3. The product sends the relevant context to XTM One.
  4. XTM One routes the request to the right assistant or agent.
  5. The result comes back into the product, or continues as a longer-running task.

From an end-user perspective, the important point is simple: you do not need to re-explain everything manually. The current product context is part of the request.

docs.title: How permissions work
docs.text:
XTM One is not meant to silently bypass the permissions of the product you are in.

In practice, this means:

  • what you can trigger still depends on your current account
  • what XTM One can read or do is scoped by the connected product and your access
  • an AI action should not grant you broader rights than you already have

docs.title: Why an action may be hidden or disabled
docs.text:
An XTM One action can be unavailable for several reasons:

  • the product is not connected to XTM One
  • the feature is not enabled in your deployment
  • no agent is bound to that use case — see Intents
  • the relevant capability is not available for your business context
  • your permissions do not allow the underlying operation

If a button or menu entry is missing, that does not automatically mean something is broken.

docs.title: What results can look like
docs.text:
Depending on the feature, the result may appear as:

  • a summary
  • extracted information
  • a proposed action or draft
  • a streamed answer
  • a background task that finishes later

Some workflows can also include a human review step before anything sensitive is applied.

docs.title: The in-product assistant panel
docs.text:
When the product's version supports it, the assistant panel of OpenCTI and OpenAEV also carries what the XTM One chat offers around a conversation:

  • Your usage quota: the same count and limit as the indicator of the XTM One chat, for the same period. It is not shown on Community Edition, where AI is off.
  • Your prompts: the prompts you can use in the XTM One chat - your own, the ones shared with you or your groups, and the company-managed ones - newest first. A prompt set to Hide from chat is not offered.
  • Rating an answer: a thumbs up or down, with an optional comment of up to 2,000 characters. It is the same rating as in the XTM One chat: rating again replaces it, removing it takes it back, the agent's managers see it in its Feedback tab, and it is still there when you reopen the conversation.

docs.title: How to use the feature well
docs.text:
• Start the action from the most relevant object, not from a generic page.
  • Expect the answer to be tailored to the current context.
  • Review the result before using it in an operational decision.
  • If the action is unavailable, check with your administrator whether the integration or routing is configured.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with XTM One in OpenCTI, then read XTM One in OpenAEV if your organization uses it.

docs.title: XTM One in OpenAEV
docs.text: In OpenAEV, XTM One supports adversarial exposure validation work without requiring you to leave the OpenAEV experience. As in OpenCTI, the capabilities appear inside the product, attached to the scenario, inject, or exercise you are working on.

docs.title: Access points inside OpenAEV
docs.text:
Each access point is powered by a named capability — an intent — answered by an agent your administrators chose. These are the agents that handle them out of the box.

Where it applies What you can do Capability Default agent The in-product AI assistant Hold a conversation about the current OpenAEV context — scenarios, simulations, results global.assistant CTEM Assistant, which hands the conversation over to the OpenAEV Assistant Text and description fields Summarize, explain, shorten, expand, fix spelling and grammar, change the tone of the content you are writing global.summarize, global.explain, global.make_it_shorter, global.make_it_longer, global.fix_spelling, global.change_tone OpenAEV Assistant Exercise content Generate the messages used in an adversary emulation exercise aev.message_generator OpenAEV Assistant Exercise content Generate a media article for an adversary emulation exercise aev.media_article_generator OpenAEV Assistant Phishing content Generate a phishing lure email (subject, HTML body, and plain-text fallback) for an authorized phishing simulation aev.phishing_email_html_generator AEV Phishing Email Generator Phishing content Generate a phishing landing page (HTML and CSS) for an authorized credential-capture simulation aev.phishing_landing_page_html_generator AEV Phishing Landing Page Generator Detection and remediation Turn a malware behavior description into detection rules, with the processes, commands, files, and ATT&CK techniques it relies on aev.detection_rules_generator AEV Detection Rules Generator Document analysis Extract tactics, techniques, and procedures from a document cti.ttp_harvester CTI TTP Harvester (Filigran AI)

The exact wording of buttons and menu entries depends on your OpenAEV version, and an administrator can bind a different agent to any of these capabilities.

Beyond these contextual actions, the OpenAEV Assistant and the scenario and payload agents can also be used from XTM One itself — to design a scenario, propose injects, or review the outcome of an exercise, with the results written back into OpenAEV.

docs.title: What to expect when you use it
docs.text:
When you trigger an XTM One action from OpenAEV:

  • the current OpenAEV context is reused, so you do not have to restate it
  • XTM One routes the request to the agent bound to that capability for the aev business context
  • the result comes back as part of the OpenAEV experience

Longer-running work can continue in the background; those runs appear in Work history in XTM One.

docs.title: Why a feature may be unavailable
docs.text:
An action can be hidden or disabled if:

  • the OpenAEV instance is not registered with XTM One
  • no agent is bound to that capability, or the bound agent is disabled
  • the bound agent is private rather than company-managed or shared with a group
  • the binding targets another business context than aev
  • your OpenAEV permissions do not allow the related operation

Administrators can review and fix the routing on the Intents page.

docs.title: Permissions and review
docs.text:
As with other suite products, you should expect:

  • the action to respect your current OpenAEV permissions
  • results to be treated as operational assistance, not final truth by default
  • some sensitive workflows to include a review or validation step

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Start the action from the scenario or exercise that already contains the relevant context.
  • Review generated proposals before applying them to an operational workflow.
  • Ask your administrator if the expected action is missing or unavailable.

docs.title: OpenAEV MCP server
docs.text:
Connecting OpenAEV to XTM One also activates a native MCP server for the platform.

Any MCP-compatible client (Cursor, Claude Desktop, custom agents) can connect to https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/openaev with a personal XTM One API key and search, read, and manage scenarios, simulations, payloads, injects, atomic tests, and findings — with your own OpenAEV permissions.

Find your endpoint and a ready-to-copy client configuration in My Profile > MCP Endpoint, and see Platform MCP servers for the full guide.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Return to the main XTM One guide for the broader platform chapters, starting with Home Dashboard when needed. Administrators who need to change which agent answers a capability should read Intents.

docs.title: XTM One in OpenCTI
docs.text:
In OpenCTI, XTM One is the AI layer on top of the threat intelligence workflow you already use. You do not open XTM One to benefit from it: the capabilities appear inside OpenCTI, on the objects you are working on.

This page lists the concrete places where the two products meet, so you know where and when you can use XTM One.

docs.title: Access points inside OpenCTI
docs.text:
Each access point is powered by a named capability — an intent — and each intent is answered by an agent that your administrators chose. Out of the box, the agents below handle them.

Where you find it What you can do Capability Default agent The in-product AI assistant Hold a conversation with the current OpenCTI context already loaded global.assistant CTEM Assistant, which hands the conversation over to the OpenCTI Assistant Text and description fields Summarize, explain, shorten, expand, fix spelling and grammar, change the tone of the content you are writing global.summarize, global.explain, global.make_it_shorter, global.make_it_longer, global.fix_spelling, global.change_tone OpenCTI Assistant Search and filters Describe what you are looking for in plain language and get an OpenCTI filter in return cti.nlq_search OpenCTI NLQ Containers — reports, groupings, cases Get a structured summary of the container, including the content of its attached files cti.container_summary OpenCTI Entity Insights Containers — Ask AI report generation Write an HTML report from the container's knowledge, with the requested length, tone and language cti.container_report OpenCTI Entity Insights Entity pages — threat actors, intrusion sets, malware, organizations, sectors, and others Get a digest of the containers that mention the entity, an activity trend analysis, a forecast of future activity, or a summary of the entity's own modification history cti.containers_digest, cti.entity_activity, cti.entity_forecast, cti.entity_history OpenCTI Entity Insights Automation playbooks Extract intelligence from documents into a STIX bundle, transform a bundle, or act on a bundle as the last step of a playbook cti.stix_harvester, cti.stix_transformer, cti.stix_consumer CTI STIX Harvester (Filigran AI) — or CTI STIX Harvester — then CTI STIX Transformer and CTI STIX Consumer

The exact wording of buttons and menu entries depends on your OpenCTI version, and an administrator can bind a different agent to any of these capabilities. What each access point does is stable; who answers it is a configuration choice.

Not the same as the MCP server

The access points above are AI actions inside OpenCTI. Connecting OpenCTI to XTM One also exposes OpenCTI's own tools to external MCP clients, which is a separate capability — see OpenCTI MCP server below.

docs.title: Using XTM One from a playbook
docs.text:
Playbooks are the access point that matters most for automation, because the agent runs without anyone watching. Three distinct roles are available, and they differ by what the step receives and what it must return:

  • A harvester receives a document — a PDF, an office file, a text report — and returns a STIX 2.1 bundle. Use it to turn incoming reports into structured knowledge.
  • A transformer receives a STIX 2.1 bundle and returns a STIX 2.1 bundle. Use it to enrich, filter, rewrite, or normalize what is flowing through the playbook.
  • A consumer receives a STIX 2.1 bundle and takes a final action instead of returning a bundle — summarize it, alert on it, post it somewhere. It is a terminal step.

Because the playbook step expects a specific shape of answer, an agent bound to one of these capabilities has to respect it. If your administrators bind a custom agent to cti.stix_harvester or cti.stix_transformer, that agent must return a valid STIX 2.1 bundle; a consumer is free to return a readable report.

Results and failures of playbook-triggered runs are visible in XTM One under Work history, which is where to look when a playbook step did not produce what you expected.

docs.title: Using OpenCTI from XTM One
docs.text:
The integration works in both directions. Once OpenCTI is registered, you can also start from XTM One:

  • Chat with an OpenCTI-aware agent. The OpenCTI Assistant and the other threat intelligence agents query your OpenCTI instance while they answer.
  • Build your own agents on OpenCTI data. The OpenCTI integration gives agents read and write tools for entities, observables, relationships, indicators, and containers. See Integrations.
  • Let agents work on a schedule. An agent can run on its own — for example to produce a recurring exposure briefing — and its runs appear in Work history.
  • Connect an external MCP client to work with OpenCTI knowledge from your own tooling.

docs.title: What to expect when you use it
docs.text:
When you trigger an XTM One action from OpenCTI:

  • the current OpenCTI context is the starting point, so you do not have to re-explain it
  • XTM One routes the request to the agent bound to that capability, for the business context declared by your OpenCTI instance — CTI, FIMI, or Fraud-oriented workflows can resolve to different agents
  • the result is returned inside the OpenCTI experience rather than as a separate generic chat

This makes the feature feel more like an OpenCTI capability than a detached AI assistant.

docs.title: Why a feature may be unavailable
docs.text:
You may not see a given XTM One action in OpenCTI if:

  • no agent is bound to that capability, or the bound agent is disabled
  • the bound agent is private, since an agent offered to platform users has to be company-managed or shared with a group
  • the binding targets a business context different from the one your OpenCTI instance declares
  • the action is not enabled for your deployment, or your OpenCTI version does not request that capability
  • your OpenCTI permissions do not allow the underlying operation

The product intentionally disables a feature when no suitable XTM One agent is available, rather than failing when you click. Administrators can check and fix all of this on the Intents page.

docs.title: Permissions and trust
docs.text:
As an end user, you should expect XTM One to act within the boundaries of your OpenCTI access.

That means:

  • the analysis is based on what your current session can access
  • results should be reviewed as contextual assistance, not as an automatic truth
  • if a workflow requires validation, your product can still ask for human review

docs.title: Good practices
docs.text:
• Launch the action from the most relevant report, case, or document.
  • Use the output to speed up investigation, not to skip validation.
  • Prefer a playbook step over a manual action when the same treatment has to apply to every incoming document.
  • If an action is missing, ask whether the relevant XTM One capability has been configured for your environment.

docs.title: OpenCTI MCP server
docs.text:
Connecting OpenCTI to XTM One also activates a native MCP server for the platform.

Any MCP-compatible client (Cursor, Claude Desktop, custom agents) can connect to https://<your-xtm-one>/mcp/opencti with a personal XTM One API key and search, read, create, and update threat intelligence knowledge — entities, observables, relationships, indicators, and containers — with your own OpenCTI permissions.

Find your endpoint and a ready-to-copy client configuration in My Profile > MCP Endpoint, and see Platform MCP servers for the full guide.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Continue with XTM One in OpenAEV if your organization also uses adversarial exposure validation workflows. Administrators who need to change which agent answers a capability should read Intents.
